setting: General practice. You are the GP. Version B of the iron-deficiency station — the same results in a pregnant patient whose pregnancy has been uneventful.
stem: Amy Kaur, 24, is pregnant and attended a week ago with tiredness. She looked pale and bloods were arranged. She has returned for the results.
Results: haemoglobin low · MCV low · MCH low · MCHC low · ferritin low · anisocytosis and poikilocytosis on film. Her pregnancy has been uneventful.
tasks: Explain the results
Take a focused, relevant history
Explain your diagnosis and differentials
Outline your management
time: 8 minutes, four tasks, same budget as MED-58 (1:30 · 3:00 · 1:30 · 1:30 · 0:30). Same six-line result explanation and the same six questions — plus obstetric interval, number of pregnancies and dietary iron. Do NOT take a full obstetric history: the stem says the pregnancy is uneventful.

back.dx: Iron deficiency anaemia of pregnancy from increased demand: three pregnancies in two years (short inter-pregnancy intervals — stores never rebuilt), on top of the physiological iron cost of each pregnancy; possibly low dietary intake. Same six questions exclude blood loss (no dark stools, no NSAIDs, no bleeding), malabsorption (no coeliac/IBD symptoms) and weight loss red flags. Differentials stated specifically: low dietary iron (e.g. vegetarian diet without red meat), blood loss (previous heavy periods, GI bleeding — dark stools, NSAIDs), malabsorption (coeliac disease, IBD), and — if any red flag or male/post-menopausal — GI malignancy needing both scopes (not indicated here). Management: treat the cause (spacing pregnancies, diet) and replace iron — IV iron is usually preferred in pregnancy when replacement must be rapid; recheck; antenatal team informed.
plan: Intro, confirm name, 'how can I help you today?'; 'I have the results — let's go through them together'

Six lines: red cells/haemoglobin/iron · total Hb low · cells smaller · haemoglobin per cell and concentration low · ferritin (store) low · anisocytosis = sizes · poikilocytosis = shapes → 'together these confirm iron deficiency anaemia'

Permission; tiredness briefly. Six questions: ★ red meat/dietary iron · surgery, bleeding, donations, ★ 'how many pregnancies, and how far apart?' → three in two years · ★ dark/black stools, blood in stool · anti-inflammatories/OTC, indigestion, vomiting (hyperemesis?) · weight change, appetite, lumps, bowel habit, family history · chronic diarrhoea, greasy stools, mouth ulcers, joints, shin rash; antenatal supplements taken?
Examination: conjunctival pallor, koilonychia, cheilitis, glossitis; pulse, postural BP; flow murmur; abdomen (fundal height appropriate, no tenderness); no rectal examination unless GI symptoms

★ 'Amy, the most likely cause is the three pregnancies you've had in the last two years. In each pregnancy your body has to build extra blood, and the baby needs a large amount of iron. We usually suggest waiting a while after a delivery so your stores can rebuild — if the next pregnancy starts soon after, you begin it already low.' Then the specific differentials and why they don't fit.

Management: ★ 'because we can't wait for tablets to work slowly in pregnancy, an iron infusion is usually preferred, and I'll recheck your blood afterwards' · dietary iron and vitamin C, avoid tea/coffee with meals · continue antenatal folate/iodine · inform the antenatal team; delivery planning if Hb low near term · postnatal contraception/spacing conversation · safety net: breathlessness at rest, palpitations, chest pain, bleeding · review after infusion
Teach-back and summary
ask: ★ 'How can I help you today?' / 'Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin, and haemoglobin is made of iron.' / 'All of these confirm iron deficiency anaemia.'
★ 'How many pregnancies have you had, and how far apart?' / ★ 'Do you eat red meat?' / ★ 'Any dark or black stools?' / 'Anything you buy yourself for pain?'
★ 'The most likely cause is the three pregnancies in two years — each one costs a large amount of iron, and the stores didn't have time to rebuild.'
★ 'In pregnancy an iron infusion is usually preferred because we can't wait for tablets to work slowly, and I'll recheck your blood afterwards.'

'Is the infusion safe for the baby?' → 'Yes — intravenous iron is used routinely in the second and third trimesters; the main risk is a reaction during the infusion, which we monitor for, and it avoids the stomach upset of tablets.' VERIFY
'Will this happen again?' → 'It can — so we'll check your iron after this baby, top it up before you're pregnant again, and talk about spacing.'
pefe: Expected: pale, conjunctival pallor; mild tachycardia; ± flow murmur; abdomen consistent with dates; no GI findings; no rectal examination indicated
Investigations: iron studies (ferritin, TSAT), CRP, ± B12/folate, coeliac serology if symptoms or poor response; no scopes in a young woman with an obvious cause and no red flags VERIFY

IV iron: ferric carboxymaltose from second trimester onward, dose by weight and Hb; oral iron acceptable in first trimester or mild deficiency (alternate-day dosing); recheck Hb/ferritin ~3–4 weeks VERIFY
Trap: a full obstetric history — the stem states the pregnancy is uneventful; one question on interval/number and one on supplements is enough
SA: antenatal shared care / midwifery (Yorke and Northern LHN), infusion at the local hospital day unit; TIS 131 450

Leading with iron before asking the six cause questions, or referring for scopes with no red flags ★
Taking a full obstetric history and never reaching management
Opening with the numbers; explaining white cells/platelets; aniso/poikilo reversed
Vague 'diet' differential; no recheck plan; no antenatal team involvement; no spacing conversation
numbers: Three pregnancies in two years · same six-line result explanation · same six cause questions + interval
Four causes: low intake · malabsorption · blood loss · increased demand (pregnancy) — pregnancy = demand
IV iron preferred in pregnancy when replacement must be rapid VERIFY · recheck ~3–4 weeks · inter-pregnancy interval ideally ≥18 months VERIFY

setting: General practice, country town. You are the GP. Online: 6-minute history, findings on screen, then diagnosis and differentials. Face to face: 4 + 2 + 2.
stem: Your next patient is John Brennan, 45, complaining of tiredness. He told the receptionist he has been tired for about three weeks and it is getting worse.
His record notes that he was told as a child that he had a heart murmur. He has no regular medications and has not attended the practice for several years.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history from the patient
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you would like
Explain your most likely diagnosis to the patient, with your reasons
Give your differential diagnoses
time: 8 minutes. Tiredness in 60 s · the murmur — three 'I don't remember's, then CHANGE TACK (long-course antibiotics, sore throats, follow-up) · screen until 'feverish' → take it as fever · the two endocarditis probes (dental work, marks on the hands) · say the timing match aloud · cardiac failure questions · examination requested by name incl. Osler/Janeway/splinters · 40-second explanation, four reasons · grouped differentials with reasons for the top two · hospital TODAY.

back.dx: Subacute infective endocarditis on a rheumatic mitral valve (mitral stenosis): childhood murmur with years of antibiotics/injections and constant sore throats and no follow-up (rheumatic fever → RHD), three weeks of worsening fatigue starting at the time of a root canal with no prophylaxis, feverish, splinter haemorrhages; T 38.5, mid-diastolic rumbling murmur at the apex, dipstick blood 1+. Four reasons to the patient: murmur as a child and a murmur today; fever; dental work three weeks ago matching the three weeks of tiredness; marks under the nails. Differentials, grouped with reasons: heart failure on the stenotic valve (less likely — no chest pain, oedema, orthopnoea, PND); blood cancers — leukaemia/lymphoma (no weight loss, lumps, night sweats); other infections — TB, EBV, HIV, hepatitis; thyroid, diabetes, anaemia, autoimmune, medications and mood, coeliac/IBD, OSA. Plan: three sets of blood cultures before any antibiotic, bloods, urine, ECG, CXR, hospital today for echocardiography and IV antibiotics. Discriminating behaviours: changing tack on the murmur, asking about dental work, naming the peripheral stigmata to the examiner.
plan: Intro, consent, 'tell me about the tiredness' → low energy, 3 weeks, constant, worse, nothing helps, can't get out of bed — 60 s

★ 'Before I go further, I want to ask about that heart murmur — it may be important': when, what, treatment → three 'I don't remember's → ★ CHANGE TACK: 'antibiotics for a long time as a child — months or years, injections? lots of sore throats? any follow-up for your heart?' → yes, yes, none
Screen: 'a checklist — most will be no' — liver, endocrine, malignancy… ★ 'any fever or chills?' → 'feverish, hot and cold' → 'have you measured it?' → 'I'll take that as a fever'

★ The two probes: 'any dental work recently — filling, extraction, root canal? other procedures?' → root canal 3 weeks ago → ★ say the timing match aloud · 'antibiotics before it?' → no · ★ 'any rashes, spots or marks on your hands or fingers?' → marks under the nails

Finish the screen in groups: ★ cardiac failure (chest pain, ankle swelling, pillows, PND), exertional dyspnoea/palpitations, joints/headache/rash, cough/snoring, bowels, medications and drugs (injecting), mood, occupation (truck driver), alcohol, smoking; 'what were you worried this might be?' (brother's bowel cancer)

Examination by name: general (pale, jaundiced, rash, unwell) · ★ temperature, HR, BP, RR, SpO2 · thyroid, lymph nodes · CVS: apex visible/displaced, JVP, murmurs, S3, opening snap — timing, site, radiation, character · chest · abdomen (hepatosplenomegaly) · urine dipstick · ★ 'specifically, the hands — Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, clubbing, splinter haemorrhages?' → photograph
★ 40-second explanation: 'infective endocarditis — a valve narrowed since childhood, bacteria from the mouth after the root canal settled on it'; four reasons; no anatomy lecture

Differentials grouped, reasons for the top two (heart failure, blood cancers), then list · ★ plan: three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics, bloods, urine, ECG, CXR, hospital TODAY for echo and IV antibiotics; who can drive you, who to call; respond to the cancer fear
ask: ★ 'Before I go further, I want to ask about that heart murmur you were told about as a child — it may be important.' → ★ 'Do you remember being on antibiotics for a long time as a child — months or years, maybe injections? Did you get a lot of sore throats? Any follow-up for your heart since?'
'Have you measured your temperature?' → ★ 'I'll take that as a fever.'

★ 'Have you had any dental work recently — a filling, an extraction, a root canal? Any other procedures?' → 'Three weeks — the same time your tiredness started. Were you given any antibiotics before it?'
★ 'Have you noticed any rashes, spots or marks on your hands or fingers?'
★ To examiner: 'May I look at the hands — Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, clubbing, or splinter haemorrhages?' (never 'any skin changes?')

'I believe you have infective endocarditis. One of your heart valves is narrowed — that's the murmur from childhood. When you had the root canal, bacteria from the mouth got into the bloodstream and settled on that damaged valve. Four reasons: the murmur then and now; a fever; dental work three weeks ago, the same three weeks you've been tired; and the marks under your fingernails.'

'The main alternative is heart failure from the long-standing valve problem — less likely because no chest pain, no leg swelling, one pillow, not waking breathless. I also thought about blood cancers like leukaemia and lymphoma — less likely, no weight loss, lumps or night sweats; other infections such as TB, glandular fever, HIV and hepatitis; thyroid, diabetes, anaemia, autoimmune conditions, medications and mood, coeliac and bowel disease, and sleep apnoea.'

★ 'Three separate sets of blood cultures before any antibiotic, other bloods, a urine test, an ECG and a chest X-ray — then hospital today, because this needs an ultrasound of the heart and antibiotics through a drip.'

'Is this because of the dentist? Can I sue?' → 'I can hear you're angry. This isn't about anyone doing anything wrong — mouth bacteria enter the bloodstream briefly in all of us. The problem is a valve that was damaged and never followed up. Right now my focus is treating the infection.'

'I can't go — I'm driving to Adelaide Monday. Give me tablets.' → 'I can't make you go, but this infection sits on a heart valve; untreated it can destroy the valve or throw clots to the brain. Tablets are not enough. Can we ring your wife and sort the driving? If you still decline, I'll do the tests today and see you tomorrow — but I'd be failing you if I didn't say how serious this is.'
'It's not cancer, is it? My brother…' → honest, one sentence: asked the questions, nothing points that way, bloods will cover it
pefe: Examiner: unwell-looking, not pale/jaundiced, no rash · T 38.5, HR 96 regular, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 97% · thyroid and nodes normal · JVP not raised, apex not displaced, mid-diastolic rumbling murmur at the mitral area, no S3 · chest clear · no hepatosplenomegaly · no Osler nodes, no Janeway lesions · photograph of splinter haemorrhages ONLY if asked by name · dipstick blood 1+

Variant — T 37.4 (2018 face-to-face version): 'a low-grade temperature rather than a frank fever, but subacute endocarditis characteristically runs low-grade; in a symptomatic patient with valve disease I regard it as supportive, not reassuring' — do not say 'afebrile' and abandon infection

Variant — Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander patient: RHD far commoner; the follow-up gap is a system failure — involve the Aboriginal Liaison Officer/ACCHS, notify to the SA RHD register, lifelong secondary prophylaxis and echo follow-up
Variant — injecting drug use, murmur louder on inspiration (Carvallo's sign): right-sided/tricuspid endocarditis, Staphylococcus aureus; look for septic pulmonary emboli on CXR

Investigations: ★ blood cultures ×3 sets, three sites, before antibiotics; FBE, ESR/CRP, UEC, LFT, urine MCS (microscopic haematuria), ECG (PR prolongation = abscess), CXR; TTE then TOE; Duke criteria — 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor VERIFY; IV antibiotics 4–6 weeks; surgical referral for heart failure, abscess, embolism, uncontrolled infection VERIFY

RHD secondary prophylaxis: benzathine benzylpenicillin every 21–28 days VERIFY; dental/procedural prophylaxis for high-risk valve lesions per Therapeutic Guidelines VERIFY; SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · RFDS · PATS · TIS 131 450 · SA RHD register
fails: Never asking about a portal of entry (dental work/procedures) ★
Never naming Osler nodes, Janeway lesions and splinter haemorrhages to the examiner — 'any skin changes?' leaves the photograph under the papers ★
Sending him home with oral antibiotics and a review — hospital TODAY ★
Running out of time before the differentials ★
Abandoning the murmur after three 'I don't remember's without changing tack
Discounting 'feverish' because there is no number; saying 'afebrile' at 37.4 and dropping infection
Skipping the heart failure questions; explaining four chambers of the heart; naming every cancer separately
numbers: Tiredness 3 weeks · root canal 3 weeks — say the match · T 38.5°C (older version 37.4) · Duke minor criterion >38°C
Murmur: mid-diastolic, rumbling, mitral area — 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line
Blood cultures ×3 sets, three sites, BEFORE antibiotics · Duke: 2 major / 1 major + 3 minor / 5 minor VERIFY · IV antibiotics 4–6 weeks
RHD prophylaxis: benzathine benzylpenicillin every 21–28 days VERIFY

setting: Rural general practice clinic with limited facilities. You are the GP. Face to face 4 + 2 + 2; online 6-minute history then findings on screen.
stem: Your next patient is Alex Wooten, 17, who presents complaining of tiredness and feeling unwell. He works on his family's farm and has been complaining that he is not able to keep up with his work.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you would like
Explain your most likely diagnosis to the patient, with your reasons
Give your differential diagnoses
time: 8 minutes. Acknowledge the concern in the stem within 30 s · tiredness in 60 s · screen until thirst and urine turn positive — record them as symptoms, never argue with his explanation · probe: polyphagia, recurrent infections, vision, feet, ★ abdominal pain/nausea/vomiting, weight · finish the whole differential screen anyway (incl. farm animal contact) · examination incl. dehydration, breathing pattern, BSL and dipstick — 'glucose and ketones' · diagnosis in 25 seconds, two layers · differentials · hospital today.

back.dx: Diabetic ketoacidosis (ketosis; acidosis still to be confirmed) complicating undiagnosed type 1 diabetes in a lean 17-year-old: months of worsening low energy, polydipsia and polyuria explained away as farm work in the sun, polyphagia, two slow-healing skin infections, weight loss (belt tighter), nausea; aunt with T1DM. Examination: tired, mildly dehydrated, observations normal, breathing not deep or sighing; BSL mid-high teens; dipstick glucose 4+, ketones 3+. Two-layer diagnosis to the patient in 25 seconds: 'diabetic ketoacidosis, a complication of diabetes you didn't know you had — sugar goes up, the body makes chemicals called ketones, which I found in your urine'; reasons: tired for months, passing more urine, drinking more, hungrier, high sugar with sugar and ketones in the urine. Differentials reasoned for two, listed for the rest: leukaemia/lymphoma (no lumps, night sweats, that kind of weight loss); infections — EBV, HIV, Q fever from the animals (no fever/flu-like illness); then hepatitis, thyroid, anaemia, autoimmune, drugs, depression/stress, coeliac/IBD, cardiorespiratory, OSA. Disposition: hospital today — IV access, fluids started, bloods, specialist team phoned. Discriminating behaviours: recording the explained-away thirst/urine as symptoms, 'glucose and ketones' on the dipstick, and a 25-second explanation that leaves time for the differentials.
plan: Intro; ★ 'not being able to keep up with the work must be really frustrating, and I can hear it's weighing on you'; consent; tiredness: low energy vs sleepy, months, constant, worse, nothing helps, impact — 60 s

Checklist — liver, thyroid (weather) … ★ 'passing more urine? more thirsty or drinking more?' → 'only because I work in the sun — that's normal, isn't it?' → 'That does make sense, and I'll still note it.'
★ Probe: hungrier/eating more · recurrent infections (skin, thrush, urine) · blurred vision · numb/tingling feet · ★ tummy pain, nausea, vomiting · weight loss without trying

★ Finish the screen anyway, in groups: malignancy (weight, appetite, lumps, sweats, family cancer) · infection (fever, chills, sore throat, sexual activity, travel, ★ animal contact on the farm — Q fever) · anaemia · autoimmune · drugs/alcohol/smoking · mood, stress at home/school, bullying, brief HEADSS (a bit down — parents think he's lazy; no self-harm) · bowels · cardiorespiratory, snoring · family history (aunt T1DM)

Examination: unwell? ★ dehydration (dry mucosa, turgor, sunken eyes), pale, jaundiced, wasted · T, HR, BP incl. postural, RR, SpO2 · thyroid, nodes · CVS · respiratory — ★ 'is his breathing deep and sighing?' · abdomen (tenderness, organomegaly) · ★ 'blood sugar level and urine dipstick' → 'what are you looking for?' → ★ 'glucose and ketones'; say the observations are normal — ketosis, acidosis needs blood ketone + venous gas

★ Diagnosis in 25 s, two layers, five reasons; no pancreas/insulin/fat metabolism/acidosis. Physiology questions → 'I'll come back to that — let me first tell you what else I've considered and what happens next.'

Differentials: reason two, list the rest · ★ 'You need to go to hospital today — I'll put a drip in, start fluid, take bloods and ring the specialist team now. Very treatable; once controlled there's no reason you can't do the farm work. Who can drive you? Would you like me to call your parents?' · close on the hidden agenda: 'I'll tell Mum it's not because you've been slacking off.'
ask: ★ 'Not being able to keep up with the work must be really frustrating.'
★ 'Are you passing more urine than usual? Are you more thirsty, or drinking more?' → ★ 'That does make sense, and I'll still note it.' (never argue)
'Are you hungrier than usual? Any infections that keep coming back?' / ★ 'Any tummy pain, nausea or vomiting?' / 'Any contact with animals on the farm?'
★ 'Could I have a blood sugar level and a urine dipstick?' → 'Glucose and ketones.'

★ 'Alex, I think you have diabetic ketoacidosis, which is a complication of diabetes you didn't know you had. In diabetes the sugar in your blood goes up; when that happens your body starts producing chemicals called ketones — that's what I've found in your urine today. The reasons: tired for months, passing more urine, drinking more, hungrier than usual, and your blood sugar is high with sugar and ketones in your urine.'
'Diabetes? But I'm not overweight.' → 'This is the type that isn't about weight — the body stops making its own insulin. It can happen to fit people.'

'Can I still drive the ute and the tractor?' → 'Once you're on insulin there are national driving rules because of the risk of a hypo at the wheel — it doesn't mean you can't drive, it means checking your sugar before you drive and carrying something sugary. Same for machinery. We'll go through it once you're stable.'

'Do my parents have to know?' → 'What you tell me is confidential, and at 17 you can make your own decisions if you understand what's involved. But this is serious and you'll need help — and knowing you've been unwell will change how they see the last few months. Would you like me to be there when you tell them?' ADDED
★ 'You need to go to hospital today — but once this is under control there's no reason you can't do your work.'
pefe: Examiner: tired, mildly dehydrated, not pale/jaundiced · T 36.5, HR 82, BP 110/70, RR 12, SpO2 normal · thyroid, nodes, CVS, chest, abdomen normal; breathing not deep or sighing · ★ BSL high (mid–high teens mmol/L) · dipstick glucose 4+, ketones 3+

Variant — frankly acidotic (Kussmaul RR 28, HR 124, abdominal tenderness, drowsy): 'clinical ketoacidosis — large-bore cannula, 0.9% sodium chloride, bloods for glucose, ketones, gas, electrolytes, call retrieval immediately — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33'
Variant — 5-year-old known T1DM, vomiting with ketones (online paediatric version): DKA until proven otherwise; cautious fluid resuscitation, insulin infusion without a bolus — cerebral oedema risk

Variant — glucose 9 with ketones 3+ and eating very little: starvation/dehydration ketosis possible — blood ketone and venous gas before calling it DKA; euglycaemic DKA only if on an SGLT2 inhibitor ADDED

Management order if asked: fluid → potassium → insulin infusion (0.05–0.1 units/kg/h), no insulin bolus in children; monitor glucose hourly, ketones/gas/K 2-hourly; find the precipitant; specialist team; then education, NDSS registration, sick-day rules, driving rules VERIFY

SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · RFDS · PATS · NDSS · Diabetes SA; adolescent confidentiality and Gillick/mature-minor competence at 17 under SA Consent to Medical Treatment and Palliative Care Act 1995 (16+ may consent) VERIFY
fails: Accepting his explanation for the thirst and urine and moving on ★
Generic dipstick answer ('leucocytes, nitrites, protein, blood') — the answer is glucose and ketones ★
Explaining ketogenesis and acidosis beautifully and the bell going during the second differential ★
Treating him in the clinic with fluids and reviewing tomorrow — same-day referral ★
Not acknowledging the concern in the stem; skipping the differentials because 'it's obviously diabetes'
Stopping at polyuria/polydipsia — missing polyphagia, infections, complication questions and the DKA questions (abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting)
Insulin bolus / insulin before fluids if asked for management; not asking farm animal contact
numbers: 7-Eleven: fasting ≥7.0 mmol/L · random ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms · Australia reports mmol/L
Dipstick here: glucose 4+, ketones 3+ · DKA triad: hyperglycaemia + ketonaemia (blood ketones ≥3.0) + acidosis (venous pH <7.3 or HCO3 <15) VERIFY
Order: fluid → potassium → insulin · no insulin bolus in children · obs normal here = ketosis, acidosis to confirm
Timing: diagnosis and mechanism 25 s · reasons 15 s · differentials the rest · watch the clock — ≥60 s left at the start of Task 3
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · RFDS · PATS · NDSS

setting: Regional general practice, Wallaroo, South Australia. You are the GP. Version A online: 6-minute history then findings on screen. Version B face to face: 4-minute history then examination from the examiner.
stem: Jane Ellery, a 45-year-old woman, presents to your general practice complaining of tiredness. There is nothing else in the stem.
tasks: Take a focused history
You will then be given the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis AND your differentials to the patient — two marked items
time: 8 minutes. Open, acknowledge, contract · define 'tired' and explore (ask even though she volunteered some) · H, then E — cold intolerance is where it turns → switch from screening to PROBING (five key-point questions) · keep sweeping M, I, A, D, C, O, P anyway · menstrual questions exclude the closest mimic · thyroid examination requested by name, pulse, reflex relaxation phase · name it, reason it from her own answers and findings · reason three differentials incl. menopause · TSH, plan, safety net, certificate.

back.dx: Primary hypothyroidism, probably Hashimoto thyroiditis: months of progressive lack of energy affecting work; cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, weight gain, hair loss with outer-eyebrow thinning, morning periorbital puffiness; examination — dressed warmly, dry coarse skin, pulse 60, diffuse non-nodular goitre moving on swallowing, no retrosternal extension, no lymphadenopathy, delayed relaxation phase of the ankle reflexes, normal power, office tests normal. Reasons given from her own answers and findings. Differentials reasoned: menopause (regular periods, no hot flushes — the single closest mimic at 45), anaemia (no exertional dyspnoea/palpitations, periods not heavy — still check), depression (mood reasonable, still enjoys things); malignancy — lymphoma/leukaemia (no weight loss, lumps, night sweats); infection — EBV, hepatitis, HIV; then diabetes, coeliac, haemochromatosis, autoimmune (SLE, RA), medications, OSA, heart failure. Plan: TSH (free T4 if abnormal, TPO antibodies for cause) plus FBE, ferritin, HbA1c, coeliac serology, UEC, LFT; levothyroxine once confirmed; recheck TSH 6–8 weeks; certificate. Automatic fails: diagnosing off the single weather-preference answer without probing; never requesting a thyroid examination; abandoning the malignancy/infection screen; omitting the differentials; describing the reflexes as brisk.
plan: Intro, open question; ★ acknowledge ('I understand that can be concerning') and contract ('questions, then examine, then a plan together')
Define: lack of energy / sleepy / feverish · duration · constant · worse · modifiers · impact (sick leave, boss unhappy — 'we'll come back to the work side')

H: tanning, jaundice, dark urine, pale stools · E: polyuria, thirst, ★ 'any weather preference — intolerant of cold or heat?' → 'always cold' → ★ SWITCH TO PROBING: dry skin · constipation · weight gain · hair loss incl. outer third of eyebrows · puffiness of eyelids/face/legs · hoarse voice · neck swelling or dysphagia

★ Keep sweeping: M (weight loss, appetite, lumps, night sweats, cancer history) · I (fever, sore throat, sexual history/safe sex, travel) · A (exertional dyspnoea/palpitations, stiffness, headache, joints, rash) · D (medicines, mood, anhedonia, stress)

C (greasy stools, blood, chest pain, pillows, ankles, cough, smoking) · O (snoring, occupation) · ★ P: LMP, regular, heavy, hot flushes · alcohol, allergies, PMH, FHx · 'anything you were worried this might be?'

Examination: general — dressed for the weather? dry skin? pallor/jaundice/rash · temperature, ★ pulse rate, BP · ★ thyroid examination with consent to expose the neck, chaperone: inspection (swelling, moves on swallowing), palpation (diffuse vs nodular, size, consistency, tenderness), percussion over the manubrium · lymph nodes · CVS · respiratory · abdomen · ★ relaxation phase of the ankle reflexes · proximal power (rise from a chair) · Pemberton's sign · office tests, ★ 'random or fasting glucose?'

★ Name it in one plain line ('the gland in the front of your neck is underactive, not making enough of its hormone — that hormone sets the pace for everything, which is why everything feels like an effort'); ★ reasons from her answers (cold, dry skin, constipation, weight gain, hair loss) and findings (dry skin, slow pulse, enlarged gland, slow-relaxing reflexes)

★ Differentials: menopause, anaemia, depression reasoned; malignancy and infection reasoned; the rest listed · plan: TSH today ('measures how hard your body is pushing the gland') + anaemia, diabetes, coeliac, liver tests; levothyroxine once confirmed, empty stomach, recheck 6–8 weeks; certificate; safety net (neck swelling, dysphagia, chest pain); questions; summary on request
ask: 'I understand that can be concerning. Let me ask you a number of questions, then examine you, and we will make a plan together.' / 'Is it a lack of energy, feeling sleepy, or feeling feverish?'
★ 'Do you have any weather preference — are you intolerant of cold or of heat?' → 'Thank you, that is helpful. Let me ask a few more about that.'

★ 'Has your skin been dry?' / ★ 'Have you been constipated?' / ★ 'Have you had any weight gain?' / ★ 'Any hair loss — and have you noticed the outer part of your eyebrows thinning?' / ★ 'Any puffiness of your eyelids, face or legs?' / 'Has your voice become hoarse? Any swelling in your neck or difficulty swallowing?'
★ 'When was your last period? Are they regular? Any hot flushes?'

★ 'I would like to perform a thyroid examination — asking her permission to expose the neck and remove any scarf, and offering a chaperone.' / ★ 'What is the relaxation phase of the ankle reflex?' / 'Can she rise from a chair without using her arms?' / 'Pemberton's sign, given the goitre' / 'Is that sugar random or fasting?'

★ 'Most likely you have hypothyroidism. The gland in the front of your neck is underactive and is not making enough of its hormone.' / ★ 'The reasons I have come to this today are your own answers and what I found when I examined you…'

★ 'I considered menopause — it can cause exactly this at your age, but it is less likely in you because your periods are regular and you have no hot flushes.' / 'Anaemia — less likely, no breathlessness or palpitations on exertion, periods not heavy, but I will still check.' / 'Depression — less likely, your mood is reasonable and you still enjoy things.'

'The main test is called TSH, which measures how hard your body is having to push the gland.' / 'Will I be on tablets forever?' → 'Usually yes — one tablet a day, inexpensive, and most people feel like themselves again.' / 'Will the weight come off?' → 'Some usually does — a lot is fluid — but treating the thyroid does not usually take off all the weight on its own; it should give you back the energy to be active.'
Never say to the patient: TSH unexplained, euthyroid, myxoedema, Woltman sign, or 'your metabolism is slow' without the plain-English version
pefe: Examiner: dressed warmly; dry, coarse skin; no pallor/jaundice/rash · T normal, ★ pulse 60 regular, BP 110/70 · ★ diffusely enlarged thyroid, moves on swallowing, no nodules, non-tender, percussion resonant (no retrosternal extension) · no lymphadenopathy · HS normal, chest clear · no hepatosplenomegaly · ★ reflexes present with delayed relaxation phase · power normal · Pemberton negative · random BSL normal, dipstick normal

If asked what you are looking for mid-thyroid exam: 'a swelling that moves upwards on swallowing — thyroid rather than node or cyst; diffuse vs nodular — a discrete nodule changes the pathway to ultrasound; percussion for retrosternal extension'
Variant — single firm nodule: thyroid ultrasound ± FNA by sonographic features and size; still TSH first (suppressed TSH → functioning nodule) VERIFY
Variant — periods stopped 8 months ago with hot flushes: menopause moves to the top, but they overlap and coexist — still check TSH before attributing everything to menopause
Variant — lithium or amiodarone: both cause hypothyroidism; check TSH (lithium: renal function and level too); discuss with the prescriber rather than stopping it
Variant — pregnant or planning: requirement rises, targets tighter — urgent TSH, start/increase early, obstetric team, monitor more often VERIFY

Bloods: TSH first → free T4 if abnormal → TPO antibodies for cause; high TSH + low fT4 = primary; high TSH + normal fT4 = subclinical · plus FBE, ferritin, HbA1c, coeliac serology, UEC, LFT · levothyroxine ~1.6 µg/kg/day full replacement, start 25–50 µg if older or cardiac VERIFY · empty stomach, separate from calcium/iron by ~4 h · recheck TSH 6–8 weeks · SA: TIS 131 450 · PATS >100 km VERIFY
fails: Naming hypothyroidism off the single weather-preference answer without the five probing questions ('what makes you say that?') ★
Never requesting a thyroid examination — running the whole spine and missing the neck ★
Abandoning the malignancy and infection screen because you already have the diagnosis ★
Explaining the diagnosis beautifully and omitting the differentials task — one out of two ★
Describing the reflexes as brisk — they are slow to relax ★
Not asking the three menstrual questions — menopause is the closest mimic
The butterfly-gland physiology lecture; starting levothyroxine before the TSH; promising all the weight will come off
numbers: Pulse 60 — the bradycardia you expect · 5 key-point probes (dry skin, constipation, weight gain, hair/eyebrows, puffiness) · 9 examination steps · 2 famous signs (delayed reflex relaxation, outer-eyebrow loss)
TSH first · free T4 if abnormal · TPO antibodies for cause · high TSH + low fT4 = primary; high TSH + normal fT4 = subclinical
Levothyroxine ~1.6 µg/kg/day; 25–50 µg start if older/cardiac VERIFY · empty stomach · separate from calcium/iron ~4 h · recheck TSH 6–8 weeks
Three menstrual questions exclude menopause: LMP, regular?, hot flushes?
TIS 131 450 · PATS >100 km VERIFY

setting: General practice. You are the GP. The patient attends alone. Version 1 — she stopped the prednisolone abruptly.
stem: Samantha (Sam) Doyle, 60, was diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica four months ago (some versions: giant cell arteritis; Version 3: sarcoidosis). She attends today concerned about tiredness and, separately, loss of weight.
tasks: Take a relevant history (7 minutes)
Give your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses (1 minute)
time: 8 minutes — 7 + 1, the longest history and shortest close in the cluster. Acknowledge the concern · both complaints explored, weight loss quantified (how much, over how long) · the steroid block and the hinge question 'abruptly, or reduced gradually?' · follow the dog into the mood · adrenal features (nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, postural dizziness, salt craving) and steroid-diabetes questions · malignancy red flags and the THREE screening programs · rest of the mnemonic, postmenopausal bleeding, geriatric screen · 60-second answer: name, two-sentence explanation, reasons, then the list fast.

back.dx: Secondary adrenal insufficiency (not crisis — stable, talking) after abrupt cessation of prednisolone four months into PMR treatment: six weeks of profound fatigue, 5–6 kg unintentional weight loss, poor appetite, nausea, abdominal pain, loose bowels, postural light-headedness; stopped the tablet abruptly six weeks ago after her dog died, nobody told her to taper, missed follow-up; no PMR/GCA relapse features; mood flat since the bereavement (grief; screen, not diagnose). Reasons: tired, weight loss, abrupt cessation after four months, GI features. Differentials (the list is the mark): malignancy — leukaemia, lymphoma, breast, bowel (no lumps, screening up to date); depression/adjustment disorder after the loss; relapse of PMR/GCA; steroid-induced diabetes; thyroid, anaemia, haemochromatosis, hepatitis, coeliac, other autoimmune, medications, heart failure, OSA. Plan: morning cortisol today (short Synacthen if needed), restart prednisolone with a proper taper, steroid card, sick-day rules, emergency advice, mood review next week. Handle 'is it my fault?' without blame.
plan: Intro, 'how would you like me to address you?'; ★ acknowledge the concern in one line; permission to proceed

Tired: feverish / low energy / sleepy → no energy · 6 weeks · constant · worse · nothing helps · can't do housework · ★ weight: 'how many kilograms, and over what period?' → 5–6 kg in 6 weeks, not trying

★ Steroid block: when diagnosed · what treatment · 'are you taking it regularly?' → stopped · why? → the dog · ★ 'did you stop it abruptly, or reduce the dose gradually?' → just stopped · side effects (weight gain) · follow-up (missed) · relapse: shoulder/hip stiffness; GCA: headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual change
★ 'I'm so sorry about your dog — how are you coping?' · mood · anhedonia (three questions, twenty seconds)
★ Adrenal features: nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, postural dizziness, salt craving · steroid-diabetes: polyuria, polydipsia, recurrent infections
Malignancy: appetite, lumps, night sweats, family cancer · ★ three screening programs: mammogram, cervical screening test, bowel cancer kit

setting: General practice. You are the GP. Version 2 of the steroid station — she is still taking the prednisolone. Stem reconstructed from the variant section.
stem: Samantha (Sam) Doyle, 60, was diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica four months ago and remains on prednisolone. She attends today concerned about tiredness and loss of weight.
tasks: Take a relevant history (7 minutes)
Give your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses (1 minute)
time: 8 minutes, 7 + 1. Identical spine to MED-63 — the steroid block comes back clean (compliant, followed up, no relapse, no side effects). Say nothing about the recall; work down the mnemonic until you reach mood, then complete the depression criteria and the safety question. Do NOT do a full psychiatric history — plan the case from the complaint, not the outcome.

back.dx: Major depressive disorder presenting as tiredness and weight loss in a bereaved 60-year-old widow living alone: low mood, anhedonia, middle-of-the-night waking, poor appetite with weight loss, poor concentration, guilt/worthlessness, fatigue — five or more of nine features over more than two weeks; no suicidal ideation on direct questioning. Steroid history clean (taking it, tapering as planned, follow-up kept, no relapse). Differentials — the same broad list: malignancy (leukaemia, lymphoma, breast, bowel — no lumps, screening up to date), adrenal insufficiency (excluded — never stopped), PMR/GCA relapse, steroid-induced diabetes, thyroid, anaemia, haemochromatosis, hepatitis, coeliac, autoimmune, medications (steroid-induced mood change), heart failure, OSA. The one exception to 'no full psychiatric history' is the safety question — never omit it. If challenged: 'I approached this as undifferentiated tiredness and screened organic causes first; having reached a mood disorder I would complete a full mental state assessment at a dedicated follow-up.'
plan: Intro, name preference, ★ acknowledge the concern, permission
Tired defined, explored; ★ weight loss quantified (amount, period)
Steroid block: diagnosed 4 months ago, prednisolone, taking it regularly (yes), tapering per plan, follow-up kept, side effects, relapse (girdle stiffness) and GCA features — all clean

Adrenal/GI and steroid-diabetes questions (negative) · malignancy red flags · ★ three screening programs · rest of the mnemonic · ★ postmenopausal bleeding · geriatric screen (lives alone, husband died, son in Perth, toast mostly)

setting: General practice. You are the GP. Online: 6-minute history, findings on screen. Face to face: 4 + 2 + 2.
stem: Your next patient is Lily Ferrand, 45, who presents complaining of tiredness and loss of energy. There is nothing else in the stem.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you would like
Explain your most likely diagnosis to the patient, with your reasons
Give your differential diagnoses
time: 8 minutes. Tiredness in 60 s · screen — two positives arrive together (night sweats, Cairns) · the travel box in FULL, signposted and closed (destination/duration then A B C D E F G S), undeflected by 'we were just on holiday' · come back OUT and finish the screen — that is where the cough and the two failed antibiotics surface · examination with percussion on both sides, RR and SpO2 · lay diagnosis with reasons · TWO differential groups announced as groups · doxycycline or a macrolide, 48-hour review, safety net.

back.dx: Atypical (community-acquired) pneumonia after four weeks in Far North Queensland: three weeks of dry cough, low-grade fever 37.8, night sweats, back/body aches, exhaustion; two failed beta-lactam courses (amoxicillin then amoxicillin-clavulanate — neither covers Mycoplasma, Chlamydia or Legionella); right middle-zone dullness with crackles, RR 18, SpO2 96%. Four reasons: dry cough for three weeks; low-grade rather than high fever; aches, night sweats and exhaustion; and the antibiotic failure points towards, not away from, this — plus right-sided chest signs. Differentials in two announced groups. Group 1, other causes of persistent cough: typical bacterial pneumonia (chesty cough, high fever, would have responded), tuberculosis (taken seriously — three weeks of cough with night sweats; no weight loss or haemoptysis; CXR and sputum settle it), lung cancer (CXR in any adult with cough >3 weeks, never-smoker or not). Group 2, travel-acquired infections: Q fever, leptospirosis, melioidosis, mosquito-borne viruses — Ross River fits the aches. Then the negative screen: anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, hepatitis, coeliac, autoimmune, medications, mood, OSA. Do not blame the previous doctor. Plan: CXR today, bloods, sputum, atypical PCR swab, travel serology; doxycycline 100 mg bd 5–7 days (macrolide if pregnant or <8 y); review 48 h; named red flags.
plan: Intro, consent; tiredness: low energy, weeks, constant, worse, nothing helps, impact — 60 s, not 90

Checklist: liver, endocrine, malignancy (weight, appetite, lumps, ★ night sweats → YES), infection (fever/chills, flu-like, sore throat, ★ 'have you travelled anywhere recently?' → Cairns) — take BOTH positives

★ 'I'd like to ask about that trip in some detail, because where you went and what you did there can matter a great deal.' Destination and duration → A activities · B bushwalking, bites (insect/tick) · C contacts (animals, unwell people) · D drugs · E exposures (tattoos, piercings, transfusion) · F food and water (street food, unbottled/creek/tank) · G GP before travel (vaccines, tablets) · S sex while away — ask every heading despite 'we were just on holiday'

★ 'Thank you — let me finish the rest of my checklist': PMR/headache, joints and body aches (back ache), bowels, chest pain/ankles, ★ 'any cough?' → ★ five questions: dry or chesty / duration / haemoptysis / smoking / 'has anyone treated you for it already, and did it help?' → amoxicillin then Augmentin, no help

★ 'A chest infection caused by an unusual group of bugs rather than the ordinary ones' — four reasons incl. ★ 'the fact those antibiotics didn't work points towards this, not away from it'; right-sided signs

★ 'I'd like to give my differentials in two groups' — cough list (typical pneumonia, TB reasoned, lung cancer → CXR), travel list (Q fever, leptospirosis, melioidosis, Ross River/arboviruses), then the negative screen · plan: CXR today, bloods, sputum, atypical swab/PCR, travel serology; doxycycline; review 48 h; ★ safety net — breathless, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, confusion/drowsiness, climbing fever → ED; someone at home?
ask: 'I'm going to run through a checklist quite quickly — most of these will be no.' / ★ 'Have you travelled anywhere recently?'

★ 'I'd like to ask about that trip in some detail, because where you went and what you did there can matter a great deal.' → 'Where, and how long? What activities? Bushwalking, insect or tick bites? ★ 'Is it a dry cough or a chesty one — are you bringing anything up? How long? Ever coughed up blood? Do you smoke? Has anyone treated you for it already, and did it help?'
★ 'Could I have percussion on both sides, and vocal resonance?' / 'Respiratory rate and oxygen saturation, please.'
★ 'A lung infection caused by an unusual group of bugs.' / ★ 'Neither antibiotic you were given works against these bugs — the fact they didn't help points towards this, not away from it.'
'So the other doctor got it wrong?' → 'No — amoxicillin was a reasonable first choice; the response tells us which group of bugs this is.'

'Is it tuberculosis? My aunt had that.' → 'A fair question and I have thought about it. TB usually causes months of cough with weight loss; yours is three weeks with none. But because of the night sweats I'm not going to guess — the chest X-ray and a sputum sample will settle it. I'd rather check than reassure you wrongly.'
★ 'I'd like to give my differentials in two groups — other causes of a persistent cough, and infections you could have picked up because of the trip.'

'Doxycycline covers these bugs; I'd like to see you again in 48 hours. Come back sooner, or go to the emergency department, if you become short of breath, get chest pain on breathing in, cough up blood, become confused or drowsy, or the fever climbs.'

Variant — overseas (SE Asia/Pacific): any fever = malaria testing regardless (thick and thin films + rapid antigen, ×3, 12–24 h apart); typhoid live
Variant — 22 weeks pregnant: macrolide, not doxycycline; CXR with abdominal shielding — not diagnosing pneumonia is the bigger risk VERIFY

Variant — deteriorates (RR 30, SpO2 90%, confused, SBP 88): severe CAP — oxygen, IV access, cultures, medical registrar for admission, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if retrieval · Variant — farm/abattoir contact: Q fever serology; ask about Q fever vaccination (needs pre-vaccination screening) ADDED · TIS 131 450

setting: Regional general practice, Wallaroo, South Australia. You are the GP. Booked for routine BP monitoring with the practice nurse; nurse's note: BP 135/85, he has asked to see you because he has been feeling tired.
stem: James Corrigan, 40, has known hypertension on perindopril for six months. He attended for routine blood pressure monitoring with the practice nurse (BP 135/85 mmHg) and has asked for a consultation because he has been feeling tired lately.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient (6 minutes)
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
No management or investigations task — do not drift into either
time: 8 minutes, 6 + 2. Acknowledge, contract · sleepy vs low energy — get the fork right in the first minute · H to D in ~90 s · C: the heart-failure screen you must be HEARD to do (clarify the ambiguous night-waking) · O: snoring/witnessed apnoeas, the sleep probe, weight, alcohol, ★ occupation → ★ sleepy at the wheel · hidden cardiac worry · plain-English diagnosis reasoned from his answers · BP link · three reasoned differentials then the list · non-blanket driving advice, safety net.

back.dx: Obstructive sleep apnoea in a treated hypertensive commercial driver: months of worsening daytime sleepiness (nodding off at his desk), wife reports chainsaw snoring and witnessed apnoeas, unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches, poor morning concentration, dry mouth, 6 kg weight gain with tighter collar, 4–5 beers nightly up to bed, brief nocturnal arousals that settle in seconds (not PND), grain-haulage truck driver with one or two episodes of sleepiness at the wheel; BP 135/85 on perindopril — close to target, not 'fine'. Reasons drawn from his own answers. BP link: OSA is a recognised cause of hypertension resistant to tablets (nocturnal sympathetic surges); treating the OSA may do more than another tablet. Differentials reasoned: heart failure (no chest pain, one pillow, no oedema — the arousals settle in seconds), lymphoma/leukaemia (no weight loss, lumps, sweats), infections — EBV, COVID, hepatitis, HIV (no fever, travel, risk); then hypothyroidism, diabetes, anaemia, haemochromatosis, coeliac, autoimmune, medications/alcohol, depression, shift work. Driving: no blanket ban, no blanket reassurance — 'I am not taking anything off you today'; do not drive sleepy; sleep study; commercial standards stricter (Austroads), specialist opinion and evidence of treatment; hidden worry is his father's MI at 58.
plan: Intro, open question; ★ acknowledge ('being tired all the time is wearing'); contract; 'some will sound unrelated — I ask everyone'
★ 'Lack of energy, sleepy, or feverish?' → sleepy · months · mornings · worse · worse after beers · nodding off at his desk, stopping more when driving

H → D in 90 s: tanning/jaundice/urine · polyuria/thirst/weather · weight (gained 6 kg), appetite, lumps, sweats, cancer FHx · fever, sore throat, sexual history, travel · exertional dyspnoea/palpitations, stiffness, headaches (mornings only — 'I'll come back to that'), joints, rash · medicines incl. ★ C — heard to do it: greasy stools/diarrhoea/blood · chest pain · pillows · ankle swelling · 'wake at night gasping?' → ★ clarify: 'breathless and needing to sit up, or settles in seconds?' → settles · cough · smoking (quit 8 y)

★ O — the station: 'has anyone ever told you that you snore, or that you stop breathing or gasp during sleep?' → wife: snores, stops breathing · refreshing? · morning headache · morning concentration · dry mouth · weight gain / collar tighter · ★ alcohol — how much and how close to bed · ★ 'what do you do for work?' → truck driver

★ 'Have you ever felt sleepy at the wheel, or had a near miss?' → pause → once or twice, pulled over · 'the gynaecological causes obviously do not apply' · allergies, PMH, FHx (father MI at 58) · ★ 'anything in particular you were worried this might be?' → the heart

Start with the worry ('I've asked the heart questions and they're reassuring'); ★ name OSA in plain English (throat muscles go floppy, airway closes, brief arousals dozens of times, never deep sleep); ★ reasons from his answers; ★ BP link; keep taking the tablet

★ Differentials: heart failure, blood cancers, infections reasoned; the rest listed — 'one blood test covers most' · ★ driving: not taking anything off you today; sleep study; don't drive sleepy, pull over, avoid long stretches alone; no alcohol 3–4 h before bed; weight later with permission · safety net (worse headaches, chest pain, ankle swelling, any episode at the wheel) · questions (mask? licence?) · summary
ask: 'Is it a lack of energy, feeling sleepy, or feeling feverish?' / 'I am going to run through some questions quickly to make sure I am not missing anything.'

★ 'Has anyone ever told you that you snore, or that you stop breathing or gasp during sleep?' / ★ 'When you wake up, is your sleep refreshing?' / 'Any headache in the morning? Any trouble concentrating in the morning? Dry mouth on waking?'
★ 'How much alcohol, and how close to bedtime?' / ★ 'What do you do for work?' / ★ 'Have you ever felt sleepy at the wheel, or had a near miss?'
'When you wake like that — are you breathless and having to sit up, or does it settle in seconds?'
'The gynaecological causes obviously do not apply here.' / ★ 'Was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?'

★ 'The muscles at the back of your throat go floppy and the airway closes over. You stop breathing for a few seconds, your body wakes you just enough to open it again, dozens of times a night. You never remember it — but you never get deep sleep, which is why eight hours leaves you wrecked.' / ★ 'The reasons I think this are your own answers…'

★ 'Sleep apnoea is one of the known reasons a blood pressure will not settle on tablets. Your reading today is close to target — treating the sleep may do more for it than another tablet. Keep taking them.'

★ 'Because you drive for a living I need to be straight with you. I am not taking anything off you today. The test is a sleep study and I'll get that moving. Until then: do not drive if you feel sleepy, pull over and rest if you do, avoid long stretches alone.'

'Will I lose my truck licence?' → 'The rules are about sleepiness, not the label. Commercial standards are stricter and need a specialist opinion and evidence that treatment is working. Most people who are treated and controlled keep driving. What I need from you is that you do not drive while sleepy.'

'I can't afford to stop. I'll push through.' → 'I don't want you to lose your income. But if you keep driving while sleepy I have a duty I cannot ignore — in South Australia doctors are required to report a driver who is unfit. I'd much rather get you treated quickly. Can we agree you won't drive on days you haven't slept?' VERIFY the SA reporting duty before quoting

'Will I need a mask?' → 'Possibly, and they work very well. If mild, a dental splint may be enough, and weight loss helps more than anything else — could we talk about weight next visit?' Never say OSA, AHI, PSG, CPAP or BMI unexplained.

Variant — normal BMI, no witnessed apnoeas: OSA still possible (blocked nose, small jaw, crowded airway); think harder about insufficient sleep, shift work, thyroid, anaemia, depression, narcolepsy; sleep diary

setting: Your general practice. Face-to-face station. The role-player is in the room even though there is no history-taking task. Notice on the door: findings are given only if you ask for them specifically.
stem: Mary Whitfield, a 40-year-old woman, has presented complaining of feeling tired, weight loss over the last few months, night sweats and loss of appetite.
tasks: Ask the examiner for the findings of the physical examination you would perform
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Request your further investigations
time: 8 minutes (2 reading). Greet the patient first, then turn to the examiner. Frame the examination in one sentence · general, vitals (temperature first), hands, face/mouth · ★ all lymph node chains, then the four node characters · thyroid with the reason · bone tenderness · chest · abdomen — name splenomegaly · bedside tests · examination gate 5:10 · turn to her, warning shot, say the word lymphoma · reasons from your findings, not her stem · differentials by group · investigations in order — FBE, film, excisional biopsy, PET-CT — then the rest.

back.dx: Lymphoma (Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin) presenting with B symptoms: four months of fatigue, ~7 kg weight loss, drenching night sweats, anorexia, generalised pruritus; examination — pallor, thin and unwell, T 37.8, HR 96, scratch marks, ecchymoses, conjunctival pallor, two to three rubbery, fixed, non-tender cervical nodes (largest ~3 cm, skin normal), bone tenderness, splenomegaly 4 cm, thyroid normal, chest clear. Clubbing is present but is NOT a lymphoma sign — it keeps an intrathoracic malignancy on the list (say so). Reasons to the patient led by your findings: rubbery, fixed, non-tender neck glands (infection glands are tender and mobile), enlarged spleen, scratch marks from the itch — plus her B symptoms. Differentials by group: other cancers — leukaemia (ecchymoses, bone tenderness), lung/bowel/breast; infections — TB, HIV, syphilis, EBV, CMV, toxoplasmosis (some need consent); hyperthyroidism (explains fatigue, sweats, weight loss; thyroid normal today). Investigations in order of priority: FBE, blood film today, excisional node biopsy (architecture, not FNA cells), PET-CT staging (or CT neck/chest/abdomen/pelvis); then LDH, ESR/CRP, HIV and syphilis serology with consent, EBV/CMV/toxoplasma serology, IGRA + CXR, TSH. Febrile neutropenia = emergency: cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour.
plan: Gel; ★ greet the patient first ('I've been asked to examine you and then talk you through what I think — give me a moment with the examiner'); ★ frame: 'a general examination with a focus on the haematological system, looking for a cause of B symptoms — general appearance, hands, face and mouth, all lymph node groups and thyroid, chest, abdomen, bedside tests'

General: cachexia, pallor, jaundice, rash · ★ vitals, temperature first, then HR, BP, RR, SpO2 · hands: clubbing, scratch marks, ecchymoses, joint swelling → ★ 'pruritus is a recognised feature of lymphoma' · ★ 'clubbing is not a lymphoma sign, so it keeps an intrathoracic malignancy on my list' · face/mouth: conjunctival pallor, gum hypertrophy/bleeding, tonsils

★ 'A full lymph node examination, all chains over the whole body — cervical and supraclavicular, axillary, epitrochlear, inguinal' → two to three cervical nodes → ★ 'consistency? mobile or fixed? tender? overlying skin? — I ask about tenderness to separate lymphadenitis from lymphadenopathy' → rubbery, fixed, non-tender, 3 cm → 'that is a malignant pattern'; ask anyway if the examiner deflects

Thyroid with the reason (hyperthyroidism explains tiredness, sweating, weight loss): mass, size, nodularity, tenderness, retrosternal percussion · ★ bone tenderness sternum/spine/long bones · chest: air entry, added sounds, S1 S2, murmur · abdomen: inspection, tenderness, masses, ★ 'specifically hepatomegaly or splenomegaly?' → spleen 4 cm · bedside BSL, dipstick — ★ stop asking at 5:10

Turn the chair fully, lower the voice, eye contact: ★ 'I have finished examining you, and I am afraid I have found some things that concern me. Is it alright if I go through them?' [pause] ★ 'I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer of the lymph glands, called lymphoma.' — say the word, stop, let it land

★ Reasons led by findings: rubbery, fixed, non-sore neck glands vs infection glands; enlarged spleen; scratch marks — then her tiredness, weight loss, sweats. 'Am I going to die?' → no number you cannot stand behind; many lymphomas respond very well; not yet a diagnosis until a gland is sampled

★ Differentials by group: other cancers (leukaemia; lung/bowel/breast less likely), infections (TB, HIV, syphilis, EBV/CMV/toxoplasma — 'some need a blood test and your permission'), overactive thyroid; 'why HIV?' answered

★ To the examiner, in order and slowly: FBE · blood film today · excisional biopsy of a cervical node ('lymphoma is classified on nodal architecture; an aspirate gives cells without architecture') · PET-CT staging (or CT N/C/A/P) · then LDH, ESR, CRP; HIV and syphilis with consent; EBV/CMV/toxoplasma; IGRA + CXR; TSH · febrile neutropenia answer if asked · safety net to Mary (fever, breathlessness, face/neck swelling, bleeding → hospital; specialist phoned; results by phone; someone with you; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20)

★ 'A full lymph node examination, all chains, over the whole body.' → ★ 'Consistency? Mobile or fixed? Tender? And the overlying skin?' / ★ 'I am asking about tenderness because I want to separate lymphadenitis from lymphadenopathy.'

★ 'I am afraid I have found some things that concern me.' → ★ 'I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer of the lymph glands, called lymphoma.'

★ 'Glands from an infection are usually tender and mobile; yours are rubbery, they do not move under my fingers, and they are not sore. I also found your spleen — an organ on the left side of your abdomen — is bigger than it should be, and I noticed the scratch marks from the itching.'
'Why HIV?' → 'Because HIV can cause swollen glands, weight loss and sweats, and it is treatable. I test for it in anyone with this picture. I'd need your consent, and the result stays confidential.'

'If she rings tonight with a fever of 39?' → 'A medical emergency until proven otherwise — present immediately; blood cultures and empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour; haematology involved; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if retrieval is needed.'

setting: Hospital ward, evening shift. TELEPHONE station — no examiner, no role-player in the room; a card says 'please pick up the telephone'. The nurse on the line is the examiner. Your consultant is unavailable. Management is NOT a task.
stem: You are the HMO. Blood results have returned on Mr Arthur Nolan, 78, a resident of a nearby aged-care facility, currently an inpatient. Sodium 118 mmol/L (135–145), chloride low, serum osmolality low. Nothing else is given.
tasks: Report and explain the investigation results to the nurse
Take a history from the nurse
Explain the most likely diagnosis and your differentials to the nurse
time: 8 minutes. Name yourself, who and where · ★ conscious state and fitting BEFORE any number · obs · report in colleague register, name what the low osmolality means · orient: admission, PMHx, ★ the whole chart including long-standing drugs, surgery · symptoms · pseudo screen (glucose, TG, protein) said out loud · three volume blocks announced · ★ ask her to EXAMINE him for fluid state · four SIADH cause groups · three-layer explanation · escalate, safety-net, offer to document.

back.dx: Drug-induced (thiazide) SIADH → euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia. Na 118, low serum osmolality = true hypotonic (not pseudo; not glucose-driven — glucose 5.4, TG and protein normal). Nurse's examination on request: moist mucosa, no postural drop, no oedema, chest clear, weight stable, fluid chart balanced ~1400/1300 → euvolaemic. Chart: hydrochlorothiazide, paracetamol, atorvastatin — nothing changed since admission (asking only 'new medications' gets 'nothing new' and you miss it). Three-layer explanation: (1) true hypotonic, euvolaemic → SIADH, most likely trigger the thiazide; (2) other SIADH causes — malignancy (lung, lymphoma), infection (pneumonia, TB, meningitis), intracranial (bleed, head injury) — clear CT, no fever/cough/weight loss make them less likely but not excluded on history; (3) outside SIADH — hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency (TSH, morning cortisol), hypovolaemic group (losses, poor intake, diuretics), hypervolaemic group (heart, liver, kidney). Confirm with paired serum/urine osmolality + urine sodium. Close: discuss with medical registrar and document — do not change the thiazide over the phone; call back if drowsy, more confused, vomiting, fitting.
plan: ★ 'This is Dr [name], the HMO covering the ward tonight. Who am I speaking with, and which ward?' → Jackie, RN 4B, bed 12
★ 'Before I go through the results — is he alert and oriented, or drowsy or more confused than usual? Any fitting? Latest obs?' → alert at baseline, no fits, BP 128/76 HR 78 RR 16 SpO2 97 T 36.6

Report as a colleague: Na 118 vs 135–145, significant; chloride low tracks Na; ★ 'serum osmolality is low — this is a true hypotonic hyponatraemia, not an artefact'. If asked what osmolality means: one technical sentence, no lay translation

Orient: admitted 3 days ago after a fall, no fracture · HTN, OA, mild memory impairment · ★ 'read me the whole chart — everything, including anything started or changed in the last few weeks' → hydrochlorothiazide, paracetamol, atorvastatin · no surgery. Note the thiazide, keep going

Symptoms (confusion vs baseline, drowsiness, headache, nausea/vomiting, unsteadiness/falls) · ★ pseudo screen: glucose 5.4, TG normal, total protein normal → say aloud 'not pseudohyponatraemia, not glucose-driven — true hypotonic; next I need his fluid state'

Three volume blocks, each announced: 1 losing — vomiting, diarrhoea, intake, burns/wounds · 2 retaining — orthopnoea/pillows, ankle swelling, jaundice/dark urine/pale stools, urine output, fluid balance chart → ~1400 in/1300 out · 3 euvolaemic — cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain

★ THE DISCRIMINATING ASK: 'Can I ask you to look at him and tell me what his fluid state looks like — dry mouth/tongue, reduced turgor, postural drop; or ankle oedema, raised JVP, basal crackles? Weight on the chart?' → euvolaemic → say 'that narrows this considerably'

SIADH cause groups, one question each: drugs (have the chart) · infection — fever, cough, SOB, headache, neck stiffness, new drowsiness · malignancy — weight loss, lumps/nodes, night sweats, past cancer · brain — head strike in the fall, imaging → CT clear · 'drinking unusually large volumes?'

Three-layer explanation (dx + cause; other SIADH causes; non-SIADH causes) · paired serum/urine osmolality + urine Na · 'Hold his morning dose?' → ★ 'I'll discuss with the medical registrar and document tonight rather than change it by phone' · safety-net · 'anything you'd like me to go over again?'
ask: ★ 'Before I go through the results — is he alert and oriented, or drowsy? Has he had any fitting? Can you give me his latest observations?'

★ 'His sodium is 118, against a range of 135 to 145. The serum osmolality is low, so this is a true hypotonic hyponatraemia.' / 'What does osmolality mean?' → 'Total concentration of dissolved particles — mostly sodium, with glucose and urea. Low sodium with low osmolality means the sodium is genuinely low.'
★ 'Can you read me his medication chart — everything on it, including anything started or changed in the last few weeks?' (not 'any new medications?')

'Can you check whether there are recent results for glucose, triglycerides and total protein?' → 'Then this isn't a pseudohyponatraemia — it's a true hypotonic hyponatraemia. Next I need his fluid state.'
'First, whether he's losing fluid… Second, whether he's retaining it… Third, the euvolaemic causes…' — three blocks, announced

★ 'Can I ask you to look at him for me and tell me what his fluid state looks like? Dry mucosa and a postural drop — or oedema, raised JVP and basal crackles? And has his weight changed on the chart?'
'Four quick groups: infection… malignancy… brain — did he hit his head, has he had imaging?… and has anyone noticed him drinking unusually large amounts of water?'

★ 'He has a true hypotonic hyponatraemia and he's clinically euvolaemic — that points to SIADH, and given his chart the most likely trigger is the thiazide.' Then layer 2 (malignancy, infection, intracranial) and layer 3 (hypothyroid, adrenal, hypovolaemic, hypervolaemic groups)
'To confirm it I'd like a paired serum and urine osmolality with a urine sodium.'

'Do you want me to hold his morning fluid tablet?' → ★ 'I'll discuss that with the medical registrar and document a clear plan tonight rather than change it over the phone. Call me straight away if he becomes drowsy, more confused than baseline, starts vomiting, or has any fitting.'
pefe: Nurse's brief: Jackie Moore RN 4B, brisk, four other patients. Withholds volume status unless you ask her to assess fluid state/hydration/oedema/JVP/turgor — 'how does he look?' gets 'well, no different to yesterday'. Never volunteers the thiazide; 'any new meds?' gets 'nothing new since admission'. Goes cool and marks you down if you talk down to her ('a salt in your blood')

Findings on request: alert at baseline, no fits · BP 128/76, HR 78, RR 16, SpO2 97 RA, T 36.6 · ★ moist mucosa, no postural drop, no oedema, chest clear, weight stable · fluid chart ~1400 in / 1300 out · glucose 5.4, TG and protein normal · CT head on admission clear · no fever, cough, headache, neck stiffness, weight loss, lumps, cancer history · drinking normal

Register cheat-sheet — to the nurse: hyponatraemia, serum osmolality, euvolaemic, SIADH. To a patient: 'a mineral, or salt, in your blood', 'a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water'. Wrong register for the listener costs marks in both directions

Variant — nurse rings back an hour later, he has seized: diagnostic problem → emergency. Attend, MET call, airway/oxygen/monitoring, urgent repeat Na and glucose; symptomatic severe hyponatraemia with seizures → small boluses of 3% NaCl to raise Na 4–6 mmol/L, enough to stop the seizure, then stop; medical registrar + ICU from the outset; afterwards correction ≤8 mmol/L per 24 h (osmotic demyelination). VERIFY regimen against Therapeutic Guidelines and local protocol
Variant — 3-month cough, 6 kg loss, smoker since 17: 'a low sodium of this kind can be caused by a chemical released by a growth in the lung — it's on my list, CXR this week, CT if it shows anything'
SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if retrieval needed · TIS 131 450
fails: Discussing a sodium of 118 before asking whether he is alert or has fitted ★
Never asking the nurse to assess his fluid state — the single commonest failure ★
Asking only about new medications (misses the long-standing thiazide) ★
Saying 'SIADH' and offering no differentials ★
Changing or stopping a medication over the telephone instead of escalating ★
Hearing the thiazide and stopping the history; not naming what the low osmolality means; running the volume groups without announcing them
Lay-register explanation to a senior nurse; failing to offer to document and escalate; no safety-net

SIADH: urine osm >100 mOsm/kg, urine Na >30–40, euvolaemic, normal thyroid/adrenal/renal · hypovolaemic hyponatraemia urine Na <20
Correction ≤8 mmol/L per 24 h · severe symptomatic: 3% NaCl to lift 4–6 mmol/L · SIADH fluid restriction 800–1000 mL/day

setting: General practice, face to face — results-discussion station. Stem reconstructed from the Version B script in the source PDF (only the age, sodium, drugs and format are given).
stem: A 50-year-old man attends for the results of routine blood tests. He feels completely well. Sodium 120 mmol/L (135–145), serum osmolality low. He takes citalopram for mood and carbamazepine, which he has had for years for nerve pain.
tasks: Explain the blood results to the patient
Take a focused history
Explain the most likely diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Why the test, then symptoms (dizziness, confusion, memory, headache, tiredness, balance) · three volume blocks · ★ every medicine — prescribed, over the counter, herbal · five-move patient-register explanation · ★ do NOT tell him to stop the SSRI or the anticonvulsant today — confirm, then plan a substitution with the prescriber.

back.dx: Drug-induced SIADH (citalopram and carbamazepine are both recognised causes) → euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia, Na 120, asymptomatic. Five-move explanation in patient register: sodium is a mineral/salt kept in careful balance → most likely cause is SIADH, 'syndrome of inappropriate secretion of ADH' → ADH tells the kidneys to hold on to water; too much → extra water dilutes the salt → the trigger is his medication, a side effect not his fault → other causes looked for: certain cancers (lung, lymphoma — CXR normal), infections (chest, lining of the brain), problems inside the head (bleed/injury — brain scan normal) → non-SIADH causes: losing fluid (vomiting, diarrhoea, poor intake), fluid tablets, underactive thyroid (ruled out), heart/liver/kidney problems (results and examination don't support). Next step: confirm with paired serum/urine osmolality and urine sodium, then talk to the prescriber — an SSRI stopped abruptly causes discontinuation symptoms, carbamazepine stopped abruptly risks seizures; plan the change, say so aloud.
plan: WIPE · 'Before we look at them — what prompted the test?' → routine · 'Any dizziness, confusion, memory trouble, headaches, tiredness, change in walking or balance?' → none, 'which is why I'm puzzled you called me in'

Result in lay words: 'your sodium is low — sodium is a mineral, or salt, your body keeps in balance in the blood'; it is a true low (osmolality low) rather than a measurement effect; not an emergency in someone well, but it needs a cause
Three volume blocks announced: losing (vomiting, diarrhoea, intake, burns) · retaining (orthopnoea, ankle swelling, jaundice, urine output) · euvolaemic (cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain)

★ 'Every medicine you take — prescribed, bought over the counter, and anything herbal' → citalopram, carbamazepine for years · SIADH groups: fever/cough/headache/neck stiffness · weight loss/lumps/sweats/past cancer · head injury/imaging · excess water drinking · smoking

Examination by name (or findings on screen): fluid state — mucosa, turgor, postural BP, JVP, oedema, chest bases · thyroid · neuro/conscious state · results already held: CXR normal, brain scan normal, TSH normal

Five-move explanation: low sodium → SIADH named and spelt out → ADH/water mechanism → medication trigger, 'a side effect rather than anything you have done wrong' → other SIADH causes looked for → non-SIADH causes

★ 'The next step is to confirm it, then talk to whoever prescribes your medicines — we don't stop an antidepressant or an anticonvulsant abruptly; we plan the change.' Paired serum/urine osmolality + urine Na · fluid guidance once confirmed · safety-net: headache, confusion, drowsiness, vomiting, fits → ED
ask: 'Before we look at them — can I ask what prompted the test in the first place?'
'Any dizziness, confusion, memory trouble, headaches, tiredness, or any change in your walking or balance?'
★ 'Can you tell me every medicine you take — prescribed, bought over the counter, and anything herbal?'
'Your blood test shows a low sodium level. Sodium is a mineral, or a salt, that your body keeps in careful balance in the blood.'

'The most likely cause is a condition called SIADH — the syndrome of inappropriate secretion of ADH. ADH is a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. Your body makes more of it than it should, so you hold on to extra water, and that extra water dilutes the salt in your blood.'
'In your case the most likely trigger is your medication — both citalopram and carbamazepine are recognised causes, and that is a side effect rather than anything you have done wrong.'

'There are other things that can cause SIADH and I've looked for them: certain cancers, particularly of the lung, and lymphoma — your chest X-ray is normal; infections of the chest or the lining of the brain; and problems inside the head such as a bleed or an injury — your brain scan is normal.'

'Causes outside SIADH: losing fluid through vomiting, diarrhoea or not drinking enough; fluid tablets; an underactive thyroid, which your test has ruled out; and heart, liver or kidney problems, which your results and examination don't support.'

★ 'Should I stop them?' → 'Not today. We confirm it first, then I talk to whoever prescribes them — stopping an antidepressant suddenly causes withdrawal symptoms, and stopping carbamazepine suddenly can bring on seizures. We plan the change together.'
'Come back straight away, or go to the emergency department, if you get a bad headache, become confused or unusually drowsy, start vomiting, or have any fitting.'

Confirmatory: paired serum and urine osmolality, urine sodium (SIADH: urine osm >100, urine Na >30–40) · TSH, morning cortisol · UEC, glucose, lipids, protein · once confirmed: fluid restriction 800–1000 mL/day, and drug substitution planned with the prescriber (psychiatry/GP for the SSRI; neurology/pain for carbamazepine) VERIFY

Register cheat-sheet — patient: 'a mineral, or salt, in your blood', 'a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water', 'your body holds on to too much water, which dilutes the salt'. Never 'euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia' to him
Variant — malignancy version (cough 3 months, 6 kg loss, smoker): name the lung as a possible source, CXR this week, CT if abnormal — 'it's on my list, I'm not telling you that you have it'
Variant — seizure at home: emergency; 3% NaCl by protocol, 4–6 mmol/L lift then stop, ICU/medical registrar, correction ≤8 mmol/L/24 h VERIFY · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33
SA: GP-endocrine/physician referral; TIS 131 450
fails: Telling him to stop citalopram or carbamazepine today ★
'SIADH' with no differentials, or a differential list with no non-SIADH layer ★
Asking 'any medications?' without over-the-counter and herbal — or never linking the two drugs to the sodium
Reporting the sodium in colleague register (osmolality, euvolaemic) to the patient
Declaring the diagnosis without offering a confirmatory paired osmolality
No safety-net for neurological symptoms in a sodium of 120
numbers: Na 120 · normal 135–145 · severe <125 · serum osm <275 = true hypotonic
SIADH: urine osm >100 mOsm/kg · urine Na >30–40 mmol/L · euvolaemic · normal TSH/cortisol/renal
Fluid restriction 800–1000 mL/day once confirmed · correction ≤8 mmol/L per 24 h
Drug triad: thiazides · SSRIs · carbamazepine
