setting: Renal unit of a metropolitan teaching hospital; you are the resident. A 12-lead ECG is supplied with the stem — read it before you enter. Vitals available on request. Older recall adds a fourth task: outline your immediate management.
stem: Mr John Whitfield, 60, known end-stage kidney disease on maintenance haemodialysis, attends for his scheduled session. He has had several days of palpitations and diarrhoea. ECG provided: tall, narrow-based, symmetrical peaked T waves, most marked in the mid-precordial leads; QRS normal; P waves preserved.
tasks: Take a further focused history (3 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant investigations
Explain the condition to the patient
time: 8 minutes: 40 s opening · 3 min history · 45 s investigations · 2.5 min explanation · 45 s safety-net and close. Read the ECG outside and say so · vitals from the examiner · warn about the pace · kidney background, ★ read the drug list ALOUD · symptom sweep in 25 s · ★ four precipitants: diet · missed dialysis · 'new — OR ANY CHANGE to' medications · fluid loss · tissue breakdown in 10 s · three named investigations · ★ diagnosis by its proper name, three causes, symptom linked · safety-net · teach-back.

back.dx: Acute kidney injury on end-stage kidney disease with hyperkalaemia (K 5.9 with ECG changes = treat as severe) — multifactorial: (1) perindopril dose increased by the GP last week (he can't say which tablet; deduce it from pharmacology — of perindopril, hydrochlorothiazide, erythropoietin, the ACE inhibitor is the one that raises potassium), (2) missed Monday's dialysis — a session's worth of potassium not removed, (3) four days of watery diarrhoea with poor intake and postural dizziness — volume depletion. eGFR 10–12 (baseline ESKD); VBG no significant acidosis → reduced clearance and retention, not a transcellular shift. 'You have hyperkalaemia' is a laboratory state, not a diagnosis — the commonest fail. Explain: 'your kidneys have taken a sudden knock on top of the long-standing damage — an acute injury on chronic kidney disease'; three reasons stacked; potassium controls the heart's electrical rhythm, hence the palpitations. Plan: cardiac monitor, dialysis brought forward to today, hold the perindopril, letter to the GP, don't stop anything else alone. Handle 'my GP did this to me' by explaining the monitoring gap (UEC 1–2 weeks after any ACE-i dose change), not the person.
plan: Outside: 'peaked narrow-based T waves V3–V4, QRS narrow, P waves present — hyperkalaemia, not yet advanced' · ★ 'Examiner, could I have BP, pulse, RR and saturations?' → 132/78, 88 reg, 16, 97% RA, afebrile → 'haemodynamically stable, I'll proceed'

WIPE, confirm identity · ★ 'I've only got a few minutes, so I'm going to ask short, direct questions — is that all right?' · 'My heart's going like a drum — should I be worried?' → name it, park it with a promise, keep the clock

setting: General practice, regional South Australia. You are the GP. Pre-operative results station; no physical examination.
stem: Mark Ellis, 50, storeman, is booked for elective open right inguinal hernia repair in 10 days and attends for his pre-operative blood results. He feels well and has no complaint. Hypertension for 6 years on a thiazide diuretic. BP 138/84, HR 78 regular, RR 14, SpO2 98% RA, T 36.7. Results: sodium 135 (135–145), potassium 3.1 (3.5–5.2), bicarbonate 30 (22–32), creatinine 82 µmol/L, eGFR >90, anion gap normal.
tasks: Explain the blood test results to the patient
Take a focused, relevant history
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes after 2 reading: results 2 min (marks earned in the first three sentences — say the kidneys are normal) · history 4 min (surgical context → ★ hypertension block incl. the dose change → intake → GI loss naming laxatives/teas → renal loss/mineralocorticoid → phaeo triad → other drugs by category, SADMA, FHx) · diagnosis + ★ four differentials aloud 2 min · plan: repeat, ECG, magnesium, replace, review the antihypertensive · answer the operation question · safety-net · summarise.

back.dx: Mild hypokalaemia (K 3.1) from thiazide-induced renal potassium wasting — the dose was doubled four weeks ago for creeping readings, which fits the timing exactly; bicarbonate 30 at the top of range is consistent. Normal renal function (say so — interpreting creatinine/eGFR is part of 'explain the results'). Four differential buckets, numbered, in plain English: (1) not enough in — restricted diet; (2) losing it through the bowel — vomiting, diarrhoea, laxatives (name tablets, powders, teas); (3) losing extra through the kidneys — a tablet like his, or 'a small gland above the kidney making too much of a hormone that dumps potassium' (primary aldosteronism: cramps, weakness, polyuria, resistant BP); (4) shift into cells — some asthma puffers, insulin, and 'a rare adrenaline-producing tumour' (phaeo triad: headache + sweating + palpitations, patients go pale, not flushed). Plan: repeat U&E to confirm, ECG today (arrhythmia is the consequence that matters 10 days from a GA), magnesium (thiazides waste Mg; low Mg makes K replacement ineffective), oral KCl supplement, review the antihypertensive for a potassium-sparing option, write to surgeon and anaesthetist, recheck in 3–7 days and again before theatre. The operation most likely proceeds — mild, asymptomatic; if it stays low a short delay is for anaesthetic safety. Never tell him to stop the antihypertensive himself. Hidden agenda: daughter's wedding in six weeks — ask an open concerns question early.
plan: WIPE, DOB · 'I've got your results — shall I take you through them?' · ★ 'The good news first: your kidneys are working normally.' Sodium 135 normal, lower end · potassium 3.1, a little below normal · 'the salt that helps your muscles and your heart work properly — worth sorting before an anaesthetic; not an emergency'
'Is that going to stop my operation?' → acknowledge, park explicitly, promise to return · ★ 'Was there anything else you were hoping to cover today?' (wedding) · permission for questions

Surgical context: when diagnosed, painful, ever stuck/hard/tender, bowel change (first GI screen, excludes obstruction) · ★ Hypertension: when, which tablet, dose, ★ 'has the dose been changed recently, or anything added?' → doubled 4 weeks ago · adherence, follow-up, control · chest pain, SOB/PND, vision, focal weakness
Intake: diet change, typical day, fruit/veg, weight, alcohol · GI loss: vomiting, diarrhoea/looser motions, ★ 'laxatives — tablets, powders or teas?', bowel surgery/stoma

Renal loss/mineralocorticoid: cramps, weakness (stairs, chair, lifting), polyuria/nocturia, thirst, paraesthesia, central weight gain/bruising/striae, liquorice · Phaeo: ★ 'episodes of bad headache, breaking out in a sweat and heart racing, all together, sudden then settling? go pale?'

Other drugs by category: puffers (how often), steroids (tablets/creams/injections), insulin/diabetes tablets, OTC/herbal/vitamins, anyone else's fluid tablets, recent antibiotics · smoking 5/day, 6 drinks/weekend, allergies, PMHx (diabetes, thyroid, kidney), FHx (BP young, endocrine)

★ Diagnosis: 'hypokalaemia — potassium lower than normal; most likely your blood pressure tablet — it makes the kidneys pass out salt and water and potassium goes with it; the dose doubling four weeks ago fits the timing exactly'

★ 'But I did think about the other reasons, and that's why I asked all those questions': ONE not enough in · TWO bowel — vomiting, diarrhoea, laxatives · THREE kidneys — a tablet like yours, or a gland above the kidney making too much of a hormone that dumps potassium · FOUR shift into cells — puffers, insulin, a rare adrenaline-producing tumour · 'nothing points to those'

Plan: repeat test, ECG today ('potassium affects the heart's rhythm'), magnesium ('if low, potassium won't come up'), potassium supplement, review the BP tablet · the operation: most likely proceeds, recheck before theatre, letter to surgeon and anaesthetist; if still low a short delay for safety · safety-net: marked weakness, palpitations, fainting, vomiting/diarrhoea → come back · summarise, 'what questions do you have?'
ask: 'I've got your results here — shall I take you through them?' / ★ 'The good news first: your kidneys are working normally.'

'There's a salt called potassium, and yours is a little below the normal range. Potassium is the salt that helps your muscles and your heart work properly. It's not an emergency, and it's usually straightforward to fix.'

'Is that going to stop my operation?' → 'That's exactly what I want to sort out for you, and I'll give you a proper answer — let me ask you some questions first.' / ★ 'Was there anything in particular you were hoping to sort out today?'
★ 'Has the dose been changed recently, or has anything been added?'

'Do you use any laxatives — tablets, powders or teas?' / 'Are you passing more urine than usual, or getting up at night to go?' / 'Any puffers, steroid tablets, insulin, anything herbal, or anyone else's fluid tablets?'
★ 'Do you get episodes of a bad headache, heavy sweating and your heart racing, all together — coming on suddenly and then settling? Do you go pale with them?' (not 'flushing')
★ 'The most likely cause is your blood pressure tablet — it makes the kidneys pass out potassium in the urine, and the dose was doubled four weeks ago, which fits the timing exactly.'
★ 'One, not enough in. Two, losing it through the bowel. Three, losing extra through the kidneys. Four, potassium shifting into the cells.'
'I'd like to repeat the test, do a heart tracing today, and check your magnesium.' / 'I'll write to your surgeon and speak to the anaesthetic team so everyone has the same information.'

'Should I just stop the blood pressure tablet?' → 'No — please keep taking it for now. I'll review it and there are options that control your pressure without stripping potassium; we'll change it properly, not suddenly.' / 'Come back straight away if you get marked weakness, palpitations or fainting.'

Variant B — K 2.5, BP 168/98 on two agents, calf cramps, heavy legs on stairs, nocturia ×3–4: primary aldosteronism — 'a small gland above the kidney making too much of a hormone called aldosterone, pushes BP up and potassium down; treatment is different — a particular tablet, sometimes surgery; there's a blood test (ARR — correct K first, adjust interfering antihypertensives VERIFY)'; ECG today; ★ talk to the surgical team about postponing — automatic fail if the plan is unchanged

Variant C — 34F, K 2.8, 'a herbal regularity tea most nights, that's not really a medicine': senna = laxative = real cause; how often, how long; 'some people use them to manage their weight or how they feel about their body — is any of that part of it? no judgement, I ask everyone'; no moralising; National Alliance for Eating Disorders helpline (not NEDA) VERIFY current Australian service

Variant D — 68 on digoxin, K 3.2, off food, nauseated, 'the telly looks yellowish': ★ digoxin toxicity potentiated by hypokalaemia — ECG and digoxin level now, repeat UEC/K/Mg, seen today not next week; automatic fail if digoxin is on the list and you neither identify it nor escalate
SA: letter to surgeon and anaesthetist (regional hospital list); pre-anaesthetic clinic; TIS 131 450 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 (not needed here)
fails: Giving the diagnosis and stopping — no four differentials said aloud in patient language ★
No concrete plan for the operation ★
Telling him to stop his blood pressure tablet himself ★
Reassuring him before proposing a repeat test; 'it's definitely just the fluid tablet' ★
Explaining results for four minutes; skipping 'your kidneys are normal'
Asking 'what medications?' and stopping — never asking about the dose change; accepting 'no other medications' without naming laxatives, puffers, steroids, insulin
Asking about 'flushing' for phaeo; 'hyperaldosteronism' or 'transcellular shift' to the patient; 'the operation will be fine, don't worry'
numbers: K normal 3.5–5.2 (3.5–5.0 safe answer) · mild 3.0–3.4 · moderate 2.5–2.9 · severe <2.5 · here K 3.1, Na 135, HCO3 30, eGFR >90, normal AG
ECG once K <~3.0: flat/inverted T → ST depression → prominent U → T–U fusion → ectopy → torsades
Mg normal ~0.7–1.1 · oral KCl slow-release 600 mg = 8 mmol; effervescent 14 mmol/tab VERIFY · IV KCl needs cardiac monitoring, rate/concentration per local protocol VERIFY
Recheck U&E + Mg 3–7 days, again before theatre · timing: results 2 · history 4 · dx + DDx 2
Phaeo triad: headache + sweating + palpitations, pallor not flushing · ARR after correcting K VERIFY

setting: General practice, regional South Australia. No physical examination; no results provided. The examiner may ask what you would order. Six minutes of history, then explanation.
stem: James Whitfield, 45, warehouse supervisor, married with two children, not seen here for two years, no recorded chronic disease: 'I've been feeling very thirsty and I'm drinking far more water than usual.' Nurse observations: BP 128/78, HR 76 regular, RR 14, SpO2 98%, T 36.8, weight 84 kg, BMI 27; blood glucose not yet done.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Explain the most likely cause and the other conditions you considered
Answer his questions and outline the plan
time: 8 minutes. Elicit his worry in the first minute (diabetes — his dad) · ★ put a number on the litres · ★ 'passing more urine?' — say aloud that no polyuria lowers diabetes · six blocks: sugar · marrow · brain · thyroid · ★ drugs and SUPPLEMENTS · lifestyle · hypercalcaemia sweep · four-link explanation: vitamin D → calcium → kidneys → thirst · ★ 'I can't be certain until I check a calcium' · separate him from his mother · safety-net.

back.dx: Excessive vitamin D supplementation (4 × 1000 IU = 4000 IU/day for six weeks, started because his mother has osteoporosis with two fractures this year) → probable hypercalcaemia → polydipsia. Ten days of constant worsening thirst, 4–5 L/day up from 2, no polyuria, nocturnal drinking not voiding, bowels sluggish this last week; no weight loss, vision change, infections; no bone pain, fatigue, sweats, bruising; no headache/vision loss; no heat intolerance, loose bowels, palpitations, tremor; no stones, nausea; lifestyle unremarkable. Four-link chain in plain words: vitamin D helps you absorb calcium → too much pushes blood calcium up → high calcium makes the kidneys pass out more water → your body feels that as thirst; the word is hypercalcaemia. Differentials, each with why less likely: diabetes (no polyuria/weight loss; finger-prick today anyway), overactive thyroid, a brain problem with the water-balance hormone (DI), a bone-marrow condition that raises calcium (myeloma — asked bone pain, tiredness, infections), everyday causes (coffee, alcohol, salt, heat). Honest uncertainty: no blood test yet, so no declared 'vitamin D poisoning'. Plan: stop the capsules today, bring the bottle in, BSL now, bloods for calcium, UEC, 25-OH vitamin D, glucose, TSH; drink to thirst 2–3 L; review when results back, phone sooner if needed. Separate him from his mother: her dose was worked out for her bones and her blood test — his wasn't; do not change her treatment.
plan: WIPE, 'can I call you James?' · open · 'I can understand why that would be worrying you' · signpost groups · ★ 'was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?' → diabetes, dad → 'I'll check your sugar before you leave either way'

Explore: duration 10 days, constant, worsening · ★ 'how much are you actually drinking — put a number on it' → 4–5 L, was 2 · better/worse (no) · night — drinking, not voiding · impact (bottle round the warehouse)

Sugar block, five questions: ★ passing more urine? (no) · hungrier? · weight loss? · blurred vision? · recurrent infections? · FHx → ★ say aloud: 'thirst without passing more urine makes diabetes a good deal less likely — I'll still check your sugar'

Marrow (bone/back pain worse at night/rest, fatigue, weight loss/sweats/infections, bruising/bleeding) · brain (morning headache, vomiting, vision) · thyroid (heat, bowels, palpitations, tremor) — four questions each, no more

★ Drugs in this order: 'regular medicines from a doctor?' (no) → 'anything you buy yourself — painkillers, herbal?' → ★ 'any vitamin D, or a multivitamin?' → 'just vitamin D, that's not really a medicine, is it?' → no change of tone: strength per capsule (1000), how many/day (4), how long (6 weeks), anything with calcium (no), ★ 'what made you start?' → mother's osteoporosis, two fractures this year → acknowledge, promise to return

Hypercalcaemia sweep: loin pain/stones, bone ache, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain/indigestion, ★ constipation (sluggish this week), mood/memory/concentration, weakness/drowsiness · lifestyle: smoking, alcohol, coffee, salt, exercise, hot workplace · PMHx, FHx

Move 1 summarise and check · Move 2 ★ the four-link chain, name 'hypercalcaemia' · Move 3 ★ 'I can't be certain until I check a calcium level' + differentials in plain English with why less likely · Move 4 ★ separate him from his mother

His questions ('I thought vitamins were safe' — stored in fat, builds up; 'have I damaged myself' — almost certainly not, bloods check the kidneys; 'should Mum stop hers' — no, her own GP; 'how long' — halves every 2–3 weeks) · plan · ★ safety-net unprompted: vomiting, bad tummy pain, bad constipation, weakness, confusion or unusual sleepiness → straight back/ED, 'you'd need a drip' · summarise, 'anything I haven't covered?'

'Any pain in your bones or your back — worse at night or at rest? Unusually tired? Weight loss, night sweats, infections you've struggled to shake? Easy bruising?' (myeloma, out loud, man over 40)

★ 'Any medicines from a doctor — and anything you buy yourself, vitamins or supplements?' / 'What does the bottle say — how many units per capsule, and how many a day? For how long? Anything with calcium in it?' / ★ 'What made you start taking it?'

★ 'Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium from your food. If you take more than you need, the calcium in your blood can drift up. High calcium makes your kidneys pass out more water, which dries you out — and what your body feels when it's drying out is thirst.'
★ 'I want to be straight with you — I can't be certain until I check a calcium level in your blood.'

★ 'Taking it because of your mum was a sensible instinct, not a silly one. The difference is that her dose was worked out for her bones and her blood test. Yours hasn't been.' / 'Please don't change your mum's treatment — that's a conversation for her own GP.'

'Am I going to end up like Mum?' → 'Osteoporosis isn't something you catch from your mother — family history is one risk among several. The right answer isn't extra vitamin D on spec; it's checking your own level, your other risks, and at the right age a bone density scan. Shall we book a longer appointment once this settles?'

★ 'Come back straight away, or go to the emergency department, if you start being sick, get bad tummy pain or become badly constipated, feel weak, or if you or your wife notice you're confused or unusually sleepy.'

setting: General practice, regional South Australia. Results-discussion station; the examiner interrupts to hand you further results after your investigation list.
stem: Ms Janine Whitfield, 45, teacher's aide, attends to discuss blood tests taken at a routine check-up two weeks ago. Hypothyroidism for eight years on levothyroxine 100 µg daily; no other regular medicines on file; non-smoker; she has no complaint and feels perfectly well. Results: TSH 2.1 (0.4–4.0), free T4 14 (10–20), albumin 31 g/L (low, 35–50), total calcium 2.56 (normal, 2.10–2.60), corrected calcium 2.78 — HIGH.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history
Explain the blood results you already have, in plain language
Tell the examiner the further investigations you would request, in order of priority
The examiner will give you those results. Explain your diagnosis and your reasoning to the patient, including the differentials you considered
time: 8 minutes after 2 reading: history 4 · explain current results 1 · investigations 1 · diagnosis + differentials 2. Write 'corrected 2.78 · albumin low · TSH normal · PTH first' and the seven history headings before you speak. Name the abnormal result early and size it · why the test, ever told before · ≥5 hypercalcaemia symptoms · ★ full malignancy screen · supplements, antacids, thiazide/lithium by use, TB/sarcoid, phaeo, thyroid · ICE before explaining · ★ corrected not total · ★ PTH first WITH a reason · four glands, one overworking · not cancer · ≥4 differentials · plan, referral, safety-net, summary.

back.dx: Primary hyperparathyroidism (single adenoma ~85%) — PTH elevated with corrected calcium 2.78, vitamin D normal, phosphate low-normal, eGFR 88, examination normal. Total calcium 2.56 reads 'normal' only because albumin is 31: corrected = 2.56 + 0.02 × (40 − 31) = 2.74 ≈ 2.78 per report — a station-ending false reassurance if you read the total line. Calcium was 'high last year'; she was told to stop her multivitamin and cut dairy — chronicity makes malignancy less likely but does not exclude it, and diet was never the driver (correct the science kindly without attacking the colleague). Only positive symptom: 'a bit more thirsty, I keep a bottle on my desk'. Malignancy screen clean (weight, appetite, lumps, sweats, breast/mammogram clear last year, cough, smoking, haematuria); mother had breast cancer at 60 — the hidden agenda; ask ICE before you explain. Investigations ranked with BECAUSE: 1 serum PTH (commonest cause; the one test that splits the differential in two) · 2 25-OH vitamin D with phosphate (read as a set; low phosphate supports PTH) · 3 UEC/eGFR (renal function, hypercalcaemic nephropathy) · then CXR (lung Ca, TB, sarcoid), FBE/ESR/SPEP + free light chains (myeloma, lymphoma), 24-h urine calcium (exclude FHH before any surgery), full examination incl. breasts and nodes. Explain: four tiny glands behind the thyroid, different job — keep blood calcium right; one is overworking, pulling calcium from bone; the hormone is raised, which confirms it; not cancer, not the thyroid tablets, not diet. Differentials named: cancers (blood, breast, lung, kidney), vitamin D/calcium antacid excess, fluid tablets, lithium, overactive thyroid (excluded), sarcoid/TB. Refer endocrinology (age <50 → surgery will be discussed, their decision with her); hydrate; do not restrict dairy; safety-net.
plan: WIPE, identity · open question · ★ 'I can see one of the numbers, your calcium, is a little higher than we'd like. It's not an emergency, but it does need explaining. Would it be alright if I asked you some questions first?'

'What made you have the test?' · ★ 'Has anyone ever told you before that your calcium was high?' → yes, last year; multivitamin stopped, dairy cut, nothing else done · 'any further tests or treatment?'

Symptoms ≥5: nausea/vomiting · abdominal pain/constipation · bone/back pain · weakness/tiredness · thirst/polyuria/nocturia (→ 'a bit more thirsty') · stones/loin pain · mood/memory/concentration — 'these cover both the symptoms and the commonest cause'

★ Malignancy screen, full, 'questions I ask everybody with this result': weight, appetite, lumps (neck/axilla/groin), night sweats, breast lump/discharge/mammogram, cough/haemoptysis/smoking, haematuria, cancer in you or family (mother, breast, 60) · 'why are you asking all this?' → stop, turn, explain honestly

Supplements: vitamin D, multivitamin, calcium — dose, duration · antacids (Gaviscon monthly) · health-food products · prescription by USE: 'anything for blood pressure or fluid, or any tablet for your mood' · SOB/chest pain/fevers/TB contact · joint pain/rash/shin lumps · headache-sweating-flushing-palpitations, endocrine FHx · thyroid duration/adherence/tremor/heat · alcohol, smoking, PMHx · ★ ICE: 'anything worrying you about these results?' → mother's cancer

★ Explain: TSH and T4 normal → thyroxine dose right · 'calcium travels two ways — free, and carried by a protein called albumin; your albumin is a bit low so the raw number looks normal; adjusted for the protein the true level is 2.78, we'd want it under 2.60 — genuinely high, mildly' · 'calcium isn't controlled by what you eat; a hormone controls it — the question is which part of that system is out' · 'so the dairy was pointless?' → reasonable first step, but not the fix

★ To the examiner, ranked with reasons: 1 PTH because… 2 25-OH vitamin D + phosphate because… 3 UEC/eGFR because… then CXR; FBE, ESR, SPEP + FLC; 24-h urine calcium; full examination incl. breasts and nodes → PTH elevated, vit D normal, PO4 low-normal, eGFR 88, examination normal

★ 'Behind your thyroid sit four tiny glands called the parathyroid glands — different glands, different job. One appears to be overworking… today's test shows that hormone is raised, which confirms it. It's called primary hyperparathyroidism. It is not a cancer, and it is not caused by your thyroid tablets or by what you eat.' · 'is it my thyroid tablets?' answered

Differentials aloud: cancer (blood, breast, lung, kidney — why I asked, CXR and bloods still) · vitamin D/antacid excess · fluid tablets, lithium · overactive thyroid (excluded) · sarcoid/TB (other reason for CXR) · plan: endocrine referral, surgery discussed because of her age — their decision; drink plenty of water; don't cut dairy · ★ safety-net: very thirsty + lots of urine, vomiting, drowsy/confused, severe abdominal/back/loin pain → same day · review ~1 week · summarise, offer to write it down
ask: ★ 'I can see one of the numbers, your calcium, is a little higher than we'd like. It's not an emergency, but it does need explaining. Would it be alright if I asked you some questions first, so I can work out why?'
★ 'Has anyone ever told you before that your calcium was high?' / 'Did anyone do any further tests, or start any treatment for it?'

★ 'I'm going to ask some questions I ask everybody with this result, just to be thorough.' → weight, appetite, lumps, night sweats, breast/mammogram, cough/blood, smoking, urine blood, cancer in you or your family

'Why are you asking all this?' → 'A high calcium has several possible causes. Most are not serious, and the commonest by far is a small gland problem. But a few cancers can also raise calcium, so I check for them in everybody — not because I suspect it in you. Nothing you've told me so far points that way.'

'Apart from the thyroid tablet, any other regular medicine — anything for blood pressure or fluid, or any tablet for your mood?' (thiazide, lithium by use) / 'Any vitamin D, multivitamins or calcium tablets? Anything for indigestion — antacid tablets or liquid?'

★ 'Calcium travels in the blood two ways — some floats free, some is carried by a protein called albumin. Your albumin is low, so the raw number looks normal; once we adjust for it, the true level is high.' / 'Calcium isn't really controlled by what you eat — your body controls it with a hormone.'

★ 'My first priority is serum parathyroid hormone, because primary hyperparathyroidism is the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia in the community and PTH is the single test that splits the differential in two.' / 'Calcium, phosphate and vitamin D are read as a set.'

★ 'Behind your thyroid gland sit four tiny glands called the parathyroid glands — different glands, different job. Their only job is keeping your blood calcium right. One of them appears to be overworking, and that pulls extra calcium out of your bones into your blood.' / ★ 'It is not a cancer, and it is not caused by your thyroid tablets or by what you eat.'

'Is it cancer?' → 'On everything I have so far, no. Your hormone result points to a gland problem, not a cancer. I'm still completing a chest x-ray and a couple of blood tests so that I'm certain rather than nearly certain.' / 'Should I stop dairy?' → 'No — diet isn't the driver, and cutting calcium hard can be bad for your bones. Drink plenty of water.' / 'Will I need an operation?' → 'Possibly — the only definitive treatment, but not everyone needs one; because you're forty-five the specialist will talk it through seriously.'

★ 'If you become very thirsty and pass a lot of urine, start vomiting, feel drowsy or confused, or get severe tummy, back or loin pain, I want you seen the same day.' / 'To summarise — is there anything I've missed, or anything you'd like me to write down?'
pefe: Role-player: Janine, 45, teacher's aide 4 days/week, husband, two teenagers, 40-min drive; levothyroxine 100 µg, never misses; stopped multivitamin last year on advice; Gaviscon ~monthly; no BP/fluid/mood tablets; never smoked, 2 wines Friday; mammogram last year clear; mother breast cancer at 60, alive. Only positive: 'a bit more thirsty, I keep a bottle on my desk' — given only if asked. Brisk, impatient at first; guarded during cancer questions; after the breast question asks 'why are you asking all this?' every time; if you read the total calcium as normal: 'so there's nothing wrong then?'; asks 'is it my thyroid tablets?' and 'will I need an operation?'; if falsely reassured before tests: 'how can you be sure?'. Hidden agenda released on ICE, else volunteered at ~7 min as you summarise

Examiner returns: PTH elevated · 25-OH vitamin D normal · phosphate low-normal · eGFR 88 · full examination normal · everything else normal. Examiner challenges: 'Why not image the parathyroids?' → 'the diagnosis is biochemical; sestamibi/ultrasound are for the surgeon to localise, not to diagnose' · 'Avoid dairy?' → 'no; severe restriction can worsen bone loss; hydration matters more' · 'Frusemide?' → 'only for overload during rehydration; not a routine calcium-lowering treatment'

Version B — high-dose health-food vitamin D for 8 months + calcium antacids most nights: examiner gives PTH suppressed <1.0, 25-OH D 310, eGFR 74, PO4 normal → 'a low parathyroid hormone tells me the gland is behaving and being switched off — the extra calcium is coming from somewhere else; your vitamin D is ~4× target — the supplement, probably with the antacids (milk–alkali)' → stop both today, hydrate, recheck 2–4 weeks; ★ suppressed PTH is the MALIGNANCY arm — still complete CXR and bloods · corrected Ca 2.88

Variant C — 62, corrected Ca 3.15, 6 kg loss since Christmas, night-waking low back ache, worn out; Hb 96, creatinine 148, PTH suppressed, ESR 88 → 'myeloma until proved otherwise': SPEP, serum FLC, urine Bence-Jones, film, LDH, whole-body low-dose CT or MRI spine (not plain films); IV normal saline now; urgent haematology; ★ ask about cord compression (numbness, leg weakness, bladder/bowel) — same-day emergency; warning-shot register, 'today rather than next week'

Variant D — 58 on indapamide + lithium, corrected 2.72, asymptomatic: switch the thiazide to another antihypertensive, recheck 2–4 weeks; ★ do NOT stop lithium unilaterally — speak with the psychiatrist, decide together; check PTH (lithium can make the glands overactive) · Variant E — 28M, Ca 2.70 pre-employment, father and sister 'high calcium', PTH mildly raised: FHH — 24-h urine calcium and Ca:Cr clearance ratio (<0.01 supports), CaSR gene testing; these patients are harmed by parathyroid surgery
SA: endocrinology referral (RAH/FMC/Lyell McEwin); PATS for travel; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 only if a Version B/C patient needs retrieval; TIS 131 450
fails: Saying 'your calcium is actually normal' because you read the total line ★
PTH not first in the investigation list, or a flat list with no BECAUSE ★
Never asking a single cancer question; abandoning the malignancy screen because it was 'high last year' ★
Falsely reassuring ('it's definitely nothing') before any tests; or finishing on the diagnosis with no differentials, plan or safety-net ★
Jargon: 'PTH-dependent hypercalcaemia secondary to a parathyroid adenoma'
Endorsing the dairy restriction to avoid contradicting a colleague; asking 'any other medications?' and accepting 'no' without naming thiazide and lithium by use
Skipping ICE so the mother's cancer lands at minute seven; stopping the supplement in Version B and declaring the case closed; stopping lithium unilaterally in Variant D
numbers: Corrected Ca = total + 0.02 × (40 − albumin g/L) · here total 2.56, albumin 31, corrected 2.78 · reference 2.10–2.60 · mild <3.0 · moderate 3.0–3.5 · severe >3.5
Top three: PTH · 25-OH vitamin D + phosphate · UEC/eGFR · causes 1 and 2: hyperparathyroidism, then malignancy · adenoma ~85% of primary disease
Surgery triggers: age <50 · Ca >0.25 above upper limit · eGFR <60 · urine Ca >10 mmol/day · stones · T-score ≤−2.5 · FHH: Ca:Cr clearance ratio <0.01 · ECG: short QT
Severe: saline 4–6 L/24 h · zoledronic acid 4 mg IV over ≥15 min after rehydration · calcitonin 4 units/kg SC/IM 12-hourly · prednisolone 20–40 mg/day if vitamin D–mediated VERIFY

Timing: 0:00 WIPE/name it · 0:30 why/before · 1:00 symptoms · 1:45 malignancy · 2:45 drugs etc + ICE · 4:15 explain · 5:15 ranked ix · 6:15 dx/DDx/plan · cut the thyroid block, never the malignancy block · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

setting: Suburban general practice; you are the GP. Vitals (including BSL) on request. 9-minute station. RECALL NOTE: the source recording verifies the stem and history; later tasks follow the standard three-task shape.
stem: Marianne Kovac, 50, presents with two days of nausea and vomiting on a week of feeling weak, tired and lethargic. She is holding a vomit bag. Known hypertension and chronic kidney disease. Current medications: perindopril 5 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the examination findings and investigations you want
Explain the most likely diagnosis and outline your immediate management
time: 9 minutes: 40 s opening · 4 min history · 1.5 min examination/investigations · 2 min explanation · 45 s safety-net and close. The diagnosis is on the medication list — the marks are for what you ask AFTER you've worked it out: ★ obs incl. BSL · acknowledge the bag, offer water · vomit content · ★ 'when did you start the PAINKILLER, who started it' + OTC/chemist separately · ★ cardiac screen unprompted · abdomen/melaena · ★ urine output, uraemic symptoms · fluid status FIRST · investigations by analyte incl. ECG and troponin · ★ diagnosis by name · triple whammy in plain English · stop, hold, ★ transfer today, no driving · teach-back.

back.dx: Acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease (stage 2 — eGFR 45 → 22, creatinine roughly doubled) with hyperkalaemia (K 6.3 + peaked T waves, narrow QRS → treat as severe) and metabolic acidosis (HCO3 18) — the 'triple whammy': NSAID (constricts the afferent arteriole) + ACE inhibitor (dilates the efferent) + thiazide (lowers circulating volume), in a woman with baseline CKD. Ibuprofen 400 mg tds for three weeks for a knee — self-bought at the chemist, then scripted by a locum who didn't have her record; she doesn't call it a medication. Uraemic symptoms: much less urine, postural dizziness, metallic taste; examination — dry mucosa, postural drop 20 systolic, JVP not visible, abdomen soft, no bladder, no asterixis. BSL 5.4 removes DKA at the door; troponin normal and cardiac screen negative (nausea + lethargy without chest pain is a recognised MI presentation in women and CKD). Explain: 'your kidneys were working at about half strength and have taken a sudden extra hit — an acute injury on chronic kidney disease; waste products build up and cause the sickness and exhaustion'; mechanism of the three drugs in plain words; 'you can buy it anywhere' → 'that's exactly why it catches people out'. Plan: ibuprofen stops today and never again without checking; hold (not stop forever) perindopril and the thiazide while unwell; ★ ED today for fluids and potassium treatment — ring ahead, results with her, don't drive; repeat UEC 48–72 h; paracetamol + physiotherapy for the knee; letter to usual GP, flag on file. Hidden agenda: mother died on dialysis — 'not today, and in most cases like yours this is reversible once we take the pressure off'.
plan: ★ 'Examiner — BP, pulse, RR, saturations, temperature AND blood sugar?' → 142/86, 72 reg, 16, 98%, afebrile, BSL 5.4 → 'stable, afebrile, normal sugar — a diabetic emergency is unlikely from the outset'
WIPE, 'how would you like me to address you?' · open · ★ 'I'm sorry — that sounds miserable. Would you like some water first?' (the vomit bag is marked)

Symptom package in one block: onset (tiredness 1 week, vomiting 2 days), worse, better/worse · 'tired — low energy, sleepy, or breathless?' · frequency 4–5/day · ★ 'what does the vomit look like — any blood, or anything green?' (UGI bleed vs obstruction; she's on an NSAID) · keeping anything down?

Background: when diagnosed CKD (5 y, 'about half') and HTN (10 y), what for them → perindopril + 'a fluid tablet' · adherence · ★ 'and when did you start the PAINKILLER — who started it, and what was it for?' → ibuprofen ~3 weeks, knee, self-bought then locum script · ★ 'did whoever prescribed it know about your kidneys?' → 'it's only ibuprofen' (don't correct now; save it) · 'anything from the chemist, or herbal?'

★ Cardiac screen, unprompted, 10 s: 'a few quick questions to make sure I'm not missing something serious — chest/arm/jaw/back discomfort, exertional SOB, cold sweats (clammy yesterday), palpitations, blackouts'
Abdomen: pain/where, bowels, ★ black/tarry stools, fevers, jaundice · ★ urine output 'more, less or the same?' → much less · dizzy standing (yes) · confusion, hiccups, itch, ★ metallic taste (yes)

★ Examination — fluid status FIRST: postural BP, mucosa, JVP, cap refill; abdomen (tenderness, guarding, organomegaly, palpable bladder); cardiorespiratory; pallor, pigmentation, oedema, asterixis → dry, postural drop 20, JVP not seen, soft abdomen, no bladder, no asterixis

★ Investigations by name: ECG now (hyperkalaemia AND ischaemia) · UEC/eGFR vs baseline — specifically K, Na, bicarbonate · VBG · troponin · FBE, Ca, PO4, Mg, LFT, lipase, urinalysis → eGFR 22 (baseline 45), creatinine ×2, K 6.3, HCO3 18, troponin normal, peaked T narrow QRS · 'why a troponin with no chest pain?' answered · read back: stage 2 AKI on CKD; K moderate by number, severe by ECG; acidosis shifts K out of cells

★ Diagnosis by name · 'will I need dialysis? my mother died on dialysis' → pause, acknowledge, honest answer · mechanism: three medicines, three directions — painkiller narrows the vessel in, perindopril widens the vessel out, fluid tablet lowers the circulating volume — 'the triple whammy' · 'you can buy it anywhere' → exactly why it catches people out · 'the locum's fault?' → missing record, not the person; letter to usual GP

Plan: 1 ibuprofen stops today, never that class without checking · 2 hold perindopril and the fluid tablet — temporary, don't stop anything else alone · 3 ★ ED today (K affects the heart's rhythm; can't keep fluids down) — ring ahead, results with her · ★ don't drive · red flags en route: chest pain, palpitations, faint, weak muscles → ambulance · repeat UEC 2–3 days · paracetamol + physio for the knee · ★ teach-back · 'anything still worrying you?'
ask: ★ 'Could I have her observations — including a blood sugar?' / 'I'm sorry, that sounds miserable. Would you like some water first?'
'When you say tired — low in energy, sleepy, or breathless when you move about?' / ★ 'What does the vomit look like — any blood, or anything green?'
★ 'When did you start the painkiller, and who started it for you?' / 'Anything from the chemist, or anything herbal?' / 'Did whoever prescribed it know about your kidneys?'
★ 'A few quick questions to make sure I'm not missing something serious. Any discomfort or tightness in the chest, arm, jaw or back?'
★ 'How much urine have you passed in the last day — more, less, or the same?' / 'Any confusion, hiccups, itch or a metallic taste?'

★ 'I'd like her fluid status first — postural blood pressure, mucous membranes, JVP and capillary refill.' / 'Why a troponin with no chest pain?' → 'Because nausea and lethargy without chest pain is a recognised presentation of infarction in women and in chronic kidney disease.'
★ 'Her eGFR has halved from 45 to 22, which meets criteria for a stage 2 acute kidney injury.' / ★ 'The potassium is 6.3, and with ECG changes I treat that as severe regardless of the number.'

★ 'Your kidneys have taken a sudden extra hit on top of the long-standing damage — an acute kidney injury on top of chronic kidney disease.' / 'Will I need dialysis?' → 'Not today, and in most cases like yours this is reversible once we take the pressure off — that's exactly why we're acting now.'

★ 'Each of these medicines is sensible on its own. Together, with kidneys like yours, they're too much — in Australia we call it the triple whammy.' / 'But it's only ibuprofen — you can buy it anywhere' → 'You can — and that's exactly why it catches people out. Being sold without a prescription doesn't make it harmless for your kidneys.'

★ 'The painkiller stops today. The other two we hold while you're unwell — that's temporary.' / ★ 'I'm sending you to the emergency department today. Please don't drive.' / 'Could you tell me back what you'll say when you get to the hospital?'
pefe: Role-player: Marianne, 50, school administrator, husband, two grown children; HTN 10 y, CKD 5 y ('about half'), never dialysed; perindopril + 'a fluid tablet' never missed; ibuprofen 400 mg tds ~3 weeks for right knee (self-bought, then locum script; usual GP on leave) — not thought of as a medication; never smoked, wine most weekends; mother died on dialysis. 'What medications?' → 'perindopril and a fluid tablet' and STOP; ibuprofen only for 'painkillers', 'from the chemist', 'over the counter'. Slow, flat, retching; withdraws if not offered water; defensive once 'it's only ibuprofen'; 'is this the locum's fault?'; pushes back once on hospital 'can't I stop the tablets and come back Friday?' — agrees only if you hold firm with a reason; 'sorry — what does that mean?' at jargon; hidden agenda dialysis/mother in the last two minutes unless asked

Examiner returns: BP 142/86, PR 72, RR 16, SpO2 98, T 36.6, BSL 5.4 · dry mucosa, postural drop 20 systolic, JVP not visible, abdomen soft non-tender, no palpable bladder, HS dual, chest clear, no pallor/oedema/asterixis · eGFR 22 (baseline 45), creatinine ~×2, K 6.3, HCO3 18, troponin normal, ECG peaked T narrow QRS

Variant A — prevention: visiting gout patient on perindopril + a fluid tablet demands indomethacin → 'I can treat that today — before I write anything, what else are you on, any kidney trouble? …an anti-inflammatory is the one thing I don't want to give you: those three together can shut the kidneys down within days' → colchicine or short prednisolone, check UEC while here VERIFY TG gout dosing/renal cautions

Variant B — ECG: ST elevation II, III, aVF → 'inferior STEMI presenting as nausea and lethargy without chest pain — ambulance now, aspirin 300 mg chewed, IV access, activate the acute coronary pathway; the renal picture is real but no longer the priority' ★ continuing the triple-whammy talk = automatic fail

Variant C — coffee-ground vomit + black sticky stools: NSAID upper GI bleed contributing to the AKI → ambulance now, bloods, fluids, PPI, endoscopy · Variant D — refuses (daughter's wedding Saturday): honest risk statement, 'I'd be failing you if I sent you home; may only be hours on a drip'; if still declines: document discussion and specific risks, confirm capacity, written red flags, same-day repeat bloods, defined review, can change her mind any time — never simply agree
SA: ED (nearest regional/metropolitan); MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if retrieval; PATS; TIS 131 450; recheck UEC 48–72 h after stopping, 1–2 weeks after restarting an ACE-i
fails: Asking only 'what medications are you on?' — walking past the ibuprofen ★
No cardiac screen without being prompted ★
'High potassium' as the diagnosis instead of AKI on CKD; not explaining the three-drug combination in her words ★
Sending her home to 'come back Friday' with K 6.3 and ECG changes; letting her drive ★
Continuing to discuss the triple whammy after an ischaemic ECG (Variant B) ★
Ignoring the vomit bag; asking only how many times, never what the vomit looked like; never asking about urine output or black stools
'Renal function tests' with no analyte; stopping perindopril and the thiazide forever rather than holding; blaming the locum; deflecting the dialysis fear; no alternative for the knee; no teach-back
numbers: Triple whammy = diuretic + NSAID + ACE-i/ARB · here eGFR 45 → 22 · creatinine ~×2 · K 6.3 · HCO3 18 · troponin normal · peaked T, narrow QRS
AKI staging: stage 1 creatinine ×1.5 · stage 2 ×2 · stage 3 ×3 or dialysis VERIFY against current KDIGO wording · K mild 5.5–5.9 · moderate 6.0–6.4 · severe ≥6.5 · any ECG change = severe
Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 2–5 min · insulin–dextrose 10 units in 50 mL 50% glucose over 15–30 min, onset ~15 min, 4–6 h, BSL hourly × 6 h · salbutamol 10–20 mg neb
Recheck UEC 48–72 h after stopping the drugs · 1–2 weeks after restarting an ACE-i · aldosterone rule: hypoaldosteronism → high K; hyperaldosteronism → low K
Timing: 40 s · 4 min · 1.5 min · 2 min · 45 s (9-minute station) · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

setting: General practice in Kadina, regional South Australia; you are the GP registrar. A results card is handed to you. Expect a prompt at 5 minutes covering tasks 1 and 2.
stem: Mr Colin Whitfield, 58, semi-retired farm contractor, returns for the results of blood tests taken a fortnight ago when he attended feeling tired. Hypothyroidism for six years on levothyroxine 100 µg daily; no other regular medication recorded. BP 138/82, HR 76 regular, RR 14, SpO2 98%, T 36.7; he looks well. Results: TSH 2.1 (0.4–4.0), free T4 15 (10–20), total calcium 2.58 (2.15–2.60), albumin 28 (low), corrected calcium 2.82 (HIGH), phosphate 0.68 (low, 0.75–1.50), creatinine 88/eGFR >60, FBE and LFT normal, PTH sent — result not yet available.
tasks: Explain these blood results in language he can understand
Take a focused, relevant history
Give your most likely diagnosis and your differentials
Explain what happens next
time: 8 minutes: results 90 s MAXIMUM (signpost → thyroid in one breath → ★ calcium in four sentences: straight reading normal, stuck to a protein, protein low, corrected is high → check understanding → permission) · history 3½ min in seven blocks: tiredness · ★ stones · bones · groans · moans · ★ cancer · drugs incl. OTC · family/alcohol · ★ ICE before the diagnosis · transition line · four glands, one overactive, usually benign, 'I'm not going to promise you that today' · ★ say the word PTH and what high and low each mean · rest of workup, referral, PATS · fluids, don't cut dairy, avoid diuretics/supplements · safety-net · summary · 'have I missed anything?'

back.dx: Primary hyperparathyroidism with end-organ disease — corrected calcium 2.82 (total 2.58 + 0.02 × (40 − 28)), phosphate 0.68 low (PTH wastes phosphate — read the whole panel), TSH/T4 normal (dose right, no change), FBE/LFT normal; PTH pending — 'I've already sent that sample, so we won't lose any time'. History: six months of tiredness; ★ renal colic three years ago (overnight at Wallaroo) + nocturia ×2 + thirst; hip ache ('forty years on tractors'); constipation new this year; 'I've been flat' — name low mood as part of the illness, not a weakness; malignancy block clean (weight steady, never smoked, no sweats/lumps/cough); thyroxine only, 'doesn't hold with vitamins'; no FHx of calcium/stones/neck surgery (FHH, MEN 1); beers Friday, more at harvest (explains the low albumin); diet plenty of milk and cheese. Hidden agenda: brother Wayne died of bowel cancer at 55 last year — ask ICE before you explain, then build the explanation around it. Explain: one of four small neck glands behind the thyroid, different job, slightly overactive, pushing calcium out of bone — fits the stone, constipation, thirst, feeling flat; usually benign and treatable; honest middle — 'a couple of other things can raise calcium, one is a cancer somewhere else, which I know you've worried about since your brother'; what makes it less likely: weight steady, never smoked, normal FBE/LFT, no bone pain or lumps. ★ PTH: high → the gland, common, treatable; low → calcium from somewhere else → CXR and further bloods. setting: General practice. No physical examination and no results — history substitutes for examination. Six minutes of history, two of explanation.
stem: Mrs Jane Halloran, 47, presents having found a lump in her neck. She noticed it while touching her neck and has been reading about it online. She is very worried.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient (approximately 6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes: 0:00 open + empathy line · 0:30 the lump — number, ★ 'show me exactly where', 'when did you first notice it', growth, four features (hard/tender/skin/mobile) · 1:30 thyroid box (ask despite lateral site) · 2:00 lymphoma + B symptoms · ★ 2:40 top-down cancer screen scalp → stomach — where all four positives live; do NOT stop at the cough · 4:20 infection box (★ toothache/dentist) · 5:10 travel, animals, sexual health, SADMA · 5:40 ICE · 6:00 'several conditions, not one' — ranked, each with its reason, benign and infective included · plan, timeframe, safety-net.

back.dx: Right lateral, hard, fixed, painless, enlarging cervical lymph node (~2 weeks) in a 47-year-old smoker (15/day × 30 years) — four buried positives found only by a systematic top-down screen: (1) dry cough for months (lung cancer), (2) non-healing buccal ulcer for two months (oral SCC), (3) food sticking on swallowing, not painful (oesophageal cancer — ask dysphagia and odynophagia separately), (4) aching back tooth, no dentist for years (dental infection with a reactive node — genuinely on the list, but a hard fixed node is not explained by it). Thyroid box negative (no movement on swallowing/tongue protrusion, no thermal intolerance); B symptoms negative — recite as relevant negatives. Explanation: 'I've been thinking about several conditions and I can't tell you today which it is' → most concerned about a cancer, and why: a gland reacting to a cancer in the lung (cough + smoking), the mouth (the ulcer), or the food pipe (food sticking) → the bad tooth as a real alternative → thyroid, other cancers that travel to the neck (skin, nose, stomach, salivary), throat/sinus/skin infections. Plan: examine properly, bloods, neck ultrasound, urgent specialist referral (ENT); organised today, hear within the week; safety-net — rapid growth, trouble breathing or swallowing → straight back. No false reassurance (she is briefed to push 'but you can't actually know that').

setting: General practice, Kadina, Yorke Peninsula. Examination findings supplied in the stem. Counselling station — two minutes of history restricted to treatments, then five minutes of talking.
stem: James Whitlock, 27: runny nose for two weeks, getting worse. Known hay fever; mother has asthma. Examination: afebrile, clear watery discharge, enlarged swollen inferior turbinates, respiratory examination normal.
tasks: Take a history for two minutes, to inquire about the treatments taken
Explain the diagnosis to the patient
Counsel the patient about your immediate and long-term management
time: 8 minutes: 2 min treatment-only history (signpost it; he opens with a symptom list — redirect) → five questions: what now · how long/how often · is it helping · what before and did each help · concerns → 45 s diagnosis (name BOTH: rhinitis medicamentosa + hay fever; rebound; reversible) → ★ 'STOP the Otrivin' first, alone, then a pause; warn 1–2 weeks worse → saline/steroid/antihistamine, cost solved → ladder by name → 5-step technique → non-drug → testing THEN immunotherapy 3–5 years → 2-week review, safety-net, summary repeating the stop.

back.dx: Rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound congestion from two weeks of xylometazoline — Otrivin — 3–4 times a day, both nostrils) on a background of allergic rhinitis. Pattern: brilliant for the first few days, now lasts an hour, nose worse than before he started. Treatment history: antihistamine tablets helped eyes not nose; a steroid spray WORKED but he stopped it because of cost (saving for a house) and switched to Otrivin — so the plan is to restart that drug cheaply, not invent a new one. Concerns: cost; 'have I wrecked my nose?' (mate said so) — answer both explicitly: completely reversible. Explain: decongestant squeezes the vessels in the lining — beautiful for 3–5 days, then the lining becomes reliant, each dose wears off into more swelling; three reasons — two weeks, helped then stopped, swollen with clear discharge and no fever (not infection). Immediate: STOP Otrivin outright (tapering prolongs it; one-nostril-at-a-time compromise only if he can't cope), warn 1–2 weeks worse, saline before a daily steroid spray (prescribed, cheaper brand in class), cetirizine 10 mg to cover. Long-term ladder by name: saline → antihistamine (oral cetirizine/loratadine/fexofenadine for eyes, or intranasal azelastine for the nose) → ★ mometasone 2 sprays each nostril daily, preventer not rescue, no immediate relief, up to 2 weeks → Dymista 1 spray bd (bitter) → montelukast if asthma. Five-step technique. Allergen measures. Allergy testing (specific IgE or skin prick) BEFORE immunotherapy (SC or SL, 3–5 years, allergy clinic in Adelaide, PATS). Review 2 weeks not 6, bring the spray.
plan: WIPE briskly · he launches into sneezing/itchy eyes → ★ 'I can see from your notes you have hay fever, so rather than go back over that, I'd like to spend the next couple of minutes on the treatments you've been using — I suspect that's where the answer is. Is that all right?'

setting: General practice. Findings are supplied on a card so four tasks fit the time. Task 3 is to the EXAMINER (diagnosis + differentials); task 4 is counselling.
stem: James Coulter, 25, warehouse storeperson, has come in with a sore throat and is asking you for antibiotics. tasks: Take a focused history
Read the physical examination findings on the card provided
Tell the examiner your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses
Counsel the patient on management

To the examiner — most likely viral pharyngitis/tonsillitis; differentials in order of what you would not miss: bacterial streptococcal tonsillitis; peritonsillar abscess; epiglottitis/deep neck space infection; infectious mononucleosis with splenomegaly; gonococcal/chlamydial pharyngitis; scarlet fever; laryngitis and sinusitis with PND; pneumonia; and in a different patient, drug-induced agranulocytosis or head and neck malignancy. Counselling: reassure first ('this will settle by itself — even bacterial ones do; that's why we're careful, not automatic'); two options — symptoms alone, or symptoms + antibiotic: benefit ~1 day; harms — up to 1 in 10 side effects, resistance, EBV rash with amoxicillin; 'what matters most to you?' → recommend no antibiotic; ★ medical certificate solves the real need (hidden agenda: casual, no sick leave, behind on rent); paracetamol 1 g qid, ibuprofen 400 mg tds with food, fluids, salt-water gargle, rest, cut smoking; safety-net: can't swallow saliva/drooling, noisy breathing, voice change, neck swelling/stiffness, rash, not improving 5–7 days; teach-back. setting: General practice, regional South Australia. No observations supplied. Prompt at 4 minutes to move to examination; a photograph is handed over when you ask for Horner's syndrome. Indirect laryngoscopy is unavailable.
stem: Margaret Ellis, 45, primary school teacher, presents with a change in her voice — hoarseness.
tasks: Take a focused history (approximately 4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you want
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Explain the further investigations you would arrange
time: 8 minutes, four tasks — lost on time far more than knowledge. 0:00 short open + agenda · 0:25 ★ timing and pattern: constant, 'does voice rest help?', 'same all day or worse by evening?' — two months is a red flag on its own · 1:15 infection, airway red flags, overuse tested and DISCARDED out loud ('I'm a teacher' is the red herring) · 2:00 cancer screen throat → oesophagus → thyroid → ★ lung: cough, haemoptysis, SOB, shoulder pain, ★ pack-years aloud · ★ the two Pancoast questions (hand numbness ulnar side; droopy eyelid) · 3:20 reflux, myasthenia, hypothyroid, neck surgery, ★ 'steroid inhalers or puffers' by class, alcohol, FHx, ICE · 4:00 examination by component with targets — Horner's, C8–T1 · ★ basal signs = effusion secondary to the apex · 5:20 warning shot, pause, plain words, two reasons · differentials in three buckets · 6:50 ★ three numbered investigations · ownership of the result, safety-net, Quitline.

back.dx: Pancoast (apical lung) tumour with left recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement, left Horner's syndrome, C8–T1 lower brachial plexus involvement and a secondary left pleural effusion. Two months of constant, slowly worsening hoarseness, no better with two weeks' voice rest at Easter, same morning and night (kills overuse); dry cough three months, puffed on stairs, left shoulder ache 'blamed on marking', couple of kilos lost; 20/day since 20 = 25 pack-years; ★ left hand numb along the ulnar edge, husband said her eye 'looked lazy in a photo'. Examination: not cachectic, no neck mass, T 36.8, throat/nose/nodes/thyroid normal; left lower zone — reduced expansion, dullness, absent breath sounds, reduced vocal resonance (effusion); photograph — partial ptosis, miosis (ask about anhidrosis) = left Horner's → sympathetic chain → lung apex; C8–T1 weakness and sensory loss. Resolve the apparent contradiction before the examiner asks: an apical mass produces no chest signs itself; the basal signs are an effusion caused by it. To her: 'a growth in the upper part of your left lung — a lung cancer; can't be certain today' + two reasons (hoarseness/cough/smoking; fluid around the lung with eye and hand changes fitting a growth at the top pressing on nerves). Never 'Pancoast', 'Horner's', 'pleural effusion' to the patient. Differentials in three buckets with a why: infections (no fever, too long), strain (rest didn't help), growths — cords, thyroid, oesophagus, lung; rarer — reflux, hypothyroid, myasthenia, inhaled steroids. Investigations: 1 CXR today · 2 urgent ENT laryngoscopy · 3 CT chest + biopsy (then PET-CT, MRI thoracic inlet, TFTs, bloods). Own the result: call her personally, see her this week, bring her husband; safety-net; Quitline once, no lecture; Cancer Council 13 11 20. Hidden agenda: mother died of lung cancer at 58 — why she waited.

Brisk, minimising ('probably nothing'); volunteers 'I'm a teacher' early and warmly — the trap; withholds the hand and eyelid unless asked directly; pushes back once on medications 'do you mean any particular medication?'; calls the clock at 4 and 6; goes QUIET (not tearful) at the warning shot, one frightened question; 'what does that mean?' at Pancoast/Horner's/pleural effusion. Hidden agenda: mother died of lung cancer at 58 — reveal if asked what worried her/why she waited, else at ~6 min. If you finish early: 'so what do you actually think it is?'

Examiner: not cachectic, no visible neck mass, T 36.8 · throat no masses/swelling/redness/exudate · nose normal · no cervical nodes · thyroid normal · chest: reduced expansion, dullness, absent breath sounds, reduced vocal resonance LEFT LOWER ZONE · left Horner's (photograph) · C8–T1 weakness and sensory loss · indirect laryngoscopy unavailable

To the examiner if asked for the differential (technical register, what-not-to-miss order): Pancoast tumour with malignant effusion · laryngeal/vocal cord carcinoma · thyroid carcinoma invading the recurrent laryngeal nerve · oesophageal carcinoma · deep neck space infection/epiglottitis · acute laryngitis/URTI · vocal overuse, nodules, polyps · laryngopharyngeal reflux · myasthenia gravis · hypothyroidism · surgical/traumatic RLN injury · inhaled corticosteroids

Variant 1 — benign (2 weeks since school camp, better mornings, worse by home time): overuse/nodules — voice rest, don't whisper, hydrate, avoid caffeine/alcohol, stop smoking, no antibiotics, speech pathology; ★ 'if still hoarse at three weeks come back — ENT laryngoscopy regardless' — the mark is the built-in review · Variant 2 — 6 weeks post-thyroidectomy: RLN injury; ★ ask stridor/exertional breathlessness first (bilateral palsy = airway emergency); ENT laryngoscopy to document the side, speech pathology, check calcium and TFTs · Variant 3 — voice fades through the day, diplopia and heavy lids by dinner, fine on waking: fatigability → myasthenia gravis; ask chewing fatigue, dysphagia, breathlessness; AChR antibodies, neurology; breathing/swallowing difficulty → ED same day

Variant 4 — examination-station version (45M smoker, neck lump; task 1 upper limb neuro → C8–T1 loss; task 2 'further relevant examination' → ★ 'a C8–T1 lesion with a neck lump in a smoker makes me think of a lesion at the lung apex involving the lower trunk of the brachial plexus — I'd examine the respiratory system and look for Horner's and cervical nodes' → left basal effusion; task 3 → Pancoast tumour with lower brachial plexus involvement, secondary effusion, metastatic node; CXR, CT chest, tissue diagnosis, lung cancer MDT)
SA: urgent ENT (RAH/FMC), respiratory/lung cancer MDT, PATS; Quitline 13 7848; Cancer Council 13 11 20; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if the airway is threatened; TIS 131 450

setting: General practice, regional South Australia. Initial observations supplied. Findings from the examiner on request. History closes at 3:00 — this station is scored in the second half.
stem: Mr Jason Whitfield, 28, warehouse team leader, presents with a three-day sore throat. He told the receptionist he needs something to fix it fast because he cannot afford to miss work. T 37.4, HR 78, RR 14, BP 124/76, SpO2 99% on air.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Ask the examiner for your examination findings
Explain the likely diagnosis and your management to the patient
Address the patient's concerns
time: 8 minutes: 0:00 greet, ★ agenda question up front, signpost · 0:45 history — course, cough/coryza/hoarseness, fever/nodes, ★ signposted red-flag sweep (saliva, drinking, muffled voice, mouth opening, one-sided, breathing, neck stiffness/rigors), ★ rheumatic fever + ATSI + medications (thyroid/mental health/arthritis), ICE and impact · 3:00 named findings from the examiner · 3:30 diagnosis in plain English — viral and why; never 'just a virus' · 4:30 ★ solve the work problem FIRST — certificate, employer letter, modified duties · 5:15 analgesia doses, fluids, rest · ★ three pillars (no benefit · harm · resistance) · 'how does that sit with you?' · 7:00 six named safety-net symptoms, destination, review 3–4 days, teach-back. He pushes three times; the 'just in case' script is a fail.

back.dx: Viral pharyngitis: three days, 6/10, bilateral, dry cough and runny/blocked nose from the start, voice normal, swallows and drinks fine, felt warm the first night only, no red flags, no rheumatic fever/ATSI risk, no meds (paracetamol irregularly), no allergies. Examiner: T 37.4, pharynx and tonsils erythematous without exudate, uvula midline, no lymphadenopathy, no trismus, normal voice, no rash, spleen not palpable — Centor 0–1. Explain: 'everything points to a virus — the same family that causes a cold: red inflamed throat but no pus, no swollen glands, normal temperature; the cough and blocked nose actually tell me it's viral; settles over 3–5 days, throat last to go' — and ★ 'viral doesn't mean mild; these can knock you flat.' Hidden agenda: short-staffed, supervisor questioning his reliability, frightened of losing the team-leader role — solve it BEFORE antibiotics: medical certificate, a short letter to the employer (unwell, infectious, rest gets him back faster), or duties away from the team; the register softens and the antibiotic request loses its force. Symptomatic: paracetamol 1 g qid max 4 g, ibuprofen 200–400 mg tds with food, fluids, rest, gargles/lozenges. Three pillars: wouldn't work (kills bacteria, not a virus — not a day shorter); can harm (~1 in 10 diarrhoea/rash; amoxicillin-clavulanate hepatitis/jaundice); costs later (resistance when he genuinely needs one). 'Last time I was better in two days' → validate natural history, never criticise the prior GP ('every throat is different'). No 'just in case' script — offer review in 3 days and name what would change your mind. Safety-net six symptoms + destination + review 3–4 days + teach-back.
plan: WIPE · ★ 'before we get into it — is there anything in particular you were hoping we'd sort out today? I'd rather know now' → 'antibiotics' (push 1) → 'fair enough — I might well be able to help with that; can I ask a few questions first so I know what we're dealing with?'
Course: onset, better/worse, /10 · cough, blocked nose, hoarseness (cough + coryza = viral evidence) · fever/shakes, neck lumps

★ Signposted: 'a few quick questions to make sure this isn't something more serious' — swallow saliva? managing to drink? voice muffled? mouth opens fully? much worse on one side? trouble/noisy breathing? neck stiffness, shakes and shivers? → all no

★ 'A couple of routine background questions I ask everyone with a sore throat' — rheumatic fever or heart-valve problem? Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander? regular medications — thyroid, mental health, arthritis? allergies? · ICE + impact: 'how's it affecting you day to day, and what were you worried it might be?' → work, short-staffed, team falls apart

★ 'Examiner, may I have my findings: temperature and observations; the tonsils and whether there is exudate; asymmetry or deviation of the uvula; anterior cervical nodes; trismus or a muffled voice; any rash; and whether the spleen is palpable' → viral picture

'Everything points to a virus…' with the four features · 'it should settle over three to five days, the throat can be the last thing to go' · 'so it's just a cold?' → ★ 'it's a viral infection, and viral doesn't mean mild — it can floor you for a few days' · 'does that make sense so far?'

★ 'Now, you mentioned work, and I want to deal with that first because I suspect that's the bit really weighing on you' — certificate for the days he needs; a short letter to the employer; or duties away from the team while infectious — 'which would be most useful?' → register softens

Analgesia with doses, fluids, rest, gargles/lozenges · ★ three pillars, signposted: 'you asked about antibiotics and I want to give you a proper answer rather than just saying no' — 1 wouldn't work · 2 can harm · 3 costs later · push 2 'better in two days last time' → natural history, no criticism · push 3 'some to have on hand?' → ★ no script; review in three days and what would change my mind

★ 'How does that sit with you?' · safety-net: can't swallow saliva/drooling; muffled voice/can't open mouth; much worse on one side; high fever with shakes; dizzy/can't keep fluids down; short of breath → back or ED · not clearly improving 3–4 days → book back · ★ 'could you tell me back the ones you'd act on?'
ask: ★ 'Before we start — is there anything in particular you were hoping we'd sort out today?' / 'I might well be able to help with that. Can I ask a few questions first?'

★ 'I'm going to ask a few quick questions to make sure this isn't something more serious.' / ★ 'Can you swallow your own saliva? Has your voice changed? Can you open your mouth fully? Is it much worse on one side?'

★ 'A couple of routine background questions I ask everyone — have you ever been told you had rheumatic fever? Do you identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander? Any regular medications — anything for thyroid, mental health or arthritis?'
★ 'Examiner, may I have my findings — observations, tonsils and exudate, uvular position, cervical nodes, trismus or voice change, rash, and spleen?'

'Everything points to a virus — the same family of bugs that causes a cold. Your throat is red and inflamed, but there's no pus on the tonsils, no swollen glands, and your temperature is normal. The cough and the blocked nose actually help me here.' / ★ 'Viral doesn't mean mild. These can knock you flat for a few days.'

★ 'Let me deal with work first, because I think that's the real worry.' / 'I can write you a medical certificate, and a letter to your employer if that would help — or we could ask about duties away from the team while you're infectious. Which would be most useful?'

★ 'I want to give you a proper answer rather than just saying no. First, they wouldn't work — antibiotics kill bacteria; they do nothing to a virus. Second, they can do harm — around one in ten get diarrhoea or a rash, and occasionally they inflame the liver. Third, they cost you later — every unnecessary course makes the bacteria more resistant, so next time you genuinely need one it's less likely to work.'

'Last time I was better in two days' → 'That's a really common experience and it makes sense — most sore throats settle in about that time either way, so it's hard to tell what did the work. If I thought an antibiotic would get you back to work faster, I'd write it right now.' (never criticise the previous prescriber)

'Some to have on hand, just in case?' → 'I'd rather see you again in three days than give you a script to hold. What would change my mind is pus on the tonsils, swollen glands, a real fever, or the cough disappearing — if any of that happens, I'll treat it.'

★ 'How does that sit with you — is there anything about it you're not comfortable with?' / 'Come straight back, or go to the emergency department, if you can't swallow your saliva or start drooling; your voice goes muffled or you can't open your mouth; the pain gets much worse on one side; a high fever with shakes; dizzy or can't keep fluids down; or short of breath. Otherwise if not clearly better in three to four days, book back in.' / ★ 'Could you tell me back the ones you'd act on?'
pefe: Role-player: Jason, 28, team leader at a produce distribution centre outside Renmark; partner, child of three; non-smoker, 4–5 beers weekends; paracetamol irregularly; no PMHx; not ATSI; grew up in Adelaide. Blunt, impatient, not rude. Three pushes: opening line; 'better in two days last time' (defensive if you criticise 'my GP for years'); 'some on hand in case?' — accepts a script with thanks then marks a fail. If work is solved first: drops to one push, 'oh — that'd actually help a lot'. 'Just a virus' → 'it doesn't feel like just anything, mate'. If never asked about concerns: at ~7 min, flat, 'so what am I supposed to tell work?'

Examiner: T 37.4, other obs normal · pharynx/tonsils erythematous, no exudate · uvula midline, no asymmetry · no cervical lymphadenopathy · no trismus, normal voice · no rash · spleen not palpable · Centor 0–1

Variant 1 — findings turn bacterial (exudate both tonsils, tender anterior nodes, T 38.5, no cough; Centor 4): 'bacterial rather than viral' — and the Australian nuance: still not automatic antibiotics in a healthy adult (shortens ~1 day); treat if very unwell, scarlet-fever rash, or high ARF risk; symptomatic + review 3 days · Variant 2 — scarlet fever (sandpaper rash, flushed cheeks with circumoral pallor, strawberry tongue): treat — phenoxymethylpenicillin bd 10 full days; not infectious after ~24 h of treatment

Variant 3 — 19-year-old Aboriginal man, exudative tonsillitis, 38.6, grew up in a remote community: high ARF risk → treat 'to protect the heart, not the throat': swab, phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg bd 10 days (or single IM benzathine benzylpenicillin); Closing the Gap PBS; Aboriginal Liaison Officer/ACCHS follow-up with permission; ARF/RHD notifiable in SA VERIFY

Variant 4 — 34F, 4 days sore throat + fevers, 'something for an overactive thyroid' → ★ carbimazole: agranulocytosis warning sign — FBE today, stop carbimazole until the result, phone the endocrinologist; low neutrophils = febrile neutropenia → urgent assessment, cultures, empirical antibiotics. Treating as viral = automatic fail
SA: medical certificate; employer letter; ACCHS/Closing the Gap where relevant; SA Health notification for ARF/RHD; TIS 131 450; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33
fails: No signposted red-flag sweep — six minutes on the character of the pain, never saying drooling, one-sided, muffled or mouth opening ★
A flat refusal with no exploration of why he wants them ★
An antibiotic prescribed to end the argument — including a 'just in case' script ★
Agranulocytosis (carbimazole) or quinsy missed in a variant ★
No safety-netting — 'come back if it gets worse' without the six symptoms, destination and review date ★
Skipping rheumatic fever and medication questions because it 'looks viral'; not naming uvular deviation and trismus in the examiner request
'Just a cold'; criticising the previous prescriber; the certificate as an afterthought; announcing the plan instead of 'how does that sit with you?'
numbers: 8 min; history closes at 3:00; counselling from 3:30 · Centor: exudate · tender anterior nodes · fever >38 · no cough; age 3–14 +1, 15–44 0, ≥45 −1 · this case 0–1
Natural history 3–7 days · antibiotics shorten strep throat by ~1 day · harm ~1 in 10 diarrhoea/rash
Paracetamol 1 g up to qid, max 4 g/24 h · ibuprofen 200–400 mg tds with food · review 3–4 days · persisting >3 weeks → think malignancy
Phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg bd 10 days when indicated (child 15 mg/kg to 500 mg) VERIFY

setting: General practice, Kadina, Yorke Peninsula. Vitals on the card. Examination findings from the examiner (Version A: all normal; Version B: boggy pale mucosa). Online variant adds a mechanism explanation task.
stem: Ms Denise Harmer, 45, part-time office worker at a grain-handling depot: blocked and runny nose, continuously for the past six months. T 36.6, BP 122/78, HR 72, RR 14, SpO2 99% RA, BMI 26; afebrile, systemically well.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (approximately 6 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Online variant: explain the mechanism of the condition in lay terms
time: 8 minutes: 6 history → 20 s PEFE → 90 s explanation. 0:00 frustration line + early ICE · timing, ★ 'one nostril or both?' (say the answer back), CCVO — colour, consistency, volume, odour, blood · better/worse, ★ season AND place, impact · atopic package — nose, eyes, chest, skin + personal/family atopy · triggers ×4 — home, work, ★ drugs incl. nasal sprays by name and duration, smoke · ★ signposted sinusitis screen · ★ signposted malignancy screen — do NOT reassure before it · PEFE by component; 'normal' doesn't change the diagnosis · hay fever + three reasons + two differentials excluded · mechanism in four plain sentences · plan, safety-net, summary.

back.dx: Allergic rhinitis (hay fever) — perennial (cat on the bed, dust mite in an older fully carpeted house, grain dust at the depot, partner smoking indoors) with a spring pollen flare; persistent and moderate–severe by ARIA (sleep, work, taste, embarrassment). Six months, intermittent weeks, ★ bilateral, clear watery copious discharge, no smell, no blood; worse in spring, worse at home in the mornings and in bed; chemist antihistamines help for hours. Atopic package: itchy nose, sneezing fits, red streaming eyes, itchy throat, no chest symptoms (harder version: night cough, puffed at netball → asthma), childhood eczema, sister asthma, mother hay fever. Occasional decongestant spray ('not really a medication') — a week here and there: counsel the 5-day limit, stop it. Two exclusions signposted and clean: chronic rhinosinusitis (no facial pain/pressure, fever, PND, upper toothache, smell loss) and sinonasal/nasopharyngeal malignancy (no epistaxis, weight loss, neck lumps, unilateral ear blockage, diplopia, facial numbness). Hidden agenda: aunt had 'a growth in her nose' — surfaces at the red-flag questions; reassure with the specific negatives, after the screen. PEFE normal → 'a normal examination doesn't change my diagnosis — it reassures me there's no infection, polyp or growth; hay fever is diagnosed on the story'. Three reasons: clear watery bilateral discharge; the travelling symptoms (sneeze, itch, eyes); trigger exposure + family atopy. 'Why all year?' → perennial (mite, cat) plus seasonal (pollen). Mechanism: allergen → mast cell → histamine → inflammation and leaky dilated vessels → blockage and watery discharge (two waves: early histamine = itch/sneeze/run, antihistamines work; late inflammatory cells = blockage, needs the steroid, 1–2 weeks). Plan: cat out of the bedroom, mite covers, hot-wash bedding, lift/vacuum the carpet, recirculate on pollen days; mometasone 2 sprays each nostril daily (technique, 2 weeks); cetirizine 10 mg; eye drops; stop the decongestant; smoke-free home, Quitline; review 4–6 weeks with the spray; escalate to combination spray or testing/immunotherapy if uncontrolled.
plan: WIPE · ★ 'I'm very sorry you've been having such a difficult time — six months is a long while, and being told it's a cold each time must be frustrating. I'll ask some questions to find the cause, then we'll make the best plan. Is that all right?' · ★ 'was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?' (she deflects — note it, move on)

Timing: constant or comes and goes, worse · ★ 'one nostril, or both?' → both → ★ 'that's reassuring — a one-sided blockage would make me look for a different set of causes' · CCVO: clear or green/yellow; watery or thick; a lot or a little; smell; blood
Better/worse · ★ 'a particular time of year?' (spring) · ★ 'a particular place — home, work, outdoors?' (home, mornings, bed) · impact — sleep, work, concentration, taste, embarrassment

Atopic package, four addresses: nose — itch, sneezing · eyes — itchy/red/watery · throat itch · chest — cough at night/exercise, wheeze, SOB · skin — eczema · own allergies · family asthma/eczema/hay fever

Triggers ×4: home — pets (cat on the bed), carpets/bedding/curtains, dust, damp/mould (older carpeted house 8 months) · work — grain dust, harvest · ★ 'any medications, including over the counter — any nasal sprays, which one, how long?' → 'a spray, not really a medication' → pursue: decongestant, a week here and there · smoke — partner indoors

★ Signposted sinusitis screen: 'to make sure this isn't a sinus infection, because that's treated quite differently' — headaches; pain/pressure cheeks, forehead, behind the eyes, bending forward; fevers; PND; upper toothache; smell → all no

★ Signposted malignancy screen: 'questions I ask everybody with a blocked nose this long, to be sure I'm not missing anything serious' — nosebleeds, weight/appetite, neck lumps, unusual tiredness, one ear blocked/muffled, double vision, facial numbness → all no → 'why are you asking — could it be cancer? my aunt had a growth' → thank her, validate, reassure WITH the negatives (bilateral, clear, no blood, no bleeds, weight stable, no lumps, hearing normal) · close: PMHx/surgery/nasal injury, alcohol, anything else

You will be given the examination findings on screen or card
