back.dx: Version A — acute viral hepatitis (A or E) after falling chest-deep into sewage five days ago while sampling for the water utility (full PPE; doesn't know if fluid entered mouth/eyes; incident report filed; no head injury): five days of fever, aches, night sweats, anorexia, RUQ pain, mild nausea, no diarrhoea; card — no jaundice yet, T 38.1, tender hepatomegaly, RUQ tenderness, no splenomegaly, no rash, no calf tenderness, ★ urine dipstick bilirubin positive (bilirubinuria precedes visible jaundice — the point of the card). Explain: 'acute hepatitis — inflammation of the liver — most probably hepatitis A or a close relative, hepatitis E; both picked up by swallowing something contaminated with sewage; not yellow yet but the pigment is already building up in the urine'; settles over weeks, doesn't become chronic; infectious via the bowel — handwashing, household vaccination. Version B card (no jaundice, no hepatomegaly, mild lower abdominal tenderness, dipstick normal; history of loose stools 4–5/day, lower abdominal pain) → gastroenteritis, said cleanly: 'not hepatitis' — no hedging with 'might be early hepatitis'. Differentials aloud: sewage-borne — gastroenteritis viral (rotavirus, norovirus, adenovirus), bacterial (Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli, Campylobacter), protozoal (Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Entamoeba); leptospirosis (rat urine; no calf pain/red eyes but treatable — test); liver abscess (needs ultrasound); PTSD/adjustment reaction (replaying it, two dreams, hasn't been back down); further down EBV, CMV, HIV, syphilis, travel infections, lymphoma/leukaemia, thyroid, diabetes, anaemia, coeliac, autoimmune ('cancer?' → 'not worried about that here — it's on the list I work through'). Plan: LFTs, clotting, hepatitis and leptospirosis serology, liver ultrasound; rest, fluids, no alcohol; notify hepatitis A; vaccinate household (3-year-old son); employer letter — off work while infectious; ReturnToWorkSA; safety-net confusion/drowsiness, bruising/bleeding, can't keep fluids down, turning yellow; review 2 days, talk about the dreams properly then.

setting: General practice. Examination card at six minutes — three versions: (1) hepatitis card, (2) HIV seroconversion card (scripted here), (3) endocarditis card. Six minutes of history.
stem: Gary, 26, attends alone feeling unwell. He has recently returned from an overseas trip in South-East Asia, and used heroin while he was away.
tasks: Take a relevant history (6 minutes)
You will be given a physical examination card
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient

'I've ruined my life over one stupid night' → pause, 'what's going through your mind?' → concern not result; treatment today — normal lifespan, undetectable = untransmissible. back.dx: Pneumonia in a man with untreated HIV (ART stopped six months ago — felt well, tablets nauseated him, long trip to Adelaide; no specialist review for a year; no prior complications), with opportunistic infection (Pneumocystis, TB) and malignancy on the list. Three to four days feverish with rigors, worsening, paracetamol useless; dry cough; new exertional breathlessness on stairs; everything else negative; smokes 10/day; mood flat. Examiner: alert, no rash/jaundice, mildly dehydrated; T 38.0, HR 104, BP 118/74, RR 24, ★ SpO2 92% RA; ★ a white patch in the mouth — scrapes off, on tongue and buccal mucosa (candidiasis — but describe before naming: Kaposi = violaceous, raised, hard palate, doesn't scrape; OHL = white, corrugated, lateral tongue, doesn't scrape); no lymphadenopathy; ★ respiratory examination entirely normal; HS dual; abdomen and dipstick normal. To the examiner: 'although the chest is normal he is febrile, tachypnoeic and hypoxic — in advanced HIV there isn't enough immune function to produce consolidation, crackles or an effusion, so a normal chest does not exclude pneumonia — the same principle as febrile neutropenia'. To Jack: 'the most likely thing is a pneumonia — fever, cough, unwell, Panadol not helping; on examination your oxygen is low and you're breathing fast — your lungs aren't picking up oxygen properly, even though listening sounded normal'; 'but my chest sounded fine?' → 'the low oxygen tells me more than my stethoscope does'. Opportunistic concern named (Pneumocystis, TB) alongside common causes (COVID-19, influenza, pneumococcus, Legionella, Mycoplasma) — don't call it Pneumocystis with no CD4, viral load, white cells or film. ★ 'HIV also raises the risk of certain cancers, and I have to be honest with you': lung cancer (cough, smoker), Kaposi sarcoma (the patch — exclude), lymphoma, leukaemia → he is shaken → contain: 'I'm not telling you that you have cancer; I'm telling you what I have to rule out; the most likely explanation today is still an infection'. Other infections named individually (tonsillitis, pharyngitis, sinusitis; gastroenteritis; hepatitis; syphilis, herpes, gonorrhoea; meningitis; cellulitis); then low mood/adjustment, anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, coeliac, OSA. Plan: send in today — CXR, bloods incl. CD4/viral load, start treatment; reconnect with the HIV team; ★ restarting ART is one of the most important things we do — and look at what made it hard last time. 'Is this because I stopped my tablets?' — hidden agenda at ~7 min.
plan: ★ 'Before I begin, could I have his observations — BP, pulse, RR, temperature AND oxygen saturation?' → 118/74, 104, 24, 38.0, 92% · 'Hello Jack, I'm sorry to hear you've not been well — let's work out what's going on together' · ★ 'I can hear that cough — we'll come to it'
Unwell: sleepy/low energy/feverish? duration (3–4 days), constant, worse, better/worse · fever block: measured? chills? (yes) taken anything, helped? (Panadol, nothing)

HIV: 'when were you diagnosed? (5 y) I know you've stopped your medication — can you tell me what led to that? (felt fine, nausea, long trip to Adelaide) — no judgement here · regular follow-up? (not for a year) · any complications before? (never)'

★ 'I'm going to run through the whole body fairly quickly, area by area — most of these will be a simple no, and that's what I'm hoping for': sore throat/coryza/facial/ear pain · ★ cough — dry or chesty? SOB? noisy breathing? (dry; puffed on the stairs — three questions, keep going) · nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain/diarrhoea · dysuria/frequency · headache/stiff neck/photophobia · ★ sexual health (active in 3 months? condoms? discharge/rash/ulcers/scrotal pain) — despite HIV · jaundice/dark urine/pale stools · rash, hot painful skin · travel · ★ recreational drugs, ever injected? chest pain/palpitations (endocarditis) · animals

★ Malignancy heading: 'a few more — weight loss without trying? appetite? lumps or bumps? night sweats? ulcers or patches in your mouth? new purple or red marks on your skin? ever coughed up blood? do you smoke? (10/day) what work — asbestos? new or changing moles?' · if time: 'how has your mood been?' (flat)

★ Examination in one run: general — alert/drowsy, rash, jaundice, dehydration · all five vitals · throat — swelling/redness, ★ any lesion in the mouth · full lymph node survey, thyroid · respiratory — expansion, percussion both sides, added sounds, ★ vocal resonance ('I'm looking for consolidation') · CVS — S1 S2, murmurs · abdomen — tenderness, splenomegaly · dipstick → 'there is a white patch in his mouth'; respiratory entirely normal

★ The patch, two questions: 'is it painful to touch with a tongue depressor? can it be scraped off? colour? where?' → white, scrapes off, tongue and buccal mucosa → describe first, name second · ★ the normal-chest sentence to the examiner

To Jack: pneumonia named + reasons (fever, cough, unwell, Panadol failed; low oxygen, fast breathing) · 'but my chest sounded fine?' answered · opportunistic concern — Pneumocystis, TB — alongside common viruses/bacteria · ★ 'HIV also raises the risk of certain cancers, and I have to be honest with you about that' — lung, Kaposi (the patch), lymphoma/leukaemia → shaken → ★ 'I'm not telling you that you have cancer; I'm telling you what I have to rule out' · other infections named individually · then low mood, anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, coeliac, OSA

'Is this because I stopped my tablets?' → honest, not blaming · plan: send in today — CXR, bloods incl. a check of the immune system, treatment started · ★ 'restarting your HIV treatment is one of the most important things we can do — and we can look at what made it hard last time' · safety-net: more short of breath, confused/drowsy, severe headache/stiff neck, haemoptysis → ambulance · confidentiality/Adelaide follow-up if he prefers · questions
ask: ★ 'All five observations, including oxygen saturation.' / ★ 'I can hear that cough — tell me about it.' / 'I'm sorry you're feeling like this, Jack. Let me ask you a few questions, and we'll work out what's going on together.'
'When were you diagnosed? Can you tell me what led to stopping?' / 'Are you still having regular follow-up with your specialist?' / 'Thank you for telling me that, and there's no judgement here.'

★ 'I'm going to run through the whole body quickly — most of these will be a simple no.' / 'Is the cough dry or chesty? Short of breath? Coughed up blood?' / 'Can I ask about sexual health? Sexually active now or in the last three months? Condoms? Any discharge, rash or ulcers?' / 'Any recreational drugs — have you ever injected? Any chest pain or racing of the heart?'
★ 'Any weight loss, appetite change, lumps, night sweats, mouth ulcers or patches, new purple or red marks on your skin, coughed-up blood? Do you smoke? Any asbestos at work?'

'Is vocal resonance increased anywhere — I'm looking for consolidation.' / ★ 'Is the patch painful to touch with a tongue depressor, and can it be scraped off? What colour is it, and where in the mouth?'

★ 'Examiner, although the respiratory examination is normal, he is febrile, tachypnoeic and hypoxic. In advanced HIV there isn't enough immune function to produce consolidation, crackles or an effusion, so a normal chest does not exclude pneumonia here — the same principle as febrile neutropenia in a child on chemotherapy.'

★ 'Jack, the most likely thing is a pneumonia — an infection in your lung. Fever, cough, feeling unwell, Panadol not helping — and on examination the oxygen level in your blood is low and you're breathing faster than normal.' / 'But you said my chest sounded fine?' → 'When the immune system is weakened the body can't mount the response I'd normally hear. The low oxygen is telling me more than my stethoscope is.'

'Because you have HIV there's a higher chance of unusual infections — we call them opportunistic — things like Pneumocystis and tuberculosis. But it could still be a common virus such as COVID-19 or influenza, or a common bacterial pneumonia — pneumococcus, Legionella or Mycoplasma.' / Examiner: 'why not just say Pneumocystis?' → 'Because I have no CD4 count, viral load, white cell count or chest film. I'm calling it a pneumonia, and Pneumocystis is at the top of the list of causes.'

★ 'I also have to be honest that HIV raises the risk of certain cancers. Because you have a cough I'm thinking about lung cancer. Because of the white patch in your mouth I want to exclude a cancer that occurs specifically in HIV called Kaposi sarcoma. Lymphoma and leukaemia are also more common.' → (shaken) ★ 'I'm not telling you that you have cancer. I'm telling you what I have to rule out, because ruling it out properly is how we make sure nothing is missed. The most likely explanation today is still an infection.'

★ 'Restarting your HIV treatment is one of the most important things we can do — and we can look at what made it difficult last time.' / 'Am I dying?' → 'I can't answer that today and I'm not going to guess. What I think is happening — an infection in your lung — is treatable, and getting you back on treatment changes your outlook a great deal.' / 'If you become more short of breath, confused or drowsy, develop a severe headache or stiff neck, or cough up blood — that's an ambulance, not a waiting room.'
pefe: Role-player: Jack, 30, grain terminal Wallaroo, lives alone in Kadina; 10 cigarettes/day; social drinker; never injected; no meds/allergies. HIV 5 years, did well on ART; stopped 6 months ago (felt well, nausea, long trip to Adelaide); no specialist for a year; never a complication. Coughs harshly mid-sentence throughout. Crisp negatives. If 'cancer' is said: visibly shaken, quiet for a beat — see if you notice and contain. If judged about stopping: defensive, shorter answers for the rest. Hidden agenda: half-suspects it's his fault — 'is this because I stopped my tablets?' at ~7 min if you're warm

Examiner: alert, no rash, no jaundice, mildly dehydrated · T 38.0, HR 104, BP 118/74, RR 24, SpO2 92% RA · 'there is a white patch in his mouth' → white, scrapes off, tongue and buccal mucosa · no lymphadenopathy, thyroid normal · respiratory examination entirely normal · HS dual, no murmur · abdomen normal · dipstick normal

Three answers for the patch: candidiasis (white, creamy, scrapes off) · Kaposi sarcoma (violaceous, raised, hard palate, doesn't scrape, painless — AIDS-defining, biopsy; can involve the lung) · oral hairy leukoplakia (white, corrugated, lateral tongue, doesn't scrape). Variant — 'raised violaceous plaque on the hard palate, doesn't scrape': ★ Kaposi, not thrush. CD4 landmarks: <200 Pneumocystis, toxoplasmosis; <50 MAC, CMV retinitis; Kaposi at any count ADDED

Investigations in hospital: CXR, ABG/VBG, FBE, UEC, LFT, CRP, LDH, CD4 count, HIV viral load, blood cultures, sputum MCS + AFB ×3 (induced sputum/BAL for PJP), COVID/influenza PCR, urinary Legionella/pneumococcal antigen, syphilis serology; PJP empirical treatment if suspected VERIFY TG · TB is notifiable — 'done discreetly; Kadina is a small town — follow-up in Adelaide if you prefer'

Variant — three weeks of diarrhoea, same stem: structure unchanged — infection screen then malignancy screen; infective: Cryptosporidium, Isospora, microsporidia, CMV colitis, MAC + Campylobacter, Salmonella, Giardia, C. difficile; malignancy: lymphoma, Kaposi of the gut
SA: admit via regional hospital → RAH ID/HIV service; PATS; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if hypoxic and deteriorating; TIS 131 450
fails: Telling him his chest was fine and therefore this was probably not serious ★
Never mentioning cancer at all — never opening the malignancy heading ★
'That's thrush' without checking anything — sticking with thrush after being handed 'violaceous' ★
Lecturing him about stopping his medication ★
Forgetting the fifth vital sign; ignoring the cough as stage direction
Turning the cough into a four-minute respiratory history; skipping the sexual history because he already has HIV; omitting the injecting/chest pain questions
'ENT infections' / 'GI infections' as differentials to the patient — categories are not diagnoses; false reassurance or blunt confirmation to 'am I dying?'

setting: General practice, Moonta. EXAMINATION-FIRST station — no history taking. Findings from the examiner for four minutes; the results card is handed over at exactly four minutes; then you explain results, diagnosis and differentials to Jane.
stem: Jane Whitmore, 40, has come in feeling unwell — tired and nauseated, no fever. She has recently returned from a trip to the Philippines. No sexual activity overseas, no mosquito bites, no needle exposures. Appendicectomy ten years ago.
tasks: Begin with a physical examination, asking the examiner for the findings — there is no history taking
At four minutes you are given the investigation results; explain them to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes: ★ 0:00 GREET JANE FIRST — name, role, what will happen, when I'll be back, is that all right (15 s) · 0:20 examination as one run across the differentials, not at the liver: general (jaundice) · four vitals · throat, ears · thyroid, full node survey · chest · heart · abdomen → 'hepatomegaly' → ★ don't accept it: span, tender?, border, shifting dullness, scratch marks, bruising, bowel sounds · DRE · ★ 'with the patient's consent and in the presence of a chaperone' pelvic · ★ two office tests: dipstick (bilirubin) and ★ pregnancy test · 4:00 turn back to Jane, acknowledge the wait · results in three sentences (test → plain English → meaning), under a minute, no numbers, no abbreviations · 5:30 'most likely' hepatitis A + reasons incl. bilirubin in the urine · 6:30 differentials — ★ TRAVEL FIRST, then liver/abdominal incl. cancer, then pregnancy, then the generic tiredness list · plan, notification, hygiene, alcohol, safety-net.

back.dx: Acute hepatitis A (most likely — confirmatory anti-HAV IgM pending): three weeks in the Philippines with relatives, home cooking and street food, back a fortnight; a week tired, nauseated, off food, afebrile; husband noticed yellow eyes two days ago. Examination: alert, ★ jaundiced, no rash/pallor, mildly dehydrated; BP 120/80, HR 88, RR 12, T 36.9; throat/ears/thyroid/nodes normal; chest clear; HS dual; abdomen not distended, ★ hepatomegaly 3 cm, non-tender, smooth regular border, no splenomegaly, no ascites, no scratch marks/bruising, bowel sounds normal; DRE and pelvic normal; ★ dipstick bilirubin positive, urobilinogen raised; ★ pregnancy test negative. Results card: WCC 13.2, bilirubin 68, ALT 780, AST 640, ALP 130, GGT 110, INR 1.1, albumin 38, HBV and HCV negative — hepatocellular pattern (to the examiner). Explain in three beats each: FBC — white cells, immune cells, raised = fighting infection/inflammation · liver test — enzymes raised = inflammation in the liver · hepatitis B and C negative. 'Damaged?' → 'inflamed rather than damaged; the two numbers that measure how well it's doing its job are normal today'. Diagnosis 'most likely', never certain: enlarged liver, jaundice, bilirubin in the urine ('made by the liver, normally never reaches the urine — finding it there tells me the problem is in your liver'), raised enzymes, B and C negative, recent travel, nausea; spreads via contaminated food/water. Settles over 2–8 weeks, no specific treatment, never chronic, lifelong immunity. Differentials in the order the case demands: (1) travel — malaria, dengue, typhoid, leptospirosis, hepatitis E, EBV, HIV, TB; (2) liver/abdominal — hepatitis B/C (negative), autoimmune hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, gallstones/cholangitis, ★ cancer of the liver or pancreas ('particularly because your liver was not tender'); (3) pregnancy (tested, negative); (4) anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, coeliac, haemochromatosis, lymphoma/leukaemia, autoimmune, depression, heart failure, OSA. Plan: anti-HAV IgM, liver ultrasound, review this week; no alcohol, check before any medication (paracetamol at reduced dose VERIFY); handwashing, don't prepare food for others, don't share towels; notify — household vaccinated (within 14 days VERIFY); safety-net confusion/drowsiness, bruising/bleeding, worsening jaundice, can't keep fluids down. Hidden agenda: sister died of pancreatic cancer — tearful at the word cancer; name it, proportion it, say what resolves it.
plan: ★ 'No questions, thank you. — Hello Jane, I'm Dr [name], one of the doctors here, and I'll be looking after you today. I'm going to speak with my colleague for a few minutes and go through an examination, then I'll come straight back to you and explain everything I've found. Is that all right?'

One continuous run: general — alert/drowsy, ★ jaundice, rash, pallor, dehydration · all four vitals · throat (swelling, redness, exudate), ears (red bulging TM) · thyroid, ★ full lymph node examination every chain · respiratory — air entry, added sounds · CVS — S1 S2, murmurs · abdomen — inspection (distension, redness, bruising), palpation (tenderness, hepatosplenomegaly)

'Hepatomegaly' → ★ 'what is the span? is it tender? border regular or irregular? shifting dullness? scratch marks? bruising? bowel sounds?' → 3 cm, non-tender, smooth, no ascites, no scratch marks/bruises, BS normal

'I would like a digital rectal examination. ★ And with the patient's consent and in the presence of a chaperone, a pelvic examination — inspection for discharge or rash, speculum for cervical discharge, bimanual for cervical motion tenderness, uterine size and tenderness, and the adnexae' → all normal (there IS time here — judge by the clock you're given)
★ 'Two office tests: a urine dipstick — I'm looking particularly for bilirubin — and a urine pregnancy test' → bilirubin positive, urobilinogen raised; pregnancy negative → results card handed over

★ Turn back: 'thank you for waiting, Jane — I've examined you and I have your results; let me talk you through them, then tell you what I think' · three sentences, test → plain English → meaning: white cells raised · liver enzymes raised · hepatitis B and C negative · 'is my liver damaged?' → inflamed, not damaged; the job-numbers (INR, albumin) are normal

'Most likely hepatitis — your liver is inflamed — most likely caused by a virus called hepatitis A' + reasons (enlarged liver, jaundice, bilirubin in the urine, raised enzymes, B and C negative, recent travel, nausea) · 'from the food?' → most likely · 'will I get better?' → 2–8 weeks, no specific medicine, never long-term, immune for life · 'can I pass it on?' → hands, food, towels; notification → household vaccine

★ Differentials, travel FIRST: malaria, dengue, typhoid, leptospirosis, hepatitis E, EBV, HIV, TB · liver/abdomen: B/C negative, autoimmune hepatitis, drug-induced (antibiotics), gallstones/cholangitis, ★ cancer of the liver or pancreas — 'particularly because your liver was not tender' → tearful, sister → name it, proportion it (travel, pattern, bilirubinuria point to a virus), what resolves it · pregnancy — tested · the generic list

Plan: confirmatory blood test, liver ultrasound, review this week · no alcohol, check before any medication ('Panadol for headaches?' → reduced dose, ask me) · handwashing, no food preparation for others, no shared towels · notification, household vaccination · work certificate · safety-net: confused/unusually sleepy, bruising/bleeding, yellowing much worse, can't keep fluids down → hospital · questions
ask: ★ 'Hello Jane, I am Doctor [name] — give me a few minutes with my colleague and I will come straight back to you.'
'Examiner, on general appearance: is she alert or drowsy? Any jaundice? Any rash? Any pallor? Any dehydration?' — findings, not regions
★ 'What is the span? Is the liver tender? Is the border regular or irregular?' / ★ 'Is there shifting dullness? Any scratch marks? Any bruising?'
★ 'With the patient's consent and in the presence of a chaperone…' / ★ 'Two office tests: a urine dipstick, looking particularly for bilirubin, and a urine pregnancy test.'

'The first test is a full blood count. The white blood cells are the cells of your immune system, and they're higher than normal — your body is fighting an infection or inflammation.' / 'Your liver enzymes are raised — that means there is inflammation in your liver.' / 'We tested for two viruses that commonly cause liver inflammation, and both are negative.'
'Is my liver damaged?' → ★ 'Inflamed rather than damaged. The liver is a remarkably good healer. There are two numbers that tell me how well it's doing its job, and both are normal today.'
★ 'Bilirubin is made by the liver and normally does not reach the urine at all — finding it there tells me the problem is in your liver.' / To the examiner: 'This is a hepatocellular pattern.'

'I think you most likely have hepatitis — your liver is inflamed — most likely caused by a virus called hepatitis A.' / 'It settles over two to eight weeks, there's no specific medicine, it does not become long-term, and afterwards you are immune for life.'

★ 'Because you have been overseas, the first group I thought about was travel-related infections: malaria, dengue fever, typhoid, leptospirosis, and hepatitis E.' / 'Is it cancer?' → 'That's a fair thing to ask, and I'd rather answer it honestly. Cancer of the liver or pancreas is on my list, and one reason it stays there is that your liver wasn't tender. But the whole picture — you've just come back from overseas, the pattern of your blood tests, the bilirubin in your urine — points much more strongly to a viral infection. The blood test I'm arranging should settle it, and the ultrasound looks directly at the liver.'

'We notify this routinely, which means your household can be offered a vaccine.' / 'Avoid alcohol completely, and check with me before any medication.' / 'Come back straight away, or go to hospital, if you become confused or unusually sleepy, if you start bruising or bleeding easily, if the yellowing gets much worse, or if you cannot keep fluids down.'

Three weeks in the Philippines with relatives, home cooking and street food, no malaria tablets, back a fortnight; a week tired, nauseated, off food, afebrile; yellow eyes noticed two days ago. Composed, tired, quietly frightened; warm if greeted at the door and returned to as promised; if ignored for four minutes: cool, short answers, 'I did not know what was happening, nobody said anything to me'. Asks at least two questions; 'I'm sorry, I don't know what that means' at jargon (hepatocellular, transaminases). setting: General practice. Vitals in the stem. Examination findings on screen/card when asked. Five minutes of history. No management task — but a plan and a safety-net still earn marks.
stem: Ben Alderton, 25, has come in feeling unwell. He attends a sauna regularly with friends, and his friends have similar symptoms. He is currently taking PrEP. T 38.4, HR 96, BP 122/76, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA.
tasks: Take a focused history (5 minutes)
You will be given the examination findings on screen or card
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses
time: 8 minutes. Acknowledge the worry · 'unwell' in four questions · ★ open the sauna: how often, ★ 'what do your friends have?', what do you do there (sex) · ★ three water infections: Legionella (cough, SOB, fever, diarrhoea, confusion) · hepatitis A (abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, jaundice, dark urine/pale stools) · Pseudomonas (itchy spots under swimwear) · ★ PrEP block, three separate marks: adherence · 3-monthly screening · hepatitis A/B vaccination · ★ normalise once, then the full sexual history (partners, number, gender, condoms, practices, previous STI, alcohol/drugs) — don't stop to counsel · STI symptoms incl. ulcers, discharge, scrotum, back passage · the rest · examination by name incl. throat, nodes, palms/soles, genitals, dipstick · acute viral hepatitis WITHOUT guessing the subtype · differentials by exposure: sauna ×3 + crypto, STIs with ★ HIV high on the list despite PrEP · ★ three-site swabs · confidentiality accurately · vaccinate · 3-monthly reviews · safety-net.

back.dx: Acute viral hepatitis (subtype deliberately not guessed — A via faecal-oral including sexual transmission between men, or B/C via sex) in an MSM on PrEP: a week of fever, anorexia, upper abdominal pain, vomiting, partner says he looks yellow, urine darker; no cough/SOB/diarrhoea/confusion (Legionella less likely), no rash (Pseudomonas less likely). Sauna 2–3×/week, same group, a couple of friends off work with unknown symptoms; 'we have sex there as well' (say it back: both a water exposure and a sexual exposure). PrEP: misses the odd dose when he stays out; last review two months ago but ★ never screened for STIs; doesn't know if he's had hepatitis A/B vaccines. Sexual history: no stable partner, several partners, all men, no condoms, oral and anal, never diagnosed, sometimes after drinks. No STI symptoms. Card: jaundiced, T 38.4, tender hepatomegaly span >13 cm, no splenomegaly, chest clear, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, no genital/perianal lesions or discharge, dipstick bilirubin positive. Differentials grouped by exposure: sauna — Legionella (warm-water spray; no cough/SOB), Pseudomonas folliculitis (no rash), cryptosporidium (chlorine-resistant; no diarrhoea); STIs — ★ HIV high on the list ('PrEP is very effective but not absolute, and it depends on taking it consistently — you miss doses; one blood test'), syphilis, herpes, gonorrhoea and chlamydia (throat and rectum often asymptomatic — urine alone misses them); then EBV/CMV, travel, lymphoma/leukaemia, depression, thyroid/diabetes/anaemia/coeliac. setting: General practice, Wallaroo. Four tasks in eight minutes — examination begins at 4:00, management at 7:00. Observations from the examiner at the door (online: 'I'm taking you through to the treatment room to check your observations').
stem: Mary Ellis, 25, is 20 weeks pregnant. She has come in because she has been feeling unwell for the past few days. First pregnancy; antenatal care so far uncomplicated.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings (2 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Explain your management plan to the patient
time: 8 minutes: observations first, one sentence · empathic sentence · ★ offer the word FEVERISH — she won't volunteer it · fever block: measured, chills, medication · urinary upper and lower: dysuria, frequency, haematuria, nausea/vomiting, ★ flank pain — site and radiation only · sexual health with a permission sentence · other infection: throat, cough, headache/neck, travel · ★ pregnancy-specific: vision, swelling, headache (pre-eclampsia) · thirst and polyuria separately (GDM) · jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, itch (cholestasis/AFLP) · palpitations/SOB (anaemia) · obstetric close — tightenings, fluid/bleeding, movements · ★ allergies BEFORE naming an antibiotic · 4:00 examination as one run: findings not regions, four vitals again, ★ fundal height, uterine tenderness, fetal heart · ★ 'is there any renal angle tenderness?' · dipstick — leucocytes and nitrites · 6:00 pyelonephritis with reasons; the baby question in one sentence; differentials LISTED not explained · 7:00 ★ ED today, admission, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, culture first.

back.dx: Acute pyelonephritis at 20 weeks: 3–4 days hot and shivery with rigors last night, worsening, paracetamol useless; dysuria and frequency, no visible haematuria; vomited 3–4 times; right flank/back pain radiating to the groin (Version B: low central suprapubic pain — the diagnosis is unchanged when renal angle tenderness is positive). Pregnancy-specific screen negative: no visual blurring, swelling, headache (pre-eclampsia); no thirst/polyuria (GDM); no jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, itch (cholestasis/AFLP); no palpitations/SOB (anaemia); no tightenings, fluid, bleeding; baby moving; pregnancy vitamins only; no allergies. Examiner: alert, flushed, mildly dehydrated; BP 110/70, HR 108, RR 18, ★ T 38.7; throat/chest/heart normal; mild suprapubic tenderness, no RUQ tenderness, no organomegaly; ★ fundal height 20 cm consistent with dates, uterus non-tender, FHR 145; ★ right renal angle tenderness POSITIVE; dipstick leucocytes +++, nitrites +, blood ++, protein trace. To Mary: 'pyelonephritis — an infection in your kidney: burning, going more often, fever, vomiting, tender over your kidney, urine test showing infection'; 'dangerous for the baby?' → 'it can be, which is exactly why we treat it properly and quickly — today is the best thing for both of you'. Differentials LISTED in 25 s: pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, other infections (STIs incl. herpes and HIV, throat, chest, meningitis), the liver conditions of pregnancy (cholestasis, acute fatty liver), appendicitis, renal stone, anaemia. Management, the four things first: ★ ED today, expect admission, IV antibiotics + IV fluids ('too serious to treat with tablets at home'), MSU for culture before antibiotics; then oral switch once afebrile 24–48 h, 10–14 days total, test-of-cure culture 1–2 weeks after, obstetric team checks the baby; 'do I have to go?' → sepsis and preterm labour risks; 'safe for the baby?' → yes, well-studied antibiotics. Safety-net: worse, shaking chills, can't keep fluids down, tightenings, bleeding, fluid, reduced movements → straight back.
plan: ★ 'Before I begin, could I have her observations — BP, pulse, RR and temperature?' → 110/70, 108, 18, 38.7 · 'Hello Mary, I'm sorry to hear you've not been well — questions, examination, then a plan together. Tell me what's been happening' → 'I'm worried about the baby' → acknowledge

Urinary: burning/pain passing urine (yes) · frequency (constantly) · blood (no) · nausea/vomiting (3–4×) · abdominal pain · ★ 'any pain in your side or back, around your kidneys — where exactly, and does it travel?' → right flank to groin (site + radiation, then MOVE)

'Can I ask a few confidential questions about sexual health? active? condoms? genital rash/ulcers? discharge? lumps or night sweats?' → husband, no condoms, nothing · other infection: sore throat/coryza/cough, headache/stiff neck, travel

setting: General practice, regional South Australia. Counselling station — the assessment is already done and summarised in the stem; no history task. 'Can I get temazepam?' arrives when you ask for her concerns at the start, or at minute seven if you never ask. Cross-reference MED-57 (sleep history version).
stem: Jane Miller, 17, Year 12 student, presenting with tiredness over two to three months. Your completed assessment: recent examinations with considerable stress; bed after 1 am, up at 6:30; easy-going personality; mood normal, no anxiety disorder; three to four cups of coffee every night while studying. No weight loss, fever, night sweats, lumps or travel; no snoring or witnessed apnoeas; no medications, alcohol or drugs; periods regular and not heavy. Examination and vital signs normal.
tasks: Explain your assessment to the patient — diagnosis and cause of the tiredness (about 3 minutes)
Counsel her regarding your management plan
Answer the patient's questions
time: 8 minutes. 30 s: open question, empathy, ★ 'anything you were hoping we'd sort out today?' (the temazepam line — park it explicitly), ★ 'is it all right if I explain what I think, then we make a plan together?' · Task 1, four blocks, three minutes: NAME it (sleep restriction) · DEFINE it (8–10 h needed; she gets ~5) · REASON it (exam trigger, pattern persisting, caffeine) · SAY WHAT YOU EXCLUDED · teach-back · Task 2, eight headings one sentence each: hygiene · diary · ★ CBT-I first line · caffeine · relaxation · lifestyle · named organisation · review 4 weeks + conditional bloods/sleep study · Task 3, ★ VALIDATE → DECLINE with ≥2 reasons → SUBSTITUTE (not second best) → CONTRACT (four weeks, a date) · safety-net incl. mood/self-harm · driving.

back.dx: Chronic insufficient sleep — behaviourally induced sleep restriction — in a 17-year-old: ~5 hours on school nights (bed 1–2 am, up 6:30), studies and scrolls in bed, 3–4 instant coffees each evening (last ~11 pm, ~380 mg, half still circulating at bedtime), set off by exam stress and persisting after it; catches up to midday at weekends and feels much better (the pattern that says 'not enough sleep', not blood or thyroid); mood normal, no self-harm, no snoring/apnoeas/sleep attacks. 'Nothing wrong with me?' → 'there is something wrong — it just isn't a disease'. Management aim: improve quantity and quality of sleep — (1) sleep hygiene: fixed bed and wake time seven days, bed for sleep only (no phone/laptop/study/TV), dark quiet cool, out of bed if not asleep in 20–30 min, warm shower/milk; (2) sleep diary two weeks (bedtime, sleep onset, hours, quality/10); (3) ★ CBT-I — first line in Australia, more effective than hypnotics and durable — psychologist referral or Australian online programmes; cognitive half (the 'if I don't sleep I'll fail' worry) + behavioural half (stimulus control, relaxation, time-in-bed matching); (4) caffeine: half-life ~5 h, nothing after early afternoon, cut the total, expect a headache; (5) relaxation — mindfulness, breathing, PMR, yoga; (6) lifestyle — daytime exercise, regular meals, no alcohol/smoking/vaping, screens off; (7) named: Sleep Health Foundation fact sheets, headspace (12–25); (8) review 4 weeks with the diary → if no better TSH, FBE, ferritin → sleep study if another disorder is suggested. Temazepam: validate (exhausted, worked for a friend) → decline with reasons (dependence/tolerance/withdrawal, next-day drowsiness for driving and study, not recommended under 18, doesn't fix the cause) → substitute (CBT-I works better and lasts) → contract (four weeks, then we look together). 'Just a few for exams?' → exam time is when grogginess costs most; two weeks is enough to start dependence. 'So you're not going to help me?' → 'I'm not doing the thing that helps for two weeks and causes a problem for two years — everything else starts today.' Safety-net: mood drops, hopelessness, self-harm thoughts, sudden daytime sleep attacks, snoring/apnoeas → sooner. Driving: don't drive sleepy, pull over (P-plater).
plan: 'Hello Jane, how have you been feeling since we last spoke?' · 'I'm sorry — that sounds miserable, especially in Year 12' · ★ 'before I start explaining — anything you were hoping we'd sort out today, or anything you've been worried about?' → temazepam → 'a really good question and I'll answer it properly — can I first tell you what I think is going on?' · ★ 'is it all right if I explain, and then we make a plan together?'

1A NAME: 'the most likely cause is a sleep problem — there are breathing types like sleep apnoea, body-clock types, nightmare disorders; yours is sleep restriction, or sleep deprivation — your sleep itself is fine, there just isn't enough of it'
1B DEFINE: 'enough good-quality sleep is a basic requirement — concentration, memory, mood, appetite, immune system; at your age eight to ten hours; bed after one, up at half six, is about five'

1C REASON: 'it started when your exams started — stressed, up late; sleep problems are often triggered by a stressful stretch and keep going after it, because the pattern is set; and three or four coffees in the evening is still working at bedtime' · 'I'm fine on weekends' → 'that's exactly what we see when the problem is not enough sleep rather than something in the blood or thyroid'

1D EXCLUDED: 'no weight loss, fevers, sweats, lumps, travel; normal periods; no snoring or breathing pauses; mood fine; normal examination — that's what lets me be confident' · 'nothing wrong with me?' → 'there is something wrong — it just isn't a disease' · 'anaemic? mum said bloods' → not needed now; bloods at review if no better · teach-back: 'if a friend asked tonight what the doctor said?'

★ 'I've looked for the other causes and not found them — that's what lets me be confident.' / 'So there's nothing wrong with me?' → 'There is something wrong — it just isn't a disease. Not getting enough sleep is a real problem with real effects and a real treatment. I'm not dismissing it.'

★ 'CBT for insomnia is first line — more effective than sleeping tablets, and it keeps working after you stop.' / 'What will the psychologist actually do?' → 'Two halves. ★ 'I can see why you're asking — you're exhausted and you've heard it worked for someone else. But I don't think a sleeping tablet is the right answer for you. It helps for a short time, but it comes with real problems. The main one is dependence — your body gets used to it, it stops working at the same dose, we end up increasing it, and if you try to stop you get withdrawal: worse sleep than before, anxiety, shakiness. The psychological treatment works better than the tablets do, and it keeps working after you finish.' / ★ 'Give me four weeks with the diary and the plan. back.dx: Cardiac (exertional) syncope from aortic stenosis. 'Out cold', <1 min, witnessed by his wife, no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence, not confused after (shaken only), grazed elbow, no head strike. ★ Walking up the driveway with the shopping (exertion), ★ no warning at all, prior light-headedness twice on the golf course walking uphill, months of chest tightness and breathlessness on hills 'put down to age' — the AS triad. No meds, none stopped; no FHx sudden death. PEFE: no postural drop, pulse regular slow-rising (ask: low volume? heave? thrill?), ESM RUSE radiating to the carotids, soft S2, neuro normal, glucose 5.6, ECG SR with LVH. To Bill: 'not a trip — a blackout from the heart rather than a simple faint: no warning (faints almost always give a few seconds of dizziness or sweating), and it happened on exertion; a murmur — a narrowed, stiff valve, the door blood leaves the heart through; on exertion the body asks for more blood, the valve can't let enough through, the brain briefly goes short'. Differentials: arrhythmia (still needs excluding), cardiomyopathy, PE, stroke/seizure. Plan: admit to a monitored bed, bloods, echo, cardiology; if severe → valve replacement, works very well. ★ 'Please don't drive until the specialists have assessed you' (Austroads; SA Registrar of Motor Vehicles; notification duty) · no heights, machinery, swimming alone · 000 if recurrent, chest pain, palpitations, severe SOB. Hidden agenda: brother-in-law's stroke; 'can I drive home and come back tomorrow?' — always asked.

ask: 'Before I start, could I please have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and temperature?' / 'I'm sorry to hear that, and that's a very reasonable thing to be worried about. Let's work out what's going on together.'

★ 'Did you lose consciousness completely, or were you aware of your surroundings?' / 'Did anyone see it happen?' / ★ 'Did you have any jerky movements of your arms or legs? Did you bite your tongue? Did you wet or soil yourself?'

'How long were you unconscious? Is this the first time? Can you describe each episode for me?' / ★ 'What were you doing when it happened?' / ★ 'Did you have any warning at all — did you know you were about to go down?'

'Had you missed any meals, and were you drinking normally that day?' / ★ 'When you came round, were you confused, or just tired?' / 'Did you injure your head, or any other part of you, when you fell?'

'For the next few questions, tell me whether you had it before this happened, after it, or not at all — I won't ask you everything twice.' / ★ 'Do you take any medications regularly, or have you recently stopped any?' / ★ 'Has anyone in your family died suddenly and unexpectedly, especially at a young age?'

★ 'Examiner, I have the blood pressure and pulse rate — may I have the postural blood pressure and the pulse rhythm?' / 'That murmur is very significant. Is the pulse volume low as well as slow-rising, and is there a heave or thrill?'

'What you had wasn't a trip — you blacked out, and I think the blackout came from your heart rather than being a simple faint. Two things point me there: you had no warning at all — simple faints almost always give a few seconds of dizziness or sweating first — and it happened while you were exerting yourself.'

'There's a murmur — an extra sound — which suggests one of the valves has become narrowed and stiff. That valve is the door blood leaves your heart through. When you exert yourself your body asks for more blood, the narrowed valve can't let enough through, your brain briefly goes short, and you black out. It also explains the chest tightness and breathlessness on hills.'

'Is it serious?' → 'I want to be straight with you: blacking out with this kind of valve problem is serious, and it's treatable. I'd like to admit you today to a bed with heart monitoring, do bloods, and arrange an echo to see exactly how narrow that valve is. If it's significantly narrowed the treatment is to repair or replace it, which works very well.'

★ 'Please don't drive until the specialists have assessed you — and don't work at heights, use machinery, or swim alone.' / Examiner on driving: 'Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive — the non-driving period depends on cause, treatment and licence type; commercial stricter; I'd check the current standard rather than quote from memory; in SA the Registrar of Motor Vehicles, and doctors carry a duty to notify where a patient is unfit and continues to drive.'

back.dx: Vasovagal (reflex) syncope — third episode, each with a textbook trigger and a prodrome: (1) jumped out of bed to answer the phone, (2) the sight of blood, (3) today after 1–2 hours standing still in a hot, packed, exciting parade — blurry vision and light-headedness first, 30 s LOC, went floppy (no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence), tired but oriented after, 'white as a sheet', hip bruise. Chronic headaches on Nurofen (distractor): no morning vomiting, weight loss, nocturnal/positional worsening; fundoscopy normal → refer to GP, medication-overuse flagged. No palpitations, chest pain, SOB; periods regular; no alcohol/drugs; no FHx sudden death. PEFE: BP 120/80 sitting → 94/62 standing (drop 26/18 — name it), pulse 82 reg, neuro/fundi/CVS/RS/abdo normal. Explain: nerves overactive → vessels in the legs widen → blood pools → brain short for seconds → lying flat fixes it. Three reasons: setting (hot, prolonged standing, crowd, excitement); earlier episodes fit classic triggers; clear prodrome. Postural drop = supporting evidence, not the diagnosis (postural hypotension causes dizziness/near-fainting more than true LOC; reflex syncope produces a transient drop). Differentials by system: cardiac (arrhythmia — no palpitations; HOCM — no chest pain/SOB/FHx, had a warning; valve/ischaemia), brain (seizure — friends' account; SOL, bleed, meningitis), chemistry (glucose, sodium), blood (anaemia — periods), drugs/alcohol/medications, panic. Management: lie down legs up or head between knees at the warning; counter-pressure; fluids in heat; don't skip meals; keep calves moving; FBC + pregnancy test today; caution heights/swimming alone; GP 1–2 weeks (headaches, ibuprofen frequency); driving — a triggered, prodromal, standing faint generally doesn't restrict; tell the GP if the pattern changes; return if no warning, supine, exertional, or chest pain/palpitations first. Hidden agenda: brain tumour fear from googling the headaches; the licence.

★ 'The most likely cause is vasovagal syncope — a simple faint. When you stand still for a long time in a hot, crowded place, some nerves become overactive and widen the blood vessels in your legs, so less blood and oxygen reach your brain for a few seconds, and you black out. Lying flat fixes it straight away — which is why you came round so quickly.'

★ 'Three reasons: the setting — hot, standing still for hours, crowded and exciting; your earlier episodes fit the same pattern — jumping up to answer the phone and fainting at the sight of blood are textbook triggers; and you had a clear warning first.' / 'Your blood pressure drops a little when you stand — that supports the same diagnosis.' / 'Is the blood pressure the real problem?' → 'Part of the same picture rather than a separate illness — a drop on standing usually makes people dizzy rather than black out completely, so it's supporting evidence rather than the cause.'

'When you feel the warning, lie down and put your legs up — don't try to walk it off.' / 'Cross your legs and squeeze your thigh and bottom muscles, or grip your hands and pull them apart.' / 'Come back if you faint with no warning, while lying down or exercising, or with chest pain or a racing heart first.'

'Could this be a brain tumour?' → 'I'm glad you told me — I did check for it: headaches that wake you at night or are worse first thing, morning vomiting, weight loss, weakness or numbness, and changes at the back of the eye. You have none, and your neurological examination is normal — so very unlikely. But two years of headaches needing regular Nurofen deserve proper attention; frequent painkillers can keep headaches going. I'll write to your GP.' / 'Will this stop me getting my licence?' → 'A faint like yours — clear trigger, clear warning, while standing — generally doesn't restrict you. What would change that is fainting with no warning, or sitting or driving, or a heart cause. Tell your GP if the pattern changes, and pull over if you ever feel the warning at the wheel.'

Hidden agenda (late, or last 30 s): 'Could this be a brain tumour? And will I still be allowed to drive?'. 'It's just a faint' → 'so it'll definitely never happen again?'; physiology >25 s → 'sorry — what does that actually mean?'; no plan → 'so what happens now?'

Examiner: alert, no pallor/dehydration/rash/injuries · BP 120/80 sitting, 94/62 standing · pulse 82 regular · RR, temp, sats normal · cranial nerves, fundoscopy, limbs, gait normal, no neck stiffness · CVS normal, no murmurs · chest clear · abdomen normal · BSL and ECG normal (stem) · dipstick unavailable

Version B — 15F, collapsed at the END of a 100 m run, mother present (online): task 2 = describe the examination to the mother in lay language in examination order (looks, colour, alertness, injury; BP lying and standing, pulse rate and regularity, breathing, temperature, oxygen; nerves — face, eyes incl. looking in the back with a light, strength/sensation/reflexes, balance and walking; heart — neck, chest, feel, listen; lungs; tummy; finger-prick sugar and urine) — not 'praecordial palpation, cranial nerves II–XII'. Extras: skipped breakfast, pallor, postural drop → still ONE provisional diagnosis (vasovagal: sprinting on a hot day, missed food and fluid, dizzy/light-headed first), rank hypoglycaemia (normal glucose NOW doesn't exclude it THEN — she had Hydralyte on recovery ADDED) and the postural drop; HOCM addressed and set aside (no chest pain/SOB/FHx, had a warning). ★ Say aloud: syncope DURING exertion = cardiac red flag; at the END/just after = usually reflex (muscle pump stops while vessels are still dilated)
Variant C — mid-game collapse, no warning, family sudden death: everything changes — admit on a monitor, echo, cardiology; no sport or driving until known; family may need checking

Scoring 0/1/2 per item: postural BP by name, fundoscopy, murmurs, glucose + ECG requested · one clear provisional diagnosis · ≥3 reasons · postural drop as evidence not diagnosis · differentials across ≥4 systems · counter-pressure · trigger avoidance · driving · safety-net · follow-up
SA: ED → GP follow-up; headache review; Austroads — reflex syncope with prodrome generally no restriction VERIFY; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 not needed
fails: Exploring only today's episode — never asking her to describe all three (the diagnosis lives in the phone rush and the sight of blood)

Skipping seizure screen because the stem says 'fainted'; hearing 'tired' and switching to seizure; deleting palpitations/FHx/meals because BSL and ECG are normal
Avoiding alcohol and drugs because she's 17; six cardiac differentials and no other system
'Just a faint' with no counter-pressure advice, no safety-net for no-warning/supine/exertional syncope, no plan for the headaches
numbers: Postural hypotension: systolic fall ≥20 or diastolic ≥10 within 3 min standing · here 120/80 → 94/62 = 26/18 · pulse 82 · LOC 30 s · third episode · standing 1–2 h
Reflex syncope typically <1 min; brief myoclonic jerks can occur and don't mean seizure · vasovagal triad: trigger + prodrome + rapid full recovery
Red flags: during exertion · supine · no prodrome · palpitations first · FHx sudden death <40–50 · abnormal ECG · injury · ECG items: QTc, delta wave, Brugada, LVH + deep TWI, AV block
Version B: end-of-exertion = reflex; during = cardiac · normal glucose now ≠ no hypo then (oral rehydration given) · skipped breakfast, pallor, postural drop — still one diagnosis
Counter-pressure: lie down legs up · head between knees · cross legs and tense · grip and pull · FBC + β-hCG today · GP 1–2 weeks

stem: Ms Chloe Danvers, 25, brought in by her parents after a 'funny turn' this morning: she got out of bed, walked to the fridge and collapsed; her parents witnessed the event. Now alert and orientated. BP 118/74, PR 78 regular, RR 16, SpO2 99% RA, T 36.8, BGL 5.4, GCS 15.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes: history 4 · PEFE 1:15 · explain + close 2:45 — watch the clock at 5:15. 'Shaking' arrives in ten seconds — stay on the TLOC spine: before → during (★ the witness account, and why) → after → causes. ★ Offer privacy before alcohol/drugs; ★ 'stopped, run out of, or missed any medication?' (Version B lives here); febrile convulsions acknowledged then set aside; pregnancy; driving/occupation; ★ concerns (epilepsy fear) · PEFE by name incl. fundoscopy, postural BP, ECG (QTc), β-hCG · name it a seizure in plain English · ★ trigger as a probability, never proof · structured differential · investigations · ★ no driving + SA notification · safety-net.

back.dx: Provoked generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Standing at the fridge after getting up late; no warning, no aura (smell/taste/déjà vu), no chest pain/palpitations; complete LOC 1–2 min, bilateral jerking, eyes rolled up, went blue, sore tongue, incontinent, bruised elbow; confused and drowsy ~15 min, whole body aches, no focal weakness. Two febrile convulsions as a toddler ('is that why?' — modestly raises later risk, doesn't explain today). No fever/headache/neck stiffness/rash, no head injury, no morning headache/vomiting/weight loss. Version A: party last night, champagne, ~2 h unaccounted for, woke at home; doesn't use drugs but 'can't tell you what happened after I blacked out' — spiking/safety asked without pressing, service offered; missed breakfast, little water yesterday. Version B: no alcohol; temazepam nightly for a year, ran out two days ago — benzodiazepine withdrawal seizure; restart the usual dose today, GP taper over weeks, never abruptly. PEFE: normal, no postural drop, GCS 15, no meningism, fundi normal, ECG normal QTc, β-hCG negative. To Chloe: 'a seizure — a brief burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain, like a short electrical storm; stopped by itself; full recovery; examination, sugar and tracing normal'; 'a single seizure with a clear trigger is not the same as epilepsy'. Trigger (A): most likely alcohol — any amount lowers the threshold ('not about how much you drank'); can't exclude something taken or spiked; missed breakfast → low sugar may have contributed. Differential named so 'nothing is brushed aside': meningitis/encephalitis, bleed (esp. after a head knock), SOL, electrolytes/glucose, cardiac arrhythmia (no prodrome keeps it live), faint, functional episode. Plan: FBC, EUC + Ca/Mg, LFT, alcohol level, urine drug screen; observe to baseline; first-seizure clinic — EEG ± MRI. ★ No driving — legal duty to notify the licensing authority; in SA the doctor is also required to notify; letter for work; no swimming/baths alone, shower, no heights, someone with her tonight; return for another seizure, >5 min, severe headache, fever, neck stiffness, weakness. Hidden agenda: 'is this epilepsy? my aunt lost her licence'.
plan: Outside: 'BP with a postural drop, pulse rate and rhythm, RR, sats, temperature, bedside glucose, GCS?' → stable, not hypoglycaemic · WIPE, DOB, comfortable? · 'that must have been very frightening for you and your parents — let me go through the whole morning with you'

setting: Emergency Department. No physical examination in this station; vitals normal on request. A full SIX minutes of history is expected — psychogenic is a diagnosis of exclusion and finishing the history at three minutes tells the examiner you guessed.
stem: Jane, 25, brought in by ambulance after collapsing at work. The episode happened immediately after her manager accused her of shoplifting.
tasks: Take a history (6 minutes)
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes: 0:00 vitals, WIPE, ★ confidentiality statement, open question, empathy, ★ declare neutrality on the allegation · 0:40 ★ 'complete LOC or aware?' → aware; witnessed; seizure screen → ★ jerking + awareness — RECONFIRM THE CONTRADICTION OUT LOUD · timing (20–30 s), first, context (mid-argument) — don't announce the diagnosis at two minutes · 2:30 BEFORE ×4 incl. ★ 'did you hit your head, or did anything happen physically?' · AFTER ×3 (★ confusion vs embarrassment) · 3:30 organic exclusion signposted — CNS, CVS, GI, drugs/meds/cessations, travel/jaundice/thermal — negatives are your reasoning · 4:45 hyperventilation, ★ 'did you feel frightened you were about to die?', mood/sleep/appetite/anhedonia, home and work, ★ RISK — self-harm and harm to others, PMHx/epilepsy/FHx · explanation: functional seizure named, ★ 'what happened to you was real', three reasons, honest differentials with EEG/ECG/glucose, no antiepileptics, driving, safety-net, crisis numbers.

back.dx: Psychogenic (functional) non-epileptic seizure — provisional, diagnosis of exclusion. Collapse mid-argument after being accused of shoplifting; 20–30 s; bilateral arm and leg shaking WITH retained awareness (heard people talking, the ambulance being called, remembers all of it) — incompatible with a generalised epileptic seizure; no tongue bite, no incontinence, no warning, clear-headed immediately (mortified, not confused), no injury, first episode; nobody touched her — shouting only; organic sweep entirely negative; no alcohol/drugs/meds/cessations; not breathing fast; ★ did not feel she was about to die (panic screened); mood stressed, sleep poor, appetite fine, still enjoys things, home fine with partner, work hard — manager 'on at me for months'; ★ no thoughts of self-harm or harming others (if positive — stop, explore ideation/plan/intent/means/previous/protective, same-day mental health); no PMHx/epilepsy/FHx. Explain: 'a psychogenic seizure — also called a functional seizure; looks very like an epileptic seizure and your arms and legs really were shaking, but it doesn't come from abnormal electrical activity in the brain'; ★ 'what happened to you was real — you weren't putting it on, and you couldn't have stopped it; under intense emotional stress the body can respond physically, outside your control'. 'So you think I faked it — that's what he said too' (scripted) → ★ 'No — I'm saying the opposite. I believe what happened, and I don't think you had any control over it. A recognised condition with a name and a treatment — the treatment isn't epilepsy tablets, it's working with someone on the stress.' Three reasons: aware throughout; clear-headed after; the exact moment of confrontation. Differentials, honestly: true epileptic seizure — frontal lobe type can mimic → EEG (video-EEG telemetry definitive); brain bleed/infection/growth (no headache, focal signs, fever); arrhythmia → ECG; glucose/electrolytes → bloods; alcohol/drugs/cessation (none); panic (didn't feel she was dying). Plan: ECG, finger-prick glucose, bloods; neurology + psychology (talking therapy is the most effective treatment); no antiepileptics; ★ no driving until assessed — after any blackout, whatever the cause; no heights/machinery/swimming alone; return if recurrent, injured, prolonged; crisis numbers. Words to avoid: 'not a real seizure', 'nothing wrong', 'all in your head', 'pseudoseizure', 'faking'. Medical certificate offered; nothing written about the allegation; anything written is hers to share.
plan: Vitals → normal · WIPE · ★ 'everything we talk about today stays between you and me, unless there's a risk of harm to you or someone else — is that alright?' · 'tell me more about what happened' → accused, argued, went down, 'I didn't take anything' · empathy · ★ 'my job here isn't to work out what happened at the shop — it's to work out why you collapsed'

Is that right?' → yes
Duration 20–30 s · ever before (never) · doing (mid-argument) · hot/stuffy, standing long, position change → no — keep excluding for another three minutes

BEFORE: warning (not really) · meals/fluids (normal) · ★ 'did you hit your head at all, or did anything happen physically during the argument?' → nobody touched me, just shouting · fever/rash · AFTER: ★ 'confused, or clear-headed straight away?' → clear-headed, just embarrassed · pale (no) · injured (no)

Interpret the ECG to your examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differentials

back.dx: Congenital long QT syndrome: three syncopal episodes over months, each while seated doing nothing (class, home, class), ~1 min, complete LOC, no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence, ★ never any warning ('I'm fine, then I'm on the floor'), not confused after, not pale, no injury; everything else negative — no chest pain/palpitations/SOB, no medications (none for acne/allergies/nausea/mood), no alcohol/drugs, no stress, no PMHx; ★ mother used to faint when younger and still does sometimes; no sudden deaths, drownings, cot deaths or congenital deafness. Vitals: pulse 50 (bradycardia — note it). ECG in seven steps: rate ~50 (six large squares), regular, P before every QRS → sinus bradycardia, PR normal, QRS normal, ST no elevation/depression, T waves and QT → ★ 'examiner, could you tell me what the QTc is?' → 0.54 s = 540 ms — markedly prolonged (expect <~460 in a girl; >500 high risk) → sinus bradycardia with a significantly prolonged QTc — long QT syndrome. Never try to measure it silently on a laminated tracing (paper-folding unavailable, Bazett under time pressure unrealistic — candidates default to sinus bradycardia/sick sinus and fail; a correct differential does not rescue a wrong primary diagnosis). To Lily: 'after each beat the electrical system takes longer than it should to reset; sometimes it tips the heart into a fast, disorganised rhythm — the heart can't pump, blood doesn't reach the brain, you black out, then it settles, which is why you wake up fine'. Three reasons: the QT on the tracing; mum's fainting (a version runs in families); no warning (cause in the heart, not a simple faint). 'Could I die?' → honest: taken seriously, occasionally dangerous — hence not home; very treatable; finding it today is good news; a tablet (beta blocker) greatly reduces the chance; a list of medicines to avoid. Differentials across systems: other rhythms (too slow, block), muscle/valve, seizure, brain, glucose/salts, PE, reflex/orthostatic (seated, no warning), panic last. Plan: admit on a monitor, K/Mg/Ca/TSH/glucose, paediatric cardiology today, beta blocker likely, QT-prolonging drug list (antibiotics, antiemetics); ★ when mum arrives — with Lily's permission — mum needs an ECG today; screen parents and siblings; sport — defer to the specialists (type-dependent), hold competitive sport, no swimming (some forms triggered by exercise and swimming).

back.dx: Aortic stenosis (commonest cause at 40: bicuspid valve) — exertional syncope with the triad: collapsed mid-rally chasing a ball, complete LOC 2–3 min, first ever, no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence, ★ no warning at all, warm day but drinking between games and had breakfast (the decoy), clear-headed on waking, looked washed out, grazed elbow; ★ chest pain while playing — left/central, radiating down the left arm and up the neck, heavy 'like a weight' (exertional angina — hold both ACS and AS; you haven't listened yet); ★ more puffed on court this season; no palpitations/oedema/PE features; non-smoker, 6–8 SD/week, no meds; cholesterol high-normal 3–4 years ago, BP normal, no diabetes, no known murmur/rheumatic fever, no FHx sudden death. Examination: no postural drop; pulse 84 regular (ask character — slow-rising/low volume/narrow pulse pressure); neuro normal; JVP not raised; ★ prominent but undisplaced LV impulse (pressure overload, concentric hypertrophy — say so), no thrill; S1 S2 normal; ★ murmur — aortic area (R 2nd ICS), systolic, radiating to the carotids, no separate carotid bruit; chest clear; abdomen normal; no oedema/calf tenderness; ECG, BSL normal (a normal ECG doesn't exclude structural disease → echo). 15-second diagnosis: 'the aortic valve is the gateway between your heart and the main blood tube carrying blood to your body — in your case that gateway has become narrowed'; two reasons: the trio with exercise, the murmur. Differentials by system: heart — MI/blocked artery (ECG normal, troponin), arrhythmia (no palpitations), HOCM, pericarditis, PE; brain — seizure, stroke, bleed, meningitis, SOL; chemistry — glucose, salts; simple — dehydration, heat, standing faint; drugs/alcohol/panic. Plan: admit on a monitor, bloods + serial ECGs (exclude MI), echo, cardiology today; valve replacement if tight — results very good; no tennis or heavy exertion; ★ no driving until cleared — SA notification, done together; return if recurrent, chest pain, SOB at rest; letter for the employer, social work. Hidden agenda: 'am I going to drop dead?' (a colleague's brother); 'will I lose my licence — I drive for work?'.

★ 'Two reasons: you have the well-known trio — chest pain, breathlessness and blacking out, all with exercise — and when I listened to your heart I heard an abnormal sound that fits with that narrowing.' / 'It's serious, but it's very treatable, and you've come to the right place.'

stem: Mrs Anita Rowe, 44, has come from the shopping centre: she was shopping this morning, felt unwell and was about to fall. Known diabetic on insulin. Vital signs stable.

Interpret the ECG for your examiner
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes: history 5 · ECG 1:15 · explain + close 1:45. WIPE, acknowledge, signpost, ★ bedside glucose · 'complete LOC or aware?' → about to, didn't; focal seizure screen; duration; first · context, ★ no warning (discordant — cardiac up), meals (skipped breakfast), fluids, head knock, fever; after ×3 · ★ diabetes block: diagnosed, adherence and today's dose, dose change, new/OTC/herbal, diet and snacks, home monitoring, hypo awareness, reviews · ★ complications — feet, eyes, kidneys, autonomic (dizzy standing, early satiety, bladder) → link microvascular disease to autonomic neuropathy · system screen incl. ★ 'chest pain — even a little?' (none — a clue in a diabetic), SADMA, exertion today, BP/lipids/FHx, ★ drives · ★ ECG one-breath hand-over: rate, rhythm, P, PR, QRS, axis, ST (elevation II, III, aVF; reciprocal aVL/I), T, Q; V1–V3 posterior; ★ V4R before nitrates · inferior STEMI, time-critical · warning shot · ★ two-part diabetes explanation · differential incl. hypo · ★ aspirin 300 mg chewed + ambulance to PCI · no party, ★ no driving, call family.

back.dx: Acute inferior STEMI, painless — diabetic autonomic neuropathy. Presyncope after three hours of walking (far more activity than usual), skipped breakfast (an apple), aware throughout, a few seconds, no jerking/incontinence, first time, ★ no warning, not confused, no injury, friend said 'washed out'; diabetes ~2 years on insulin, adherent (took it this morning, slightly offended at the question), no dose change, nothing new/herbal, usually eats and snacks properly, sugars in the 7s, 3-monthly reviews; ★ feet tingle at night, ★ early retinal changes at the last eye check (microvascular disease → painless ischaemia plausible); ★ 'no chest pain at all' (firm); no SOB/palpitations/oedema; non-smoker, occasional wine; BP and cholesterol 'a bit up'; father MI at 58; ★ drove herself here; husband at work. Bedside glucose 6.1 (Version B). ECG: rate ~70, regular sinus, PR normal, QRS narrow, axis normal, ★ ST elevation II, III, aVF with reciprocal ST depression aVL and I (reciprocal change = infarction, not pericarditis/early repolarisation), no Q waves, T upright; examine V1–V3 for posterior extension; ★ right-sided leads (V4R) before any nitrate → 'acute inferior STEMI — a time-critical emergency' (RCA ~80%; ST III > II favours RCA). Warning shot, then: 'your heart tracing shows you are having a heart attack right now'; 'no chest pain' → two-part explanation: diabetes damages the small vessels (blocks → heart attack) AND the nerves carrying pain from the heart → a silent heart attack; 'the tracing tells us more than how you feel'. 'Am I going to die?' → serious and very treatable; the safest thing is what we're doing now. Differential: hypoglycaemia (skipped breakfast, hours of walking — may still be part of it), hyperglycaemia/DKA, arrhythmia/valve, PE, TIA, seizure, electrolytes, dehydration, anaemia, medication — the tracing puts MI at the top. Action: ★ aspirin 300 mg chewed, IV access, monitor with a defibrillator available, oxygen only if SpO2 <93%, V4R before nitrates, ★ 000 to a PCI-capable centre, ECG transmitted ahead, stay with her; no party; ★ no driving today or until cleared (~2 weeks after successful PCI); call the husband; car stays.

'Any numbness, tingling or burning in your feet, or ulcers? Any blurring of vision — when was your last eye check? Any kidney problems? Do you get dizzy on standing, feel full very quickly after meals, or have bladder trouble?'
★ 'Any chest pain, tightness or heaviness — even a little?' / 'Have you done more physical activity than usual today?' / ★ 'Do you drive, and who's at home with you?'

★ 'Rate, rhythm, P waves, PR, QRS, axis, ST segments, T waves, Q waves.' / ★ 'ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with reciprocal ST depression in aVL — an acute inferior STEMI.' / ★ 'I would obtain right-sided leads, particularly V4R, before giving any nitrate.'

Examiner: 'which artery?' → 'Most often the right coronary artery — about 80% of inferior infarcts; the circumflex in the rest. ST elevation taller in III than II favours the RCA.' / 'why no chest pain?' → 'Diabetic autonomic neuropathy impairs the afferent pain pathway; painless infarction is well described in diabetes, in women and in older patients.'
★ 'I need to tell you something important, and I'd like you to hear all of it. Your heart tracing shows that you are having a heart attack right now — the medical name is a myocardial infarction.'

★ 'Diabetes does two separate things here. First, over years, it damages the small blood vessels that supply the heart muscle — if one suddenly blocks, that part of the muscle stops getting blood, and that is a heart attack. Second, the same diabetes damages the nerves that carry pain from the heart — so instead of chest pain, the only thing you felt was being unwell and about to fall. We call that a silent heart attack, and it's why the tracing tells us more than how you feel.' / 'This is serious, and it is also very treatable — the safest thing possible is what we're doing now.'

★ 'I'd like you to chew this aspirin. I'm calling an ambulance, and you'll go straight to a hospital that can open the blocked vessel — the sooner that's done, the more heart muscle we save. I'll stay with you, put a drip in, keep you on a monitor, and send your tracing ahead.'

★ 'I'm sorry — the party isn't possible tonight, and you must not drive: not today, and not until the specialist clears you. Your car can stay here safely. Is there someone I can call — your husband?' / Refuses the ambulance: 'Part of your heart muscle is losing its blood supply right now, and every minute counts. It must be an ambulance rather than your car because the most dangerous moments are the first hours, when the rhythm can go wrong suddenly — the paramedics carry the equipment to fix that. You can decline — I'll respect it — but I'd be failing you if I didn't say plainly that I think it would be a very dangerous choice. Can I call your husband before you decide?'
