setting: Orthopaedic ward; you are the resident. Day 1 after TKR under spinal. Vitals in the stem (ask for them anyway, lying and standing). No examination required. Task 3 is investigations to the examiner. The one sentence the station is marked on: PE named first, CTPA named.
stem: John Whittaker, 60, had an elective total knee replacement yesterday morning under spinal anaesthetic. Overnight he walked to the ward toilet with a frame and was found on the floor by a nurse. He is back in bed, alert and talking. BP 118/74 lying, 104/66 standing; HR 104 regular; RR 20; SpO2 94% RA; T 36.9; BSL 6.2; GCS 15.
tasks: Take a focused history (approx. 6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials to the patient
Tell the examiner your investigations
time: 8 minutes: leave 2 for explanation + investigations. Vitals lying/standing — interpret aloud (tachycardic, borderline sats, postural drop) · WIPE, sit, open question, empathy · ★ true LOC (a fresh TKR gives every mechanical reason to fall) · last memory, duration, witnessed (no), first time · context: doing, standing long, pain, ★ micturition/defecation/straining, heat · ★ prodrome (none) · chest pain/palpitations · during: shaking, tongue, incontinence, pallor · after: confusion, how long · ★ 'did you hit your head?' · ★ full respiratory and calf screen despite negatives · CNS, GI, fever · ★ opioids/pregabalin, antihypertensive restarted, ★ VTE prophylaxis — which, missed doses · intake · VTE risk factors (previous VTE, cancer, travel, FHx clotting/sudden death), smoking, PMHx · ★ concerns · ★ PE named FIRST — 'guided by your situation as well as your symptoms' · vasovagal, peri-op MI, orthostatic/opioid/blood loss, rhythm/glucose/salts as differentials · check understanding · investigations tied to differentials — ★ CTPA, ★ no D-dimer · escalation, safety-net, summary.

back.dx: Pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise — provoked by post-operative immobilisation, day 1 after TKR (syncope occurs in ~1 in 7 PE presentations and suggests a central clot with RV strain). Complete LOC ('there's a gap', last memory reaching for the rail), unwitnessed, found a few minutes later, first ever; had just passed urine, not straining, not standing long, bathroom not hot, knee sore but no worse; ★ no warning; no chest pain/palpitations; nobody saw shaking; 'white as a sheet'; muddled ~1 min then himself; grazed elbow, shoulder took the impact, 'I don't think I hit my head' (if he clipped the sink and is on enoxaparin → CT head too); ★ entirely negative respiratory and calf screen — do NOT downgrade PE (that is the designed reaction); no CNS/GI/fever; oxycodone at midnight, paracetamol; ★ nightly abdominal injection, name unknown, ★ one dose missed on the day of surgery; perindopril restarted this morning; nil by mouth pre-op, eaten little; no previous VTE/cancer/travel/FHx; ex-smoker 20/day quit 10 y; BP tablet only. Vitals: HR 104, SpO2 94%, postural drop 118/74 → 104/66. To John, lead with the dangerous diagnosis: 'the thing I am most concerned about is a pulmonary embolism — a clot in the blood tubes of your lungs; the reason isn't your symptoms, it's your situation — major knee surgery yesterday, hardly able to move that leg; blood clots in the deep veins and a piece travels to the lungs; it can cause exactly this sort of blackout, sometimes with no chest symptoms at all; even though your breathing is fine I'm not prepared to leave that untested'. Then: vasovagal (pain, toilet, first stand after surgery — may well be it), peri-operative MI (days 0–3, can be quiet), orthostatic hypotension (surgical blood loss + opioids), rhythm, glucose, salts. 'But I feel fine' → 'a clot in the lung doesn't always announce itself — sometimes a blackout is the only thing it does; treatable, very treatable early; the scan takes twenty minutes'. Investigations tied to differentials: bedside — lying/standing obs, continuous sats and cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG, BSL, oxygen to 94–98%, two large-bore cannulae; PE — ★ urgent CTPA after renal function and contrast allergy (V/Q if contrast contraindicated); ★ no D-dimer (raised in virtually everyone a day after surgery, wouldn't change management); MI — ECG + serial troponin; bleeding — FBE, coags, group and hold, wound and drains; metabolic — UEC (also for contrast), Ca, Mg; CXR (collapse/effusion/pneumothorax); CT head if head strike or persistent confusion; bedside echo for RV strain if hypotensive; discuss empirical anticoagulation with orthopaedics while awaiting the scan; bed rest, supervised mobilisation, mechanical prophylaxis; escalate to the registrar now; MET if he deteriorates; ★ 'press the buzzer before you get up'. Hidden agenda: home Friday — wife Margaret has early dementia; social work either way.
plan: 'May I have the vital signs — BP lying and standing, HR, RR, sats, temperature, blood sugar?' → interpret aloud: 'stable but tachycardic, borderline saturations, a postural drop — I'll keep monitoring running' · WIPE, hands washed, sits · 'tell me about it in your own words' · 'I'm so sorry — that must have been frightening; let's find out what's going on together'

★ 'Did you black out completely, or go down but stay aware?' → right out, a gap · last thing you remember (reaching for the rail) · how long, anyone with you (unwitnessed, found minutes later) · ever before (never)

Context: doing (just got there, passed urine) · standing a while · pain (sore, no worse) · ★ passing urine/opening bowels/straining · bathroom hot · ★ 'any warning — light-headed, sweaty, sick, ringing, vision closing in?' → none · chest pain/racing heart → no

During: anyone see it (no) · told you shook/stiffened, bit your tongue, wet yourself (nobody mentioned) · pale (white as a sheet) · after: confused/drowsy, how long (muddled a minute) · quickly yourself · ★ 'did you hurt yourself — did you hit your head?' → elbow, shoulder, doesn't think so (Variant 2: clipped the sink)

★ Systems, all of it, despite negatives: chest pain/tightness, SOB even on moving, cough/haemoptysis, calf pain/swelling/redness · headache, vision, speech, weakness, numbness · nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain/melaena · fever/sweats/rash → all no — do not downgrade PE

★ Medications: pain relief — anything strong (oxycodone, midnight), pregabalin · usual BP tablets restarted (perindopril this morning) · ★ 'a blood-thinning injection since the operation — which one, any doses missed?' → nightly abdominal injection, name unknown, one missed on the day of surgery · eating/drinking (little, NBM) · alcohol/substances

VTE risk and background: previous clot leg/lung, cancer, long flights/drives, FHx clotting or sudden death young, smoking (ex 20/day ×30 y, quit 10 y), PMHx (BP), ★ 'is there anything you've been particularly worried about?' → home Friday, wife unwell → acknowledge, promise to return, don't derail

★ Explain — PE FIRST: 'everything you've told me is reassuring, and I have to be guided by your situation as well as your symptoms; what concerns me most is a pulmonary embolism…' · 'but I feel fine — is it dangerous?' → answered · differentials: simple faint (pain/straining/first stand), quiet peri-op heart attack, low BP from blood loss + strong painkillers, rhythm/sugar/salts · 'does that make sense — what questions?' · Friday: can't promise; team told about Margaret; social work either way

★ To the examiner, each test tied to a differential: bedside obs lying/standing, monitoring, ECG, BSL, O2 to 94–98%, two large-bore cannulae · PE — ★ urgent CTPA after UEC and contrast allergy (V/Q if contraindicated); ★ no D-dimer and why · MI — ECG + serial troponin · bleeding — FBE, coags, G&H, wound/drains · metabolic — UEC, Ca, Mg · CXR · CT head if head strike/confusion · bedside echo for RV strain if hypotensive · empirical anticoagulation discussed with orthopaedics · bed rest, supervised mobilisation, mechanical prophylaxis · registrar now, MET if deteriorates · summary
ask: 'Before I begin, may I have the vital signs, including lying and standing blood pressure?' / 'I'm so sorry to hear that — let's find out what's happening together.' / ★ 'Did you black out completely, or did you go down but stay aware?'
'Did it happen while you were passing urine or opening your bowels, or straining? Was the bathroom hot?' / ★ 'Did you get any warning?' / ★ 'Did you hit your head?'

★ 'Have you had a blood-thinning injection since the operation — do you know which one, and have any doses been missed?' / 'What have they been giving you for pain — anything strong like morphine or oxycodone, or a nerve tablet such as pregabalin? Were your usual blood-pressure tablets restarted this morning?'

'Have you ever had a clot in the leg or the lung? Any cancer? Long flights or drives? Anyone in the family with clotting problems, or died suddenly and young?' / ★ 'Is there anything you have been particularly worried about?'

★ 'Everything you've told me is reassuring, and I want to be honest about where that leaves us. The thing I am most concerned about is a pulmonary embolism — a clot in the blood tubes of your lungs. The reason I am concerned is not your symptoms — it is your situation. You had major knee surgery yesterday and you have hardly been able to move that leg; when the legs stay still, blood can clot in the deep veins, and a piece can travel to the lungs. That can cause exactly this sort of blackout, sometimes with no chest symptoms at all. So even though your breathing is fine, I am not prepared to leave that untested.'

'But I feel fine — how can it be a clot?' → 'I know, and that's a good sign. But a clot in the lung doesn't always announce itself — sometimes a blackout is the only thing it does. It is treatable, and very treatable when we find it early, which is exactly what I'm trying to do. The scan takes about twenty minutes and we'll know today.'

'A simple faint — a vasovagal faint — is common when people are in pain, or straining on the toilet, or standing up for the first time after an operation, and that may well be what happened. Heart attacks are more common in the first few days after a big operation and can be surprisingly quiet, so I want to check that. Low blood pressure from blood loss during surgery, together with the strong painkillers, can also drop you when you stand.' / 'A simple faint is a diagnosis I can only make after ruling out the dangerous ones.'

★ 'For pulmonary embolism, which is my leading diagnosis: an urgent CT pulmonary angiogram, after checking renal function and contrast allergy — a V/Q scan if contrast is contraindicated.' / ★ 'I would not order a D-dimer, because it is elevated in virtually every patient a day after major surgery and would not change my management either way.'

'For myocardial infarction: the ECG plus serial troponin. For bleeding and anaemia: full blood examination, coagulation profile, group and hold, and inspection of the wound and drains. For metabolic causes: urea, electrolytes and creatinine — which I also need before contrast — plus calcium and magnesium. A chest X-ray; a CT head if he struck his head or remains confused; a bedside echo looking for right ventricular strain if he becomes hypotensive.' / 'I'd discuss empirical anticoagulation with the orthopaedic team while awaiting the scan, escalate to my registrar now, and call a MET if he deteriorates.'

'Am I still getting home Friday? My wife's not well' → 'Thank you for telling me — I can hear how much it matters. I can't promise, but I'll make sure the team knows about your wife and that social work is involved either way.' / ★ 'Please press the buzzer before you get up — do not walk to the toilet on your own.'

setting: Suburban GP, South Australia. Vitals on the door (all normal, no postural drop). You do not examine — findings are supplied only for what you NAME; ask for nystagmus and Dix–Hallpike by name or the station never discloses them. History hard-stops at 5:00. Five recalls share this stem with different answers to the defining question — the answer decides the structure, not the stem.
stem: James Whitfield, 60, has come in complaining of dizziness. Reception note: 'dizzy spells, 5 days'. HR 78 reg · BP 132/80 sitting, 128/78 standing · RR 14 · SpO2 98% RA · T 36.7 · BGL 5.8 · GCS 15.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history
Ask the examiner for the examination findings you require
Explain the most likely diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
Outline your management plan to the patient
time: 8 minutes: history stops at 5:00, PEFE 45 s, tasks 3–4 = last 2½ min (half the marks). HD stability · WIPE · open question · ★ ideas/concerns in minute one (brother's stroke at 62) · ★ TRIAGE TRIAD: define dizziness (spinning / light-headed / off-balance) → LOC? → falls? · timing: 5 d, bursts <60 s, symptom-free between, settles when still · triggers open then ★ NAME 'rolling over in bed' (patients under-report it) · ★ EAR ×5: hearing loss, N/V, tinnitus, pain/discharge, recent URTI · ★ BRAIN ×9: speech, diplopia/blur, weakness, numbness, gait between spells, head knock/falls (→ anticoagulant), headache/morning vomiting/weight loss, photophobia/aura, fever · CVS: chest pain, SOB, palpitations, oedema · meds/changes, alcohol, drugs · eyesight, foot numbness, diabetes/thyroid, fatigue · geriatric/social, SADMA, FHx · ★ impact and DRIVING · summarise back · PEFE named item by item · interpret aloud · check understanding · dx + ★ TWO REASONS · grouped DDx · Epley with warning + consent · home exercises · antiemetic caveat · driving + SA duty · home safety · review 1–2 wk · 7-item safety-net · teach-back.

back.dx: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (posterior canal) — Version A. True spinning ('like six beers'), bursts of 20–30 s, completely normal between, ★ set off by rolling over in bed, getting up, looking up to the top shelf; settles lying still; no LOC, no falls (grabbed the bedpost); all five ear questions negative; all nine brain questions negative; no CVS symptoms; perindopril 5 mg × 6 y unchanged, 2–3 beers Friday, ex-smoker at 40; widowed, lives alone, drives grandson to school Thursdays. Hidden agenda: brother's stroke at 62 — he will not volunteer it unless asked concerns; if never asked he interrupts at ~6 min 'is this a stroke?'. PEFE: positional nystagmus present, Dix–Hallpike positive, everything else normal → 'that combination is what lets me call this peripheral and benign'. Reassurance without reasons = 'but how do you know?' and a lost mark.
plan: 'Before I begin, may I confirm the patient is haemodynamically stable?' · WIPE, sits at an angle · 'what's brought you in?' · acknowledge ('that sounds unpleasant and I can see it's worrying you') · signpost · ★ 'was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?' → brother's stroke → name it, promise to return, actually return

★ Triage triad: 'dizziness means different things — spinning, light-headed as if about to faint, or off-balance?' → spinning (light-headed on standing = Version B → switch to falls structure) · 'any fainting or blacking out, even a second?' · 'any falls?'

Duration 5 d · episode length (20–30 s) · constant or gone between (gone) · getting worse · settles when still · 'what makes it better or worse?' (nothing noticed) → ★ 'does a change of position — rolling over in bed — set it off?' → 'now you say it, every time' · exertional onset = cardiac story, not vestibular
★ Ear ×5 as a named block: hearing change/loss either side · nausea/vomiting · ringing/buzzing · pain/discharge · cold or flu in recent weeks → all negative = permission to say 'benign'

★ Brain ×9: slurred speech · double/blurred vision · limb weakness · numbness/pins and needles · balance/walking between spells · recent head knock or fall (→ blood thinners, urgent CT) · headache, morning vomiting, weight loss · flashing lights/photophobia · fever

CVS: chest pain, SOB, palpitations, ankle swelling · meds incl OTC, anything started/changed · alcohol, drugs · eyesight, foot numbness, diabetes/thyroid, tiredness · memory, mood, who's at home, ADLs, near-misses · smoking, allergies, PMHx, FHx · ★ 'how is this affecting day-to-day life, work and driving?' → grandson Thursdays
Summarise back in 15 s: 5 d, short bursts <1 min, rolling over/looking up, settles still, no hearing loss/tinnitus/vomiting/headache/weakness/numbness/LOC/falls · 'have I missed anything?'

★ PEFE named items: appearance/pallor · postural BP + pulse rhythm · gait, tandem, Romberg · CN with fundoscopy + acuity, ★ 'specifically — nystagmus present or absent, direction, does it fatigue?' · limbs incl foot sensation · otoscopy, Rinne, Weber, hearing · CVS/resp · ★ 'I'd like to perform the Dix–Hallpike' · BGL, ECG → interpret aloud

Check understanding ('heard of vertigo, or crystals in the ear?' — 'fear of heights?' → correct gently) · name BPPV, mechanism in one sentence · ★ TWO REASONS: (1) positional spinning <1 min, (2) 'I looked specifically for the serious causes and they aren't there' · answer the brother directly · grouped DDx: ear (neuronitis, labyrinthitis, Ménière's, acoustic neuroma), brain (stroke/TIA, subdural, tumour, vestibular migraine, MS), heart (arrhythmia, ischaemia), meds/postural drop · scan request → explain, give the conditions under which you would image

Epley: describe, ★ warn (very dizzy, maybe sick — expected, passes), ~8/10 success, ★ consent · fact sheet + Brandt–Daroff · antiemetic ≤3 d only ('longer slows recovery — the brain needs the symptom to retrain') · betahistine = Ménière's, not this · ★ driving: not while attacks continue, not straight after the manoeuvre, SA legal duty to notify if unsafe · home: rise in stages, night light, clear path, no loose rugs · review 1–2 wk, vestibular physio if 2–3 manoeuvres fail · ★ safety-net ×7 · summary + teach-back
ask: 'Before I begin, may I confirm the patient is haemodynamically stable?' / 'Was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?'

★ 'Dizziness means different things to different people. Do you mean a spinning sensation — the room going round, or you going round? Or light-headed as if you're about to faint? Or off-balance and unsteady on your feet?' / 'Any fainting or blacking out, even for a second? … And any falls?'
'When you get an episode, how long does it last? Is it there all the time or does it come and go?' / ★ 'Does a change of position — for instance rolling over in bed — set it off?'

★ 'A few questions about your ears: any change in your hearing on either side? Any nausea or vomiting with the spells? Any ringing, buzzing or roaring? Any pain or discharge? A cold or flu-like illness in the last few weeks?'

'Any slurred speech? Double or blurred vision? Weakness in the arms or legs? Numbness or pins and needles? Trouble with balance or walking between the spells? Any recent knocks to the head or falls? Any headache — particularly vomiting first thing in the morning — or weight loss? Flashing lights or sensitivity to light? Any fever?'
★ To examiner: 'specifically, is there any nystagmus — present or absent, in which direction, and does it fatigue?' / 'As a special test I'd like to perform the Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre.'

★ 'You have a condition called benign positional vertigo. It happens because of a disruption of the normal fluid circulation in the balance organ of your inner ear, so when you move your head your brain briefly gets a false signal that you're spinning.' / ★ 'There are two reasons I'm saying that. First, true spinning brought on by changing position and lasting under a minute is very characteristic. Second — and just as important — I've looked specifically for the serious causes and they aren't there.'

'A stroke affecting the balance centres almost always causes constant dizziness rather than short bursts, and nearly always brings something else with it — slurred speech, double vision, weakness, or being unable to walk. You have none of those.' / scan: 'this is diagnosed by the story and the positional test, not by a scan — where I would arrange one is if you developed hearing loss on one side, any of the warning signs, or didn't improve as expected.'

★ 'The main treatment isn't a tablet — it's a manoeuvre I can do right now. I need to warn you it will make you feel very dizzy for a few seconds and possibly a bit sick — that's expected and it passes. It fixes it in about eight out of ten people. Are you happy for me to go ahead?' / 'Only a couple of days of the anti-sickness tablet — taking it longer actually slows your recovery.'

★ 'While you're still having attacks you shouldn't drive — including the school run. Don't drive straight home after the manoeuvre today. Here in South Australia doctors have a legal duty to notify the licensing authority about anyone who isn't safe to drive, so I'd much rather we sort this out together and get you back behind the wheel quickly.' / ★ 'Come back straight away, or call an ambulance, if you get slurred speech, weakness or numbness down one side, double vision, trouble swallowing, a severe headache or new neck pain, hearing loss or ringing in one ear, if the dizziness becomes constant instead of coming in bursts, or you can't walk without help.' / 'What will you do if you get any of those warning signs?'

Guarded and gruff, warms up if you do; anxious at the word 'brain'/'stroke'; relieved only if given REASONS. Will not say 'spinning' unless offered the three options. Unhelpful on the open trigger question — make them ask about bed. Asks 'shouldn't I have a scan?' and 'will it make me sick?' once

'Horizontal nystagmus' on the card → lateral canal: supine roll test, log-roll (barbecue) manoeuvre, not Epley

Variant 3 — tripped 12 d ago, head on door frame, on apixaban (volunteered late, only if asked): chronic subdural until proven otherwise → urgent non-contrast CT head today, ask headache/memory/vagueness; if positive: neurosurgery, withhold apixaban, local reversal protocol · Variant 4 (2023 re-skin) — 'not spinning, light-headed and grey on standing, legs went twice': switch structure openly to the falls spine; lying/standing BP at 1 and 3 min (138 → 106), falls-risk assessment, medication review (antihypertensive + prostate tablet); do not force the ear questions on him

setting: Regional SA general practice, standard appointment. Walks in unaided, alert. Vitals in the stem; the postural BP, glucose and dipstick are given only if you ask. Version C is the spine — four causes stack, and the case hands you the first one in the words 'rushing to the toilet'. Aim history 4½ · PEFE 1½ · explanation 2.
stem: John Halloran, 70, retired farmhand, has come in because he has fallen twice in the last two nights. T 36.9 · HR 82 reg · BP 120/80 sitting · RR 16 · SpO2 97% RA.
tasks: Take a relevant focused history (about 5 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings — you will not examine the patient
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Open, acknowledge, signpost ('some questions won't seem related — that's deliberate') · ★ concern in minute one (brother's stroke / ending up in a home) · ★ fall vs faint SECOND, always (LOC, remember hitting the floor, shake/tongue/wet) · number, timeline ('never in my life' = acute, 48 h), context (out of bed, hurrying to the toilet — register it, keep the structure), warning ('swimmy'), ★ injury, ★ long lie · organic screen: numbness, weakness, speech, vision, headache, vertigo · chest pain, palpitations, SOB · V/D, melaena · ★ 'eating regularly, or skipping meals?' → skipping tea · PMHx ×4 (conditions, ops, meds incl sleep/pain/OTC, allergies) → nil · ★ six risk domains in order: home (hallway light poor, toilet far end) · urinary (frequency, urgency, nocturia ×3–4, stinging, no blood) · ★ fever/shivers/flank/abdo pain (excludes pyelo) · MSK/feet/footwear (old slippers) · eyes/ears · alcohol QUANTIFIED, smoking, drugs · geriatric/social: who's home, ADLs, memory, mood, weight, driving, ★ fear of falling · stop at 5:00 → PEFE → four numbered causes → answer the stroke by name → DDx still being checked → plan → red flags → teach-back.

back.dx: Multifactorial acute falls — FOUR causes, numbered: (1) symptomatic UTI (48 h frequency, urgency, nocturia, dysuria; suprapubic tenderness; nitrites + leucocytes) — the reason he is rushing at night; (2) postural hypotension 120/80 → 94/60 (26 systolic), likely from reduced intake + infection, no meds; (3) hypoglycaemia border — capillary glucose exactly 4.0 after skipping dinner ('cooking for one's a nuisance, I go to bed early'); (4) the situation — woken from sleep, drowsy, dark hallway, toilet at the far end, hurrying because he can't hold on. Nothing points to stroke: never blacked out, awake the whole way down, speech/vision/strength/sensation normal. Hidden agenda: brother's stroke at 68 — if never asked he interrupts the explanation with 'is this a stroke?'. Naming only the UTI is the single commonest fail.
plan: 'I can see your observations are stable, so I'll take a history' · WIPE, name · 'tell me what's been happening' · 'that sounds frightening, I'm glad you came in' · ★ 'Falls at your age almost always have a reason, and usually more than one … some questions won't seem related — that's deliberate' · ★ 'anything in particular you were worried this might be?' → brother's stroke → promise a straight answer at the end

★ 'When you went down, did you black out or lose consciousness, even for a second?' · 'remember hitting the floor?' · 'shook or jerked, bit your tongue, wet yourself?' → awake the whole way down ('my legs just went')

How many, since when ('just the two, never before in my life' → acute) · 'talk me through each one — what were you doing?' (out of bed, hurrying to the toilet) · warning: light-headed, spinning, racing, chest tightness → 'a bit swimmy standing' · ★ 'did you hurt yourself?' (bruised hip) · ★ 'could you get yourself up, or were you on the floor a while?'

Organic screen, closed and fast: numbness/pins and needles, weakness, slurred speech, vision, headache, spinning · chest pain, palpitations, SOB · vomiting/diarrhoea, black or bloody motions · ★ 'are you eating regularly, or skipping meals?' → skipping tea → flag it, come back to it
PMHx ×4: conditions and who follows them · operations/admissions · ★ medicines including anything for sleep, pain or over the counter · allergies → all nil (bank the time for the risk screen)

★ Six domains, same order every time: HOME — rugs, cords, steps, night lighting, toilet distance · URINARY — 'you mentioned rushing: more often, more urgently? up at night? burning? blood?' → 2 d of frequency/urgency/nocturia 3–4, stinging, no blood · ★ 'fever, shivers, pain in your tummy or your back?' → none · MSK — joints, balance, feet, indoor footwear (old slippers) · EYES/EARS last checked · ALCOHOL — how much, how often (one beer Sunday), smoking (quit 40s), drugs

Geriatric/social: who's at home (alone since Marg died; daughter Adelaide) · ADLs · memory · mood (bit flat) · weight loss · driving (in town) · ★ 'have the falls made you afraid to move about?' → 'nervous getting up in the dark'

★ PEFE: appearance/hydration/bruising · gait + Timed Up and Go · ★ lying and standing BP at 1 and 3 min, pulse rhythm · ★ bedside glucose · LL neuro incl vibration/proprioception, Romberg, heel–shin · acuity, fundoscopy · CVS (aortic stenosis murmur), resp · LL MSK, feet, footwear · ★ abdomen for suprapubic tenderness/palpable bladder · ★ urine dipstick → 'a postural drop of 26, a glucose right on 4, and a symptomatic UTI'

★ 'Falls at your age almost never come from one single thing — several small things stack up, and that's good news because each one is fixable. I've found four.' Number them, tie each to something he said · ★ answer the brother: 'nothing you've told me and nothing I've found points to a stroke — and here's why' · DDx still being checked: rhythm (ECG today), leg nerves (diabetes, B12), sodium, anaemia, home hazards · plan: MSU + antibiotic today (symptomatic, not asymptomatic bacteriuria), fluids, ECG, bloods · ★ tonight: night light, bottle/urinal by the bed, count to ten on the edge of the bed, eat something · OT home visit, My Aged Care meals · review 48 h · red flags · ★ 'tell me back the two things you'll change tonight'
ask: 'Falls at your age almost always have a reason, and usually more than one, so I'm going to ask a fairly long list of questions — some won't seem related to falling, but that's deliberate.' / 'Was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?'

★ 'When you went down, did you black out or lose consciousness, even for a second? Do you remember hitting the floor? Has anyone told you that you shook or jerked, or did you bite your tongue or wet yourself?'

'Talk me through each one — what were you doing at the time? Any warning beforehand — light-headed, spinning, heart racing, chest tightness?' / ★ 'Did you hurt yourself? Could you get yourself up, or were you on the floor for a while?'
★ 'Are you eating regularly, or skipping meals?' / 'Any medicines at all, including anything for sleep, for pain, or anything you buy over the counter?'

'You mentioned rushing. Are you passing urine more often, or more urgently? Getting up at night? Any burning or stinging? Any blood?' / ★ 'Any fever, shivers, or pain in your tummy or your back?' / 'Do you drink alcohol — how much, and how often?'
'Who's at home with you, and who helps if you need a hand?' / 'Have the falls made you afraid to move about?'

★ To examiner: 'the lying and standing blood pressure at one and three minutes, the pulse rhythm, a bedside blood glucose … an abdominal examination for suprapubic tenderness or a palpable bladder, and a urine dipstick.'

★ 'Falls at your age almost never come from one single thing — they're usually several small things stacking up, and that's actually good news, because each one is something we can do something about. I've found four in your case.' / 'Sitting it was 120 over 80; standing it fell to 94 over 60 — we call it postural hypotension.' / 'Your sugar today was exactly 4, right on the line we call low; overnight without dinner it can drop further.'

★ 'You mentioned your brother's stroke, and I want to answer that directly. Nothing you've told me and nothing I've found points to a stroke — you never blacked out, your speech, vision, strength and sensation are all normal.' / examiner challenge: 'it would be asymptomatic bacteriuria if he had no symptoms, and I wouldn't treat that — he has new frequency, urgency, dysuria and suprapubic tenderness over 48 hours, so this is a symptomatic infection and I'd treat it while awaiting culture.'

★ 'A night light in the hallway, a bottle by the bed so you're not making that trip in the dark, and when you get up, sit on the edge of the bed and count to ten before you stand. And please eat something at night.' / 'I want to see you in 48 hours. Come back sooner, or go to the hospital, if you get a fever or shivers, pain in your back or tummy, blood in the urine, if you become confused or drowsy, if you fall again, or if you hit your head or can't get up.' / ★ 'Can you tell me back the two things you'll change tonight?'
pefe: Role-player: John, 70, retired farmhand, alone in a single-storey house since Marg died 3 y ago; daughter rings Sundays; independent, drives in town; proud, minimising ('I'm alright'); no meds, no PMHx; one beer Sunday; quit smoking 40s. Urinary symptoms given fully but ONLY when asked about waterworks or what he was doing — if never asked, volunteers at ~6 min 'is it normal to be up four times a night?'. Skipped meals only under a direct meals question. Pushes once: 'can't you just give me something for it?'. 'Sorry doctor, what does that mean?' once on jargon

PEFE: well, hydrated, gait normal · ★ 120/80 sitting → 94/60 standing · 82 reg · ★ capillary glucose 4.0 · LL neuro normal incl proprioception · CVS/resp/MSK normal · ★ suprapubic tenderness · ★ dipstick nitrites + leucocytes. Postural hypotension ≥20 systolic or ≥10 diastolic within 3 min; adult hypoglycaemia <4.0; TUG >12 s abnormal

Versions A (alcohol, 70 M), B/B2 (medications), D (TIA, 77 M) and E (PMR on steroids) share this spine and are separate cards (MED-103–106). Same stem, different answers → the six-domain screen finds the causes; the numbered multifactorial explanation is the discriminator in all of them

Treatment: trimethoprim 300 mg nocte 3 d in women / longer in men VERIFY TG · MSU before antibiotic · fluids · 15 g fast carbohydrate then recheck if <4 · staged rising, recheck postural BP at review · OT home assessment · My Aged Care 1800 200 422 · a dipstick alone never diagnoses UTI in an older person — say 'he is symptomatic'

Examiner challenge 'why treat postural hypotension on no medications?' → 'because it is demonstrated on today's measurement and in his case likely from reduced intake and the infection — treat the reversible causes, teach staged rising, recheck at review'
SA: Country Health Connect / OT · My Aged Care · Motor Vehicles Act notification if unfit · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if pyelonephritis/sepsis from a rural site
fails: ★ Never establishing loss of consciousness — the fork of the whole differential tree, listened for in the first 90 seconds
★ Not asking about injury or a long lie on the floor
Naming ONE cause ('it's a urine infection') — the commonest fail; causes must be numbered and each tied to something he said
Forgetting fever and flank pain — the questions that exclude pyelonephritis; accepting 'do you drink?' without quantifying
Rattling the organic screen so fast you miss 'skipping tea'; cutting the social screen (fear of falling, driving, meals in context)
PEFE shopping list without lying/standing BP at 1 and 3 min, glucose, abdomen and dipstick — no dipstick, no diagnosis

Ending at the diagnosis: no antibiotic, ECG, home modification, review date or red flags = fail with the right diagnosis; reassuring before anything is excluded; never answering the brother by name; still in the history at 5:00
numbers: Recurrent falls ≥2 in 12 months · postural drop ≥20 / ≥10 mmHg within 3 min · John 120/80 → 94/60 = 26 systolic · adult hypoglycaemia <4.0 (his 4.0) · 15 g fast carbohydrate / 15 min
TUG >12 s abnormal · NHMRC alcohol ≤10/week, ≤4/day · 7–8 standard drinks in a bottle of wine · thiamine 100 mg daily before glucose in a heavy drinker
Trimethoprim 300 mg nocte, 3 d women / longer men VERIFY TG · review 48 h · My Aged Care 1800 200 422
Aspirin 300 mg stat after suspected TIA unless contraindicated · no private driving ≥2 wk (4 wk commercial) after TIA VERIFY Austroads
History 4½ · PEFE 1½ · explanation 2 · four causes, never one · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

setting: General practice. Version A of the recurrent-falls spine (reconstructed stem from the older-person Part 2 §7 — patient name reconstructed). Examiner findings: bilateral distal sensory loss with loss of proprioception, glucose normal, no postural drop. The alcohol hits three systems plus sedation — name all of them.
stem: A 70-year-old man has come to see you about three falls over recent months; on one occasion he struck his head and was taken to hospital. Observations are normal.
tasks: Take a relevant focused history (about 5 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Same spine as MED-102: WIPE · concern · ★ LOC/seizure screen · describe each fall, ★ head strike → hospital, imaging, anticoagulants, headache/confusion since · injury, long lie · organic screen → ★ 'numbness in both legs' · ★ meals → one meal a day · PMHx ×4 · six domains → ★ ALCOHOL: 'how much, how often' → a bottle of wine every night, always has · family interstate, no help · geriatric screen → PEFE (postural BP, glucose, ★ LL sensation and proprioception, Romberg, cerebellar, gait, head/scalp) → four numbered causes → thiamine, bloods, safe reduction, meals and company.

back.dx: Alcohol-related multifactorial falls: (1) alcoholic peripheral neuropathy — numbness and loss of proprioception in both legs ('when you can't feel the ground, you fall'); (2) cerebellar degeneration — unsteady gait; (3) nutrition — one meal a day, nocturnal hypoglycaemia risk; (4) sedation from the alcohol itself at night. Plus social isolation (family interstate, no one to help cook). Glucose normal today and no postural drop do not exonerate — the history carries it. Head strike with hospital attendance: establish imaging, anticoagulation, symptoms since (subdural). Do not lecture; be straight; do NOT advise abrupt cessation; thiamine BEFORE any glucose.
plan: WIPE, acknowledge, signpost the long list · concern (brother's stroke / losing independence)

★ LOC, remember the floor, shake/tongue/wet → falls, not faints · number and timeline · ★ 'talk me through each' · ★ the head strike: taken to hospital, scan, told anything, on any blood thinner, headache/vagueness/drowsiness since · injury, long lie

Organic screen → ★ 'numbness in both legs' (note, keep going) · weakness, speech, vision, vertigo · CVS · GI, melaena · ★ 'eating regularly?' → one meal a day, 'can't be bothered cooking, no one to help'
PMHx ×4 · meds incl sleep/pain/OTC · allergies

Six domains: home/lighting · urinary · MSK/feet · eyes/ears · ★ ALCOHOL — 'do you drink, how much, how often?' → full bottle of wine nightly 'always have' · quantify: 'a bottle is about seven or eight standard drinks; the national guidance is no more than ten in a whole week' · smoking, drugs
Social: ★ 'who's at home, who helps?' → family all interstate · ADLs, memory, mood, weight, driving, fear of falling

PEFE: appearance, nutrition, bruising, scalp · gait, TUG, Romberg, heel–shin, tandem · lying/standing BP · glucose · ★ LL sensation incl vibration and proprioception, reflexes, power · CN, fundi, acuity · CVS, resp · abdomen (liver) · dipstick, ECG → sensory loss + proprioception loss both legs; glucose normal; no postural drop

★ 'There are four things going on, and I need to be straight with you because the alcohol explains three of them': neuropathy → cerebellar degeneration → nutrition/overnight sugar → sedation · plan: thiamine today, bloods (FBE, MCV, LFT, GGT, UEC, Mg, B12, folate, glucose/HbA1c), ★ 'cutting down safely — stopping suddenly on that amount can be dangerous', meals and company (My Aged Care, Meals on Wheels, social work), OT home visit, physio balance, hip protectors/alarm · CT head if not already done post-strike · driving · review · red flags
ask: ★ 'When you went down, did you black out at any point, even for a second?' / 'You hit your head that time — did they scan your head at the hospital? Are you on any blood thinners? Any headache, vagueness or drowsiness since?'
★ 'Do you drink alcohol — and how much, and how often?' / 'A bottle of wine is around seven or eight standard drinks — the national guidance is no more than ten in a whole week.'
'Are you eating regularly?' / 'Who's at home with you, and who helps if you need a hand?'
★ To examiner: 'lower limb sensation including vibration and proprioception, Romberg, heel–shin and tandem gait, and the lying and standing blood pressure and a glucose.'

★ 'I'm not here to lecture you, but I do need to be straight with you, because the alcohol explains three of the four things I've found. One: the numbness and loss of feeling in your legs comes from damage to the nerves — when you can't feel the ground properly, you fall. Two: alcohol also affects the balance centre at the back of the brain, and that makes you unsteady. Three: you're eating one meal a day, so your blood sugar can drop overnight. And four: the alcohol itself makes you drowsy at night.'

★ 'I'd like to start you on vitamin B1 — thiamine — today, do some blood tests, and talk about cutting down safely, because stopping suddenly on that amount can be dangerous.' / 'I'd also like to arrange some help with meals and some company, because doing this alone is making everything harder.'
pefe: Role-player (reconstructed): 70 M, three falls, one head strike → hospital; 'I have numbness in both legs'; 'I have a full bottle of wine every night, always have'; 'I only eat one meal a day — can't be bothered cooking and there's no one to help'; 'my family are all interstate'. Examiner: bilateral sensory loss + loss of proprioception, glucose normal, no postural drop

Alcohol falls mechanisms: peripheral neuropathy (sensory ataxia — Romberg +ve) · cerebellar degeneration (gait/truncal ataxia, heel–shin) · malnutrition/hypoglycaemia · sedation/impaired reaction · also hyponatraemia, subdural (head strike + coagulopathy), withdrawal seizures, Wernicke's. Bloods: FBE (macrocytosis), LFT/GGT, UEC/Na/Mg, B12/folate, glucose, INR

Thiamine 100 mg daily oral (300 mg IV/IM if Wernicke's suspected — confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia) BEFORE glucose VERIFY TG · never abrupt cessation at this intake — supervised reduction / withdrawal management (diazepam-based) VERIFY · AUDIT-C, brief intervention, Drug and Alcohol Services SA / Alcohol and Drug Information Service 1300 13 1340

Trap: naming the neuropathy and stopping — alcohol hits nerves, cerebellum, nutrition AND sedation. Trap: 'you need to stop drinking' as the plan. Trap: not revisiting the head strike (subdural can declare weeks later)
SA: My Aged Care 1800 200 422, Meals on Wheels, Country Health Connect OT/social work, DASSA, Motor Vehicles Act notification if unfit to drive
fails: Not establishing LOC; not exploring the head strike (imaging, anticoagulation, symptoms since)
Accepting 'I drink a bit' without 'how much, how often' — the whole case hides behind quantification
Naming the neuropathy alone; missing cerebellar, nutrition and sedation as separate numbered causes
Advising abrupt cessation at a bottle a night; giving glucose before thiamine; moralising instead of being straight
Skipping the social screen — isolation and no help cooking are the reason for the one meal a day and the lever for the plan
numbers: Bottle of wine ≈ 7–8 standard drinks · NHMRC ≤10/week and ≤4/day · thiamine 100 mg daily (300 mg parenteral if Wernicke's) before glucose VERIFY
Hypoglycaemia <4.0 · postural drop ≥20/≥10 within 3 min (absent here) · Romberg +ve = sensory ataxia

Examiner findings in both: NORMAL postural BP, normal sensation, normal lower limbs. The examination is deliberately normal — the causes are all in the medication list. Do not go quiet.
stem: A 70-year-old woman has come to see you about recurrent falls. Observations are normal.

Version B: on a 'fluid tablet' and a blood-pressure tablet 'ending in -sartan'; has depression and takes temazepam to sleep; 'numbness in my legs'. Version B2 (2024): on clonidine and a fluid tablet, recently changed by the GP, and amitriptyline instead of temazepam.
tasks: Take a relevant focused history
Ask the examiner for the relevant examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Same spine: WIPE, concern · ★ LOC/seizure screen · each fall, context, ★ injury, long lie · organic screen → 'numbness in my legs' (subjective; keep going) · ★ PMHx ×4 for EACH condition: hypertension (when, what, adherence, follow-up, complications), depression (control, sleep, who manages it) · ★ MEDS one by one incl anything for sleep, recent changes (B2), timing · six domains (home, urinary, MSK, senses, ★ drugs/alcohol) · social/geriatric → PEFE (lying/standing BP at 1 and 3 min, glucose, LL neuro incl proprioception, gait/TUG, cognition) → all normal → ★ four numbered medication-driven causes, deprescribe slowly, never stop clonidine abruptly.

back.dx: Medication-related multifactorial falls with a normal examination: (1) intermittent postural hypotension from diuretic + ARB (B) / clonidine + diuretic (B2) — 'measured normally today, but the drop is intermittent and at home getting up quickly it can fall further, so it stays on my list'; (2) ★ temazepam — persists overnight, drowsy and slow to react, roughly doubles fall risk at her age; B2: amitriptyline — sedating, postural drop, anticholinergic, a poor choice in an older faller; (3) subjective leg numbness — a fall risk in itself even with normal testing; check B12/glucose; (4) depression + poor sleep — awake at night, drowsy by day. Plan: reduce temazepam slowly (not stop), sleep hygiene/CBT-i, review antihypertensive doses and timing with her GP, ★ never stop clonidine abruptly (rebound hypertension), review the amitriptyline indication rather than cease it yourself.

'Your blood pressure was steady when we measured it today — but that doesn't rule the problem out, because the drop is intermittent, and you're on two tablets that lower blood pressure. At home, getting up quickly first thing, it can fall further than it did here. So it stays on my list.'

'Although the testing of the nerves in your legs came back normal, the fact that you feel numbness in them is itself something that makes falls more likely, so I'm not dismissing it — I'll check your B12 and your sugar.'

stem: A 77-year-old man has come to see you about recurrent falls; the most recent happened while he was working in the garden. Observations are normal.
tasks: Take a relevant focused history
Ask the examiner for the relevant examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Same spine: WIPE, concern · ★ LOC ('never') · each fall — ★ garden fall: 'my vision blurred just before, and for a bit afterwards'; 'no chest pain, no sweating, just felt cold' · one fall as he stood up · ★ chase the blur: one eye or both, half the world or all of it, how long, speech/weakness/numbness/face droop with it, resolved fully · exertional context → cardiac questions · injury, long lie · organic screen · PMHx ×4 (vascular risk: BP, lipids, diabetes, AF, smoking) · meds, ★ antiplatelet/anticoagulant · six domains · social/driving → PEFE (postural BP, rhythm/AF, carotid bruits, murmur of AS, full neuro, fundi, glucose, ECG) → all normal → ★ TIA first, cardiac second, postural third → aspirin now, urgent imaging, ★ no driving.

back.dx: Transient ischaemic attack — transient visual blurring around the exertional fall, fully resolved (normal examination is what a resolved TIA looks like) — needs same-day assessment, not next week. Any jerky movements?' → never → 'so these are falls rather than blackouts' · 'how many?' → four · ★ 'describe each' → couch, bed, getting up · ★ 'does a change of position — sitting or lying to standing — set them off?' → 'exactly' · ★ 'did you injure yourself or fracture any bones?' → bruised hip

Organic screen: speech (fine now), ★ weakness → left arm and leg still · numbness · chest pain, palpitations, ★ SOB → gardening → 'with exertion, settles with rest? any cough?' · N/V, ★ abdo pain → points to epigastrium → 'reflux or heartburn? ★ any anti-inflammatories — Nurofen, Voltaren, aspirin? weight loss?' → no ×3 → 'I'll come back to that separately' · spinning · missed meals

★ 'You mentioned the stroke — full recovery, or left with weakness, numbness or speech difficulty?' → left side weak, speech back · 'other conditions?' → hypertension: when (10 y), treatment (one tablet mane), adherence (every day), follow-up (yes), complications (heart, eyes)

Risk domains: home (two front steps, slippers) · urinary (sleeps through) · MSK (no joint pain), ★ balance ('sometimes that persists after a stroke' — a bit off) · vision/hearing · other meds, alcohol, drugs · geriatric: memory, mood (flat since stroke), support (Marie), diet

★ PEFE: appearance/pallor · ★ postural BP + rhythm · neuro: ★ power upper and lower limbs, tone, reflexes, plantars, sensation, gait · fundi, acuity · CVS/resp · ★ abdomen — epigastric tenderness, mass · TUG, BSL, dipstick, ECG → 120/80 → 94/56; L arm/leg 3/5, R normal, sensation intact; fundi normal; mild epigastric tenderness; TUG prolonged; glucose normal; ECG SR
★ Arithmetic aloud: 'a fall of 26 systolic and 24 diastolic — positive on both criteria' · '3 out of 5 = movement against gravity but not against resistance — a significant residual deficit'

★ 'Falls usually have more than one cause, and I've found several' → four, each reasoned · 'should I stop the tablet?' → ★ firm no + review dose/timing + staged rising, fluids, avoid standing fast after a big meal · 'is this another stroke coming?' → honest: nothing today suggests a new stroke, but risk is higher — that's why we treat; FAST → 000 · epigastric pain: look into it separately · risk-factor DDx then collapse DDx · ★ consequences: head injury/intracranial bleed, hip fracture → surgery, rehab, loss of independence, fear of falling, recurrence · ★ 'we aim to prevent falls by reducing the risk factors' → physio, OT, tablet review, cardiac work-up, driving (Austroads, SA notification), summary
ask: ★ 'When you fall, do you lose consciousness, or are you still aware of your surroundings? Any jerky movements?' / 'So these are falls rather than blackouts.' / ★ 'Does a change of position — from sitting or lying to standing — trigger the falls?' / ★ 'When you fell, did you injure yourself or fracture any bones?'

'Does the breathlessness come on with exertion and settle with rest? Any cough with it?' / ★ 'Tell me about that pain — any reflux or heartburn with it? Are you taking any anti-inflammatory painkillers — Nurofen, Voltaren, or aspirin? Have you lost any weight?'

★ 'You mentioned the stroke two years ago — did you make a full recovery, or are you left with any weakness, numbness or difficulty with speech?' / 'Any balance problems — sometimes that persists after a stroke?'

★ To examiner: 'a postural blood pressure and the pulse rhythm; power in the upper and lower limbs, tone, reflexes, plantars, sensation and gait; fundoscopy and acuity; cardiovascular and respiratory; the abdomen — any epigastric tenderness or mass; a Timed Up and Go, glucose, dipstick and ECG.' / ★ 'That's a fall of 26 millimetres systolic and 24 diastolic on standing — a positive postural drop on both criteria. And power of 3 out of 5 means movement against gravity but not against resistance — a significant residual deficit.'

★ 'First, your blood pressure drops when you stand up — postural hypotension. I'm confident for two reasons: I found it on examination, and almost every fall you described happened as you changed position. The history and the examination agree. Your blood pressure tablet is likely contributing, so we'll review the dose and timing — but please don't stop it yourself, because it's protecting you from another stroke.' / 'Second, the remaining weakness in your left arm and leg makes you less steady on your feet.'

'Third, I'm also concerned about the shortness of breath when you garden. With your blood pressure and your previous stroke, there's a chance of narrowing of the arteries supplying the heart, and I'd like to investigate that.' / ★ 'Fourth, and I want to be honest with you: having had a stroke means you're at higher risk of another one, or a mini-stroke, and those can cause falls too. That's not to alarm you — it's exactly why we treat your blood pressure and keep you on preventive medication.' / 'And separately, I don't want to leave that pain in your upper tummy — it may be unrelated, but let's look into it.'

'Should I stop the blood pressure tablet?' → ★ 'No — please don't stop it. It's doing an important job. I'll review the dose and when you take it, and in the meantime: sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before standing, get up in stages, keep your fluids up, and avoid standing up quickly after a big meal.' / 'Is this another stroke coming? Tell me straight' → 'Nothing today suggests a stroke right now — your examination fits your old one, not a new one. But your risk of another is higher than average, and that's why we keep your blood pressure controlled. Warning signs: face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty — ring 000.'

★ 'A fall can cause a head injury — bleeding around the brain — which can be life-threatening. It can cause fractures, most importantly the hip, which usually means an operation and a long rehabilitation. People often lose independence afterwards. And falls create a fear of falling — people move less, get weaker, and fall more; having fallen is the strongest predictor of falling again. So what we aim to do is prevent falls by reducing the risk factors.'

Examiner: 'He has already had a stroke — why is stroke still on your list?' → ★ 'Because a previous stroke is the single strongest predictor of a further stroke, and a recurrent stroke or TIA can present as falls rather than as an obvious deficit. Excluding it because he has already had one would be the wrong way round — it is the reason he is on secondary prevention.'
pefe: Role-player: John, 60, retired storeman, married to Marie, single-storey house with two front steps; straightforward, a bit deflated since the stroke; frightened it means another stroke. Four falls, all on getting up; never LOC; bruised hip once. Residual left arm/leg weakness, speech recovered. Hypertension 10 y, one tablet every morning, adherent, regular GP. SOB gardening volunteered only under CVS questions — if you move on without follow-up, he never raises it again. Points to epigastrium under abdo pain; 'no, no and no' to reflux/NSAIDs/weight loss. Asks once 'should I stop the tablet?' and 'is this another stroke coming?'. Does not volunteer flat mood, balance, or the exact number of falls

PEFE: alert, no pallor · ★ sitting 120/80 → standing 94/56 · pulse regular · ★ L arm and leg 3/5, R normal, sensation intact · fundi/acuity normal · HS normal, chest clear · mild epigastric tenderness, no mass · TUG prolonged · glucose normal · dipstick negative · ECG SR. Postural drop criterion: ≥20 systolic OR ≥10 diastolic within 3 min (some references 15 systolic; no dispute about the 10) — EITHER is enough

Variant A — diastolic-only drop: 134/86 → 122/72 = 12 systolic (below), ★ 14 diastolic (above) → positive; this has appeared because candidates check the systolic, see 12, and call it negative — read both numbers every time · Variant B — 'actually I think I do go out for a moment' → syncope structure: prodrome, standing/exertion/head-turn, duration, recovery, witness, tongue/incontinence, FHx sudden cardiac death; examination + ECG carry the weight

Non-drug measures for postural drop: rise in stages · fluids · avoid large hot meals and alcohol · compression stockings · head-up bed tilt · review all BP-lowering drugs (every antihypertensive class can cause it — adherence does not exonerate the drug) · IHD work-up: ECG, troponin if acute, echo, stress testing, lipids, HbA1c · epigastric pain: FBE (anaemia), H. pylori/endoscopy if persistent, consider cardiac referral · secondary prevention: antiplatelet, statin, BP; check adherence
MRC power: 0 nil · 1 flicker · 2 moves with gravity eliminated · ★ 3 against gravity not resistance · 4 against some resistance · 5 normal · Case 1 companion (Robert, diabetic) = MED-107

SA: physio (post-stroke balance), OT home (two front steps, rails), Country Health Connect, stroke secondary-prevention review, Austroads fitness to drive with residual weakness + postural drop + possible IHD — Motor Vehicles Act 1959 notification duty (confirm current requirement) · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if acute stroke

★ Never asking about residual weakness — treating the stroke as background, so cause two is missed
Skipping past the breathlessness; dropping the epigastric pain entirely (or never asking about anti-inflammatories)
★ Leaving stroke/TIA off the differentials 'because he's already had one' — backwards; a previous stroke raises the risk
Telling him to stop his antihypertensive; not offering non-drug measures
Not asking the change-of-position trigger question directly, so the pattern is never a documented positive; never asking about injury
No consequences (head injury, hip fracture) and no prevention line — fluent, confident, failed

setting: MM5 rural general practice, routine session. History 5 minutes (prompted at 5:00), then the PEFE card is handed over, then diagnosis and differentials. stem: Jenny, 40, presents with widespread aches and pains all over her body. Her ESR and CRP are normal. Her mother has rheumatoid arthritis and she is worried she has it too. She has previously been diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (5 minutes — you will be prompted)
Physical examination findings will be given to you on a card
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. First 30 s: WIPE · ★ 'are you in any pain right now — would you like something for it?' · open question → hostile opener ('nobody listens') → ★ VALIDATE the experience, promise the process, promise NOTHING about the outcome · ★ name the RA agenda and promise to return to it · site: 'joints or muscles?' → 'name me two or three spots' (ask twice, gently, never argue) · duration, onset, constant, character, severity, ★ 'how is this affecting your life?' (early) · ★ PATTERN: night, morning vs evening, rest vs activity, morning stiffness duration → 'makes no difference' = the diagnosis · swelling, rash, trauma · ★ announce EIGHT differential groups aloud, organic first: (1) malignancy (2) infection incl travel/bites/sexual (3) joints/family/psoriasis/Raynaud/gout/reactive (4) muscle/drugs/statin, PMR girdle + GCA screen (5) neuro incl concentration (6) endocrine thyroid/diabetes (7) psychosocial LAST and announced — mood, sleep, home, work, function, one risk question, 45 s (8) SADMA → concerns · card → synthesise, not recite · name fibromyalgia, explain, ★ refute RA with five features she does not have · DDx by group · plan, safety-net, review 4 wk.

back.dx: Fibromyalgia (Version A) — >1 year of constant deep dull ache in neck, shoulders, back, arms, legs (7–8/10), neither inflammatory nor mechanical ('it makes no difference'), few minutes of morning stiffness only, unrefreshing sleep, exhaustion, cognitive 'fog', IBS, two stressors (daughter's final school year, relentless work), reduced function; all organic groups negative; card: tender points at trapezius, occiput, 2nd costochondral, lateral epicondyles, greater trochanters, medial knees with NO swelling/redness/deformity, full painless ROM, normal neuro/thyroid/dipstick; ESR 8, CRP 2, FBE/TSH/CK/Ca normal. Diagnosis of exclusion reached in a defensible order. Hidden agenda: 'do I have what my mother has?' — refute RA with her own findings, not reassurance.

('I'm always in pain — that's the point') · 'tell me in your own words' → 'four doctors, all normal, nobody listens, mum has RA' · ★ 'I can hear how overwhelming this has been, and I'm sorry you've had that experience. Your pain is real and I take it seriously.' · ★ 'thank you for telling me about your mum — I'll ask specifically about RA and come back to it before you leave'

Site: 'where exactly?' → 'everywhere' → 'joints or muscles?' → 'I don't know' → ★ 'name me two or three spots' → neck, shoulders, back, arms, legs · duration (>1 y), onset (crept), constant, dull/sharp, /10, better/worse (nothing) · ★ 'how is this affecting your life?' → exhausted, cut hours, no friends
★ Pattern: wakes at night? morning or evening? rest or activity? ★ morning stiffness — how long? → 'makes no difference', a few minutes · swelling, redness/rash, injury/trauma/MVA

★ 'I'm going to run through a checklist of causes — some will sound unrelated' · 'first some serious causes': weight loss, appetite, lumps, night sweats, bone pain at night · 'now infections': fever/chills, flu-like illness, travel, sick/animal contacts, tick/insect bites, sexually active/condoms

'Now your joints': occupation/repetitive work, ★ FHx arthritis (mum RA), deformity, rash/scaly patches/nail change (psoriatic), fingers change colour in cold (Raynaud), worse after red meat/alcohol (gout), diarrhoea/blood/discharge (reactive/IBD) → IBS · 'now muscles': ★ any medications incl chemist (statin), ★ shoulder + hip girdle stiffness, rising from chair, combing hair, ★ new headache/scalp tenderness/jaw pain chewing/vision (PMR/GCA)

'A few nerve questions': pins and needles, weakness, walking, speech, vision, ★ concentration → 'fog' (note; use later as fibromyalgia evidence, not a red flag) · 'hormone questions': cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair, weight; thirst, polyuria

★ Psychosocial, announced, 45 s: 'pain that goes on this long affects far more than the body — may I ask how you've been in yourself?' → mood (flat, frustrated), sleep (bad, never refreshed), home (husband, daughter final year), work (relentless), function, ★ 'I ask everyone with long-standing pain — any thoughts of harming yourself?' → never · SADMA: smoking, alcohol (2 glasses/wk), drugs, allergies, PMHx/ops, FHx · 'anything I haven't asked that you were hoping to discuss?'

Card → ★ synthesise aloud: 'looks well, afebrile, no rash/cachexia/lymphadenopathy; tenderness at multiple sites but no swelling, no redness, no deformity, full painless ROM; neuro and thyroid normal; ESR 8, CRP 2, FBE/TSH/CK/Ca normal — the combination of widespread tenderness with a normal joint examination and normal inflammatory markers excludes an inflammatory arthritis and supports fibromyalgia'

★ Name fibromyalgia · explain: widespread pain without structural damage; pain-signalling system over-sensitive — 'volume dial turned up too high' — also the tiredness, poor sleep, fog and IBS · ★ 'it is a real, recognised medical condition — not in your head and not your fault' · ★ RA refuted with HER findings: swollen joints, >1 h morning stiffness, worse after rest/better with movement, deformity, raised markers — 'you have none of those' — 'the two can occasionally coexist, so if anything changes we look again' · DDx by group with why set aside: cancers (no weight loss/sweats/lumps, FBE normal), infections, other arthritides (psoriatic, gout, reactive, lupus), muscle (no statin, CK normal), PMR (age, not girdle), MS (no neuro), thyroid/Ca normal

Plan: ★ graded gentle exercise (start lower than you think), sleep work, psychologist for coping ('not because it's imaginary'), a night-time tablet for pain and sleep, chronic disease management plan → physio/exercise physiologist · safety-net: fever, weight loss, swollen joint, new weakness/numbness · review 4 wk · written info · 'any questions?'
ask: ★ 'Before we start — are you in any pain right now? Would you like something for it before we talk?' / ★ 'I can hear how overwhelming this has been for you, and I'm sorry you've had that experience with other doctors. Your pain is real and I take it seriously.'

★ 'Thank you for telling me about your mum — I'll ask specifically about rheumatoid arthritis and I'll come back to it before you leave.' / 'Is it the joints that ache, or the muscles? … Can you name me two or three spots where you feel it most?' / 'How is this pain affecting your life?'
★ 'Is it worse in the morning or the end of the day? Worse with rest or with activity? Do you feel stiff in the mornings, and roughly how long before you loosen up?'

★ 'I'm going to run through a checklist of possible causes — some questions will sound unrelated, but I ask them of everyone with this problem. Let me first check some serious causes … now some questions about infections … now about your joints … now your muscles and soft tissues … a few nerve questions … some hormone questions.'

'Any pain and stiffness across both shoulders and hips? Do you struggle to get out of a chair or comb your hair? Any new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain on chewing, or change in vision?' / 'Are you taking any medications at all, including from the chemist?'

★ 'Jenny, pain that goes on this long affects far more than the body — may I ask a few questions about how you've been in yourself? How has your mood been? Your sleep? Who's at home, and is anything stressful going on? Work? Are you managing your usual activities? And I ask this of everyone with long-standing pain — have you had any thoughts of harming yourself?'
★ To examiner/aloud: 'There is tenderness in many places, but your joints are not swollen, not red, not deformed, they all move fully and painlessly, and your inflammation tests are normal.'

★ 'I think the most likely explanation is a condition called fibromyalgia. It causes widespread pain all over the body without any structural damage in the muscles or the joints. The system that carries pain signals becomes over-sensitive — a bit like a volume dial turned up too high, so ordinary signals are felt as pain. That's also why it brings the tiredness, the poor sleep, the foggy concentration and the irritable bowel. It is a real, recognised medical condition. It is not in your head and it is not your fault.'

★ 'I promised I'd come back to rheumatoid arthritis. In rheumatoid arthritis I would expect swollen joints, stiffness lasting more than an hour in the mornings, pain worse after rest and better with movement, often joint deformity, and raised inflammation in the blood. You have none of those. So I don't think you have rheumatoid arthritis — though the two can occasionally occur together, so if anything changes we will look again.'

'The most useful treatment is gentle, graded exercise — starting much lower than you think and building slowly. We'll work on your sleep, and I'd like to offer you a psychologist to help with coping — not because the pain is imaginary, but because pain this persistent wears people down. Come back if you get fever, weight loss, a swollen joint, or new weakness or numbness.' / if 'so it's in my head as well?' → 'No. It is a real condition with a physical mechanism; the stress makes it worse, it did not create it.'

Volunteers the concern in the last minute if never asked: 'I just want to know whether I've got what my mother has'. If explained badly: 'so you're saying it's in my head as well'

PEFE card: looks well, not cachectic/pale, no rash · T 36.8, P 76, BP 122/78, weight stable · tender: trapezius, occiput, 2nd costochondral junctions, lateral epicondyles, greater trochanters, medial knees · no swelling/redness/deformity, full painless ROM · neuro normal, no lymphadenopathy, thyroid normal, dipstick negative · ESR 8, CRP 2, FBE/TSH/CK/corrected Ca normal

CORRECTION: do not count tender points — 1990 ACR 11/18 superseded; current: widespread pain in ≥4 of 5 body regions for ≥3 months with the symptom cluster (fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive symptoms), after exclusion; no confirmatory test · brief morning stiffness of minutes is compatible with fibromyalgia; inflammatory threshold ~45–60 min in a girdle distribution

stem: A 72-year-old man presents with aches and pains all over his body for the past few weeks. He is otherwise well. Observations are normal.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history
Physical examination findings will be given to you on a card
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. WIPE, pain now, validate · site: 'where exactly?' → ★ 'mainly my shoulders — both — and my hips' (the answer that changes everything) · ★ pattern: morning vs evening, rest vs activity, ★ 'how long does the stiffness last?' → 'a good hour and a half' = inflammatory · function: rising from a chair, combing hair, turning in bed, getting out of the car · ★ GCA screen — the marked item: new headache esp temples, scalp tenderness combing hair/on the pillow, jaw pain chewing that eases when stopping, visual change/blurring/diplopia/curtain · red flags: weight loss, appetite, sweats, fever, night bone pain · joints/swelling/rash/family · meds incl statin · neuro · endocrine · psychosocial briefly · SADMA · card → interpret · dx PMR with reasons · DDx: GCA, RA (late-onset/EORA), malignancy/myeloma, hypothyroidism, statin myopathy, fibromyalgia, OA, polymyositis (weakness not pain, CK), infection · plan: bloods + prednisolone 15 mg, response confirms, taper, bone protection, ★ GCA safety-net same day.

back.dx: Polymyalgia rheumatica — bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain, much worse in the morning, stiffness ~90 min, worse sitting still, eases with movement, age >50, systemically well; no GCA symptoms in the base version (harder variant: 'my scalp is sore when I comb my hair and my jaw aches after a few mouthfuls' → GCA — same-day high-dose steroid, do not wait for biopsy). Explain PMR as inflammation of the tissues around the shoulder and hip joints — bursae and tendon sheaths — NOT 'the immune system attacking the blood vessels in your shoulder' (that conflates it with GCA). Dramatic response to low-dose prednisolone within days helps confirm the diagnosis.

★ 'Where exactly is the pain?' → 'mainly my shoulders, both of them, and my hips' · onset (weeks), constant, character, severity · ★ 'how is it affecting your life?' → can't get out of a chair, can't lift arms to dress

★ 'I think you most likely have polymyalgia rheumatica. back.dx: Counselling: minimally displaced extra-articular Colles' fracture in POP — cast care, follow-up plan, and the minimal-trauma fracture conversation. Version A: straightforward trip on a hose, no presyncope; hidden agenda — husband Ray has Parkinson's, she does everything for him and is frightened she can't with one hand; deflects the first concern question ('not really, I just want to get home'), tells you on the second ask or a home-specific question, otherwise blurts it at 7:40. plan: 'I'm Dr —, one of the doctors here in Emergency. Are you Mrs Harper — Denise? Do you mind if I pull up a chair?' · ★ 'before we start on the plaster — how's the pain right now, out of ten?' (3/10) · ★ 'is there anything in particular worrying you about going home with this on?' → pause, 'not really' → note it

★ 'I'd like to cover five things: what you've actually broken, how to look after the plaster, the warning signs that would bring you straight back, the plan over the next six weeks, and one important thing about your bones. I'll stop at each so you can ask.'

(1) 'You've broken the end of the radius just above the wrist; the broken end has tipped slightly backwards — a Colles' fracture. The pieces are lined up well, so plaster rather than an operation. The plaster holds the ends still so the bone can knit, about six weeks. Thumb left out deliberately — a scaphoid would have the thumb wrapped in.'

(2) SWELLING: 'the plaster can't stretch, so we keep the swelling down three ways — arm up (sling by day; at night forearm on pillows, ★ hand above the heart), ice on top of the plaster in a bag/thin towel 15–20 min every 2–3 h for the first days, and ★ keep the fingers moving — full fist, straighten, every hour awake; moving them pumps the swelling out' · DRY: 'plaster of Paris goes soft if wet — two plastic bags taped to skin for showers, no baths/swimming for six weeks; if damp, hairdryer on ★ COOL only — never warm; you can burn skin you can't see' (sister's wet cast → 'hers may have been fibreglass; yours is plaster') · CLEAN: 'nothing down inside — no needles, pens, coat hangers; cool air for the itch; no powder/lotion/oil; don't trim the edges — ring us; rest it on something soft for a day or two while it hardens' · itch is normal — a fixed burning pain in one spot is a pressure sore · MOVING: 'fingers, elbow, shoulder all free and I want them used — the wrist is the only thing that stays still' · ★ 'let's get the rings off — if the fingers swell overnight a ring turns into a tourniquet'

(3) ★ 'Two things would make me want to see you straight away. First, if the plaster becomes too tight: pain getting worse rather than better, painkillers stop touching it, fingers numb or tingly, pale, blue or cold, can't move them or it hurts to straighten them — ★ come straight back here to Emergency, don't wait for the clinic; we can split the plaster in two minutes and that fixes it. Second, the skin underneath: fever, a bad smell, ooze or staining through the plaster, or a burning rubbing pain in one fixed spot — ★ same day, us or your GP. I'll write both lists down.' ('would I need a new one?' → 're-do once the swelling settles; splitting costs nothing, a tight plaster can cost you the use of your hand')

(4) Plan: ★ 'fracture clinic in one week with another X-ray — these occasionally slip in the first week or two and it's far easier to fix early; if it's holding, plaster stays until about six weeks and comes off at the clinic, not at home' · distance → PATS, coordinate the film locally VERIFY · ★ 'expect a stiff wrist and weaker arm when it comes off — normal, not a complication — I'll arrange physiotherapy / hand therapy; a couple of months of exercises to get movement and grip back' · 'will it go back to normal?' → honest

(5) ★ 'The most important part: you broke this bone falling from standing height, on the flat. A healthy bone at your age shouldn't break from a fall like that. We call that a minimal-trauma fracture — a signal the bone may be thinner than it should be: osteoporosis. I'd like to arrange a bone-density scan, a DEXA, and some blood tests, and your GP will go through the results. If the bones are thin there are very good treatments, and starting now substantially cuts the chance of the next fracture — which could be a hip. Is that something you'd be happy for me to organise?' ('my mother had a hip' → 'all the more worth doing — it runs in families')

I'd like to do three things: go through the picture with you, explain why it has happened, and talk about what we do about it — today and longer term. Please stop me at any point.' · ★ 'Before I start — has anything in particular been on your mind?' → 'no, not really'

★ Pick the film up, turn it to her: 'On any X-ray there are really only three colours. White is bone, grey is soft tissue and muscle, black is air. Today we're only interested in the white. This white column is your spine — built out of little blocks of bone stacked on each other; each block is a vertebra. Can you see them?' → 'like a row of bricks'

★ 'And in one of those blocks, here, I can see a break.' → 'actually broken?' → 'Yes. It's called a compression fracture, or a wedge fracture. It happens when the bone has become weak and fragile — so weak that even a small strain like lifting a bag is enough for the block to squash down and collapse at the front. When the front squashes and the back stays put, the block stops being a square and becomes a wedge — see it there, next to the square ones above and below?' · bound the fear: 'the spinal cord is not involved, the back wall is intact, your legs are working — this is not a break that needs an operation or a plaster' · 'does that make sense so far?'

★ 'But I only picked up a bag of shopping' → 'That is exactly the point — the most important thing I'll say today. A healthy bone would not break from lifting a bag of shopping. The fact that yours did tells us the bone itself is the problem. Can I explain why?'

★ 'The main cause is osteoporosis — which simply means the bones have become thin, weak and fragile. Picture the inside of a bone as a honeycomb: in osteoporosis the walls thin out and the spaces get bigger. There's usually more than one reason:' AGE · ★ MENOPAUSE — 'once the periods stop the drop in oestrogen speeds bone loss up a lot — the main reason women get this more than men' · CALCIUM/dairy · VITAMIN D/sunlight · EXERCISE ('if we don't use it we lose it') · ★ CONDITIONS AND MEDICINES — steroid tablets, long-term stomach-acid tablets · she offers PPI + no milk → ★ 'that's really useful — both are on my list and both are things we can do something about' (do NOT start asking smoking/menopause questions; 'that's something I'd want to check today')

Mother's hip surfaces ('am I going to end up like that?') → ★ 'Thank you for telling me — I can hear that it frightens you. I'm not going to pretend the risk is nothing. Treatment makes the bone stronger and lowers the chance of the next fracture — and a big part of what I'll suggest is aimed at making sure you don't have that fall in the first place.'

★ 'Two things to sort out, in order. First, the broken bone itself: pain relief taken REGULARLY — paracetamol 1 g four times a day, not just when it hurts; if that isn't holding it, something stronger for a few days with something for your bowels alongside. Rest when the pain demands it, but ★ NOT bed rest — lying in bed makes the bone thinner and you weaker; I want you up and doing as much of your normal day as the pain allows.
