'Are you in pain right now? Would you like something for it?' → 'I'll ask the nurse to organise pain relief now and we'll keep going' (no drug/dose/allergy detour)

'Show me where' → ★ 'Where did it start — was it always there, or did it begin somewhere else?' → belly button, moved overnight (do not diagnose aloud) · /10 (6) · sharp/dull (dull → sharper) · when (yesterday late afternoon) · constant · worse · travel (no) · better/worse (nothing; every bump in the car)

GI as a heading: nausea/vomiting (sick once this morning, after the pain), bloating, wind, D/C, fever ('might have felt hot last night') · ★ 'a few questions I ask everybody with tummy pain': weight loss, ★ appetite (none since yesterday — couldn't face toast), lumps, dizziness, blood/black motions, habit, FHx bowel cancer

Waterworks: burning, frequency, blood · groin lump · ★ 'I need to ask a few personal questions about your periods and sexual health, because some causes of this pain start in that area — is that all right?' → bleeding, discharge, LMP + regular (3 wk, regular), sexually active/condoms (one partner, most of the time), STI ever · ops, meds, allergies

★ Bell → examiner: general appearance · postural BP · inspection — moves with respiration, distension, scars, hernia, bruising · superficial and deep palpation — site of maximal tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound, mass · percussion tenderness · bowel sounds · inguinal region · DRE with consent and chaperone · ★ Rovsing and psoas

★ 'With the patient's consent and a chaperone present, I'd like to perform a pelvic examination: inspection — rash, lumps, bleeding, discharge; speculum — cervical discharge; bimanual — cervical motion tenderness, uterine size and tenderness, adnexal tenderness or mass' · ★ 'bedside tests — urine dipstick, urinary βhCG, capillary glucose' (LMP unreliable in early pregnancy; a missed ectopic is a preventable death)

★ 'Jenna, most likely you have acute appendicitis. The appendix is a small finger-shaped pouch attached to the large bowel on the right lower side of your tummy, and at the moment it's inflamed.' · 'Is it serious? will I need an operation?' → ★ 'it is something we take seriously, and yes — very likely an operation to remove it; usually keyhole, home within a day or two' · ★ four reasons: pain moved, appetite gone, feeling sick/vomited, specific tests positive

DDx in groups with a reason each: pregnancy — ectopic (normal period 3 wk ago, βhCG negative) · gynae — PID/torsion (no discharge, internal exam normal) · urinary — UTI/ureteric stone (no burning/blood, dipstick clear) · bowel — gastroenteritis/mesenteric adenitis (bug gives vomiting first + diarrhoea; neither) · plan: NBM, IV, fluids, analgesia, bloods, USS, surgical team on their way · safety-net: 'if the pain suddenly gets much worse or spreads across your whole tummy, tell the nurse straight away' · questions
ask: ★ 'Examiner, before I start — is my patient haemodynamically stable, and could I have the vital signs, please?' / ★ 'I'm really sorry to hear that, Jenna. The pain you're describing is concerning to me too. I'll need to ask you a few questions to get a better idea of what's going on, and I promise I'll take good care of you. Is that all right?'

★ 'Where did the pain start? Was it always in that spot, or did it begin somewhere else?' / 'On a scale of one to ten, how bad is it? Sharp or a dull ache? There all the time? Getting better or worse? Does it travel anywhere? Anything that makes it better or worse — food, movement, position?'

'A few questions I ask everybody with tummy pain: any weight loss? How has your appetite been? Lumps or bumps? Dizziness? Blood in the motions or black tarry motions? Change in bowel habit? Anyone in the family with bowel cancer?'

★ 'I need to ask a few personal questions about your periods and your sexual health, because some causes of this pain start in that area. Is that all right? Any vaginal bleeding or discharge? When was your last period, and are they regular? Are you sexually active, and do you use condoms? Have you ever been told you had a sexually transmitted infection?'

★ To examiner: '…on superficial and deep palpation — where is the tenderness maximal, is there guarding, is there rigidity, is there rebound tenderness, any mass? … the inguinal region, and with consent and a chaperone a rectal examination? And I'd like Rovsing sign and the psoas sign.' / ★ 'With the patient's consent and with a chaperone present, I would like to perform a pelvic examination … is there cervical motion tenderness, is the uterus of normal size and non-tender, and is there any adnexal tenderness or mass?' / ★ 'Bedside tests — a urine dipstick, a urinary βhCG, and a capillary blood glucose.'

If pushed on βhCG: 'I would still request it. The last menstrual period is unreliable in early pregnancy, and a missed ectopic is a preventable death, so I test every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain.'

★ 'Jenna, most likely you have a condition we call acute appendicitis. The appendix is a small finger-shaped pouch attached to the large bowel, on the right lower side of your tummy. At the moment that pouch is inflamed. There are four reasons I think that: your pain moved — it started around your belly button and settled in the right lower side; your appetite has gone since yesterday; you've been feeling sick and vomited; and when I examined you, the specific tests we use for appendicitis were positive.'

★ 'It is something we take seriously, and yes — it's very likely you'll need an operation to take the appendix out. It's usually keyhole surgery and most people go home within a day or two. The surgical team will come and talk you through it.' / 'A pregnancy sitting outside the womb — but your period was normal three weeks ago and the pregnancy test is negative. An infection of the womb and tubes, or a twisted ovary — but no discharge and the internal examination was normal. A bladder infection or a stone in the kidney tube — no burning, no blood, urine clear. A stomach bug or inflamed glands — a bug usually gives vomiting first and diarrhoea, and you have neither.'

'We'll keep you nil by mouth, put a drip in, give you fluids and pain relief, take some blood tests, and arrange an ultrasound. I'm asking the surgical team to come and see you. If at any point the pain suddenly gets much worse or spreads across your whole tummy, tell the nurse straight away.'

Version B: 'Those observations concern me. I can see you're not well — I'm going to ask a few quick questions and start treatment at the same time.' → examiner: two large-bore cannulas, bloods incl cultures and βhCG, fluid bolus, IV antibiotics, antiemetic, analgesia, NBM, urgent surgical review; 'in a rural site I would be ringing MedSTAR now' · ★ 'the pain that eased and then became generalised — I'm concerned about a perforated appendix with peritonitis and sepsis. Is the abdomen rigid, are bowel sounds absent, is there generalised rebound?' · 'I think the appendix has burst and the infection has spread; fluids and antibiotics now, the surgical team is coming — you'll need an operation today.'

Only says 'started around the belly button' if asked WHERE IT STARTED; only mentions the lost appetite if asked. Vomit came after the pain. Asks 'will I need an operation? how long in hospital?' once the diagnosis is named. 'Sorry, what does that mean?' to 'peritonism'/'ectopic'

PEFE Version A: uncomfortable, well hydrated, no postural drop · moves with respiration, no distension/scars/hernia · ★ RIF maximal tenderness with rebound + percussion tenderness, no guarding/rigidity, no mass · BS normal · inguinal normal · DRE unremarkable · ★ Rovsing +, psoas + · pelvic normal (no CMT, uterus normal, no adnexal tenderness/mass) · dipstick negative, βhCG negative, BSL 5.4

Three history key points: migration, anorexia, nausea/vomiting after pain. Three peritonism words: guarding, rigidity, rebound. Two named tests: Rovsing + psoas (or obturator). Alvarado 5–6 compatible, 7–8 probable, 9–10 very probable — not an Australian decision rule. Escalate: SBP <100, HR >100, T >38, rigid silent abdomen, positive βhCG with pain

Version B — day 3 perforated: 96/58, 118, 22, 38.7, lying still; resuscitate while talking (sepsis pathway: cultures, IV antibiotics per TG — e.g. amoxicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole or piperacillin-tazobactam VERIFY, fluids, analgesia, NBM, theatre) · Pregnant variant: tenderness may be higher; USS first, MRI if non-diagnostic, no CT; obstetrics + surgery; SA transfer to WCH · Adolescent with parent: add mesenteric adenitis question (recent sore throat/viral illness); no DRE; ask for time alone if a sexual history is needed

Investigations: FBE, CRP, UEC, LFT, lipase, βhCG, group and hold, urinalysis/MSU; USS first line (esp women of reproductive age), CT if USS non-diagnostic and not pregnant · management: NBM, IV fluids, analgesia (opioid does not mask signs), antiemetic, prophylactic antibiotics at induction, laparoscopic appendicectomy; interval/non-operative pathways are specialist decisions
SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · WCH for the pregnant patient · TIS 131 450
fails: Never asking where the pain STARTED — the single most valuable item; never asking appetite or the vomiting-versus-pain order
Skipping the stability question because the numbers are on the door (in Version B it is the whole station)
Ninety seconds on allergies/what she took/which drug/dose — a whole differential group unasked; going straight from her sentence to 'when did it start?' with no acknowledgement
Omitting the gynae/sexual group, or asking it without permission; 'her period was three weeks ago so I wouldn't test' — no βhCG
A vague 'examine the abdomen' — findings only come for named items; no pelvic exam with consent/chaperone; not naming a special test
Differentials as a flat list without ectopic, or without a reason each; leaving 'will I need an operation?' to the surgeons
Version B: taking a leisurely history without starting resuscitation; not naming the eased-then-generalised pain as perforation

Escalate: SBP <100, HR >100, T >38, rigid silent abdomen, +βhCG with pain · pregnant: USS → MRI, no CT · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

setting: ED. Version A of the central/periumbilical pain trio (Doug / Marion / Reg — Versions B and C are MED-118 and MED-119). Findings only for what you name; the inguinal region and the rectum are two separate named steps. Four cardinal features of obstruction, four adult causes, and a cause must be named — 'obstruction' with no cause is a fail.

Ask the examiner for the examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient

(colicky), onset, worse, radiation, better/worse · ★ obstruction block: vomiting — how many, ★ colour ('is any of it green?'), faeculent smell; distension; ★ 'when did you last pass WIND? when did you last open your bowels?' (absolute constipation — patients don't use the word) · ★ cause block: previous abdominal operation (appendicectomy in his 20s), groin lump/hernia, weight loss/PR blood/change in habit (tumour), chronic constipation · ischaemia block: palpitations/AF, MI/stroke/DVT, post-prandial pain and food fear · closure: urinary, rash/injury, smoking/alcohol/drugs/meds (anticoagulants, NSAIDs)/allergies, PMHx/FHx · examiner, seven steps named: appearance, four vitals, inspection (distension, scars, ★ visible peristalsis), palpation (tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound, masses), percussion (tympanic/dull), ★ auscultation (present/absent/tinkling), ★ inguinal region and scrotum, ★ DRE — rectum full or empty, dipstick + BSL · dx + CAUSE + layman explanation · grouped DDx · management: drip and suck.

back.dx: Small bowel obstruction from adhesions (appendicectomy in his twenties) — colicky central pain 8/10, four vomits with the last two green and bitter, distended, no flatus for two days, no motion for three; no groin lump. PEFE: distended, generally tender with guarding, hyper-resonant, bowel sounds absent, appendicectomy scar, no groin lump, rectum empty. Explain adhesions without sounding accusatory: 'bands of scar are normal healing, not a mistake; years later one can kink or squeeze a loop'. Management: drip and suck (NBM, IV fluids, NG tube), analgesia, antiemetic, IDC for fluid balance, bloods, AXR/CT, surgical team; most adhesive SBO settles in 1–2 days; operate if it doesn't or if any sign of strangulation.
plan: ★ Stability question · 'I'm Dr —, am I speaking with Doug? I can see you're in a lot of pain — would you like something for it before we start? Tell me what's been happening.'

★ Cause: 'ever had an operation on your abdomen?' → appendix in his 20s · 'any lump or swelling in your groin, ever told you have a hernia?' · weight loss, blood in motions, change in habit · long-term constipation · ischaemia: racing/irregular heartbeat, AF, heart attacks/strokes/clots, pain after meals/avoiding food
Closure: burning/frequency/haematuria · rash/injury · smoking, alcohol, drugs, ★ medicines incl blood thinners and anti-inflammatories, allergies · PMHx, FHx · summarise back

★ Examiner, seven steps: appearance (alert, distressed, dehydrated) · four vitals incl temperature · inspection — distended, moves with respiration, scars, ★ visible peristalsis · palpation — tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound, masses · percussion — tenderness, resonant or dull · ★ auscultation — present, absent, or high-pitched tinkling · ★ inguinal region and scrotum — any lump · ★ DRE — rectum full or empty · dipstick, BSL → distended, generally tender with guarding, hyper-resonant, BS absent, scar, no groin lump, rectum empty

★ 'Doug, your bowel is blocked — a small bowel obstruction — and the most likely cause is scar tissue from your appendix operation. Whenever the inside of the tummy is operated on, the body lays down bands of scar — that's normal healing, not a mistake. Years later one of those bands can kink or squeeze a loop of bowel and nothing gets past. That explains the gripping pain, the vomiting, the swelling and no wind.' · DDx grouped with a reason: other blockage causes — hernia (groin normal), growth (no weight loss/bleeding/habit change), twist; outside blockage — blocked blood supply, pancreatitis, ulcer, kidney stone (pain pattern and clear urine argue against)

'You stay in hospital. Nothing by mouth, a drip for fluids, a small tube through the nose to drain the stomach — drip and suck. Pain relief, anti-nausea, a catheter to measure fluid balance, bloods and an X-ray/CT of the abdomen, and the surgical team will see you. Most blockages from scar tissue settle in a day or two without an operation. If it doesn't settle, or there's any sign the bowel is being strangled, we operate.' · questions, someone to call
ask: ★ 'Examiner, before I begin — may I confirm the patient is haemodynamically stable? Blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation.' / 'I can see you're in a lot of pain. Would you like something for it before we start?'

★ 'And — this is important — when did you last pass wind? When did you last open your bowels?'

★ 'Have you ever had an operation on your abdomen? Any lump or swelling in your groin, or have you ever been told you have a hernia? Any weight loss, blood in your bowel motions, or change in your bowel habit?' / 'Any racing or irregular beating of your heart? Do you get cramping pain in your tummy after meals?'

★ To examiner: 'Inspection — is the abdomen distended, moving with respiration, any scars, any visible peristalsis? … Auscultation — are bowel sounds present, absent, or high pitched and tinkling? The inguinal region and scrotum — any lump or swelling? Digital rectal examination — is the rectum full or empty?'

★ 'Doug, your bowel is blocked — a small bowel obstruction — and the most likely cause is scar tissue from your appendix operation. Any operation inside the tummy leaves bands of scar tissue — that is normal healing, not a mistake. Years later a band can kink or squeeze a loop of bowel, and nothing gets past.'

'Nothing by mouth, a drip for fluids, and a small tube through the nose to drain the stomach — we call it drip and suck. Pain relief, something for the nausea, a catheter so we can measure your fluid balance, bloods and an X-ray of the abdomen, and the surgical team will see you. pefe: Role-player: Doug, 50; colicky central pain 8 h, 8/10; four vomits, last two green; distended; no wind 2 d, no motion 3 d; appendicectomy in his twenties; no groin lump; doesn't volunteer flatus until asked
PEFE: distended, generally tender with guarding, hyper-resonant, bowel sounds absent, appendicectomy scar, no groin lump, rectum empty

Four cardinal features: colicky pain · vomiting (bilious → faeculent) · distension · absolute constipation (no flatus). Four adult causes: adhesions · hernia · tumour · volvulus. Small bowel on AXR: valvulae conniventes, full width, central; large bowel: haustra, partial, peripheral; erect film for air-fluid levels. CT abdomen with contrast is the definitive test (transition point, closed loop, ischaemia). Gastrografin challenge: contrast reaching the colon within 24 h predicts non-operative resolution VERIFY

Eight-step resuscitation — imaging is step seven: NBM · IV access + bloods (FBE, UEC, VBG/lactate, lipase, G&H) · fluids · NG tube · analgesia · antiemetic · IDC · imaging · surgical referral. Strangulation signs: constant pain, peritonism, fever, tachycardia, leucocytosis, raised lactate → theatre. Harder variants: sigmoid volvulus (elderly, gross distension, coffee-bean loop from the pelvis → flexible sigmoidoscopic decompression, surgery if it fails/ischaemia) · ruptured AAA (older smoker, central/back pain, faint, pulsatile mass — stop the history and say so; recognising when to stop is scored) · ischaemic colitis (anticoagulated, crampy left pain, bloody diarrhoea settling — supportive care; thumbprinting is colonic)
SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for a rural site needing theatre · TIS 131 450
fails: Skipping the stability question in an ED stem
Accepting 'no constipation' — never asking about flatus; not probing vomit colour
★ Naming obstruction with no cause; never asking about previous surgery or a groin lump
Not requesting the inguinal region and the rectum as named steps; ★ claiming a finding never requested
Explaining adhesions as a surgical error; omitting NG tube/drip-and-suck; sending for imaging before resuscitation in a peritonitic patient
numbers: Four cardinal features · four adult causes · eight-step resuscitation, imaging step seven · adhesive SBO settles in 1–2 d in most
AXR: SB valvulae conniventes central full-width; LB haustra peripheral · erect film air-fluid levels · Gastrografin to colon within 24 h predicts resolution VERIFY

★ 'Marion, that lump in your groin is a hernia — a weak spot in the muscle wall that a loop of bowel pushes through. Normally it slides back. Yours has become trapped, and the opening has tightened enough to squeeze off its blood supply. That's what's causing the pain around your belly button and the vomiting, because the bowel is also blocked.' · 'but I've had it for years' → 'while it was going back in, it was safe; what has changed is that it stopped going back and became sore — that's the point it becomes an emergency, and you were right to come in' · DDx grouped: adhesions (no surgery), tumour, volvulus; ischaemia, pancreatitis, ulcer, stone

Acute mesenteric ischaemia: SMA embolus (AF, recent MI, valve) ~50%; SMA thrombosis on chronic atherosclerosis (post-prandial pain, food fear, weight loss = 'intestinal angina'); non-occlusive (low flow, vasopressors); mesenteric venous thrombosis (hypercoagulable). Early: pain out of proportion, soft abdomen, gut emptying (vomiting/diarrhoea); late: peritonitis, bloody stool, sepsis, acidosis. Lactate/VBG (normal early does not exclude), leucocytosis, amylase; CT angiography (arterial + venous phase) is the test — plain CT misses it. Erythema nodosum causes: IBD and sarcoidosis first; then streptococcal infection, TB, drugs (OCP, sulfonamides), pregnancy, idiopathic. Extra-intestinal IBD: EN, pyoderma, aphthous ulcers, uveitis/episcleritis, arthritis/spondylitis, PSC, clubbing. Crohn vs UC: Crohn — mouth to anus, skip lesions, perianal disease, strictures/fistulae, transmural; UC — rectum upward, continuous, bloody diarrhoea. Paediatric Crohn induction: exclusive enteral nutrition first line; UC: 5-ASA; steroids/immunomodulators/biologics per specialist; growth monitoring; bone health; vaccination before immunosuppression

Faecal calprotectin distinguishes inflammatory from functional (normal makes IBD very unlikely — harder variant: otherwise well teen with normal bloods and calprotectin → functional named, with exclusion criteria said aloud). IBS: no alarm features, generally <50, no nocturnal symptoms. Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA + total IgA) while eating gluten. Stool MCS, C. difficile, Giardia

back.dx: Coeliac disease — gluten-related bloating and discomfort for months, steatorrhoea (bulky, pale, offensive, floats, needs two flushes = fat malabsorption), iron deficiency anaemia unresponsive to oral iron, tiredness. Explain: gluten (wheat, barley, rye) triggers the immune system to attack the small bowel lining; the finger-like villi flatten so fat and iron aren't absorbed — greasy stools and iron tablets that don't work. Before I say another word about diet, one thing matters more than everything else: keep eating your normal diet, including bread and pasta, until the tests are done. If you stop gluten now, the blood test and the biopsy can both come back falsely normal, and we'd have to ask you to eat it again for six weeks and start over.' · three reasons: bloating with bread/pasta; bulky pale stools hard to flush = fat not absorbed; iron deficiency not responding to iron · DDx: IBS, lactose intolerance, IBD, giardiasis, pancreatic insufficiency, other causes of iron deficiency (GI blood loss — ask)

Plan: ★ blood test today (tTG-IgA + total IgA; FBE, iron studies, B12, folate, vitamin D, LFT, TSH, Ca), then gastroscopy with small-bowel biopsies, and only then the diet — lifelong, with a dietitian · 'is it serious? forever? will my kids get it?' → manageable; yes, for life — small amounts keep the damage going; it runs in families — first-degree relatives should be tested; Coeliac Australia · bone density if long-standing · safety-net

★ 'Josh, I think this is coeliac disease. Before I say another word about diet, one thing matters more than everything else: keep eating your normal diet, including bread and pasta, until the tests are done. If you stop gluten now, the blood test and the biopsy can both come back falsely normal, and we'd have to ask you to eat it again for six weeks and start over. So the order is: blood test, then a gastroscopy with small biopsies, and only then the diet — which will be lifelong, and which a dietitian will help you with.'

'Gluten — a protein in wheat, barley and rye — triggers your immune system to attack the lining of your small bowel. The tiny finger-like folds that absorb food get flattened, so you don't absorb fat or iron properly. That is why the stools are greasy and why the iron tablets haven't worked.'

'It's a lifelong condition, but it's completely manageable, and people who stick to the diet feel entirely well. Yes, it is for life — even small amounts of gluten keep the damage going. It does run in families, so your first-degree relatives should be tested, and that will include any children. Coeliac Australia is genuinely useful for the practical side.'

Coeliac in Australia: ~1 in 70; first-degree relatives ~1 in 10; associations — T1DM, autoimmune thyroid, Down syndrome, IgA deficiency (hence total IgA), dermatitis herpetiformis. Gluten challenge ~4 slices bread/day for 6 weeks VERIFY. Treatment: strict lifelong GFD, dietitian, correct deficiencies (iron, folate, B12, vit D, Ca), DEXA, pneumococcal vaccine (hyposplenism) VERIFY, repeat serology at 6–12 months, screen relatives; oats controversial in Australia VERIFY

Iron deficiency in a young man is GI until proven otherwise — coeliac serology + consider endoscopy; ask about PR blood, melaena, NSAIDs. Secondary lactose intolerance is common at diagnosis and improves on GFD

Opioid-induced constipation: reduced motility, increased tone/sphincter, reduced secretions — dose-related, no tolerance. Panadeine Forte = paracetamol 500 mg + codeine 30 mg (S4; OTC codeine ended in Australia 2018). Management: stop/reduce opioid; osmotic laxative (macrogol) ± stimulant (senna/bisacodyl); suppository/enema for rectal loading; PAMORAs for chronic opioid use (specialist). Avoid bulk-forming alone in opioid constipation. Fibre 25–30 g/day, fluids, exercise VERIFY

Always βhCG in a 20-year-old with lower abdominal pain
Codeine counselling: also drowsiness, dependence, not for chronic non-cancer pain; ultra-rapid metabolisers; not in breastfeeding · SA: healthdirect 1800 022 222

stem: Ron Falzon, 60, presents with alternating constipation and diarrhoea, 5 kg of unintentional weight loss and some rectal bleeding. His aunt had bowel cancer. He says his screening test last year was normal.

Break the concern honestly: 'I am concerned about the possibility of a bowel cancer' — concerned, not certain; the test gives the answer within weeks.

I say this as a positive diagnosis of exclusion: no weight loss, no bleeding, no anaemia, no nocturnal symptoms, no mass, no family history, no dietary trigger, no travel, and she is not pregnant.' B: 'coeliac disease — gluten-related symptoms, steatorrhoeic stools, an iron deficiency anaemia I do not accept as menstrual until malabsorption is excluded, an itchy elbow rash consistent with dermatitis herpetiformis, and a sister with a gluten problem; a second contributor is the oral iron.' · DDx by group: malignancy (bowel; ★ ovarian — presents exactly like this) · obstruction (adhesions, hernia, volvulus, constipation — normal flatus, no surgery) · dietary (coeliac, lactose) · infection (giardia, post-infectious) · motility (drugs, diabetic enteropathy, hypothyroidism) · IBD · functional — IBS last, a diagnosis of exclusion · exclude pregnancy
ask: ★ 'When you say bloated, can you describe it for me? Is it that you're burping a lot, or passing more wind than usual, or is it that your tummy actually looks and feels swollen?' / ★ 'Does it ever wake you at night?'

★ 'I ask everybody these next questions, just to be safe. Any weight loss without trying? Change in appetite? Lumps or bumps? Unusually tired? Any blood or very dark stools? Any lasting change in bowel habit? Family history of bowel or ovarian cancer?'

★ 'Do you get full very quickly, after only a small amount of food? Any change in how often you pass urine? Have you ever had surgery on your tummy? Any lump or swelling in your groin? Are you passing wind normally?'

★ 'Heavy periods may well be part of it, but low iron can also mean the bowel isn't absorbing properly — are your stools greasy or bulky? Do they float, stick to the pan, or need flushing twice?' / 'Any rashes — particularly an itchy rash on the elbows or knees?'
★ 'When was your last period, are they regular, and is there any chance you could be pregnant?'

★ To examiner (A): 'My most likely diagnosis is irritable bowel syndrome … I say this as a positive diagnosis of exclusion …' / (B): 'My most likely diagnosis is coeliac disease. The symptoms are gluten-related, the stools are steatorrhoeic, and there is an iron deficiency anaemia that I do not accept as menstrual until malabsorption is excluded. She also describes an itchy rash on her elbows, which would be dermatitis herpetiformis. A genuine second contributor is her oral iron supplement.'

'In any woman with persistent bloating I would want to exclude ovarian cancer.' / 'I place irritable bowel syndrome last because it is a diagnosis of exclusion.' / B to patient: 'Please keep eating gluten until we've tested you — stopping it makes the tests come back falsely normal. Blood test today; if positive, a camera test with a small biopsy; then a dietitian, iron, vitamin D and bone checks, and testing for your sister and close relatives.'

Variant — already gluten-free: 'the blood test only works while you're eating gluten — I'd ask you to go back onto a normal diet for about six weeks before we test; a wrong answer here would follow you for life.' / 'Isn't this just IBS?' → 'It might be — but you have two things that don't fit it: stools that suggest you're not absorbing fat, and low iron. I'd rather check than assume.' / Ovarian version (she is 52): 'bloating, early fullness and passing urine more often can occasionally come from the ovaries — a pelvic ultrasound and a CA-125; not telling you it's sinister, telling you it's something I always check for.'
pefe: Role-player: Jenny Walker, 25, council depot admin, lives with partner, non-smoker, 4–6 SD/week, never had surgery; polite, self-conscious, braced for 'it's nothing'. Volunteers nothing; 'not really' to the general trigger question — pizza/bread only when food is named; stool character only when asked directly (flushes twice, thought it normal); offers the anaemia readily, always with 'they said it's my heavy periods'; sister's gluten problem and the elbow rash only if asked. Pushes at ~4 min 'do you think it's serious?'; volunteers the aunt's bowel cancer at 5:30 if concerns never asked. If told to stop gluten before testing: 'I'll start tonight' — marks an error

No examination in the standard station (piloted variant: 5 min history → examination → diagnosis). Version A key positives: bloating settles after defecation, alternating hard/loose, work stress. Version B: worse after pizza/bread, greasy bulky floating stools, iron-deficiency anaemia on iron tablets, itchy blistery rash on elbows, sister 'something to do with gluten', periods regular but heavy

Rome IV IBS: recurrent abdominal pain ≥1 day/week in the last 3 months, onset ≥6 months ago, with ≥2 of: related to defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form; no alarm features. Four meanings of 'bloating' → four differential groups (aerophagia/burping; flatulence — diet, lactose, coeliac, SIBO; distension — constipation, ascites, mass, obstruction; sensation — functional). Ovarian symptom index: persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic/abdominal pain, urinary frequency — >12 times a month, new onset → USS + CA-125 (mainly >50). Red-flag age for new bowel symptoms: >50

Coeliac: ~1 in 70; first-degree relatives ~1 in 10; tTG-IgA + total IgA while eating gluten; gluten challenge ~4 slices/day × 6 weeks VERIFY; biopsy confirmation; dermatitis herpetiformis = coeliac until proven otherwise; oral iron side effects — bloating, cramping, constipation, dark stools. setting: Regional SA general practice. Six-minute history, then diagnosis with reasons and differentials spoken to the examiner. Rare recall. The whole case turns on one exchange: the general aggravating-factor question gets 'no, not really' — the dairy trigger appears only when food is named, and then dairy is named. If the examiner says 'the group calls this abdominal migraine', don't just agree.
stem: Daniel Roberts, 20, apprentice diesel mechanic, complains of abdominal pain. T 36.6 · P 68 · BP 118/74 · RR 14 · BMI 23. Well.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Tell the examiner your most likely diagnosis, with your reasons
Give the examiner your differential diagnoses
time: 6 min. Intro, acknowledge, consent (pain, bowels, diet), concerns ('my mate reckons it's an ulcer') · ★ 'point to it with one finger' (vague periumbilical → small bowel), character (dull, crampy), radiation, /10 (3–4) · onset (6 mo), ★ episode duration (1–2 h), worse?, ★ 'does it ever wake you at night?' (never) · ★ 'anything that makes it better or worse?' → 'no, not really' → ★ DO NOT ACCEPT: 'what about food — dairy like milk, cheese, yoghurt or ice-cream? bread or pasta? fatty or fried meals?' → milk and ice-cream, an hour after, every time · ★ dose: small amount or big serve? hard cheese? · GI screen: N/V, ★ bloating/wind (lots, after dairy), ★ bowels (alternate), fever · ★ red flags 'I ask everybody': weight, appetite, tiredness, blood/mucus, fever/sweats · ★ IBD screen: mouth ulcers, joints, eyes, shin lumps, perianal pain/discharge, FHx Crohn/UC · ★ coeliac despite the dairy answer: bread/pasta/beer, greasy/pale/floating/hard-to-flush stools, FHx · infection/upper GI/surgical: travel/camping/tank water, reflux, NSAIDs, previous surgery, groin lump, ★ passing wind · IBS/social: relief with defecation, FHx bowel/cancer (mum's migraines), home/work stress ('honestly none'), smoking, alcohol, drugs · dairy named by 4:25, stop at 6:00 → speak the diagnosis → DDx by group.

back.dx: Lactose intolerance — reproducible bloating, wind, cramping and loose stools 30 min–2 h after milk and ice-cream (a milkshake is worst; cheese on toast is fine — dose-dependent), well between exposures, no red flags, no nocturnal symptoms, bread fine. IBS placed below it (stools alternate, but a reproducible food trigger takes precedence and IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion). Still exclude coeliac (causes secondary lactose intolerance) and IBD (must-not-miss at 20). Explain: enzyme (lactase) shortage, not an allergy — depends on the amount. Plan: FBE, iron, CRP, coeliac serology (while eating gluten); 2–4 week lactose exclusion then structured rechallenge to find his limit; dietitian for calcium/vitamin D; safety-net.
plan: Intro · 'months is a long time to put up with that — I'll ask about the pain, your bowels and your diet, then tell you what I think; anything you were worried about?' → ulcer

★ 'Where exactly — can you point with one finger?' (circles the umbilicus) · what does it feel like (dull, crampy) · moves anywhere (no) · /10 at worst (3–4) · when (6 mo) · ★ each bout (1–2 h) · worse? · ★ 'does it ever wake you at night?' (never)

★ 'Is there anything that makes it better or worse?' → 'no, not really' → ★ 'can I ask more specifically about food — is it worse after dairy, so milk, cheese, yoghurt or ice-cream? What about bread or pasta? Fatty or fried meals?' → 'actually — yeah. Milk and ice-cream. About an hour after, every time. Bread's fine.' → ★ 'does a small amount do it, or only a big serve? how about hard cheese?' → milkshake worst; cheese on toast fine

GI screen: N/V (no) · ★ bloating/wind (loads, after dairy) · ★ bowels (constipated ↔ loose) · fever · ★ 'these next ones I ask everybody': weight loss, appetite, tiredness, blood/mucus, fevers/night sweats · ★ IBD: mouth ulcers, joints, eyes, shin lumps, perianal pain/discharge, FHx Crohn/colitis → all no

★ Coeliac anyway: 'worse after bread, pasta or beer? stools ever greasy, bulky, pale, floating, hard to flush? family history?' → no · travel/camping/tank water · reflux/heartburn · ★ anti-inflammatories · previous surgery, groin lump · ★ passing wind normally

IBS/social: relief with defecation (not particularly) · FHx bowel problems/cancer (mum — migraines) · home/apprenticeship stress ('honestly, no stress') · smoking (social), alcohol (5–6 beers weekend), drugs · summarise

★ Aloud: 'My most likely diagnosis is lactose intolerance. His symptoms are reproducibly triggered within an hour or two of dairy, with bloating, wind and cramping, and he is well between exposures. I place irritable bowel syndrome below it: his stools do alternate, but IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion and a reproducible food trigger takes precedence. I would still exclude coeliac disease, because it causes secondary lactose intolerance, and inflammatory bowel disease, the must-not-miss diagnosis at his age.' · DDx by group: dietary/malabsorptive (lactose, coeliac, other carbohydrate intolerance) · inflammatory (Crohn, UC — no blood, nocturnal, weight loss, extra-intestinal features) · infective (giardia — no travel/tank water) · upper GI (PUD, functional dyspepsia, gallstones, chronic pancreatitis) · structural/surgical (constipation, hernia, adhesions) · functional (IBS, abdominal migraine — both require no better explanation, and here one exists)
ask: ★ 'Where exactly is the pain — can you point to it with one finger?' / ★ 'Does it ever wake you at night?' / 'How long does each bout last?'

★ 'Is there anything that makes it better or worse?' → 'no, not really' → ★ 'What about food? Is it worse after any particular food — dairy like milk, cheese, yoghurt or ice-cream? Bread or pasta? Fatty or fried meals?' / 'How soon afterwards, and does a small amount do it? How about hard cheese?'

★ 'These next ones I ask everybody. Any weight loss without trying? Change in appetite? Unusually tired? Any blood or mucus in your stool? Any mouth ulcers, joint pains, sore eyes, or tender red lumps on your shins? Any pain or discharge around the back passage? Anyone in the family with Crohn disease or colitis?'

★ 'Is it worse after bread, pasta or beer? Are your stools ever greasy, bulky, pale, floating or hard to flush?' / 'Any anti-inflammatory tablets? Any previous surgery, or a lump in your groin? Are you passing wind normally?'

★ To examiner: 'My most likely diagnosis is lactose intolerance … I place irritable bowel syndrome below it … I would still exclude coeliac disease, because it causes secondary lactose intolerance, and inflammatory bowel disease, which is the must-not-miss diagnosis at his age.'

To patient: ★ 'Your bowel is short of an enzyme called lactase, which normally breaks down a sugar called lactose in dairy foods. Without enough of it, the sugar passes through undigested, pulls water into the bowel and is fermented by the bacteria there — that produces the gas, bloating, cramping and loose motions an hour or so after dairy.' / 'So I'm allergic to milk?' → ★ 'Not quite — an allergy is the immune system reacting, and even a tiny amount causes trouble. This is an enzyme shortage, so it depends on the amount: a milkshake floors you, a bit of cheese may be fine.'

'Blood tests — full blood count, iron, an inflammation marker and a coeliac screen, because coeliac disease can cause exactly this as a knock-on effect. Then cut lactose out completely for two to four weeks, and if it settles bring it back gradually to find your limit. A dietitian so you don't lose calcium — that matters for your bones at your age. Come back sooner if you see blood, lose weight, get fevers, or the pain wakes you at night.'

Examiner 'isn't this abdominal migraine?' → ★ 'I did consider it. Abdominal migraine requires discrete episodes of midline pain with complete wellness between them, usually with anorexia, nausea or pallor, and critically the final criterion is that the pain is not better accounted for by another disorder. Here it is — there is a reproducible dairy trigger. The family history of migraine is background rather than evidence.' / 'My mate said it's an ulcer' → 'ulcers give burning pain higher up, often at night or when hungry, linked to anti-inflammatories or Helicobacter — none of that fits; yours is tied to dairy.'
pefe: Role-player: Daniel Roberts, 20, second-year apprentice diesel mechanic, lives with parents, social smoker, 5–6 beers on the weekend, no meds; laid back, brief, volunteers nothing, genuinely believes nothing makes it worse. 'No, not really' flatly to the general question — reveals dairy ONLY when milk/cheese/ice-cream is named; if never named, never revealed and the station fails. 'Honestly, there's no stress.' Mum's migraines only if family history asked. Pushes at ~4 min 'is it something serious?'. Marks an error if told to stop all dairy without calcium/bones/dietitian

No examination. Positives: periumbilical dull crampy pain 3–4/10, 1–2 h bouts, 6 months, never at night; reproducible after milk/ice-cream within an hour; bloating, wind, alternating stools; all red flags, IBD, coeliac, infection, surgical screens negative

Lactose intolerance: primary (adult-type hypolactasia — common in East Asian, Aboriginal, African, Mediterranean ancestry), secondary (coeliac, gastroenteritis, Crohn, giardia), congenital (rare). Onset 30 min–2 h after lactose. Hydrogen breath test: rise ≥20 ppm over baseline after 25–50 g lactose VERIFY; exclusion/rechallenge is the pragmatic GP test. Most tolerate ~12–15 g lactose/day (≈1 cup milk) in divided doses; hard cheese and yoghurt low-lactose; lactase enzyme drops/lactose-free milk; calcium 1000 mg/day + vitamin D VERIFY. IBS Rome IV: pain ≥1 day/week over 3 months, onset ≥6 months, 2 of 3. Abdominal migraine (Rome IV): paroxysmal midline pain ≥1 h, complete wellness between, ≥2 of anorexia/nausea/vomiting/headache/photophobia/pallor, not better explained

Harder version with red flags (blood, weight loss, night pain): 'not features I put down to a food intolerance' → FBE/CRP/iron, faecal calprotectin, gastroenterology for colonoscopy — 'these are the symptoms we don't sit on'
SA: Country Health Connect dietitian · healthdirect 1800 022 222

★ Not speaking the diagnosis aloud in full sentences
Skipping the nocturnal question, the one-finger localisation, or the episode duration
Omitting red flags/IBD screen because he's 20; finding the dairy trigger and stopping — no coeliac questions

Stopping all dairy with no calcium/vitamin D/dietitian; using 'no stress' to exclude IBS or the mother's migraines to reach for abdominal migraine; agreeing with the examiner's abdominal migraine prompt without argument

setting: ED. Door sheet: WCC raised, lipase markedly raised, AST/ALT 2–3× ULN, bilirubin normal. Three versions, one patient: A — twelve drinks on Saturday; B1 — known hypertriglyceridaemia (father too); B2 (the 2025 case) — semaglutide six months, 3 kg intentional loss, previous cholecystectomy. Four automatic fails: no cardiac question/ECG; mild transaminase rise called a second disease; weight loss treated as a red flag without asking intent; pancreatitis named with no cause sought.
stem: Steph Corrigan, 25, presents with severe epigastric pain since last night and repeated vomiting. Results: WCC raised · lipase markedly raised · AST and ALT 2–3× upper limit · bilirubin normal.
tasks: Take a focused history
Explain the results and your diagnosis
Give your differentials and management
time: 8 min. Stability (118/72, 104, 20, 37.4, 98%) · intro, ★ analgesia first, open · pain: where, /10 (9), ★ three epigastric add-ons — 'through to your back?' (yes), 'sitting forward or curling up help?' (a bit), 'what does food do?' (worse, not eating) · vomits ×5–6, bilious, blood?, bloating/wind/D/C/fever · ★ six cause questions in order: alcohol (standard drinks/week, heavy session?) · gallstones/gallbladder surgery (cholecystectomy 4 y) · medicines — NSAIDs, steroids, diuretics, ★ 'any injections for weight loss or diabetes — Ozempic, Wegovy, Trulicity?' · cholesterol/triglycerides/FHx, calcium · ERCP/trauma · viral illness · ★ cardiac: chest pain/tightness, SOB, sweating, jaw/arm — 'I would like an ECG' · red flags: weight loss → ★ 'was that on purpose?' (yes — the injection), appetite, dysphagia, haematemesis/melaena, lumps, FHx · urinary · SADMA · summarise · explain each result in plain words · dx + CAUSE · DDx · management spoken: admit, fluids (the single most important treatment), analgesia, antiemetic, USS, lipids + Ca, early feeding, no routine antibiotics, stop the GLP-1 and report the reaction.

back.dx: Acute pancreatitis — 9/10 epigastric pain boring through to the back, eased sitting forward, food makes it worse, bilious vomiting ×5–6, lipase markedly raised. Cause by version: A alcohol (twelve drinks Saturday); B1 severe hypertriglyceridaemia (inherited — father); B2 semaglutide — no alcohol, no lipid disorder, gallbladder out four years ago (choledocholithiasis still possible — look), pancreatitis is a recognised uncommon effect of GLP-1 agonists → stop it, report it, 'you haven't done anything wrong'. Mildly raised AST/ALT are expected with pancreatitis and prompt a gallstone look, not a second disease; normal bilirubin suggests the main duct isn't blocked. 3 kg loss was intentional — a therapeutic effect, not a red flag.
plan: ★ 'Examiner, may I confirm she is haemodynamically stable — BP, HR, RR, T, sats?' · 'I'm Dr —, am I speaking with Steph? You look like you're in a lot of pain — would you like something for it before we start? Tell me what's been happening.'

'Show me where. Out of ten? Sharp, or deep and boring? ★ Does it go through to your back? ★ Does sitting forward or curling up make any difference? ★ And what does food do to it — better, worse, no change?' → 9, through to the back, forward helps, hasn't eaten

★ Six causes: 'alcohol — standard drinks in a usual week, any heavy session in the last few days?' · 'ever told you have gallstones, or had surgery on your gallbladder?' (out 4 y) · 'anti-inflammatories, steroids, water tablets? ★ any injections for weight loss or diabetes — Ozempic, Wegovy, Trulicity?' (Ozempic 6 months) · 'high cholesterol or triglycerides — anyone in the family? calcium/parathyroid?' · 'recent camera test of the bile duct, injury to the tummy?' · 'recent viral illness?'

★ Cardiac: chest pain/tightness, SOB, sweating, jaw/arm, cough/fever → 'I would like an ECG' · red flags: 'any weight loss?' → 3 kg → ★ 'was that on purpose?' → yes → 'that's the treatment working, not a warning sign' · appetite, dysphagia, haematemesis, melaena, lumps, FHx GI cancer · urinary · smoking, drugs, meds, allergies, PMHx/ops · summarise back

★ Results in plain words: lipase — 'an enzyme your pancreas makes; when it's inflamed it leaks into the blood; yours is very high — with this pain, the pancreas is inflamed' · WCC — 'your body's response to inflammation, not necessarily infection' · AST/ALT — 'liver tests only slightly up; expected with pancreatitis, not a separate liver problem — but it makes me want to check for a gallstone' · bilirubin normal — 'reassuring; the main bile tube isn't blocked at the moment'

★ Dx + cause: A 'acute pancreatitis, most likely caused by alcohol' (without moralising; offer help) · B1 'caused by very high triglycerides — high enough to inflame the pancreas directly; inherited — family should be checked' · B2 'the most likely trigger is the weight-loss injection, and we should stop it' → 'but why? I don't drink, no gallbladder' → 'the two commonest causes don't fit; stones can still form in the duct, so we'll look; the injection can, uncommonly, inflame the pancreas — I can't prove it today but it's high on my list' → 'have I done something wrong?' → 'not at all — an uncommon reaction to a medicine used properly' · DDx: duct stone, perforated ulcer (abdomen not rigid), cholecystitis (no gallbladder), MI (ECG)

★ Management: 'you need to come into hospital: rest the gut, a drip and plenty of fluids — the single most important treatment; strong pain relief; anti-nausea; ultrasound of the bile ducts; more bloods including cholesterol and calcium; regular review over 48 h; ★ eating again as soon as you can tolerate it — starving for days is old practice; ★ no antibiotics unless a specific infection' · B2: stop semaglutide, report the adverse reaction (TGA), discuss a safer option later · B1: fasting, sometimes insulin infusion, then fibrate, low-fat diet, no alcohol · A: alcohol conversation · rural → MedSTAR if severe
ask: ★ 'Does the pain go through to your back? Does sitting forward or curling up make any difference? And what does food do to it — better, worse, or no change?'

★ 'Alcohol — how much in a usual week, in standard drinks, and any heavy session in the last few days? Have you ever been told you have gallstones, or had surgery on your gallbladder? Any anti-inflammatories, steroids or water tablets? Any injections for weight loss or diabetes — Ozempic, Wegovy, Trulicity? High cholesterol or triglycerides — anyone in the family? Any recent camera test of the bile duct, or injury? Any recent viral illness?'
★ 'Any chest pain or tightness, shortness of breath, sweating, pain to the jaw or arm?' — 'Examiner, I would like an ECG.' / ★ 'Any weight loss? … Was that on purpose?'

★ 'The important one is an enzyme called lipase, which your pancreas makes — yours is very high. With this pattern of pain, that tells me your pancreas is inflamed: acute pancreatitis. Your white cells are up, which is your body responding. Your liver tests are slightly raised — that is expected with pancreatitis and does not mean a separate liver problem, but it makes me want to check for a gallstone. Your bilirubin is normal, which suggests the main bile tube isn't blocked.'

B2: ★ 'The two commonest causes are gallstones and alcohol, and neither fits you well — though stones can still form in the tube even after the gallbladder is removed, so we will look. But there is another possibility I have to raise: the weight-loss injection can, uncommonly, inflame the pancreas. I can't prove that today, but it is high on my list, and I think we should stop it while we sort this out.' / 'Have I done something wrong?' → ★ 'Not at all. This is an uncommon reaction to a medicine used properly — it isn't a mistake on your part or anyone else's.'

A: 'The most likely cause is the alcohol, and I want to explain that without any judgement. A large amount at once can trigger the pancreas to digest itself. The single most useful thing for preventing this again is stopping alcohol, and I'd like to help you with that rather than just tell you to.' / B1: 'Your blood carries a fat called triglyceride — yours is extremely high, high enough to inflame the pancreas directly. Fluids and pain relief first, then we bring the triglycerides down: fasting, sometimes an insulin drip, then a fibrate, a low-fat diet and no alcohol. Your family should be checked.'

★ 'You need to come into hospital. We'll rest your gut, put a drip in and give you plenty of fluids — that is the single most important treatment. Strong pain relief and something for the nausea. An ultrasound of your gallbladder and ducts, more bloods including cholesterol and calcium, and regular checks over the next two days. We'll start you eating again as soon as you can tolerate it. You won't need antibiotics unless there is a specific infection.'

Restless, rocks forward, frightened; visibly relieved by early analgesia. Two decoys: 'about three kilos' and nothing more until asked 'was it intentional?'; gallbladder surgery only when asked about gallstones/operations; Ozempic only when injections are named. Upset when the injection is blamed: 'have I done something wrong?', 'will I have to stop it? I've worked so hard'

Vitals 118/72 · 104 · 20 · 37.4 · 98%. Diagnosis: 2 of 3 — typical pain, lipase ≥3× ULN, imaging; lipase height ≠ severity. Gallstones + alcohol ≈ 80%; ALT >3× ULN points to gallstones; other causes: hypertriglyceridaemia (>11 mmol/L), hypercalcaemia, drugs (GLP-1 agonists, azathioprine, valproate, thiazides, steroids, oestrogens), post-ERCP, trauma, viral (mumps, CMV), autoimmune, idiopathic. Severity: CRP >150 at 48 h VERIFY, SIRS, BISAP/Glasgow; CT at ≥72 h for necrosis, not at presentation; ERCP within 24 h for cholangitis/persistent obstruction; cholecystectomy same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis

Management: aggressive IV crystalloid (goal-directed), analgesia (opioids fine), antiemetic, early oral feeding when tolerated (no routine NBM/NG), no prophylactic antibiotics, USS, lipids/Ca, monitor for organ failure, HDU if severe; hypertriglyceridaemic — insulin infusion ± plasmapheresis VERIFY; GLP-1 — cease and report to TGA, do not rechallenge

Harder variants: rigid abdomen = perforated ulcer → erect CXR, resuscitate, antibiotics, theatre · pancreatitis with jaundice + fever = gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis → ERCP within 24 h · diabetic with epigastric pain and vomiting → ketones/glucose first (DKA)

Generic SOCRATES without the three epigastric add-ons; never asking about weight-loss injections
Blaming the patient for the drug reaction; keeping her NBM for days; routine antibiotics
Missing that a stone can still lodge in the duct after cholecystectomy; no lipids/calcium

stem: Warren Diggs, 40, presents with epigastric pain for six weeks, worse when he eats; antacids help for an hour or two. He takes ibuprofen daily for back pain. Ultrasound: gallstones present; no wall thickening, no duct dilatation, no inflammation.

Explain the ultrasound to the patient
Give your diagnosis, differentials and management
time: 8 min. Intro, open, concerns · pain: gnawing, 5/10, ★ worse after eating, ★ antacids relieve, through to back? (no), sitting forward? · vomiting, blood · six cause questions incl ★ NSAIDs (2–3 Nurofen most days for months), alcohol, gallstones (known), steroids, GLP-1, lipids · cardiac screen + ECG if any doubt · red flags: weight loss (intent), dysphagia, haematemesis/melaena, anaemia symptoms, FHx · biliary specifics: fatty food, RUQ, shoulder tip, episodic hours-long attacks (no) · SADMA · explain the USS: 'stones sitting there quietly — common, we don't operate on quiet stones' · dx: NSAID-associated peptic (gastric) ulcer with reasons; DDx: GORD, gastritis, functional dyspepsia, biliary colic (doesn't fit), pancreatitis, gastric cancer (age 40, no red flags — low threshold) · ★ management: stop ibuprofen first → PPI → H. pylori test (off PPI 2 weeks) → treat if positive → alarm-feature safety-net → review; endoscopy if not settling/red flags.

back.dx: NSAID-associated peptic ulcer disease — six weeks of gnawing epigastric pain, worse after eating, relieved by antacids for an hour or two, daily ibuprofen for months; gallstones on ultrasound are incidental (no wall thickening, no duct dilatation, no inflammation, and the story is not biliary). Explain the ultrasound: 'stones in your gallbladder, but the wall isn't thickened, the tubes aren't blocked and there's no inflammation — these stones are sitting there quietly; very common; we don't operate on quiet stones.' Three things: stop the ibuprofen (the cause — no acid tablet fixes it while it continues), PPI, H. pylori breath/stool test off PPI for two weeks; eradicate if positive; red flags → hospital.

pefe: Role-player (reconstructed): Warren, 40; gnawing epigastric pain six weeks, 5/10, worse after eating, antacids help an hour or two; 2–3 Nurofen daily for months for back pain; no weight loss, no haematemesis, no melaena. USS: gallstones, normal wall, no duct dilatation, no inflammation

Asymptomatic gallstones: ~10–15% of adults; most never cause symptoms; cholecystectomy only for symptomatic stones or complications (exceptions: porcelain gallbladder, large polyps, certain risk groups) VERIFY. Biliary colic pattern: postprandial (fatty), RUQ/epigastric, radiates to right scapula, 1–6 h, no fever

PUD: NSAIDs and H. pylori are the two causes; gastric ulcer pain classically worse with food (15–60 min), duodenal 2–5 h after/at night relieved by food. H. pylori testing: urea breath test or stool antigen — off PPI ≥2 weeks and antibiotics ≥4 weeks; eradication 7-day triple therapy (esomeprazole 20 mg + amoxicillin 1 g + clarithromycin 500 mg, all bd; metronidazole 400 mg if penicillin-allergic) VERIFY TG; test of cure ≥4 weeks after antibiotics. PPI 4–8 weeks; gastric ulcers need repeat endoscopy to confirm healing/biopsy. Endoscopy: alarm features at any age; new dyspepsia ≥50 (some say 55–60); NSAID ulcer with continued need → PPI cover, COX-2, review
Back pain alternatives: paracetamol, physio, exercise, heat, topical NSAID (less systemic), review cause; if NSAID unavoidable — lowest dose, shortest time, PPI co-prescription
SA: healthdirect 1800 022 222 · gastroenterology via LHN if scope needed
fails: Attributing the pain to the gallstones — the scan is a decoy; recommending cholecystectomy
Prescribing a PPI without stopping the NSAID first
Testing for H. pylori while on a PPI (false negative); no test of cure
No alarm-feature screen; no red-flag safety-net; no scope threshold
Missing the OTC ibuprofen in the medication history
numbers: Gastric ulcer pain 15–60 min after food · duodenal 2–5 h/night · asymptomatic stones ~10–15% of adults

setting: Regional SA general practice. Six-minute history (warning at 6:00), then diagnosis to the patient with reasons, then differentials to the examiner. No examination, no investigations. Two things must be audible: the upper-GI red flags — melaena, haematemesis, dysphagia — and gastric cancer named as a differential. The reflux screen is written negative on purpose: saying 'GORD' is the commonest single fail.
stem: James Whitlock, 32, long-haul truck driver, presents with pain in the upper part of his abdomen. T 36.8 · P 78 reg · BP 124/78 · RR 14 · SpO2 98% · BMI 27. Comfortable at rest.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis to the patient, with your reasons
Give the examiner your differential diagnoses
time: 8 min. 'Could you confirm the patient is haemodynamically stable and give me the vital signs?' · intro, 'comfortable enough to talk?', open · acknowledge, bridge · pain in one breath: site (LUQ/epigastric — don't freeze if he points elsewhere), radiation, /10 (4–5), ★ quality (dull ache, NOT burning), duration (weeks–months), constant/intermittent, worse?, better/worse ('nothing') → ★ 'what about food — any different when you eat?' → worse → ★ two probes: 'particular food — spicy, dairy, bread/pasta, fatty?' (any) and ★ 'how soon after eating?' (within the hour = gastric; 2–3 h/night = duodenal) · ★ red flags signposted: weight loss, appetite, lumps, tiredness, ★ black tarry stools, ★ vomited blood/coffee grounds, ★ dysphagia, FHx stomach/gullet/bowel cancer · ★ group one aloud — reflux/ulcer: heartburn, bitter/metallic taste, water brash, worse lying/bending (all no) · ★ risk factors: 'medications including anything over the counter' (Quick-Eze, Panadol → ★ Nurofen most days), smoking (ex, 20/day, quit 3 y), alcohol (4–5 beers most nights), coffee, night pain · group two — pancreas: through to back, forward, trauma, fever, lipids · group three — liver/gallbladder: jaundice, itch, dark urine/pale stools, fatty-meal attacks, rigors · ★ chest: exertional tightness, SOB, cough, fever · closure: drugs, allergies, PMHx/ops, FHx, ★ 'what were you most worried this might be?' (cancer — mate) · 6:00 dx to James · 7:00 DDx to examiner: gastric malignancy first.

back.dx: NSAID-associated peptic ulcer disease (gastric pattern — pain within the hour of eating) — weeks to months of intermittent dull (not burning) LUQ/epigastric ache 4/10, worse after any food, partially relieved by Quick-Eze, daily ibuprofen for months for back pain, ex-smoker, 4–5 beers nightly; clean negative reflux screen; no red flags; no pancreatic, biliary, cardiac or respiratory features. Most important differential: gastric malignancy — ulcer and cancer are indistinguishable on history; only endoscopy with biopsy separates them. Hidden agenda: a mate's 'stomach trouble' was cancer and he died.
plan: 'Before I begin, could you confirm the patient is haemodynamically stable and give me the vital signs?' · 'Good morning James, I'm Dr —. Are you comfortable enough to talk right now? What has brought you in today?' → 'I'm sorry you've been putting up with that, and I can hear it's worrying you. Let's go through it together.'

In one breath: 'show me exactly where … travel anywhere? … out of ten? … burning, gnawing, dull ache? … how long? … constant or comes and goes? … getting worse? … anything better or worse?' → 'nothing, really' → ★ 'what about food — is it any different when you eat?' → worse → ★ 'two things: any particular food — spicy, dairy, bread and pasta, fatty? and how soon after you eat — straight away, or hours later?' → any food, within the hour

★ 'I now need to ask some questions to make sure we're not missing anything serious': weight loss without trying, appetite, lumps, tiredness, ★ 'stools turning black or tarry?', ★ 'ever vomited blood, or something like coffee grounds?', ★ 'difficulty or pain swallowing, food sticking?', FHx cancer of stomach/gullet/bowel → all negative

★ 'I'll ask about reflux and ulcers first, because that's what most often causes pain here': heartburn behind the breastbone, bitter/metallic taste, mouth filling with saliva, worse lying flat/bending → all no · ★ 'what medications are you taking, including anything you buy yourself over the counter?' → Quick-Eze, Panadol… 'anything else?' → Nurofen most days for months (write it down visibly; 'does the Quick-Eze help?') · smoked/ever smoked · alcohol how much, how often · coffee, spicy · 'does the pain wake you at night?'

'Next, the pancreas': through to the back, better leaning forward, injury, fever/flu-like illness, high blood fats · 'now liver and gallbladder': yellowing, itching, dark urine/pale stools, ★ 'severe pain after a large fatty meal?', fevers with shaking chills · ★ 'two last ones, because problems in the chest can be felt in the upper tummy': chest pain/tightness esp on exertion, SOB, cough, fever
'Almost done': recreational drugs, allergies, other conditions/operations, family · ★ 'and what were you most worried this might be?' → cancer, the mate

★ To James: 'the most likely explanation is a peptic ulcer — a small raw area in the lining of the stomach or the first part of the bowel. The likeliest cause is the Nurofen you take most days for your back: it's an anti-inflammatory, and that group strips away the mucus layer that protects the lining. I say that because the pain sits in the upper tummy, it's a dull ache rather than a burn, it's clearly worse after eating, and the anti-inflammatories are a real risk factor on top of the smoking history and the alcohol. Just as importantly, I looked for the warning signs of anything more serious — weight loss, trouble swallowing, black stools, vomiting blood — and you have none of them. That's why I'm not more worried about the cancer you mentioned. I can't rule it out from a conversation alone, so if things don't settle we look with a camera. I'd also test for a common stomach germ, Helicobacter pylori.' · plan four things: stop the Nurofen (sort the back another way), PPI, H. pylori breath/stool test → 7 days of antibiotics if positive, cut the alcohol; review 4 weeks · ★ safety-net: haematemesis, melaena, sudden severe pain with a hard tummy, faint → ambulance/ED, don't drive

★ To examiner: 'My most likely diagnosis is NSAID-associated peptic ulcer disease. My most important differential is a gastric malignancy — gastric ulcers can be malignant and a stomach cancer presents exactly like this, so I would not exclude it on history alone. I would also consider pancreatic and oesophageal cancer. Grouping the rest: upper GI — reflux and gastritis, unlikely given the negative reflux screen; pancreatic — acute and chronic pancreatitis; hepatobiliary — biliary colic, cholecystitis, cholangitis, hepatitis, HCC; outside the abdomen — acute coronary syndrome and left lower lobe pneumonia, both screened for.' · if only one differential: gastric cancer

Variant B (duodenal timing — 2–3 h after meals, wakes him at 2 am, settles with a sandwich or milk): 'that pattern points to an ulcer in the duodenum rather than the stomach; treatment is the same, and ulcers there do not turn cancerous.' / Variant A (6 kg loss, black stools): 'those two things change my plan — black stools usually mean bleeding in the stomach, and unintentional weight loss always needs explaining; blood count today and an urgent gastroscopy rather than treating and waiting.' / Variant C (exertional, sweaty, fist on sternum): 'James, I need to stop there — pain brought on by exertion and relieved by rest can come from the heart. ECG now, hospital today.' / Variant D ('a drink settles it'): 'a drink can dull it for a while, but alcohol irritates the lining and makes ulcers worse, so cutting down is part of the treatment.'
pefe: Role-player: James Whitlock, 32, Port Augusta run, married, two young kids; practical, blunt, not medically minded; put it off because stopping work costs money. Flat hand LUQ/epigastric, dull ache 4/10, weeks–months, not positional, worse within the hour of any food, doesn't wake him. Holds the food clue once ('not really' → only on a specific food question). Holds the Nurofen once (Quick-Eze and Panadol first; Nurofen only on 'over the counter' or 'anything else'). Ex-smoker 20/day quit 3 y; 4–5 beers most nights; lots of coffee. All red flags absent. Hidden: frightened of cancer — a mate died; raises it only if asked concerns, else flatly at 6:00: 'it's not cancer, is it?'. Goes quiet when cancer is named; warms if the fear is addressed directly. Pushes: 'so what actually is it?', 'am I going to be all right?'
No examination or investigations in the station. Vitals normal, BMI 27

Brand-name trap: Quick-Eze/Mylanta = antacids; Gaviscon = alginate-antacid; Somac = pantoprazole (PPI, not an antacid); Micardis = telmisartan (ARB); Nurofen = ibuprofen — the diagnosis. Gastric ulcer: pain 15–60 min after food, food worsens, can be malignant → biopsy at index scope, PPI 8 weeks, repeat endoscopy 6–8 weeks. Duodenal: 2–5 h after food and at night, relieved by food/antacid, benign, PPI 4 weeks, no repeat scope

H. pylori eradication (7 days, all bd): esomeprazole 20 mg + amoxicillin 1 g + clarithromycin 500 mg; penicillin allergy — metronidazole 400 mg replaces amoxicillin VERIFY TG. Confirm cure: urea breath test ≥4 weeks after antibiotics, ≥2 weeks off PPI. Scope: any age with alarm features; new dyspepsia from ~50 without them. Alcohol NHMRC ≤10/week, ≤4/day. ACS and lower-lobe pneumonia present as upper abdominal pain — twenty seconds buys the domain
SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450 · truck driving — no sedating analgesia; fitness to drive unaffected by the ulcer itself
fails: ★ Saying 'GORD' — the reflux screen is negative on purpose
Asking only about fresh rectal blood — no melaena/haematemesis/dysphagia questions; never naming gastric cancer as the leading differential
A medication history without 'anything over the counter' — no Nurofen, no diagnosis, no station
Asking only 'is it related to food?' — missing the food-type and lag-time probes; freezing when he points to the LUQ
Finishing the abdomen and stopping — no chest screen; never asking what he's worried about; no safety-net for bleeding/perforation
numbers: 6 min history · warning 6:00 · 8 min · gastric 15–60 min after food, biopsy, PPI 8 wk, rescope 6–8 wk · duodenal 2–5 h/night, benign, PPI 4 wk
Eradication 7 d bd: esomeprazole 20 + amoxicillin 1 g + clarithromycin 500 (metronidazole 400 if allergic) VERIFY · UBT ≥4 wk post-antibiotics, ≥2 wk off PPI
Scope: alarm features any age; new dyspepsia ~≥50 · alcohol ≤10/wk, ≤4/d · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

stem: Susan Hartley, 57, presents with new difficulty swallowing.

Versions: A — 6 weeks (or 6 months), worsening; 6 kg unintentional loss; ex-smoker (quit 10 y); alcohol; long reflux history, Mylanta no longer helping; solids only, now on soft food. B — identical plus a normal examination card. C — no red flags; heartburn, metallic taste, water brash, spicy food; not progressive.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis, with your reasons, to Susan
Give your differential diagnoses
time: 8 min. Intro, open · match the reply to what she said (no canned 'I understand your concern' unless she voiced one) · ★ 'hard to swallow, or painful to swallow?' · ★ 'hard to start — cough or choke as you begin? or goes down then sticks? throat or chest?' · ★ 'solid food only, or liquids as well?' (solids = obstructive; both = motility) · duration, first time, daily/intermittent, ★ progressive, foods (bread, meat), impact (soft food, not eating enough) · general GI · ★ red flags: weight loss (6 kg, 2 months, not trying), appetite, lumps, tiredness, night sweats · ★ four cancer sites: throat (persistent sore throat, ★ ear pain, ★ voice change), oesophagus/stomach (haematemesis, melaena), thyroid (neck lump, weather preference), lung (persistent cough, haemoptysis) · reflux: heartburn, metallic taste, water brash, ★ 'have you taken anything — is it still working?' (Mylanta used to help, now nothing) · motility/neuro: weakness, numbness, diplopia, ptosis, tremor, stroke, diabetes · autoimmune: rash, joints, tight skin, dry eyes/mouth · meds · ★ 'do you smoke, or have you EVER smoked?' · alcohol, spicy, coffee · PMHx, FHx · concerns (sister-in-law died of oesophageal cancer) · card → 'a normal examination does not exclude an oesophageal malignancy — my concern is unchanged' · dx, six DDx groups, urgent scope, PATS, dietitian, safety-net.

back.dx: Oesophageal carcinoma until proven otherwise (A/B) — 6 weeks of progressive dysphagia to solids only (goes down then catches at mid-sternum, no choking), on soft food, 6 kg unintentional loss over two months, tired, years of reflux with Mylanta that has stopped working, ex-smoker 20/day quit 10 years, two glasses of wine most nights; no site-specific symptoms from throat, thyroid or lung. Reasons: reflux with antacid failure, progression, weight loss, solids-only pattern. A normal examination (B) changes nothing — early tumours produce no signs. Version C (no red flags, heartburn/metallic taste/water brash/spicy food, not progressive): peptic stricture secondary to chronic GORD — cancer named second, biopsy still required because a malignant stricture can look benign. Hidden agenda: sister-in-law died of oesophageal cancer.
plan: 'Am I speaking with Susan? How can I help?' → 'food sticking, a few weeks, I'm worried' → 'that does sound worrying, and you were right to come in — I'd like to ask a number of questions to work out what's causing it'

★ 'Is it hard to swallow, or painful to swallow?' (hard) · ★ 'hard to start the swallow — cough or choke as you begin? or does it go down and then get stuck — in your throat or your chest?' (goes down, catches mid-sternum) · ★ 'solid food only, or liquids as well?' (solids only; bread and meat worst)

How long (6 wk) · first time · every day or on and off · ★ 'gradually getting worse?' (definitely) · better/worse, particular foods · impact: 'managing to eat enough?' (soft/mashed food, not enjoying eating)
General GI: N/V, bloating, bowels, fever · ★ 'some I ask everyone': weight loss — ★ how many kilos, over what period, trying? (6 kg, 2 months, no) · appetite · lumps · tiredness (yes) · night sweats

★ Four sites: 'sore throat that won't settle? ★ any pain in your ear? ★ any change in your voice?' · 'ever vomited blood, or black tarry stools?' · 'lump in your neck? prefer hot or cold weather more than you used to?' · 'cough that won't go, coughed up blood?' → all no

Reflux: heartburn (years), acidic/metallic taste (yes), sudden rush of saliva · ★ 'have you taken anything for it, and is it still working?' → 'Mylanta used to help — it doesn't do anything now' → 'thank you, that change matters' · motility: weakness, numbness/pins and needles, blurred/double vision, droopy eyelids, tremor, previous stroke, diabetic · autoimmune: rashes, joint pains, tight skin on the hands, dry eyes/mouth · medications (none regular) · ★ 'do you smoke, or have you ever smoked?' (ever → 20/day, quit 10 y) · alcohol (2 glasses most nights) · spicy, coffee · other conditions, FHx (mother bowel cancer at 70) · ★ 'is there anything particular on your mind?' → sister-in-law

(B) Card: general/vitals normal, no lymphadenopathy, no goitre, chest clear, abdomen soft, neuro normal → ★ aloud: 'I note the examination is entirely normal. A normal examination does not exclude an oesophageal malignancy and my concern is unchanged.'

★ 'Susan, I've been thinking about a number of conditions that cause difficulty swallowing. In your case I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer in the food pipe. It is not confirmed, and that is exactly why I want to arrange a test. My reasons: reflux for a long time and the Mylanta that used to help has stopped working; it is getting worse; you have lost six kilograms without meaning to; and it happens only with solid food, which suggests something is physically blocking the way rather than a problem with the muscle movement.' · 'but the examination was normal?' → ★ 'you're right, and I want to be honest — I examined you and could not find anything abnormal, but a normal examination does not rule out a cancer; early tumours very often produce no physical signs. My concern comes from your symptoms, and it has not changed.' · DDx in groups, ~9 s each: other cancers pressing on the pipe — throat, thyroid, lung; narrowing from long-standing reflux — a stricture; infections in the throat; movement problems — nerve conditions (stroke, MS, myasthenia, diabetes), immune conditions (scleroderma), achalasia; medications. 'The camera test sorts between them.'

★ 'I'll arrange the camera test urgently and refer you to Adelaide today; our nurse will start the travel scheme paperwork. I'd like our dietitian to see you in the meantime. If you reach the point where you cannot swallow your own saliva, if food becomes completely stuck, or if you vomit blood, go straight to the emergency department.' · 'am I going to be alright?' → no false reassurance: 'I don't know yet — that's what the test is for, and I'm not waiting' · questions

Or does it go down and then get stuck? And if it sticks, is that in your throat or in your chest?' / ★ 'Does it happen with solid food only, or with liquids as well?'

First investigation: gastroscopy with biopsy (Category 1, urgent VERIFY timeframe); barium swallow first only for suspected pharyngeal pouch; CT/PET for staging after tissue; MDT. Pain an hour or two after fatty food, lasting a couple of hours then settling, going to the right shoulder blade, recurring over months, no fever, no jaundice — and a normal examination between attacks, which is expected. I want to be clear that a normal examination today does not mean nothing is wrong; with gallstones, between attacks there's usually nothing to find. Your diagnosis comes from the story, and the story is a textbook one.' · ★ one picture, three diseases: 'your gallbladder is a small bag under the liver that stores bile, which helps digest fat. When you eat something fatty the bag squeezes; if there are stones, one can block the outlet — pain for an hour or two until it falls back. If the stone stays stuck, the bag becomes inflamed and infected — more serious, needs hospital. If a stone escapes into the main drainage tube and blocks it, bile backs up into the blood, you turn yellow, and the tube gets infected — the most dangerous of the three.' · DDx: PUD, GORD, pancreatitis, hepatitis, right lower lobe pneumonia, renal colic, IBS, cardiac

Your diagnosis comes from the story, and the story is a textbook one. The next step is an ultrasound to confirm the stones and blood tests to check your liver. 'Can't you just dissolve the stones?' → 'Dissolving tablets exist but they work poorly, take a long time and the stones usually come back, so we rarely use them.' / 'Do I have to have surgery?' → 'You don't have to — it's your decision. Removing the gallbladder is a common keyhole operation and you can live perfectly well without it.'

First, liver function tests — bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT — because a rise tells me whether the bile duct is obstructed, which changes this from a gallbladder problem to a duct problem; plus FBC, CRP and lipase. Second, an abdominal ultrasound — stones, gallbladder wall thickness, fluid around the gallbladder, and whether the common bile duct is dilated. Bloods tell me whether it is obstructed; the ultrasound tells me why.' / Version E (hard, nodular, non-tender hepatomegaly, weight loss): 'the liver is enlarged, hard and knobbly but not tender — that pattern suggests a cancer that has spread to the liver; a smooth tender liver would suggest congestion, hepatitis or abscess. With weight loss this needs urgent imaging to find the primary.'

Asks 'can't you just dissolve the stones?', 'do I have to have surgery?', 'what if I do nothing?'

PEFE: everything normal — no tenderness, Murphy negative, no jaundice, obs normal. Version C (acute cholecystitis): constant pain >1 day, T 38.5, HR 96, RUQ tenderness with guarding, Murphy positive, no jaundice, WCC/CRP raised → admit, NBM, IV fluids, analgesia, IV antibiotics (amoxicillin + gentamicin, or amoxicillin-clavulanate VERIFY TG), USS, laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 h/same admission VERIFY. Version E: hard nodular non-tender hepatomegaly + 6 kg loss → metastatic malignancy; urgent CT, LFTs, tumour markers, find the primary

Numbers: biliary colic <6 h; cholecystitis >6 h; GB wall normal <3 mm; cholecystitis fever 38–38.5; cholangitis 39 with rigors; CBD normal ≤6 mm (age-adjusted); obstructive picture = bilirubin, ALP, GGT up, ALT mildly up. Risk factors: female, forty, fertile, fat, FHx, OCP, rapid weight loss, diabetes, haemolysis, Aboriginal women. Complications: cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis, gallstone ileus, Mirizzi, GB cancer (porcelain)
