setting: ED, rural SA (Moonta/Wallaroo). Version B of the RUQ set. T 39.1 with rigors: take the vitals and VISIBLY change gear — fluids, cultures, antibiotics within the hour — or the examiner records that you did not recognise sepsis. The jaundice block is the station: he does not volunteer yellow eyes, dark urine, pale stools or itching. Murphy is positive in both cholecystitis and cholangitis — the jaundice and the obstructive LFTs decide it.
stem: Mr Okoye, 58, presents with constant right upper quadrant pain for two days and a temperature of 39 °C with rigors. T 39.1 · HR 112 · BP 108/64 · RR 22 · SpO2 96%.
tasks: Take a focused history
Ask the examiner for the examination findings
Explain your diagnosis, differentials and immediate management
time: 8 min. ★ Stability → 'those observations concern me and I'll be moving quickly' · analgesia, open · pain: /10 (8), after dinner, ★ constant now, to the back/shoulder blade, ★ 'had anything like this before?' (a couple of shorter episodes last year) · ★ jaundice ×4: yellow eyes (wife noticed), dark tea-coloured urine, pale stools, itching · ★ 'was the shivering a proper rigor — teeth chattering, couldn't stop?' · confusion, drowsiness, dizziness on standing (light-headed) · N/V, bowels · weight loss/intent, dysphagia, haematemesis, melaena, lumps · liver risk: alcohol, transfusions/tattoos/IVDU/travel, paracetamol/herbal, FHx · ★ chest ×2 · SADMA, ops (none) · summarise · ★ examiner every step incl scleral icterus, scratch marks, palpable GB/liver character, ★ Murphy's, chest bases, DRE stool colour, dipstick → unwell, jaundiced, RUQ tender with guarding, Murphy +, liver not enlarged, chest clear, dipstick bilirubin; WCC 18, CRP 210, bili 74, ALP/GGT clearly raised, ALT mildly, lipase normal · ★ 'Murphy positive tells me the gallbladder is inflamed — true in cholecystitis and cholangitis — before I commit: is there scleral icterus, and what is the bilirubin?' · dx ascending cholangitis (Charcot's triad) · honest about seriousness · management spoken: drip ×2, cultures, ★ antibiotics within the hour, fluids, analgesia/antiemetic, USS, ★ ERCP within 24 h, MedSTAR transfer, cholecystectomy after recovery · DDx.

back.dx: Ascending cholangitis — Charcot's triad: constant RUQ pain (two days, 8/10, after dinner, round to the right back, previous shorter episodes = prior biliary colic), fever 39.1 with a true rigor, and obstructive jaundice (yellow sclerae per his wife, tea-coloured urine, pale stools, itching); light-headed on standing (early Reynolds' — hypotension/confusion make the pentad). PEFE: unwell, scleral icterus, RUQ tenderness with guarding, Murphy positive, liver not enlarged, chest clear, dipstick bilirubin; WCC 18, CRP 210, bilirubin 74, ALP/GGT clearly raised, ALT mildly raised, lipase normal. Sepsis from an obstructed, infected duct — almost certainly a stone. Antibiotics within the hour, biliary decompression by ERCP within 24 h (not available locally → MedSTAR), cholecystectomy on the same admission once recovered.
plan: ★ 'Examiner, may I confirm he is haemodynamically stable — all four observations and saturations?' → 39.1, 112, 108/64, 22, 96% → ★ 'those observations concern me and I'll be moving quickly' · 'I'm Dr —. Would you like something for the pain before we start? Tell me what's been happening.'

Pain: where (under the right ribs), /10 (8), after a meal (dinner), ★ 'travel to your right shoulder blade?' (round to the back), ★ 'constant, or comes and goes?' (constant now), ★ 'had anything like this before?' (couple of times last year, went in an hour or two)

N/V (sick twice), bloating, wind, D/C · weight loss — on purpose?, dysphagia, haematemesis, melaena, lumps → no · liver risk: alcohol (2 beers weekend), transfusions, tattoos, IVDU, overseas travel, paracetamol, herbal/OTC, FHx liver → none · ★ chest: cough, phlegm, SOB, pain on deep breath → none · smoking, meds (BP tablet), allergies, ops (none), PMHx · ★ summarise back

'Am I alright?' → 'I'm going to be honest with you shortly — let me get the examination findings first' · ★ examiner: 'general appearance — distressed, dehydrated, ★ scleral icterus or skin jaundice · inspection — scars, distension, ★ scratch marks · palpation — tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound, ★ palpable gallbladder, liver edge and its character · ★ Murphy's sign · percussion — tenderness, liver span · bowel sounds and ★ chest bases · rectal — stool colour · dipstick' → unwell, jaundiced with scleral icterus; RUQ tender with guarding, no mass; Murphy +; liver not enlarged; chest clear; dipstick bilirubin; WCC 18, CRP 210, bili 74, ALP/GGT clearly up, ALT mildly, lipase normal

You have an infection in the drainage tubes of your liver, which are blocked — almost certainly by a gallstone. The medical name is ascending cholangitis. It is serious, and you are already showing signs the infection is affecting your whole body. But it is very treatable and we are going to start straight away.' · 'serious how?' → 'serious enough that you need to be in hospital now and on antibiotics within the hour. The three things that told me were the pain, the fever with the shaking, and the yellow colour — a recognised pattern we treat urgently. The good news is we know exactly what to do.'

An ultrasound to confirm where the blockage is. Then the key treatment — unblocking the tube: a camera passed down through the mouth to the drainage tube, an ERCP; we aim to do that within 24 hours. That isn't done here, so I'm arranging transfer to Adelaide and speaking with the retrieval service now.' · 'and the gallbladder?' → 'once you've recovered, it should come out — ideally the same admission — so this can't happen again' · DDx: cholecystitis alone, a duct stone without infection, hepatitis, pancreatitis (lipase normal), liver abscess — 'the fever, the rigor and the pattern of your liver tests point to an infected, blocked duct' · 'is there someone we should call?'

pefe: Role-player: Mr Okoye, 58, retired shearer near Moonta, married; one BP tablet, no allergies, no operations; two beers on the weekend, non-smoker; no tattoos/transfusions/travel. Understated country manner, minimises, frightened but won't say; sits still, winces, sounds tired. Does NOT volunteer yellow eyes, dark urine, pale stools or itching — only when asked directly (if never asked, never mentioned — the whole station). 'Am I alright?' midway; 'serious how?' and 'and the gallbladder?' after the diagnosis

PEFE: unwell, jaundiced, scleral icterus · RUQ tender with guarding, no mass · Murphy + · liver not enlarged · chest clear · dipstick bilirubin · bloods: WCC 18, CRP 210, bilirubin 74, ALP + GGT clearly raised, ALT mildly raised, lipase normal. Vitals 39.1 · 112 · 108/64 · 22 · 96%

Cholangitis: Charcot's triad (pain, fever/rigors, jaundice) → Reynolds' pentad adds hypotension + confusion (severe). Tokyo criteria (systemic inflammation + cholestasis + imaging). Causes: choledocholithiasis (commonest), strictures, malignancy, post-ERCP, stents. Management: sepsis bundle — two large-bore IVs, cultures, lactate, ★ IV antibiotics within 1 h (e.g. amoxicillin + gentamicin ± metronidazole, or piperacillin-tazobactam/ceftriaxone + metronidazole VERIFY TG), fluids (30 mL/kg if hypotensive), analgesia, antiemetic, NBM, monitor urine output; USS (dilated CBD, stones); ★ biliary decompression — ERCP with sphincterotomy/stent within 24 h (urgent if severe/not improving), PTC or surgery if ERCP fails; correct coagulopathy (vitamin K); cholecystectomy same admission after recovery. Beware paracetamol dosing in liver dysfunction; no NSAIDs if renal impairment

Cholecystitis vs cholangitis: both Murphy +; cholangitis has jaundice + obstructive LFTs + higher fever/rigors; cholecystitis fever 38–38.5, no jaundice (unless Mirizzi), treated with antibiotics + early cholecystectomy. Gallstone pancreatitis: raised lipase (his is normal). Hepatitis: ALT dominant. Liver abscess: fever, tender hepatomegaly, imaging
SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 — ring now, not after the ultrasound; ERCP is in Adelaide · TIS 131 450 · family notified

Not asking rigors specifically, or confusion/postural dizziness; not asking previous episodes
False reassurance, or frightening him without a plan; forgetting the gallbladder needs to come out; not offering to call someone

setting: Regional SA general practice. The master diarrhoea history: six minutes, then diagnosis and differentials to the patient. Duration is deliberately not on the door. The role-play version (David, 41) is the multiple-findings case — five days of watery diarrhoea, amoxicillin finished three days ago, Bali six weeks ago with street food, father with bowel cancer at 71. Name ONE most likely diagnosis with reasons, then the rest grouped, each justified from what he said.
stem: A 37-year-old woman (role-play: David Bennett, 41) presents complaining of diarrhoea. Duration not given.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 min. Identity, open, ★ respond to the stated worry, permission ('some are personal') · ★ timing box: when, constant/intermittent, worse, ★ 'does it wake you at night?' · ★ CCCVO: count, consistency (watery vs loose), colour, ★ blood, volume/bulky, ★ offensive/floats/hard to flush (coeliac trigger → weight, FHx immediately) · better/worse, ★ impact on life · general GI: N/V, bloating/wind, ★ constipation before it started, pain, fever · differential blocks as headings: travel/contacts → ★ full seven-part travel history once a destination is named · hepatitis (jaundice, itch, dark urine) · IBD ×4 · coeliac (greasy/float/flush, FHx) · lactose · ★ medications incl chemist → ★ 'which antibiotic, how long, what for?' · thyroid (heat, palpitations) · ★ red flags: weight loss (how much/how long), appetite, lumps, tiredness, blood, ★ FHx bowel cancer + ★ 'how old were they when diagnosed?', bowel screening · sexual screen (converts to the PrEP station if 'my partner has it too') · IBS (relief with defecation, alternating, stress) · summarise back · name one dx, reasons, grouped DDx, cancer named with why unlikely, safety-net, review.

back.dx: Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (amoxicillin 5 days for a sore throat, finished 3 days ago; diarrhoea began during the course) — five days of watery stools 6–7/day, no blood, no fever, low crampy pain, not nocturnal; the more serious version, pseudomembranous colitis (C. difficile toxin), must be excluded with a stool test. Still considering a Bali-acquired infection (street food, ice, six weeks ago) and the travel group; bowel cancer stays on the list because of his father (diagnosed at 71) but is unlikely — no bleeding, no weight loss. Plan: stool MCS + C. difficile toxin PCR, oral rehydration (Hydralyte), avoid loperamide for now, safety-net, review 2–3 days.
plan: 'I'm Dr —; can I confirm your name and date of birth? What's brought you in?' → 'five days of bad diarrhoea, worried' → ★ 'that's exhausting, and I can understand the worry. I'd like to ask a series of questions about your bowels — some are personal — then tell you what I think. Is that all right?'

★ Timing: when (5 d), constant, worse?, ★ 'does it ever wake you at night?' (no) · ★ CCCVO: 'how many times a day? watery, or soft and loose? any blood? large bulky amount? particularly offensive — floats, sticks to the pan, hard to flush?' (6–7, watery, no blood, not bulky) · better/worse (Gastro-Stop hasn't helped) · 'how is this affecting day to day?'
General GI: nausea/vomiting (queasy), bloating, ★ 'constipated at all before it started?', tummy pain (low crampy), fever

★ 'Have you travelled anywhere recently? anyone at home or work the same?' → Bali 6 weeks ago → ★ full travel: where/how long/what (Seminyak, 2 wk, beach), bushwalking/bites, sick or animal contacts, drugs, tattoos/piercings/medical treatment, ★ street food/ice/unbottled water (warungs, ice), pre-travel GP/vaccines (none) · hepatitis: yellowing, itch, dark urine · IBD: joints, eyes, rash, mouth ulcers · coeliac: greasy/float/flush, FHx coeliac/bowel disease · lactose: dairy trigger · ★ 'any medications, including anything from the chemist or supermarket?' → 'finished some antibiotics' → ★ 'which antibiotic, how long, and what for?' (amoxicillin, 5 d, sore throat; diarrhoea started while on it) · Gastro-Stop, Nurofen · thyroid: heat, racing heart

★ Red flags despite five days: 'weight loss without trying — how much, over how long? appetite? lumps or bumps? more tired? blood in the stool? ★ family history of bowel cancer — and how old were they when diagnosed?' (dad, 71) · 'have you done the bowel screening test?' (kit came, never did it)

Sexual screen (married, wife) · IBS: settles after going? alternating? stress? · PMHx · ★ summarise back: 'five days of watery diarrhoea 6–7×/day, no blood, no fever, low crampy pain; amoxicillin finished a few days ago; Bali six weeks ago with street food; father bowel cancer at 71 — have I missed anything?' · 'was there anything you were particularly worried about?' → 'is this cancer? my dad…'

★ 'There are a few things that could be causing this, and I'd rather be honest about that than pick one and ignore the rest. The most likely is antibiotic-associated diarrhoea — antibiotics upset the balance of the normal bacteria in your bowel, and that causes loose stools.' · ★ 'There is a more serious version I need to make sure you don't have, called pseudomembranous colitis — one particular bug overgrows and produces a toxin. It's checked with a simple stool test.' · 'I'm also still considering an infection picked up in Bali, given the street food, along with the travel-related infections as a group. And because your father had bowel cancer I keep that on my list — unlikely, no bleeding, no weight loss, and he was diagnosed at 71, but I don't leave it off.' · 'which one?' → 'my money is on the antibiotics; the stool test tells us whether it's the serious version' · plan: fluids/Hydralyte, ★ avoid Gastro-Stop for now, stool test, ★ safety-net (fever, blood, severe pain, faint → ED), review 2–3 days with results; do the screening kit
ask: ★ 'Some of these questions are quite personal, but they'll help me work out what's going on.' / ★ 'Does it ever wake you up at night to go to the toilet?' / ★ 'Do the stools float, stick to the pan, or are they hard to flush?' / ★ 'Were you constipated at all before the diarrhoea started?'

★ 'Because you've been overseas I'd like to go through that trip in detail — where did you go, how long, what did you do? Any bushwalking or insect bites? Contact with anyone unwell, or with animals? Any drug use? Tattoos, piercings or medical treatment? Street food, ice, unbottled water? Did you see a GP before you went?'

★ 'Which antibiotic was it, how long for, and what was it for?' / ★ 'Have you lost any weight without meaning to — how much, and over how long?' / ★ 'Any family history of bowel cancer — and how old were they when they were diagnosed?' / 'Have you done the bowel screening test that comes in the post?'

★ 'Based on what you've told me, the most likely explanation is …' (never 'Bali belly' or 'traveller's diarrhoea' — neither is a diagnosis) / ★ 'Antibiotics upset the balance of the normal bacteria that live in your bowel.' / 'There are several possibilities and I'd rather be honest with you about that.'

★ 'I've specifically checked for the things that would worry me, and they're not there.' / ★ 'Come back straight away, or go to the emergency department, if you develop a fever, blood in the stool, severe pain, or you feel faint.' / 'Was there anything you were particularly worried about today?'

Gastroenteritis version (recent travel, street food): 'Most likely you have a condition called gastroenteritis — an infection in your bowel. Three reasons: you've just come back from overseas; you ate street food, an important risk factor for a food-borne infection; and watery diarrhoea coming on over a few days with cramping fits an infection. I'm not going to guess the exact bug — knowing which doesn't change what we do first.' / DDx: 'because you've travelled — typhoid, malaria, bacterial infections, which is why I asked about mosquito bites; hepatitis A; inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease, dairy intolerance, medication side effects, an overactive thyroid, irritable bowel — and I always think about bowel cancer in anyone with a change in their bowels.'

Tired, embarrassed, cooperative; answers only the last part of a compound question; tense at 'cancer'. No examination task. Versions: acute traveller (gastroenteritis), antibiotic-associated (this), Version F chronic coeliac (MED-137), norovirus cruise ship (MED-138); 'I'm gay and my partner has it too' converts to the PrEP station (MED-139)

Definitions: acute <14 d · persistent 14–30 d · chronic >4 wk. C. difficile onset during the course or up to 8 weeks after, most within 2 weeks. Coeliac serology: tTG-IgA + total IgA on a gluten-containing diet. iFOBT 2-yearly 45–74 (average risk); moderate risk (first-degree relative <60, or two relatives): colonoscopy 5-yearly from 10 years before the earliest diagnosis or 50, whichever earlier VERIFY — father at 71 = average/slightly above. Brand names: Nexium/Somac = PPI; Gastro-Stop = loperamide; Hydralyte/Gastrolyte = ORS

Investigations when indicated: stool MCS/PCR (bacterial, viral, parasitic), C. difficile toxin, ova/cysts/parasites (Giardia after travel), FBE/UEC/CRP, coeliac serology, TSH, faecal calprotectin for chronic; notifiable in SA: shigella, salmonella, campylobacter, giardia, hepatitis A, typhoid VERIFY. Loperamide avoided in bloody/febrile diarrhoea and suspected C. difficile. Travel DDx: typhoid, malaria (fever + travel = malaria until excluded), hepatitis A/E, amoebiasis, giardia, cholera

setting: Cruise ship berthed in Sydney after sailing from New Zealand; you are the ship's medical officer. A different task set: four-minute focused history, then an assessment — directed to the examiner — of whether this patient can be released home. He is furious about being held on board. The 2025 finding: a cannula-site infection photograph handed over on request, which does not by itself prevent discharge.
stem: A 40-year-old man on a cruise ship berthed in Sydney has been diagnosed with norovirus gastroenteritis. He is insisting on being discharged home.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Perform an assessment, directed to the examiner, of whether this patient can be released home
time: 8 min. ★ Opening for the approach marks: 'I can hear how frustrating this is — I'd be frustrated too; can I ask what's making you so keen to get home? There may be something I can help with. Whatever you tell me stays between us.' (cat alone at home → 'we can almost certainly arrange for someone to look in on her') · ★ 'when did it start? is it still going? if it has stopped — when was the last symptom?' (the exclusion criterion is time since the last symptom) · count, consistency, ★ blood (would change the diagnosis) · fever/chills, abdominal pain, N/V, dizziness (must be asymptomatic, not just diarrhoea-free) · ★ 'eating and drinking normally and keeping it down?' · ★ immunocompromise: diabetes, cancer, steroids, chemo · ★ 'what treatment did you receive on board?' → IV fluids → the cannula · ★ occupation: food handler, childcare, healthcare (changes the exclusion period, public health duty) · to examiner: appearance/dehydration, vitals incl postural BP, full abdominal examination, ★ 'look at the cannula site' → photo: erythema, swelling, purulent discharge · ★ release criteria stated: no diarrhoea/vomiting for 48 h, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, no dehydration, normal abdomen → release, remove cannula, oral flucloxacillin, mark the edge, GP 48 h / ED if fever or spreading.

back.dx: Resolved norovirus gastroenteritis meeting exclusion criteria for release (symptom-free ≥48 h, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, no clinical dehydration, normal abdominal examination) — plus a peripheral cannula-site infection (erythema, swelling, purulent discharge at the insertion point) from the IV fluids given on board: remove the cannula, oral flucloxacillin as for a skin and soft tissue infection, mark the margin, GP review in 48 h, ED if fever, spreading redness or unwell. IV antibiotics only for systemic features (high fever, hypotension, tachycardia, drowsiness) — he has none. Not a reason to keep him on board.
plan: 'I'm furious, stuck in the harbour' → ★ 'I can hear how frustrating this is, and I'd be frustrated too — being held on board past your disembarkation date is really hard. Can I ask what's making you so keen to get home? There may be something I can help with. Whatever you tell me stays between us.' → cat alone → 'that's a real worry — we can almost certainly arrange for someone to look in on her today. Let me ask a few questions and then I'll tell you exactly where we stand.'

★ 'When did it start? Is it still going? If it has stopped — when exactly was your last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting?' · count, consistency, ★ blood · 'fever or chills? tummy pain? nausea? dizziness?' · ★ 'are you eating and drinking normally and keeping it down?'

★ 'Examiner, before I decide about release I'd like: general appearance — does he look well, any evidence of dehydration? Vital signs — temperature, pulse, BP including a postural BP, respiratory rate. A full abdominal examination, because I would not release anyone with abdominal tenderness. And I'd like to look at the cannula site, since he had intravenous fluids on board.' → photo: erythema, swelling, purulent discharge at the insertion point → describe it

★ 'My criteria for release are: no diarrhoea and no vomiting for 48 hours, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, no clinical dehydration and a normal abdominal examination — he meets them.' · challenge 'would you still release him with that cannula site?' → ★ 'Yes. He meets the exclusion criteria for norovirus. The cannula site needs treatment, but that is oral antibiotics I can prescribe, and there is no reason to keep him on board to give it. I would remove the cannula, start flucloxacillin, mark the edge of the redness, and ask him to see his own GP in 48 hours or attend an emergency department if he develops fever, spreading redness or feels unwell. IV antibiotics would be indicated only for systemic features — high fever, hypotension, tachycardia, drowsiness — and he has none.' · public health: notify the ship's outbreak log/port health; hand hygiene (soap and water — alcohol gel is less effective against norovirus), stay off food handling for 48 h after symptoms; the cat

★ To examiner: 'General appearance and any evidence of dehydration; temperature, pulse, blood pressure including a postural blood pressure, and respiratory rate; a full abdominal examination; and I would like to look at the cannula site, since he tells me he had intravenous fluids on board.'

★ 'My criteria for release are: no diarrhoea and no vomiting for 48 hours, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, no clinical dehydration and a normal abdominal examination.' / ★ 'Yes, I would still release him … I would remove the cannula, start flucloxacillin, mark the edge of the redness, and ask him to see his own GP in 48 hours or attend an emergency department if he develops fever, spreading redness or feels unwell.'

Examiner hands over the cannula-site photo on request

Photo: peripheral cannula site with erythema, swelling and purulent discharge at the insertion point — phlebitis/cellulitis. Management: remove cannula, swab, oral flucloxacillin 500 mg qid 5–7 d (cefalexin/clindamycin if allergic) VERIFY TG, mark margin, review 48 h; IV/admission if systemic features, spreading, or purulent thrombophlebitis with a cord

Norovirus: incubation 12–48 h; symptoms 24–72 h; highly infectious; shedding continues after symptoms — exclusion 48 h symptom-free (some services 48–72 h VERIFY SA Health/national guidance); food handlers, childcare and healthcare workers excluded 48 h after symptoms resolve; soap and water hand hygiene; bleach-based cleaning; outbreak reporting (ships: port health/Department of Agriculture and state health); prolonged/severe in the immunocompromised, elderly, infants

Discharge criteria in any gastroenteritis: symptom-free window, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, no dehydration (postural BP), normal abdomen, safe home situation, not a public-health risk; document the shared decision
fails: Arguing with the angry passenger or lecturing him; never asking why he wants to get home
Not asking when the last symptom was — the single exclusion criterion; not asking about oral intake or immunocompromise
Not asking what treatment he had (missing the cannula), or not asking to look at the site
Keeping him on board for IV antibiotics for a localised cannula infection; or ignoring it entirely
Not stating the release criteria explicitly to the examiner; forgetting occupation/public-health duty

Cannula infection: remove, flucloxacillin 500 mg qid 5–7 d VERIFY, mark margin, GP 48 h · IV only if systemic
Soap and water (alcohol gel less effective) · food handlers excluded 48 h post-symptoms · port/state health notification

setting: General practice. Within the first minute he volunteers that he is gay and his male partner has the same symptoms — every candidate received that without digging. Reorder the consultation: sexual history to the front. Three traps in task 2: avoiding the word HIV; testing without consent and a pre-test discussion; saying 'PrEP protects you, so it can't be HIV' (untrue — the reassurance trap the case is built to catch).
stem: Michael Reid, 32, presents with diarrhoea for two weeks. 'I'm gay, and my boyfriend has exactly the same thing.'
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 min. Identity, open → disclosure → ★ 'thank you for telling me that so openly — it's directly relevant. I'd like to ask about your bowels, and also about your sexual health, because that may well be part of what's going on. Everything is confidential. Is that all right?' · ★ PrEP first: on it? every day, missed doses? since when, who prescribes? ★ 'last HIV/STI check and did you get the results?' (a month ago, never got them → 'I'll retrieve them today — not the same as a negative') · ★ three boxes — partners (stable? multiple? male/female/both), practices (condoms? oral/anal? receptive/insertive?), risk (previous STIs — chlamydia ×2, gonorrhoea, syphilis; sex under alcohol/drugs; sex work) · say it back · ★ seroconversion: fevers/night sweats, sore throat, glands, rash, mouth ulcers, myalgia · ★ anorectal: pain, discharge, tenesmus, bleeding · generic structure at pace: timing, CCCVO, general GI, travel/contacts, hepatitis + hep A/B vaccination, IBD/coeliac/lactose, other meds, thyroid, red flags · summarise · ★ name HIV as the condition to exclude, reasons, PrEP not absolute, grouped DDx (PrEP side effect, proctitis — chlamydia/gonorrhoea/LGV, enteric STIs — shigella/giardia, hepatitis A, general causes), ★ consent + pre-test discussion (window, repeat 6 and 12 weeks, result in person), three-site STI screen, ★ partner in for the same tests.

back.dx: Acute HIV infection to be excluded — two weeks of watery diarrhoea 4–5/day in a man on PrEP with ~fortnightly missed doses, a fluey illness with sore throat, fever, myalgia and a chest rash two weeks ago, persistent cervical lymphadenopathy, mouth ulcers, some anal discharge; risk profile: open relationship, several male partners, condomless receptive anal sex, chlamydia ×2, gonorrhoea, syphilis, chemsex; last screen a month ago with results never seen. Most probable diagnoses are a PrEP side effect or a sexually transmitted enteric infection/proctitis — HIV is first as the diagnosis I most need to exclude because the consequence of missing it is greatest and the seroconversion picture fits. PrEP substantially reduces but does not eliminate risk; breakthrough is described.
plan: Identity, 'what's brought you in?' → disclosure → ★ 'thank you for telling me that so openly — it's directly relevant, so I'd like to ask about your sexual health now rather than later. Everything you tell me here is confidential.'

★ 'Are you taking PrEP? every day, without missing doses? since when, who prescribes it? ★ when was your last HIV and STI check, and did you get the results?' → ~a year; misses one a fortnight; a month ago, never told → 'I'll look those up today — a test you haven't had a result for isn't the same as a negative'

★ Partners: 'stable relationship? ever multiple partners? male, female or both?' · practices: 'condoms? oral, anal or both? receptive, insertive or both?' · risk: 'ever diagnosed with an STI? sex under the influence of alcohol or drugs? ever paid for sex?' → open relationship, several men, no condoms with the boyfriend, mostly receptive, chlamydia ×2/gonorrhoea/syphilis, parties · say it back without flinching

Timing/CCCVO: 2 wk, constant, 4–5/day, watery, no blood, not nocturnal · general GI: nausea, cramps, no constipation, felt feverish · ★ 'alongside the diarrhoea — fevers or night sweats? sore throat? swollen glands? rash? mouth ulcers? aching muscles?' → sore throat + fluey 2 wk ago, neck glands up, chest rash · ★ 'pain in the back passage? discharge? needing to go when there's nothing there? bleeding?' → some discharge

Travel/contacts (none; just the partner) · hepatitis symptoms; ★ 'vaccinated against hepatitis A and B?' (not sure) · IBD ×4 (mouth ulcers yes), greasy stools, dairy · other meds/chemist, thyroid · red flags: weight, appetite, lumps, tiredness (bit), blood, FHx · ★ summarise back the whole picture

★ 'Thank you for being so open — I want to be straight with you. The most serious condition I need to rule out is an HIV infection. I'm not telling you that you have it; it's the thing I most need to exclude, and I want to explain why: diarrhoea can be one of the first symptoms of HIV in the first weeks after someone catches it — often with fever, sore throat, swollen glands and a rash, which is close to what you've described; and the risk factors line up. ★ You're taking PrEP, which is genuinely very good protection — but it isn't one hundred per cent, and it works best taken every single day. It lowers the risk a lot; it doesn't remove it.' · 'but I'm on PrEP — I thought I couldn't get it' → hold the line · DDx grouped: the PrEP itself (nausea, loose stools) · proctitis — chlamydia, gonorrhoea, LGV, herpes · enteric STIs — shigella, giardia · hepatitis A · general: IBD, coeliac, lactose, thyroid, IBS; bowel cancer very unlikely at 32

★ Consent: 'I'd like to do a blood test for HIV today — it looks for the virus and your body's response. There's a window in the first weeks where it can be negative even if someone has been infected, so if it's negative I'll repeat it at six and twelve weeks. The result comes back to me and I'll give it to you in person. It's confidential. Are you happy for me to do that?' · 'how long? will anyone find out?' → answered · three-site screen (anorectal, pharyngeal, urine NAAT), syphilis serology, hepatitis serology/vaccination, stool MCS/PCR (shigella, giardia, campylobacter), UEC (PrEP), FBE · ★ 'I'd like your partner to come in too — he needs the same tests' · partner notification support; do not stop PrEP without advice; SHINE SA/Clinic 275
ask: ★ 'Thank you for telling me that — it's directly relevant, so I'd like to ask about your sexual health now rather than later. Everything you tell me here is confidential.' / ★ 'Are you taking PrEP? And are you taking it every day, without missing doses? When was your last HIV and STI check, and did you get the results?' / 'A test you haven't had a result for isn't the same as a negative.'

★ 'Are you in a stable relationship? Have you ever had multiple partners? Are your partners male, female or both? Do you use condoms? What kind of sex do you practise — oral, anal or both — receptive, insertive or both? Have you ever been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection? Have you ever had sex under the influence of alcohol or drugs? Ever paid for sex?'

Any feeling that you need to go when there's nothing there? Any bleeding?' / 'Are you vaccinated against hepatitis A and B?'

I'm telling you it's the thing I most need to exclude, and I want to explain why.' / ★ 'Diarrhoea can be one of the first symptoms, in the first few weeks after someone catches it.' / ★ 'PrEP is very good protection, but it isn't absolute, and it works best taken every day.'

★ 'I'd like to do a blood test for HIV today … There's a window early on when the test can be negative, so I'd repeat it at six and twelve weeks. The result comes back to me and I'll give it to you in person. It's confidential. Are you happy for me to do that?' / ★ 'I'd like your partner to come in as well — he needs the same tests.'

Examiner 'he's adherent — is HIV really top?' → ★ 'I would not put it at the top as the most probable diagnosis — that is a PrEP side effect or a sexually transmissible enteric infection. I put HIV first as the condition I most need to exclude, because the consequence of missing it is the greatest and the seroconversion picture fits. PrEP substantially reduces risk but does not eliminate it, particularly with intermittent missed doses, and breakthrough infection is described. Testing costs him one blood test.' / 'Should I tell my partner?' → 'He should be tested and he needs to know he may have been exposed. You don't have to do that alone — there are services that notify partners anonymously, and I can help with the conversation. What I can't do is tell him your results without your permission.' / Proctitis variant (tenesmus, mucus, blood, pain): 'that sounds like inflammation of the rectum — proctitis — most often chlamydia or gonorrhoea, sometimes LGV or herpes; I'd examine with consent and a chaperone, take swabs, and start treatment today rather than wait (regimen VERIFY TG).'
pefe: Role-player: Michael Reid, 32, hospitality supervisor, Adelaide, boyfriend of two years (open); PrEP (TDF/FTC) ~1 year via a sexual health clinic, misses ~1 dose/fortnight; social drinker, MDMA/GHB at parties; chlamydia ×2, gonorrhoea, syphilis (treated); condoms inconsistent, none with boyfriend; receptive and insertive anal, oral. Volunteers the disclosure in sentence one and nothing else — STI history, missed doses and seroconversion symptoms must each be asked. 'Are you sexually active?' alone → 'yes' and stop. Guarded if the doctor is uncomfortable/apologetic; warm if straightforward. Hidden: frightened it's HIV, feels foolish because of PrEP; if HIV named: 'but I'm on PrEP — I thought that meant I couldn't get it'; if never named, at ~7 min 'should I be worried about HIV?'; if told PrEP means he can't have HIV → 'oh good' and let them fail

No examination task. Seroconversion illness 2–4 weeks after exposure (fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, maculopapular rash, mucosal ulcers, myalgia, diarrhoea, headache); fourth-generation Ag/Ab assay detects p24 from ~2 weeks; HIV RNA PCR if acute infection suspected; repeat at 6 and 12 weeks (window). PrEP: TDF/FTC daily (on-demand 2-1-1 for MSM); monitoring — HIV Ag/Ab and STI screen 3-monthly, creatinine/eGFR baseline and periodically, hepatitis B status; breakthrough rare with adherence, resistance risk if started during undiagnosed acute infection — do not continue PrEP blindly if HIV suspected; discuss with a sexual health physician

STI screen for MSM: anorectal + pharyngeal + first-pass urine NAAT (chlamydia/gonorrhoea), syphilis serology, HIV, hepatitis A/B/C serology; enteric STIs — shigella, giardia, campylobacter, amoebiasis; proctitis empirical treatment ceftriaxone + doxycycline (21 days if LGV) VERIFY TG; vaccinate hep A/B, HPV, meningococcal per guidelines. Notifiable in SA: HIV, syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, shigella, giardia, hepatitis A

Partner notification: contact tracing services (SHINE SA, Clinic 275, letyouknow.org.au / Drama Downunder resources) · confidentiality — cannot disclose his result to the partner · SA: SHINE SA · Clinic 275 (Adelaide Sexual Health Centre) · TIS 131 450 · PrEP prescriber for review

Not addressing the partner as a second patient; not chasing the unretrieved result; no window-period repeat plan

setting: General practice. No history-taking task and no examination task — the long stem carries the findings (read it for four things: the antibiotic, the stool description, the absent features, the hydration finding). Three tasks: diagnosis + differentials, investigations with reasons, management. The starred omissions: not saying 'stop the antibiotic'; recommending loperamide; no named red flags and no review interval.
stem: A 40-year-old man presents with diarrhoea for three days — watery stools six times a day with abdominal cramps, no blood, no travel. Recent bronchitis treated with amoxicillin for five days. Examination: dry mucous membranes, vital signs within normal limits, abdominal examination normal.
tasks: Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Explain the further investigations you would arrange, and why
Explain your management plan to the patient
time: 8 min. Identity, ★ 'before I tell you what I think, talk me through what's been happening' (rapport even without a history task), signpost three parts, concerns ('it's not cancer, is it?') · 0:50 ★ 'I'm concerned you may have pseudomembranous colitis' → mechanism in four steps with the word ★ TOXIN (balance of bacteria → antibiotic disturbs → C. difficile overgrows → produces a toxin that inflames the lining) · 'pseudomembranous' explained · ★ second diagnosis: simple antibiotic-associated diarrhoea — the difference matters, the stool test decides · differentials each with a reason from the stem: food/travel infection (no travel, no eating out, no contacts), IBD (no blood/mucus, not nocturnal, 3 days), coeliac (not greasy), lactose (no dairy link), thyroid, other medications, bowel cancer (40, no bleeding/weight/FHx — very unlikely) · 3:20 ★ investigations: stool C. difficile toxin PCR FIRST ('because…') → stool MCS/PCR for other pathogens → FBE + CRP (inflammation) + UEC (he's dry) → faecal calprotectin (IBD screen) → coeliac antibodies (keep eating gluten) → sigmoidoscopy mentioned and deferred · 5:00 ★ management: STOP the antibiotic → oral vancomycin 10 days if confirmed (the paradox answered) → ORS, avoid loperamide → soap and water, bleach → red flags → review 2–3 days.

back.dx: Pseudomembranous colitis (C. difficile toxin-mediated colitis) 'may have' — three days of profuse watery diarrhoea 6–7/day with cramps starting ~10 days after a five-day amoxicillin course for bronchitis; no blood, no travel, mild dehydration, normal obs and abdomen. Second (and more common): plain antibiotic-associated diarrhoea — settles alone; a stool toxin test tells them apart, and only the first needs specific treatment. Management: stop the antibiotic (chest infection settled), oral vancomycin 125 mg qid 10 days if confirmed (metronidazole alternative for non-severe VERIFY), oral rehydration, no loperamide (prolongs toxin contact, toxic megacolon risk), soap-and-water hand hygiene and bleach cleaning (spores resist alcohol gel), red flags, review 2–3 days. Recurrence ~1 in 5.
plan: 'I'm Dr —; can I confirm your name and date of birth? Before I tell you what I think is going on, talk me through what's been happening over the last few days.' → 'thank you — I've read your notes and I have a clear picture. I'll explain what I think this is, what tests I want, and what we'll do. Was there anything you were particularly worried about?' ('been reading online — it's not cancer, is it?')

★ 'I'm concerned you may have a condition called pseudomembranous colitis. Your bowel normally has a large population of harmless bacteria living in balance. When you take an antibiotic, it doesn't only kill the bug causing your chest infection — it disturbs that balance. One particular bug, Clostridioides difficile, can take over and overgrow. That bug produces a toxin — a poison — and it is the toxin that inflames the lining of the bowel and causes the diarrhoea and cramps. It's called pseudomembranous because with a camera we'd see whitish patches on the lining.' · 'is that serious? do I need hospital?' → non-severe form, treatable as an outpatient if the plan is followed

★ 'The other possibility — and the more common one — is simply that the antibiotic itself has loosened your bowels. That settles by itself. The difference matters, because the first needs specific treatment and the second doesn't, and a stool test tells us which it is.' · DDx with reasons from the stem: food/travel infection (no travel, no eating out, nobody unwell), IBD (no blood/mucus, not nocturnal, only 3 days), coeliac (not greasy/floating), dairy (no link), thyroid (no weight loss/heat), other medications (I'll check — Somac), bowel cancer (at 40 with no bleeding, weight loss or FHx — very unlikely; it stays on the list with any habit change)

★ Investigations, each with 'because': 'the most important test is a stool sample looking for that toxin — a PCR — that confirms or rules out this diagnosis · on the same sample, other bowel infections — viral, bacterial, parasitic · bloods: FBC and CRP for the degree of inflammation; kidney function and salts, because diarrhoea upsets those and you're a bit dry · faecal calprotectin — our best screening test for inflammatory bowel disease · coeliac antibodies — keep eating gluten normally until it's done · there's also a camera test, a sigmoidoscopy, because this condition has a characteristic appearance — I wouldn't do that first; the stool test is simpler and should give the answer'

★ 'The first and most important thing is that we stop the antibiotic — your chest infection has settled, and it's what triggered this.' · ★ 'If the stool test confirms it, we treat the overgrowth with a medicine that targets that bug — usually vancomycin by mouth for ten days.' · 'antibiotics caused it and you're giving me another one?' → ★ 'I know how that sounds. We're not treating a new infection — one bug has overgrown, and this medicine targets that one bug specifically, so the normal balance can re-establish itself.' · ★ 'Drink plenty — Hydralyte or Gastrolyte is ideal, plain water is fine. Avoid Gastro-Stop or anything that stops diarrhoea for now — if this is the infection I think it might be, slowing the bowel keeps the toxin in contact with it longer.' · ★ 'The germ spreads through spores that alcohol hand gel doesn't kill — wash your hands with soap and water, and clean the bathroom with a bleach-based cleaner.'

★ 'Come back, or go straight to the emergency department, if you develop a fever, severe tummy pain or bloating, blood in the stool, dizziness or light-headedness, or you can't keep fluids down. Otherwise I'll see you in two to three days — I should have the results — and we'll go through them together.' · address the cancer worry with the reasons · 'when will I hear?' · 'does all of that make sense? what questions do you have?'

Antibiotics disturb that balance, and one particular bug can overgrow. That bug produces a toxin, and it's the toxin that inflames the bowel lining.'

I'll see you again in two to three days with the results.'

Examiner challenges: 'toxin on every post-antibiotic diarrhoea?' → 'No — most is mild and self-limiting. I test where the stool is profuse and watery, with systemic features, in hospital or aged care, in the elderly, or not settling — he meets that threshold.' / 'always severe?' → 'No — a non-severe form with watery diarrhoea, cramps, low-grade fever and normal observations, which is what he has; severe and fulminant sit further along the spectrum.' / 'severe disease?' → 'oral vancomycin; fulminant with ileus or toxic megacolon — oral or per-rectal vancomycin plus IV metronidazole and urgent surgical review; IV vancomycin does not reach the lumen.' / 'finished ten days ago — can it still be that?' → 'yes — during the course or up to eight weeks after, most commonly within two.'
pefe: Role-player: Peter Doyle, 40, grain handler, Wallaroo, partner and one child; 3 d watery diarrhoea 6–7/day, cramps easing after going, no blood/mucus, nothing at night, thirsty/dry mouth, no vomiting; amoxicillin 5 d for bronchitis finished ~10 d ago (name/duration/indication only if asked separately); Somac for reflux, Panadol; Gastro-Stop ×2 (little help); no travel/eating out/contacts; all other blocks negative. Practical, fed up, wants a plan; anxious at 'colitis'; asks 'antibiotics caused it and you're giving me another antibiotic?' at ~5:30 regardless; 'can I just keep taking the Gastro-Stop?' if loperamide not mentioned. Hidden: reading online, frightened of cancer — 'it's not cancer, is it?' if asked concerns, else at ~6:30

Findings given: dry mucous membranes; vitals within normal limits; abdomen normal. Severity markers (non-severe here): WCC ≥15, creatinine >1.5× baseline, albumin <30, T >38.5, ileus/megacolon/hypotension = severe/fulminant VERIFY

C. difficile: onset during the course or up to 8 weeks after (most within 2); risk — any antibiotic (clindamycin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, amoxicillin), PPIs, age, hospital, IBD; test liquid stool only (GDH/toxin/PCR algorithm), do not repeat to prove cure. Treatment VERIFY TG: non-severe — oral vancomycin 125 mg qid 10 d (metronidazole 400 mg tds 10 d alternative); severe — oral vancomycin; fulminant — oral/PR vancomycin + IV metronidazole, surgery; recurrence ~20% → vancomycin taper/fidaxomicin/FMT (specialist); stop offending antibiotic and PPI if possible; no antimotility agents; contact precautions, soap and water, sporicidal (bleach) cleaning; notifiable? (C. difficile is not routinely notifiable in SA — hospital surveillance) VERIFY
Version B (post-op day 4, 67 F) = MED-141 · SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · healthdirect 1800 022 222
fails: Delivering a diagnosis to a patient who hasn't spoken; saying only 'a side effect of your antibiotics' (that is antibiotic-associated diarrhoea, which needs no investigation or management — and the station asked for both)
Explaining the mechanism without the word toxin; listing tests without 'because'; leading with sigmoidoscopy
★ Not saying 'stop the antibiotic'; ★ recommending or allowing loperamide; ★ no named red flags and no review interval
No infection-control advice (soap and water, bleach); not answering the antibiotic paradox; not addressing the cancer worry
numbers: Onset during course or ≤8 wk after (most ≤2 wk) · oral vancomycin 125 mg qid 10 d VERIFY · metronidazole 400 mg tds 10 d (non-severe alternative) · fulminant: oral/PR vancomycin + IV metronidazole; never IV vancomycin alone
Recurrence ~1 in 5 · test liquid stool only · no test of cure · review 2–3 d · soap and water, bleach · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

setting: Surgical ward; you are the HMO. Version B of the pseudomembranous colitis document (August 2025). No differential task — deliberately; the history must follow the lead point in the stem (the cancer, its treatment, the operation four days ago). Observation chart handed over at five minutes: interpret it to the examiner, then order investigations with reasons. Name C. difficile first — then add the anastomotic leak/collection the source leaves out.
stem: A 67-year-old woman with known bowel adenocarcinoma underwent bowel resection four days ago and now reports diarrhoea.
tasks: Take a focused history (5 minutes)
Interpret the observation chart to the examiner (given at 5 minutes)
Order your investigations, with reasons
time: 8 min. Identity, open, acknowledge · usual diarrhoea questions: started this morning, ★ watery, ★ large volume, 5–6 episodes, blood/mucus, ★ 'feel hot/feverish?' · ★ lead-point block: 'when were you first diagnosed? besides surgery, chemotherapy or radiotherapy? who follows you up?' · ★ 'the last four days: nausea/vomiting? tummy pain — different from the pain you'd expect after surgery? bloated or distended? wound problems? started eating and drinking — keeping it down?' · ★ 'what medications have you been given? which antibiotic, how many days?' (antibiotics since the operation, 5 days, name unknown) · analgesics (opioids/laxatives given?), DVT prophylaxis, other meds · 5:00 chart: ★ RR 14–17 normal · SpO2 97–98% → 94% day 4 · HR high 70s → 112 · T 36.6 → 38.4 day 4 · BP ~120/80 → ~160/110 → 'a deteriorating patient on day four after bowel resection — new fever, new tachycardia, falling saturations, alongside new profuse watery diarrhoea after five days of antibiotics' · ★ investigations with reasons: stool C. difficile toxin PCR · stool MCS/PCR panel · FBE + CRP · UEC + albumin · blood cultures + lactate · ★ CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast — anastomotic leak or collection, discussed with the surgical team · erect CXR · not calprotectin/coeliac here · isolate, contact precautions, soap and water.

back.dx: Probable C. difficile colitis in a deteriorating post-operative patient — day 4 after bowel resection for adenocarcinoma (neoadjuvant chemotherapy), five days of antibiotics, new profuse large-volume watery diarrhoea from this morning (5–6 episodes), feverish; chart: new fever 38.4, HR 112, SpO2 94%, BP risen to ~160/110. The safer reasoning names C. difficile first and then insists on excluding an anastomotic leak or intra-abdominal/pelvic collection (day 4 is the classic timing; diarrhoea can be the early sign of a pelvic collection) with contrast CT and surgical discussion, plus a sepsis screen. Isolate with contact precautions and soap-and-water hand hygiene while awaiting the toxin result.
plan: Identity, 'tell me what's been happening' → acknowledge · diarrhoea: when (this morning), ★ watery, ★ volume (large), episodes (5–6), blood/mucus, urgency, ★ 'do you feel hot or feverish? any shivers?'

★ Lead point: 'when were you first diagnosed with the bowel cancer? besides the surgery, any other treatment — chemotherapy or radiotherapy? who follows you up, and how often?' (6 months; chemo before the op)

★ The last four days: nausea/vomiting · tummy pain — ★ 'different from the pain you'd expect after surgery?' · bloating/distension · passing wind · wound — pain, ooze, redness · ★ 'have you started eating and drinking, and are you keeping it down?' (fluids yesterday, soup today) · urine output · breathing, cough, calf pain

★ 'What medications have you been given? which antibiotic, and how many days?' (since the op, ~5 d, name unknown) · painkillers (opioids), laxatives/aperients (osmotic laxatives cause diarrhoea), PPI, DVT prophylaxis, usual meds · allergies · summarise

★ Chart: 'Examiner — respiratory rate 14 to 17 throughout, normal. Oxygen saturation 97–98% on days one to three, falling to 94% on day four. Heart rate high seventies rising to 112 — she is now tachycardic. Temperature 36.6 rising to 38.4 — a new fever on day four. Blood pressure has risen from about 120/80 to about 160/110. My interpretation is a deteriorating patient on day four after bowel resection, with new fever, new tachycardia and falling saturations, alongside new profuse watery diarrhoea after five days of antibiotics.'

★ Investigations with reasons: 'stool C. difficile toxin PCR — antibiotics plus new watery diarrhoea in hospital makes this my leading diagnosis · stool MCS and PCR panel — other enteric pathogens and ward infection control · FBE and CRP — inflammation and severity · UEC, creatinine and albumin — NBM then large losses; also C. difficile severity markers · blood cultures and venous lactate — febrile and tachycardic; sepsis screen · ★ CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast, discussed with the surgical team — to exclude an anastomotic leak or intra-abdominal collection; day four is the classic timing, and diarrhoea can be an early symptom of a pelvic collection · erect chest X-ray — falling saturations · I would not order faecal calprotectin or coeliac serology here — appropriate in an undifferentiated community presentation, not this context' · ★ 'and I would isolate her in a single room with contact precautions and soap-and-water hand hygiene while awaiting the result' · escalate: registrar/surgical team, sepsis pathway, fluids, hold laxatives/opioids review, no antimotility agents
ask: ★ 'I'd like to ask about your bowel condition and the operation. When were you first diagnosed? Besides the surgery, have you had any other treatment — chemotherapy or radiotherapy? Who follows you up, and how often?'

★ 'Now about the last four days. Any nausea or vomiting? Any tummy pain — and is it different from the pain you'd expect after surgery? Is your tummy bloated or distended? Any problems with the wound? Have you started eating and drinking, and are you keeping it down?' / ★ 'What medications have you been given? Which antibiotic, and how many days?'

★ To examiner: 'Respiratory rate 14 to 17 throughout, normal. Saturations 97–98% on days one to three, falling to 94% on day four. Heart rate high seventies rising to 112 — now tachycardic. Temperature 36.6 rising to 38.4 — a new fever on day four. Blood pressure risen from about 120/80 to about 160/110. My interpretation is a deteriorating patient on day four after bowel resection, with new fever, new tachycardia and falling saturations, alongside new profuse watery diarrhoea after five days of antibiotics.'

★ 'Stool C. difficile toxin PCR — antibiotics plus new watery diarrhoea in hospital makes this my leading diagnosis … And I would want a CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast, discussed with the surgical team, because I need to exclude an anastomotic leak or an intra-abdominal collection — day four is the classic timing, and diarrhoea can be an early symptom of a pelvic collection.' / 'I would not order faecal calprotectin or coeliac serology here.' / 'I would isolate her in a single room with contact precautions and soap-and-water hand hygiene while awaiting the result.'
pefe: Role-player (reconstructed): 67 F, bowel adenocarcinoma diagnosed 6 months ago, neoadjuvant chemotherapy, resection 4 days ago; watery large-volume diarrhoea from this morning ×5–6, feels hot; antibiotics since the operation ~5 days, name unknown; fluids yesterday, soup today

Chart: RR 14–17 · SpO2 97–98 → 94% day 4 · HR 70s → 112 · T 36.6 → 38.4 · BP ~120/80 → ~160/110. Post-op day 3–5 DDx for fever + diarrhoea: C. difficile (hospital, antibiotics), anastomotic leak (day 3–7; fever, tachycardia, pain, ileus, diarrhoea, raised CRP), pelvic/intra-abdominal collection, wound infection, pneumonia/atelectasis (SpO2 fall), UTI (IDC), DVT/PE, medication (laxatives, magnesium, antibiotics), overflow around impaction, early enteral feeding intolerance

C. difficile severity (VERIFY): WCC ≥15, creatinine rise, albumin <30, T >38.5, hypotension, ileus, megacolon → severe/fulminant; treat oral vancomycin ± IV metronidazole; surgical review; stop offending antibiotics where possible; isolate; no loperamide. Anastomotic leak → CT with contrast, NBM, IV antibiotics, surgical team — drainage or re-laparotomy
Escalation: MET criteria (HR >130, RR >25, SpO2 <90, SBP <90, T >38.5 in some charts) VERIFY local; sepsis bundle; inform the surgical registrar/consultant; document

Not asking which antibiotic/how long, oral intake, wound, distension, or pain character
Reading the chart without interpreting the trend or stating 'deteriorating patient'
Investigations without reasons; ordering calprotectin/coeliac serology; no CT/leak consideration; no blood cultures/lactate
No isolation/contact precautions; no escalation to the surgical team

setting: Regional SA general practice. ~4 min history, 2 min examination findings from the examiner, 2 min explanation. Every red flag is NEGATIVE — the patient gives no prompt to think of cancer; the findings outrank the history. Without the rectal examination you get hepatomegaly alone and spend the explanation talking about a big liver with no cause. Consent and chaperone must be said aloud.
stem: Mrs Margaret Harding, 67, presents with diarrhoea for two weeks. Gastro-Stop from the chemist is not helping — if anything it's worse. Lower abdominal ache.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history
Ask the examiner for your physical examination findings
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 min. Identity, open → 'two weeks is worth sorting properly — and worsening despite treatment tells me we need the cause, not more symptom relief' · permission · timing, nocturnal, CCCVO (4–5/day, watery, no blood) · pain: where (low, no side), radiation, relation to bowels, ★ tenesmus ('feel you haven't fully emptied, or need to go and nothing comes?' — yes) · general GI · ★ 2:10 red-flag block 'I ask everybody with a change in their bowels': weight loss (how much/how long), appetite, lumps, tiredness, blood/black stools, ★ 'before this, had your bowels changed — more/less often, different shape?', FHx bowel cancer + age, ★ 'done the bowel screening kit?' (never sent it back) → all negative — do not change course · at speed: travel/contacts, meds incl chemist/antibiotics/anticoagulants, IBD ×4, coeliac/lactose, thyroid, alcohol · 3:50 hands off · ★ seven named PEFE steps: appearance (well/unwell, dehydration, pallor, jaundice, cachexia, rash) · vitals + postural BP · neck — thyroid, cervical + supraclavicular nodes · abdomen inspection · palpation (tenderness, masses, ★ organomegaly) → hepatomegaly 4 cm → ★ pursue: smooth or irregular/nodular? tender? pulsatile? · percussion (liver span, shifting dullness), auscultation, groins · ★ 'I would like to perform a digital rectal examination, with the patient's consent and with a chaperone present' → perianal inspection; digital: mass → ★ pursue: cm from the verge, fixed/mobile, proportion of circumference, blood on the glove · dipstick · warning shot → findings → concern → ★ pause → her three questions → plan → DDx → stop loperamide → obstruction safety-net → support.

back.dx: Colorectal (rectal) carcinoma with hepatic metastases until proven otherwise — two weeks of worsening watery diarrhoea 4–5/day despite loperamide, dull lower abdominal ache, tenesmus, slightly dry, all red flags negative, never did the screening kit; PEFE: irregular non-tender hepatomegaly 4 cm below the costal margin, no splenomegaly/ascites, and on DRE a firm fixed rectal mass ~6 cm from the anal verge involving half the circumference with blood on the glove. Explain with a warning shot, name the findings, name the concern ('may be a cancer … may have spread to the liver'), pause, never give a prognosis; urgent colonoscopy + biopsy, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, bloods (FBE, iron, UEC, LFT, coags, CEA baseline), referral today with a follow-up call, stop the Gastro-Stop, obstruction red flags, Cancer Council SA.
plan: Identity, open → ★ 'two weeks is worth sorting out properly, and it's getting worse despite what you've tried — so we need to find the cause rather than keep treating the symptom. I'll ask some questions, examine you, then tell you what I think. Some are personal — is that all right?'

Timing: 2 wk, constant, worse, not nocturnal · CCCVO: 4–5/day, watery, no blood, not bulky · pain: low, no side, no radiation, relation to defecation, ★ 'do you ever feel you haven't fully emptied, or need to go and nothing comes?' → yes (register, move on)

General GI: N/V, bloating (a bit), constipated before (no), fever · ★ 2:10 'there are some questions I ask everybody with a change in their bowels': weight loss — how much/how long (none), appetite (normal), lumps, tiredness (a bit), blood/black stools (no), ★ 'before this, had your bowels changed at all — more often, less often, a different shape?' (no), FHx bowel cancer + age (none), ★ 'have you done the bowel screening test that comes in the post?' (got it, never sent it back)

At speed: travel/contacts · meds incl chemist (perindopril, Gastro-Stop), antibiotics, blood thinners · IBD ×4 · greasy stools, dairy · thyroid · alcohol (glass most nights) · concerns ('I just want it to stop — granddaughter's wedding in three weeks') · 3:50 hands off

★ 'Examiner, I'd like specific findings — yes or no is fine. General appearance — well or unwell? dehydration — dry mucous membranes, skin turgor? pallor, jaundice, cachexia? rashes? · vital signs incl postural BP, RR, sats · neck — thyroid, cervical and supraclavicular nodes · abdomen inspection — moves with respiration, distension, scars, visible masses · palpation — tenderness, guarding, rebound, masses, ★ organomegaly' → 'hepatomegaly, 4 cm below the costal margin' → ★ 'is the edge smooth, or irregular and nodular? tender? pulsatile? splenomegaly, ascites, jaundice?' → irregular, non-tender, no spleen, no ascites · 'percussion — liver span, shifting dullness; bowel sounds; groins — hernias, nodes'

★ 'And I would like to perform a digital rectal examination, with the patient's consent and with a chaperone present. On inspection of the perianal area — fissures, tags, piles, masses? On digital examination — is there a mass, how far from the anal verge, fixed or mobile, what proportion of the circumference, and is there blood on the glove?' → firm mass → ★ '~6 cm, fixed, half the circumference, blood on the glove' · dipstick (ketones)

★ Warning shot: 'Mrs Harding, I'd like to talk to you about what I found when I examined you. I'd rather be straight with you than vague — is that all right? Is there anyone you'd like to have with you?' → ★ 'I found two things. There is a lump in your back passage, and your liver is enlarged — I can feel it below your ribs, which I shouldn't normally be able to do.' [★ pause 2–3 s — do not fill it] → ★ 'I'm concerned that the lump may be a cancer in the bowel, and that the enlarged liver may mean it has spread there. I can't be certain today — I need tests to confirm it — but I don't want to tell you it's nothing when I'm worried that it isn't.' · 'but I feel fine, no weight loss' → 'that's true, and it's a good thing — but those symptoms don't always appear early; what I can feel on examination matters more than what the symptoms have shown so far' · 'are you sure?' → 'no, not yet — I'm sure of what I felt, and that it needs investigating quickly' · ★ 'how long have I got?' → 'I genuinely can't answer that, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I guessed — we don't yet know what it is, how big, or whether it has spread; once we have the camera test and the scan the specialist team can talk to you properly'

Plan: urgent colonoscopy with biopsy · CT chest/abdomen/pelvis · bloods today (FBE, iron, UEC, LFT, coags, CEA baseline) · ★ 'I'll do the referral this afternoon and ring you myself with the appointment' · DDx honestly: inflammation of the bowel, reduced blood supply, infection, a liver problem itself — 'the tests will sort them out; I'm telling you my main concern because I think you'd want to know' · ★ stop the Gastro-Stop · ★ safety-net: 'very painful or bloated tummy, vomiting, stop passing wind, or blood → sooner or ED' · review in a few days regardless · Cancer Council 13 11 20 — support and transport to Adelaide (PATS) · 'what questions do you have?'

Is it pulsatile?' / ★ 'How far from the anal verge? Is it mobile or fixed to surrounding tissue? What proportion of the circumference? Is there blood on the glove?'

Is there anyone you'd like to have with you?' / ★ 'I found two things. There is a lump in your back passage, and your liver is enlarged.' [pause] / ★ 'I'm concerned that the lump may be a cancer in the bowel, and that the enlarged liver may mean it has spread there. I can't be certain today — I need tests to confirm it — but I don't want to tell you it's nothing when I'm worried that it isn't.'

'But I haven't lost any weight' → ★ 'That's true, and it's a good thing. But those symptoms don't always appear early. What I can feel on examination is more important than what the symptoms have shown so far, and that's why I'm not letting it go.' / 'How long have I got?' → ★ 'I genuinely can't answer that, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I guessed. We don't yet know what it is, how big it is, or whether it has spread. Once we have the camera test and the scan, the specialist team will be able to talk to you properly about treatment. What I can tell you is that this is being taken seriously and it's being done quickly.'

'I'm going to arrange an urgent camera test of the bowel — a colonoscopy — and a CT scan of your chest, tummy and pelvis. Bloods today. I'll do the referral this afternoon and I'll ring you myself with the appointment. Please stop the Gastro-Stop. Antibiotics as an adjunct for surrounding cellulitis, diabetes, immunosuppression or valvular heart disease.' / 'perianal vs pilonidal?' → 'Site. Perianal — immediately adjacent to the anal verge, from an infected anal gland at the dentate line. Pilonidal — midline of the natal cleft in hair-bearing skin, from a midline pit with ingrown hair, typically pointing slightly off the midline.' / 'three abscesses in two years?' → 'raises Crohn disease — ask about diarrhoea, blood, weight loss, mouth ulcers; colonoscopy and pelvic MRI with gastroenterology; check for diabetes and immunosuppression.' / 'diabetic, 39.5, tachycardic, dusky skin' → 'Fournier's gangrene — a surgical emergency: resuscitate, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately, cultures and lactate, urgent surgical debridement — immediate MedSTAR retrieval on 1300 13 12 33.' / 'irregular ulcerated bleeding lesion' → 'anal cancer — usually squamous cell, HPV-associated: urgent specialist referral for examination and biopsy, examine the inguinal nodes, offer HIV testing with consent.'

Never volunteers the beer cans — only to a direct alcohol question ('the notes say she stopped, so I won't ask' → silence). No examination. Findings by proxy: fluctuating forgetfulness with intact recognition, sleep reversal, intermittent confusion, easy bruising, abdominal distension (ascites), constipation, poor intake, low mood, no falls; non-adherence, lost to follow-up; hidden alcohol

Hepatic encephalopathy: West Haven grades 1–4 (sleep reversal/subtle → lethargy/disorientation → somnolence/confusion → coma); asterixis, fetor; ammonia not required for diagnosis. Six precipitants: alcohol, infection (SBP, UTI, chest), medications (sedatives, opioids, diuretics), constipation, GI bleeding, dehydration/electrolytes (also hypokalaemia, TIPS, HCC). Treatment: identify/treat the trigger; lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools/day; rifaximin for recurrence VERIFY; avoid sedatives; nutrition (don't restrict protein); thiamine. SBP: ascitic neutrophils ≥250/mm³ → IV ceftriaxone VERIFY, albumin, prophylaxis. HCC surveillance 6-monthly USS ± AFP. Standard drink 10 g; NHMRC ≤10/week. Cirrhosis follow-up: 6-monthly, varices screening, vaccinations

★ Results in plain words: 'as you know, you have cirrhosis — the tissue of your liver has been damaged by long-term alcohol. Albumin is the main protein your liver makes and it's low — your liver isn't producing proteins properly. Platelets are tiny particles that help your blood clot, and they're low. Your liver has also stopped making the factors that clot your blood, so your blood takes longer to clot — that's what the INR shows, and it's why you're bruising. Haemoglobin, which carries oxygen, is low. More importantly, your white cells are raised, which means there's an infection somewhere, and the type — the neutrophils — points to a bacterial infection.'

★ 'That brings me to what I think is going on. I'm suspecting spontaneous bacterial peritonitis — an infection in the fluid that has collected in your abdomen because your liver isn't working properly. Four reasons: you have a fever; your white cells and neutrophils are raised, pointing to a bacterial infection; on examination you have fluid in your abdomen; and you have a clear reason for your liver to have got worse — you've started drinking again. back.dx: Stage IV colorectal cancer — liver metastases two years after resection with no adjuvant therapy and no surveillance (no follow-up, no CEA, no imaging since); six months of 6 kg weight loss, anorexia, fatigue, early jaundice and itch; lives alone, daughter in Perth. The communication task: explain 'metastasis' plainly, offer support, an empathic line, silence, and reassurance of care. The management task in order: multidisciplinary team → confirm the liver lesion is colorectal in origin (biopsy/MRI liver; CEA) before committing to palliation → palliative intent explained honestly (symptom control; systemic therapy to prolong and control, not cure; selected patients may be candidates for liver resection — the MDT decides) → advance care directive and substitute decision-maker now, plus practical supports for a man living alone.
plan: ★ 'Good morning, I'm Dr —, the doctor looking after you today. Am I speaking with James? I've been through your file and I can see you were here yesterday. I imagine yesterday was a hard day. How are you feeling today?' → 'not great, didn't sleep' → 'I'm sorry to hear that'

★ 'Can you tell me a little more about yesterday — what were you told?' → 'something in my liver; they said metastasis — what does that actually mean?' → ★ 'Metastasis means a cancer that started in one part of the body has spread to another part. In your case I think it is most likely that the bowel cancer you were treated for has spread to your liver.' → [quiet] → ★ 'Before we go further, would you like anyone to be with you while we talk about this? How are you feeling right now? I understand this may be shocking news. I wish I had better news for you today.' [water, tissues, a few seconds] → ★ 'What I do want to say is that my team and I are here to support you, and we will provide the best care we can.'

'Is it all right if I ask some questions? ★ When were you diagnosed with the bowel cancer? What treatment did you receive? Have you been having regular follow-up with your GP and your specialist?' → 2 y; operation, told no chemo/RT; ★ never went back → 'thank you for telling me — that's important, because follow-up is how we pick up any return early' (no blame; if gently asked why: 'felt well, hate hospitals — I suppose I should have')

'Lost weight recently, change in appetite? lumps? unusual tiredness? any cough, or bone pain?' → 6 kg, poor, very tired; no cough/bone pain · 'yellowing of skin or eyes, itching, dark urine, pale stools?' → eyes a bit yellow, a bit itchy · pain, bowels, bleeding · ★ 'do you have enough support at home?' → alone; daughter in Perth · mood, sleep; who else knows

★ Step 1 — the team: 'James, let me tell you how we're going to look after you. First, you will not be doing this alone. You'll be cared for by a team — myself, an oncologist who specialises in cancer treatment, a surgeon, a cancer care nurse, a psychologist and a social worker.'

★ Step 2 — confirm the source: 'The first thing we need to do is be sure the lump in your liver has come from your bowel cancer. It's important not to assume. We may take a small sample using a needle passed through the skin, and arrange a special MRI scan of the liver to look more closely.' → 'could it be something else?' → 'most likely from the bowel cancer, so I don't want to raise your hopes — but it's important we confirm it, because a different cause would mean a different treatment'

★ Step 3 — palliative intent: 'Once we know where it's come from, the aim of treatment is to control your symptoms and keep you as comfortable and as well as possible. We call that palliative care. That means good pain relief, medication for nausea if you need it, and sometimes chemotherapy, radiotherapy or an operation — used to control symptoms and slow things down rather than to cure the cancer.' → 'so chemo wouldn't cure it' → 'No, it would not. I'm sorry. Its purpose would be to slow things down and keep you feeling better for longer.' → 'is palliative care giving up?' → 'No — it's active care focused on you living as well as possible for as long as possible.'

★ Step 4 — plan ahead: 'I'd also recommend we make an advance care directive — a document recording what treatment you would and wouldn't want — and that you choose someone as your substitute decision-maker in case there comes a time when you can't tell us yourself. Now, while you're well, is the right time.' · ★ 'You told me you live alone, so I'll also arrange a cancer care nurse and a social worker, and community palliative care support at home' — and offer to help contact his daughter · summary: 'the scan shows the cancer has most likely spread to your liver; we'll confirm where it's come from; a team will look after you; treatment will focus on keeping you comfortable; and we'll plan ahead together. Is there anything you'd like to ask me?'

★ 'Would you like anyone to be with you while we talk about this?' / ★ 'I am so sorry to have to give you this news. I wish I had better news today.' / 'Take a sip of water. Take your time.' / 'My team and I are here to support you, and we will provide the best care we can.'

★ 'You will be cared for by a team, and you will not be doing this alone.' / ★ 'First we need to be sure this has come from your bowel cancer.' / ★ 'The aim of treatment is to control your symptoms — we call that palliative care.' / ★ 'I would recommend an advance care directive and a substitute decision-maker.'

Version A (multiple lesions, no known cancer, Jenny — indigestion, iron deficiency, back pain): [turn the scan toward her] 'This is a slice through your liver. I can see a number of rounded areas that look different from the surrounding tissue, which suggests there are lumps or growths there. Jenny, unfortunately I do not have good news for you today. Would you like anyone to be with you?' → 'We usually see this picture when a cancer has spread to the liver — we call that metastasis. Based on your indigestion and the iron deficiency in your blood, which tells me you've been losing blood somewhere, the most likely source is a cancer in your bowel or your stomach. I'm also concerned your back pain may mean spread to the bones.' → gastroscopy + colonoscopy with biopsies, PET, bone scan, liver MRI/biopsy

Version D (incidental lesion, no cancer history — gallstones, liver lesion, diverticula): good news → concern → irrelevant finding: 'gallbladder — a few stones, none blocking the tubes, no inflammation; liver — a lump that looks darker than the surrounding tissue, with a few possible causes; bowel — small pouches called diverticula, not the cause of your pain and not inflamed.' → 'stones can cause short-lived pain — biliary colic — but this is your first episode and there's no inflammation, so I don't think that's the whole story. I'm concerned about the lump in your liver. It could be a cancer starting in the liver, or one that has spread there, but it could equally be benign — an adenoma, a cyst, an abscess or a haemangioma. I can't tell from this scan, and that's exactly why I want to investigate it.' → contrast MRI liver, ± biopsy, LFTs, AFP, colonoscopy + gastroscopy, chase lipase/amylase, FBE, CRP
pefe: Role-player: James Whitlock, 68, retired shearer, widowed, alone on a property outside town, daughter in Perth; ex-smoker; bowel cancer resected 2 y ago, told no chemo/RT, never returned for follow-up (felt well, hates hospitals); 6 kg loss, anorexia, fatigue; sister-in-law says eyes yellow; some itch. Flat, tired; asks 'what does metastasis mean?' early; quiet and looks down rather than crying — stays silent for seconds if no support/pause is offered; 'could it be something else?' (hopeful); 'will chemotherapy cure it?' (wants a straight answer); 'is palliative care giving up?' at ~6 min if the phrase is unexplained; defensive and closed if blamed for missing follow-up; at 7 min if never asked: 'doctor, I do live on my own, you know'. Hidden: frightened of dying alone; ashamed about follow-up

No examination task. Colorectal spread: liver > lung > nodes > peritoneum; bone less often. Markers: CEA (colorectal), AFP (HCC). Best lesion imaging: multiphase contrast MRI; staging PET-CT; bone scan if bone pain. Biopsy if it changes management (or if the primary is unknown). Selected patients with limited liver-only metastases may be candidates for resection/ablation with curative intent — the MDT decides; do not promise. Systemic therapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± biologics) for palliative control; symptom control; early palliative care improves quality of life

SA Advance Care Directive; substitute decision-maker; enduring power of attorney; SA Health palliative care services; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20; Country Health Connect; social work; PATS; My Aged Care; Lifeline 13 11 14 if distress; TIS 131 450. Explanation of a result ≤90 s. Iron deficiency (Version A): low Hb, MCV, MCH, MCHC, ferritin; anisocytosis = size, poikilocytosis = shape
Version C (single lesion with a bowel cancer history, two-minute history): four cancer questions plus a red-flag sweep only — no full pain history; the marks are in the explanation
fails: Opening with 'how can I help you today?'; skipping straight to history because 'he already knows' — losing the whole communication domain (no plain-English metastasis, no support offer, no empathic line, no silence, no reassurance)
Blaming him for missing follow-up; not saying the missed surveillance back and using it
Not asking about support at home; not addressing living alone in the plan
★ Starting the plan at palliation — assuming the source, skipping the team, never reaching advance care planning
Promising a cure from chemotherapy; using 'palliative care' without explaining it; giving a prognosis timeframe; no summary or invitation for questions
