setting: General practice. Four-minute history, PEFE from the examiner, diagnosis, differentials. The stem's 'sore throat two weeks ago' is designed to pull you to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. The question that decides the station is asked by 1:20: 'have your stools become pale?' — commit the branch aloud. Then: 'did you see a doctor, and were you given any antibiotics?' The antibiotic is the diagnosis.
stem: Jenny Marsh, 45, presents with dark urine. She had a sore throat two weeks ago.
tasks: Take a focused history (about 4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
Explain your differential diagnoses
time: 8 min. 'May I have her vital signs?' → stable · intro, permission, open · characterise the urine: ★ colour exactly (Coca-Cola, brown, dark yellow — 'strong tea'), ★ through the stream or start/end, blood/clots, smell, when, every time, worse · ★ by 1:20: 'along with the dark urine, have your stools become pale or clay-coloured?' → yes → ★ commit: 'dark urine with pale stools tells me this is very likely the liver or the drainage tubes rather than the kidneys — let me just check a few kidney questions: burning, fever, leg swelling, injury?' → none → 'I'll focus on the liver' · red flags: weight, appetite, lumps, tiredness, FHx cancer · ★ yellowing (eyes yes), itching (all over, worse at night) · risk factors ABP FIT NO SEX: alcohol (barely), ★ 'you mentioned a sore throat — did you see a doctor, and were you given any medication or antibiotics?' (Augmentin, finished a week ago), blood transfusions/piercings/tattoos, food/water, IVDU, travel, occupation, sexual · gallbladder: fatty-meal pain, operations · ★ fever/chills (none) · concerns (mother died of liver failure — transplant fear) · PEFE named: jaundice, scratch marks, cachexia, conscious level; vitals esp temperature; abdomen — symmetry, distension; tenderness ± guarding/rigidity/rebound; ★ hepatomegaly/splenomegaly; ★ shifting dullness; bowel sounds; ★ dipstick bilirubin, blood, protein → jaundiced, RUQ tenderness, enlarged liver, no spleen, no ascites, bilirubin +, blood −, protein − · dx drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis with three reasons · large liver list, small kidney list · stop and document the drug, bloods, USS, safety-net.

back.dx: Antibiotic-induced cholestatic hepatitis (amoxicillin–clavulanate) — four to five days of tea-coloured urine dark throughout the stream, pale stools, yellow sclerae and generalised itch worse at night, one week after finishing a course of Augmentin for a sore throat; no fever, no fatty-meal pain, no operations, no viral risk factors, barely drinks. PEFE: jaundiced, afebrile, RUQ tenderness without peritonism, tender enlarged liver, no splenomegaly, no ascites; dipstick bilirubin positive, blood and protein negative. Three reasons: the dark urine/pale stools/yellow eyes combination localises to liver/ducts; a well-known culprit drug with the right timing; a tender enlarged liver with bilirubinuria and no fever (cholangitis unlikely). Stop and document the drug (never again), LFTs/coags/hepatitis serology/USS, most recover fully over weeks; safety-net for fever with rigors, drowsiness/confusion, bruising/bleeding, deepening jaundice. Version A (32 F, stools normal, sore throat 3 days ago, no antibiotics, BP 152/94, dipstick blood + protein −) = IgA nephropathy — MED-154.
plan: 'May I have her vital signs?' → 124/78, 76, 14, 36.8 · 'I'm Dr —; am I speaking with Jenny? is it all right if I ask a few questions? how can I help?' → dark urine, worried → 'that would worry me too, and I'm glad you came in — I'll ask some questions, examine you, then explain'

★ 'Can you describe the colour exactly — Coca-Cola, brown, or dark yellow? Does the change happen right through the stream, or only at the start or the end? Any actual blood or clots? Has the smell changed? When did it start, does it happen every time, is it getting worse?' → strong tea; all the way through; no blood/clots; smell same; 4–5 days, every time, darker

★ 'Along with the dark urine, have your stools become pale or clay coloured?' → yes → ★ 'Thank you, that's important. Dark urine together with pale stools tells me this is very likely coming from your liver or the drainage tubes rather than your kidneys. Let me just check a few kidney questions first — any burning passing urine, any fever, any swelling of your legs, any injury to your tummy?' → none → 'Good. I'll focus on your liver now.'

Red flags: weight loss, appetite, lumps, tiredness, FHx bowel/liver/pancreas cancer → none · ★ 'any yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes? any itching?' → eyes yellow; itching all over, worse at night

★ Risk factors — ABP FIT NO SEX: 'do you drink alcohol, how much?' (barely) · ★ 'you mentioned a sore throat — did you see a doctor, and were you given any medication or antibiotics?' → Augmentin, finished about a week ago → 'thank you, very helpful' · blood transfusions, piercings, tattoos · street food/unusual water · injected drugs · travel · occupation (admin) · sexually active, condoms (married, monogamous) · 'ever had pain after a large fatty meal? any operations, particularly abdominal? ★ any fever or shaking chills?' → no, no, none · concerns → mother died of liver failure

★ Examiner: 'general appearance — is she jaundiced, scratch marks, cachectic, level of consciousness · vital signs, particularly temperature · abdomen — inspection: moving symmetrically, distension; superficial and deep palpation — tenderness, and if so guarding, rigidity, rebound; masses, specifically ★ hepatomegaly or splenomegaly; percussion — ★ shifting dullness; auscultation · office test — ★ urine dipstick for bilirubin, and also blood and protein' → jaundiced, no cachexia, T 36.8, BP 124/78, RUQ tenderness without guarding/rebound, liver palpable and enlarged, no splenomegaly, no shifting dullness, dipstick bilirubin +, blood −, protein −

★ 'Jenny, I think you have inflammation of your liver, and the most likely trigger is the antibiotic you took for your throat. Some antibiotics — and amoxicillin–clavulanate is the best known — can inflame the liver as a side effect and slow the flow of bile. When bile cannot drain, the yellow pigment backs up into your blood and spills into your urine, which is why your urine is dark; and because it is not reaching your bowel, your stools have gone pale. The itching comes from the same backing up. Three reasons: the combination of dark urine, pale stools and yellow eyes tells me the problem is in the liver or the bile ducts; you took an antibiotic well known for this, and the timing fits; and on examining you I found a tender enlarged liver and bilirubin in your urine, with no fever, which makes a serious duct infection unlikely.' · 'is my liver damaged permanently?' → uncommon but well recognised; most recover completely once the drug is stopped, though it can take several weeks; 'I'm stopping it now and recording it so you're never given it again' · the mother/transplant fear addressed

★ Two lists: 'in the liver and bile ducts — viral hepatitis A, B and C; alcohol; autoimmune hepatitis; gallstones causing blockage, gallbladder inflammation, or a duct infection called cholangitis — unlikely with no fever; and cancers of the pancreas, bile ducts or liver, which I keep on the list although no weight loss and no family history. In the kidneys and bladder, which I checked briefly at the start — infection, stones, inflammation of the kidney filters, and cancer — all made unlikely by your normal stream, no burning or fever, and no blood on the dipstick.' · plan: stop + document (allergy/adverse reaction record; TGA report), LFTs (cholestatic: ALP/GGT/bilirubin ↑), INR, hepatitis serology, FBE, USS to exclude obstruction; avoid alcohol/paracetamol excess; itch — cholestyramine/antihistamine VERIFY · ★ safety-net: fever with rigors, drowsiness/confusion, bruising/bleeding, deepening jaundice → straight back · review with results · summary
ask: ★ 'Can you describe the colour exactly — Coca-Cola, brown, or dark yellow?' / ★ 'Does the change happen right through the stream, or at the beginning or the end?' / ★ 'Along with the dark urine, have your stools become pale?' → ★ 'That tells me this is coming from the liver rather than the kidney.'
★ 'You mentioned a sore throat — did you see a doctor for that, and were you given any medication or antibiotics?' / ★ 'And have you had any fever or shaking chills?'
★ To examiner: 'Specifically, is there hepatomegaly or splenomegaly, and is there shifting dullness? … I would like a urine dipstick, looking for bilirubin, blood and protein.'

★ 'When bile cannot drain, the yellow pigment backs up into your blood and spills into your urine, which is why your urine is dark; and because it is not reaching your bowel, your stools have gone pale. The itching comes from the same backing up.' / ★ 'I am stopping that antibiotic and recording it so it is never given again.' / 'Most people recover completely once the drug is stopped, but it can take several weeks.'

★ 'Come back straight away if you get a fever with shaking chills, if you become drowsy or confused, if you start bruising or bleeding easily, or if the yellowing gets worse.' / examiner 'cholestasis or cholestatic hepatitis?' → 'the same process — drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis; I keep the jargon for you, not the patient.'
pefe: Role-player: Jenny Marsh, 45, administration officer, married, one teenager; 4–5 days of strong-tea urine, pale stools, yellow eyes, itch worse at night; sore throat 2 weeks ago → Augmentin, finished a week ago; rarely drinks; no exposures, operations, fatty-meal pain, fever, weight loss, FHx. Anxious but composed; relieved when told the liver usually recovers; 'sorry, what does that mean?' once to jargon. Pale stools ONLY when asked directly. Antibiotic ONLY to 'did you see a doctor / were you given medication or antibiotics' — 'when was the sore throat?' → 'about two weeks ago' and nothing more. Hidden: mother died of liver failure — 'is that going to happen to me? will I need a transplant?' if asked concerns or at ~7 min. Pushes once: 'will my liver recover?'
PEFE: jaundiced, no cachexia · T 36.8, BP 124/78 · RUQ tenderness, no guarding/rebound · liver palpable, enlarged · no splenomegaly · no shifting dullness · dipstick bilirubin +, blood −, protein −

Drug-induced liver injury: amoxicillin–clavulanate is the commonest cause in Australia (cholestatic/mixed, onset up to weeks after finishing); also flucloxacillin, dicloxacillin (cholestatic), erythromycin, statins, methotrexate, anti-TB drugs, herbal/supplements. Cholestatic LFTs: ALP/GGT ↑↑, bilirubin ↑, ALT mild; R-ratio (ALT/ULN ÷ ALP/ULN) <2 cholestatic, >5 hepatocellular VERIFY. Work-up: stop the drug, LFTs/INR, hepatitis A/B/C serology, EBV/CMV, autoimmune screen (ANA, SMA, AMA), USS for duct dilatation; refer if INR up, encephalopathy, bilirubin very high or not improving over weeks; document as adverse drug reaction (never re-challenge); TGA report. Dipstick three pads: blood, protein, bilirubin; urobilinogen alone is normal; bilirubin normal <20 µmol/L

Kidney branch (Version A): IgA nephropathy — visible haematuria 1–3 days after a URTI ('synpharyngitic'), normal complement; post-streptococcal GN 1–3 weeks after a throat/3–6 weeks after skin infection, low C3; visible haematuria >40 needs cancer exclusion regardless of a benign finding · SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450

tasks: Take a focused history (about 4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
Explain your differential diagnoses
time: 8 min. Vitals · intro, open · characterise: ★ colour (Coca-Cola), ★ stream (throughout), blood/clots, smell, when, every time · ★ 'have your stools become pale?' → no → ★ commit: 'because your stools are a normal colour, this is more likely your kidneys or bladder — let me check two things: any yellowing? itching?' → no → 'I'll focus on your kidneys' · kidney blocks: red flags (weight, appetite, lumps, tiredness, ★ FHx kidney/bladder cancer) · infection: fever, dysuria, frequency · stones: flank pain, previous stones, FHx · ★ 'any recent flu-like illness or sore throat — exactly when? any antibiotics for it? any swelling of your legs?' → sore throat 3 days ago, nearly gone, nothing taken · exercise (rhabdo), ★ medications (statins, rifampicin, NSAIDs), trauma · smoking (bladder cancer), occupation · periods (LMP — menstrual contamination), sexual · PEFE named: pallor, jaundice, ★ oedema; ★ BP; temperature; abdomen — distension, tenderness, masses, ★ ballot both kidneys, ★ palpate the bladder, ★ renal angle tenderness; bowel sounds; ★ dipstick blood/protein/bilirubin → no pallor/jaundice/oedema, BP 152/94, afebrile, abdomen soft, kidneys not ballotable, bladder not palpable, no renal angle tenderness, dipstick blood +, protein −, bilirubin − · dx IgA nephropathy with reasons (synpharyngitic timing, blood without protein, raised BP) · DDx: post-streptococcal GN (interval, low C3), UTI, stones, cancer, other GN, menstrual, exercise, drugs, rhabdo · plan: MSU, UEC, FBE, C3/C4, ASOT, ANA, urine ACR/microscopy (dysmorphic RBCs/casts), USS, BP recheck, nephrology.

back.dx: IgA nephropathy — Coca-Cola urine throughout the stream starting within a few days of a sore throat (synpharyngitic haematuria, 1–3 days after the URTI rather than 1–3 weeks), no pale stools, no jaundice, no itch, no dysuria/fever/flank pain; PEFE: no oedema, BP 152/94, kidneys not ballotable, bladder not palpable, no renal angle tenderness, dipstick blood positive, protein negative, bilirubin negative. Distinguish from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis by the interval (1–3 weeks after throat, 3–6 weeks after skin) and complement (C3 low in PSGN, normal in IgA) — only renal biopsy is definitive. Work-up: urine microscopy (dysmorphic red cells, casts), ACR, MSU, UEC/eGFR, FBE, C3/C4, ASOT/anti-DNase B, ANA/ANCA, USS; recheck BP; nephrology referral; visible haematuria over 40 (or with risk factors) needs urological cancer exclusion regardless.
plan: Vitals (BP 152/94 may be given) · intro, permission, open
★ Characterise: colour exactly (Coca-Cola/brown), through the stream or start/end (throughout), blood/clots, smell, when (few days), every time, worse

★ 'Have your stools become pale or clay coloured?' → 'no, completely normal' → ★ 'Thank you. Because your stools are a normal colour, this is more likely coming from your kidneys or bladder. I'll check two things to be sure — any yellowing of your skin or eyes, any itching?' → no → 'I'll focus on your kidneys.'

Kidney blocks: weight loss, appetite, lumps, tiredness, ★ FHx kidney/bladder cancer or kidney disease · fever, burning/pain passing urine, frequency · flank/tummy pain, previous stones, FHx stones · ★ 'any recent flu-like illness or sore throat — and exactly when? did you take any antibiotics for it? any swelling of your legs or puffiness around the eyes?' → sore throat 3 days ago, nearly gone; nothing taken; no swelling · heavy exercise recently · ★ medications — cholesterol tablets, anti-inflammatories, rifampicin, anticoagulants · injury to tummy/back · smoking, occupation (dyes/rubber) · LMP — could it be menstrual? · sexual history · concerns

★ Examiner: 'general appearance — pale, jaundiced, any oedema (legs, periorbital) · vital signs, particularly temperature and ★ blood pressure · abdomen — inspection for distension; superficial and deep palpation for tenderness and masses; specifically ★ ballot both kidneys and palpate the bladder; ★ renal angle tenderness; auscultation · office test — urine dipstick for blood, protein and bilirubin' → no pallor/jaundice/oedema; BP 152/94; afebrile; abdomen soft, non-tender, no masses; kidneys not ballotable; bladder not palpable; no renal angle tenderness; dipstick blood +, protein −, bilirubin −

★ 'I think the blood in your urine is coming from the filters in your kidneys. After an infection like your sore throat, the immune system makes particles called antibodies, and in some people those antibodies settle in the kidney filters and cause inflammation. That lets blood leak into the urine, which is why it looks like Coca-Cola. The condition is called IgA nephropathy. Three reasons: bloating/girth (wind and fluid), the persistent symptom cluster (early satiety, constipation, frequency — nothing alone, together and lasting this long they matter), and the lump. Two lists: bowel — bowel cancer (no bleeding), coeliac/lactose, IBD, obstruction (passing wind, no surgery), IBS ('a label I can't use when there's a lump'); other causes of a bigger tummy — fluid from heart/kidney/liver, hypothyroidism, hormonal (Cushing's), medications, ordinary weight gain. PEFE: settled, T 36.8, mild right-sided tenderness, no peritonism/mass, BS normal, right renal angle tender, groin and scrotum normal, dipstick blood ++, nitrites −, leucocytes −, protein trace. Three reasons: flank-to-groin path, waves, blood in the urine. The fork: loin tenderness + haematuria could mean pyelonephritis — no fever, no nitrites, no leucocytes → no infection → not hospital today. Investigations: non-contrast CT KUB (site and size), urine MCS (no infection behind the block), UEC/eGFR (kidney function changes the plan). Management by size: ≤5 mm — home, NSAID first (± opioid), antiemetic, tamsulosin, strain the urine, normal fluids (don't force), review 2–3 days; >7 mm — urology (ureteroscopy + laser for a low stone, ESWL, PCNL for large renal stones, stent if the kidney needs relieving). Long term: 2.5–3 L/day, low salt, normal calcium/dairy, stone analysis, metabolic work-up. Hidden agenda: uncle died of bladder cancer at 58.
plan: 'I'm Dr —; am I speaking with James? Before we start — are you comfortable enough to talk to me now? … Tell me what's been happening.' → 'pain out of nowhere loading the truck, worst ever, pacing the yard; eased off now — feel a bit stupid coming in' → ★ 'that sounds horrible, and you're not being stupid at all — that kind of pain always deserves looking at. I'm glad it has eased. I'll ask a series of questions to work out what caused it.' · 'Examiner, may I have his vital signs, in particular his temperature?' → afebrile, stable

★ 'Where exactly did it start — point with one finger? … And where is it now?' (high right flank → right groin) · 'how bad at its worst, out of ten? (9) sharp, dull, cramping? (sharp, stabbing) when did it start — suddenly? (2 h ago, instant) ★ there all the time, or coming and going in waves? (waves) travel — back, groin, testicles? (groin, top of the leg) anything better or worse — moving, lying still, eating? painkillers?' (nothing; couldn't sit still; two Panadol did nothing)
GI: nausea/vomiting (once), appetite (off), bowels, bloating/wind · ★ 'and have you had any fevers, chills or shaking episodes?' → no → 'good — that matters more here than you'd think'

★ Pivot: 'the way you've described that — one side, coming in waves, travelling to your groin — makes me want to ask about your waterworks next.' → 'burning or stinging? (a bit) passing urine more often? (a lot) ★ any blood — pink, red or tea-coloured?' → 'pink this morning — that's really why I came' (tense) → 'thank you for telling me — important, we'll come back to it' · 'dribbling at the end, trouble starting? sudden urges you can't hold? up at night? passing normal amounts? ★ have you, or anyone in your family, ever had a kidney stone?' (dad, twice, about my age)

'Two quick ones — yellowing of the eyes or skin, pale stools, cramping after fatty food? any lump in your groin, or pain/swelling in your testicles?' (no) · if the clock allows: smoking (10/day), alcohol, meds/allergies, gout/high calcium, operations/kidney surgery, one kidney?, ★ 'how much fluid do you drink in a day?' ('hardly any water — hot in that shed') · ★ 4:00 HARD STOP: 'before I examine you — was there something in particular you were worried this might be?' → [pause] 'my uncle died of bladder cancer at 58 — when I saw the blood I thought, that's it' → ★ 'thank you for telling me. That must have been a frightening morning. I can't promise you anything before I've examined you and done a scan, but I will tell you honestly what I think, and we will not leave that question hanging.'

★ Examiner: 'general appearance — distress, restlessness, dehydration, pallor, jaundice · vital signs, temperature first · full abdominal examination — inspection for distension and scars; palpation superficial then deep for tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound, organomegaly and any pulsatile mass; percussion for tenderness and a distended bladder; auscultation for bowel sounds and renal bruits · inguinal region, external genitalia, digital rectal examination · ★ as a special test — renal angle tenderness on both sides · ★ as an office test — a urine dipstick' → uncomfortable but settled; T 36.8; abdomen soft, mild right-sided tenderness, no guarding/rebound, no mass, BS normal; right renal angle tender; groin/scrotum normal; dipstick blood ++, nitrites −, leucocytes −, protein trace

★ 'James, I think you have what we call a ureteric colic — most people say a kidney stone. A small stone has formed in your kidney and started moving down the narrow tube that carries urine to your bladder. It presses on the wall of that tube and blocks it, and that is what causes the pain. Three things point to it: where the pain is — it started in your flank and travelled toward your groin, exactly the path that tube takes; it comes in waves, which is typical; and there's blood in your urine, which happens as the stone scrapes its way down.' · ★ discriminating sentence: 'I also want to be clear about something. You're tender over your kidney and there's blood in your urine, and those can suggest a kidney infection. But you have no fever, and your dipstick shows no nitrites and no white cells, so there's no sign of infection — and that's important, because a stone with an infection would mean hospital today.' · ★ the cancer worry: 'I can't rule anything out until the scan is back, and I won't pretend otherwise. But blood in the urine with this exact pattern of pain, at forty, with your father's history, points strongly to a stone. The scan will settle it.' · DDx by group: kidney/bladder — pyelonephritis, less likely a growth; liver/gallbladder (right-sided) — gallstones, inflammation, hepatitis; bowel — appendicitis, inflammation, rarely a growth; groin/testicle — hernia, torsion/epididymitis (excluded); the main abdominal blood vessel — very unlikely at forty

★ 'Three tests. One, a special CT scan of the kidneys, ureters and bladder without dye — the best test we have; it shows me where the stone is and how big. Two, your urine to the laboratory for culture, because I want to be certain there's no infection sitting behind the blockage. Three, a blood test — UEC — to check your kidney function, because if the kidney is struggling that changes what I recommend.' (pushed: FBE/CRP if infection suspected, cultures if febrile, calcium/urate if recurrent; ultrasound if pregnant) · ★ safety-net: 'come straight back, or go to the emergency department, if you get a fever or shakes, if the pain becomes uncontrollable despite the tablets, if you stop passing urine, or if you're vomiting so much you can't keep fluids down' · analgesia now (NSAID) · summary: 'sudden severe colicky right pain, flank to groin, blood in the urine, no fever — most likely a kidney stone on the move; scan, check for infection and kidney function, then decide together how to get it out. What questions do you have?' ('how long? work? will it happen again?')
V-B

'I have your scan here — let me take you through what it shows, then what it means, then what we do' · ★ orient: 'this is a slice through your lower tummy, looking from your feet upward; these bright white shapes either side are your hip bones; this big grey circle in the middle is your bladder' → 'two narrow tubes carry urine from your kidneys into the bladder — the ureters. This small bright dot is a stone, sitting in one of those tubes right where it joins your bladder — the vesicoureteric junction, or simply the last centimetre before the bladder' · dx: 'a kidney stone on the move — I can see it, and your story fits exactly' · ★ the fork before 4:15: 'what we do next depends on how big the stone is. But before any of that, two things: I need to be certain there's no infection sitting behind the blockage — urine for culture; a stone and an infection together is the one combination that means hospital the same day. And a blood test for kidney function, because that changes what I recommend.' · ★ small (≤5 mm): home — NSAID first (ibuprofen 400 mg tds with food / indometacin 100 mg PR), oxycodone 5 mg if inadequate, ondansetron, tamsulosin 400 mcg daily (light-headed on standing — get up slowly) VERIFY, ★ strain the urine and catch the stone, ★ drink normally — don't force water, review 2–3 days · ★ large (>7 mm): urology — ureteroscopy + laser (suits a low stone), ESWL, PCNL for large renal stones, stent if the kidney needs relieving; analgesia and tamsulosin meanwhile · long term: 2.5–3 L/day especially in the heat, low salt, ★ keep dairy/calcium normal ('cutting calcium out makes stones more likely'), stone analysis, blood/urine tests · safety-net · 'how big is it?' → 'the report doesn't give a measurement and I'm not going to guess from the picture — so here are both possibilities'
ask: ★ 'Before we start — are you comfortable enough to talk to me right now?' / ★ 'I'm glad it has eased. We'll come back to pain relief at the end — first I need to work out what caused it.' / ★ 'Where exactly did it start? … And where is it now?' / ★ 'Is it there all the time, or does it come and go in waves?' / ★ 'Have you had any fevers, chills or shaking episodes?'

★ 'The way you've described that — one side, coming in waves, travelling to your groin — makes me want to ask about your waterworks next.' / 'Any burning? Passing urine more often? Any blood — pink, red or tea-coloured? Dribbling or trouble starting? Sudden urges? Up at night? Normal amounts?' / ★ 'Have you or anyone in your family ever had a kidney stone?' / 'How much fluid do you drink in a day?'

★ To examiner: '…auscultation for bowel sounds and renal bruits; then the inguinal region, external genitalia and a digital rectal examination. As a special test I'd like renal angle tenderness on both sides. And as an office test, a urine dipstick.'

★ 'A small stone has started moving down the narrow tube from your kidney to your bladder, and the pressure on that tube is what causes the pain.' / ★ 'You have no fever, and no nitrites or white cells on the dipstick, so there is no sign of infection — and that matters, because a stone with an infection would mean hospital today.' / 'I can't rule anything out until the scan is back, and I won't pretend otherwise. But blood in the urine with this exact pattern of pain, at forty, with your father's history, points strongly to a stone. The scan will settle it.'

★ 'What we do next depends on how big the stone is — but before any of that, I need to be certain there is no infection and to check your kidney function.' / ★ 'If it is small, most stones pass on their own … if it is larger, it is unlikely to pass and I'd refer you to a urologist.' / ★ 'Strain your urine and catch the stone, so we can analyse what it is made of.' / 'Please don't force large amounts of water — it won't push the stone out and it makes the pain worse.' / 'Keep your dairy and calcium normal — cutting calcium out actually makes stones more likely.' / ★ 'Come back straight away if you get a fever or shakes, if the pain becomes uncontrollable, or if you stop passing urine.'

Variant 1 (T 38.7, rigor, HR 118, BP 96/58, nitrites + leucocytes +): ★ 'This changes things completely — an obstructing stone with evidence of infection is an infected obstructed kidney, a urological emergency. James, the picture has changed: a stone blocking the tube with signs of infection behind it; antibiotics alone will not fix it — the blockage has to be relieved. Hospital today: IV fluids, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, urgent urological decompression — a stent up the tube or a drain through the back into the kidney — and from here that means MedSTAR on 1300 13 12 33.' / Variant 3 ('just give me the Endone'): 'I'm not going to leave you in pain. The most effective drug for this particular pain is actually an anti-inflammatory, so I'll start there; if that isn't enough I'll add something stronger — a short course, and you must not drive or operate the forklift on it.' / Variant 4 (24 weeks pregnant): ultrasound not CT; paracetamol ± opioid, no NSAIDs; obstetrics + urology early; UTI commoner and more serious VERIFY / Variant 5 (solitary kidney, anuria, creatinine 210): 'size is irrelevant — an obstructing stone in a solitary kidney with a rising creatinine needs urology today for decompression.'
pefe: Role-player: James Whitmore, 40, storeman/forklift driver in a hot shed outside Wallaroo, married, two children; 10 cigs/day × 20 y; 4–6 beers weekends; almost no water at work (sheepish); two Panadol this morning; no PMHx/ops; two kidneys; father stones twice in his forties; mother hypertension; uncle died of bladder cancer at 58. Relieved, slightly embarrassed; tense and short-sentenced once blood is mentioned. Fever: answers 'no' plainly — never offered if not asked. Hidden: convinced the pink urine is bladder cancer — releases it to 'was there something you were worried this might be?'; if never asked, at ~6 min 'Doctor — can I ask you something? Is this cancer?'; false reassurance ('definitely not cancer') → 'how can you know that without a scan?'. End questions: 'how long till it comes out? can I still go to work? will it happen again?'

Examiner: uncomfortable but settled; T 36.8; abdomen soft, mild right-sided tenderness, no guarding/rebound/mass; BS normal; right renal angle tender; groin and scrotum normal; dipstick blood ++, nitrites −, leucocytes −, protein trace. Version B CT: stone at the right VUJ; no size reported (don't guess — give both pathways)

Stone size: ≤5 mm usually passes (~70–90%) · 5–7 mm grey zone · >7 mm unlikely — refer · not passed by 4 weeks → urology VERIFY. Drugs VERIFY TG: ibuprofen 400 mg tds with food or indometacin 100 mg PR; oxycodone 5 mg PO if inadequate; ondansetron 4–8 mg; tamsulosin 400 mcg daily (medical expulsive therapy for distal stones ≥5 mm — evidence strongest 5–10 mm). Tests: non-contrast CT KUB (gold standard; low-dose protocols), urine MCS, UEC/eGFR; ultrasound if pregnant; FBE/CRP/cultures if infection; Ca/PO4/PTH/urate and 24-h urine (calcium, oxalate, citrate, urate) for recurrence; stone analysis. Urology now: infected obstructed kidney (stent/nephrostomy), solitary kidney, AKI, uncontrolled pain/vomiting, bilateral obstruction. Prevention: 2.5–3 L/day (urine >2 L), low salt, normal dietary calcium (1000–1200 mg), limit oxalate/animal protein, citrate; thiazide/allopurinol/potassium citrate by stone type (specialist)

Automatic fails: fever never asked · no dipstick · pyelonephritis on loin tenderness + blood · Version B one pathway / infection never excluded · 'definitely not cancer' before a scan · 'drink as much water as possible' · 'cut out calcium/dairy' · history past 4:00 and investigations never reached. Visible haematuria >40 with risk factors needs urothelial cancer exclusion once the stone episode is over (smoker) — cystoscopy/CT urogram VERIFY · SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450 · review 48–72 h
fails: Opening with painkillers when the pain has settled; accepting 'my side' — never asking where it is NOW; not asking waves vs constant
★ The word fever never used; ★ no urine dipstick / renal angle not named ('an abdominal examination'); ★ diagnosis switched to pyelonephritis on loin tenderness + blood
History running past 4:00 — investigations never reached; never asking family history of stones or fluid intake; never eliciting the cancer worry, or 'definitely not cancer' before any scan
★ Version B: one management pathway; ★ infection/renal function fork never said before 4:15; estimating stone size off the film; going from 'you have a stone' straight to painkillers
'Drink as much water as possible'; 'cut out calcium/dairy'; no strain-the-urine; no review interval; no safety-net (fever, uncontrolled pain, anuria, vomiting)
numbers: History 4 min (hard stop) · say 'infection' by 4:15 (V-B) · stone ≤5 mm passes · 5–7 mm grey · >7 mm refer · not passed by 4 wk → urology VERIFY
Ibuprofen 400 mg tds / indometacin 100 mg PR · oxycodone 5 mg if needed · ondansetron 4–8 mg · tamsulosin 400 mcg daily VERIFY · CT KUB non-contrast · urine MCS · UEC/eGFR · USS if pregnant
Review 48–72 h · fluids 2.5–3 L/day · low salt · normal calcium · stone analysis + Ca/PO4/PTH/urate + 24-h urine · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450

setting: Regional SA general practice. Four-minute history, PEFE from the examiner, then diagnosis + differentials (2 min). A differential-listing station wearing a history-taking coat: the role-player hands you BPH if you ask three voiding questions; the marks are in the breadth and order of the list, and in excluding cancer before you settle. Automatic fail: 'it's only BPH, nothing to worry about'; no cancer screening; no DRE.
stem: James Whitmore, 55, urgent appointment — he has been passing red urine. BP 148/92 · HR 78 · T 36.8 · RR 16 · SpO2 98% · BMI 28.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings
Explain your provisional diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient (2 minutes)
time: 8 min. Identity, 'what's brought you in?' → empathise ONCE ('that does sound worrying, and you were right to come in today'), frame · complaint: when (4 d), every time/intermittent, worse, ★ 'pink, or frankly red?', ★ clots or streaks, ★ start/end/throughout, smell, pain · ★ cancers FIRST: weight loss, appetite, lumps (groin/tummy), tiredness, tummy/loin pain, FHx kidney/bladder/prostate cancer · prostate second — obstructive: hesitancy, weak stream, straining, terminal dribbling, incomplete emptying; irritative: urgency, ★ 'wake at night — HOW MANY TIMES?' (3–4) · infection: fever/chills, dysuria, frequency, N/V, discharge, perineal pain; one line sexual · stones/kidney/trauma: loin pain, ★ previous stones (6 y), FHx stones/kidney disease, recent sore throat/viral, heavy exercise, injury · ★ medications incl OTC — 'any blood thinners — aspirin, warfarin, apixaban?' (aspirin), bruising/nosebleeds · pseudohaematuria (beetroot, rhubarb, new medicines), travel/fresh-water swimming (TB, schistosomiasis) · summarise; concerns (mate Kev — bladder cancer) · 4:00 examiner: appearance (pallor, pain, cachexia, oedema), full vitals, abdomen (distension, Grey Turner/Cullen), suprapubic + renal angle tenderness, ★ ballot kidneys, suprapubic mass, ★ percuss the bladder, ★ 'DRE — size, consistency, surface/nodularity, median sulcus, tenderness', ★ 'may I have the urine dipstick?' · dx BPH, walnut explanation, two consequences · ★ 'I cannot exclude a cancer on examination alone' → urology: cystoscopy + CT urography, bloods/urine today · list in groups · safety-net retention/clots/fever.

back.dx: Benign prostatic hyperplasia with haematuria from the friable surface of an enlarged gland — four days of painless total haematuria (pink → frankly red, one small clot), a year of LUTS (hesitancy, weak stream, terminal dribbling, incomplete emptying, urgency, nocturia ×3–4), previous stone six years ago, aspirin 100 mg and perindopril; PEFE: comfortable, bladder palpable and dull to percussion, no tenderness, kidneys not ballotable, DRE — enlarged, smooth, firm-rubbery, no nodules, median sulcus preserved, non-tender; dipstick blood +++, nitrites −, leucocytes −, protein trace. BUT painless visible haematuria at 55 is urothelial carcinoma until proven otherwise: 'I cannot exclude a cancer of the bladder, kidney or prostate on examination alone' → urology for cystoscopy + CT urography, FBE/UEC/PSA (after the bleed settles)/urine MCS + cytology today. Grouped list: cancers (bladder, kidney, prostate); infection (cystitis, pyelonephritis, urethritis, prostatitis — no fever/dysuria/discharge); stones (previous); glomerulonephritis (post-URTI); aspirin (unmasks, doesn't cause); hypertension (polycystic/CKD); exercise, trauma, bleeding disorder, coloured foods, schistosomiasis/TB. Hidden agenda: mate Kev died of bladder cancer.
plan: 'Good morning, I'm Dr —. Can I check I have the right person — James Whitmore, date of birth? What's brought you in?' → 'red urine, worried' → ★ 'That does sound worrying, and you were right to come in today. I'm concerned enough to look into it properly — I'll ask some questions, examine you, and we'll make a plan.' (empathy once, then move)

'When did you first notice it? every time, or comes and goes? getting worse? ★ pink, or frankly red? ★ any clots or streaks? ★ at the start of the stream, the end, or right the way through? does it smell? any pain or burning when you go?' → 4 d; every time now; pink → red; one dark bit; throughout; no smell; ★ no pain at all

★ 'Some questions I ask everyone with blood in the urine: lost any weight without trying? appetite? lumps or bumps — groin, tummy? more tired than usual? tummy or loin pain? family history of cancer — kidney, bladder, prostate?' → all no (tired — up all night)

'Now the waterworks: do you have to wait before the stream starts? weak stream? strain or push? dribbling at the end? feel the bladder has emptied fully? sudden strong urge? ★ wake at night to pass urine — how many times?' → yes to all; 'three, sometimes four' → 'once a night would be ordinary; three or four is a finding'

Infection: fever/chills, burning, frequency, N/V, penile discharge, deep perineal pain → no · 'sexually active? safe sex?' (married, always) · stones/kidney/trauma: loin pain, ★ 'ever had kidney stones?' (one, 6 y ago, passed), FHx stones/kidney disease, recent sore throat/flu, heavy exercise, injury · ★ 'what medications, including over the counter? any blood thinners — aspirin, warfarin, apixaban? easy bruising, nosebleeds?' → aspirin low dose + BP tablet · 'told your blood pressure is high?' (5 y) · beetroot/rhubarb/red lollies/new medicine; overseas travel, freshwater swimming → no · ★ summarise; 'anything you particularly want me to cover?' → Kev

★ Examiner: 'general appearance — pale, in pain, cachectic, peripheral oedema · full vitals incl RR · abdomen — inspection: distension, symmetrical movement, Grey Turner or Cullen · palpation: general tenderness, specifically suprapubic and renal angle tenderness; masses — ★ may I ballot the kidneys, and is there a suprapubic mass · ★ percuss the bladder · ★ I would then like to perform a digital rectal examination — assessing the prostate for size, consistency, surface or nodularity, whether the median sulcus is preserved, and tenderness · finally, ★ may I have a urine dipstick?' → not pale, comfortable, no oedema; vitals as stem; abdomen soft, bladder palpable and dull to percussion; no renal angle/suprapubic tenderness; kidneys not ballotable; DRE enlarged, smooth, no nodules, firm-rubbery, sulcus felt, non-tender; dipstick blood +++, nitrites −, leucocytes −, protein trace

★ 'James, the most likely explanation is benign prostatic hyperplasia — benign prostate enlargement. The prostate is a small walnut-shaped gland just underneath the bladder, and the tube that carries urine out runs straight through the middle of it. As men get older it commonly enlarges. Benign means not a cancer. Two things follow: it squeezes the tube — which is why the stream is weak, you dribble, never feel empty, and you're up three or four times a night; and the surface of an enlarged prostate carries fragile blood vessels that bleed easily — which is where the blood is coming from.' · 'so it's not cancer? my father had prostate trouble' → ★ 'That's the most likely answer, and the examination today is reassuring — the gland felt smooth and even, which is what we expect with the benign kind. But I want to be straight with you: visible blood in the urine at your age always has to be properly investigated, because I cannot exclude a cancer of the bladder, kidney or prostate on examination alone. That's not because I think you have one — it's the one thing I'm not willing to guess about.'

★ The list in groups: 'cancers of the bladder, kidney or prostate — the ones I must exclude; infection in the bladder, kidney, urine tube or prostate — less likely, no fever, burning or discharge; kidney stones — you've had one before; inflammation of the kidney filters, which can follow a throat or viral illness; the aspirin, which doesn't cause bleeding but can unmask it; your blood pressure, which raises polycystic or chronic kidney disease; and much less likely — strenuous exercise, injury, a bleeding disorder, coloured foods, or an infection picked up overseas' · Kev: acknowledge, honest, commit · plan: urology referral — cystoscopy and CT urography; today FBE, UEC, urine MCS + cytology, PSA once the bleeding settles; if it is the prostate — 'very good tablets' (tamsulosin, finasteride) · ★ safety-net: 'if you can't pass urine at all, your lower tummy becomes painful and swollen, you pass large clots, or you get fever and shakes — come straight back or go to the emergency department' · ring with results, review 1 week; PATS
ask: ★ 'You were right to come in today.' / ★ 'Pink, or frankly red? Any clots?' / 'Is the blood at the start of the stream, at the end, or right the way through?' / ★ 'Have you lost weight without trying?'

★ 'Do you wake at night to pass urine? How many times?' / ★ 'Is the stream weak? Do you have to strain?' / ★ 'Are you on any blood thinners — including aspirin?' / 'Ever had kidney stones? Any recent sore throat or viral illness? Any beetroot or red lollies? Any travel overseas or swimming in fresh water?'

★ To examiner: 'May I ballot the kidneys, and is there a suprapubic mass? I'd like to percuss the bladder. I would then like to perform a digital rectal examination — size, consistency, surface or nodularity, median sulcus, and tenderness. Finally, may I have the urine dipstick?'

★ 'A walnut-shaped gland just below the bladder … Benign means not a cancer.' / ★ 'I cannot exclude a cancer of the bladder, kidney or prostate on examination alone. That's not because I think you have one — it's because it's the one thing I'm not willing to guess about.'

★ 'If you cannot pass urine at all, or your lower tummy becomes painful and swollen, or you pass large clots, or you get fever and shakes, don't wait for the appointment — come straight back or go to the emergency department.'

Variant A (painless clots two weeks, pack-a-day smoker, 4 kg loss, normal DRE, no LUTS): 'I'm not going to be able to tell you today exactly what this is, and I won't guess. Painless bleeding with clots, in a smoker, with weight loss, needs to be looked at urgently — this week, not in a few months. The commonest cause of this pattern is a growth in the lining of the bladder. Many are picked up early and treated successfully with a camera procedure, but I can't promise anything until we've looked.' / Variant B (clot retention — nothing passed since last night, belly killing him): 'that changes what we do right now — your bladder is full and can't empty; I'm going to pass a catheter, and because there are clots a wider three-way catheter so we can flush it, and I'm calling urology while we do that' (3-way catheter, irrigation, FBE/coags, same-day urology; MedSTAR if unstable; watch post-obstructive diuresis) / Variant C (refuses cystoscopy — 'you said it's benign, just give me the tablets'): 'It's your decision and I won't push you. What I owe you is a clear picture: the enlargement explains most of what you've told me, but it doesn't rule out a growth in the bladder, and the camera is the only way to see that lining. If we find nothing you've lost an afternoon. Would it help if I explained what it involves, or if we booked the CT first and talked again after?' — name it as his decision, state the risk once, offer a partial step, document; don't cave, don't refuse to prescribe
pefe: Role-player: James Whitmore, 55, fitter and turner at a Yorke Peninsula grain depot, married to Denise, two daughters; ten beers/week; never smoked (say so clearly); aspirin 100 mg + perindopril (forgets weekends); one stone 6 y ago; hypertension 5 y; father 'prostate trouble' — an operation, not cancer. Worried but understated ('probably nothing'); volunteers only the red urine; animated once the waterworks are asked ('nobody has asked'); nocturia number only if asked how many; aspirin only if medications/blood thinners asked. Hidden: 'my mate Kev had blood in his water — his bladder — gone in fourteen months' (looking at the floor; ~5 min if concerns not asked). Told benign → relief then 'so why do I need more tests?' — push once. 'Nothing to worry about' → accepts happily and marks you down

PEFE: not pale, comfortable, no oedema · vitals as stem · abdomen soft, bladder palpable and dull to percussion · no renal angle/suprapubic tenderness · kidneys not ballotable · DRE: enlarged, smooth, no nodules, firm-rubbery, median sulcus felt, non-tender · dipstick: blood +++, nitrites −, leucocytes −, protein trace. DRE patterns: BPH — enlarged, smooth, firm-rubbery, sulcus preserved; carcinoma — nodular, stony hard, sulcus lost; prostatitis — boggy, exquisitely tender

Visible haematuria ≥45 (any age with risk) → urology: cystoscopy + CT urography (VERIFY age threshold 35–45); risks for urothelial cancer — smoking, age, male, occupational dyes/rubber, cyclophosphamide, pelvic radiation, chronic cystitis, schistosomiasis. Investigations: FBE, UEC/eGFR, coags if on anticoagulant, PSA (defer during haematuria/infection), urine MCS + cytology, ± USS KUB. Anticoagulants/aspirin do not explain haematuria — investigate as if not on them. IPSS 0–35 (mild ≤7, moderate 8–19, severe ≥20). BPH management: watchful waiting/lifestyle (evening fluids, caffeine/alcohol, bladder training) → tamsulosin 400 mcg MR daily (works in days–weeks; postural hypotension, retrograde ejaculation) → finasteride 5 mg daily (3–6 months; halves PSA — double the result; sexual side effects) or combination → TURP/newer endoscopic procedures; avoid anticholinergics if retention risk. Nocturia once a night at 55 normal; 3–4 is the finding

Indication: 'your bladder has filled up but can't empty. That's very common after bowel surgery — the anaesthetic, the strong pain relief you're pressing, and lying flat all switch off the signal that lets the bladder squeeze. The scan shows nearly 800 mL — about three cups. If we leave it, the bladder muscle can be stretched and damaged, and the pressure can back up to the kidneys.' · 'can I just have another go, standing?' → 'reasonable — standing genuinely helps some people. My honest view: at three cups and eight hours, waiting isn't safe, and the longer we leave it the harder it is for the bladder to recover. Better pain relief and fifteen minutes at the sink with the tap running — but if nothing comes, I'd want to drain it. Could you live with that?' → 'let's just do it'

'A catheter is a soft, thin, flexible tube — about the thickness of a drinking straw. It goes in through the opening at the tip of the penis, along the water pipe, and into the bladder, so the urine drains into a bag. A tiny balloon near the end is filled with a little sterile water once it's inside so it can't fall out. You stay awake; the only anaesthetic is a numbing jelly.' · ★ 'To do it I need to uncover you from the waist down — only for the minute or two it takes, with a sheet over you the rest of the time. Curtain and door closed. I'd also like one of the nurses in the room with us — routine for this, there for your comfort as much as mine. Would you prefer a male or a female nurse? ★ Contraindication screen: 'a few quick safety questions. Any injury to your pelvis or the area between your legs — a fall, a straddle injury? Any blood at the tip? Ever had a catheter before, or an operation on the prostate or the water pipe? Ever told the water pipe is narrowed? Any allergies — latex in particular? And has anything changed in the feeling around your bottom or in your legs since the anaesthetic?' → no to all (excludes urethral injury and cauda equina aloud)

★ Risks and alternatives: 'the common things — it can sting going in, a little blood in the urine for a day, a feeling of needing to go even though the bladder is empty. The one I most want you to know about is infection — the risk climbs for every day the tube stays in, so we check every morning whether it can come out. Less commonly it can graze the water pipe. Rarely people react to the material. And occasionally it won't pass — then I stop and ask the urology team rather than force it. The alternatives are to wait a bit longer with better pain relief and privacy, or, if it can't go in, a tube through the skin above the pubic bone by the specialists. Doing nothing isn't safe at this volume.' · brother → ★ 'that's real, and it's the risk I'd worry about most too — nursing-home catheters stay in for months; yours: sterile insertion, a sealed drainage system, a review every morning, out the moment you're walking — a day or two, not weeks' · ★ teach-back: 'if you were telling your wife what we're about to do, what would you say?' → 'tube to drain the bladder, small infection risk, out in a day or two' → 'exactly. Any questions? ★ Are you happy for me to go ahead? Thank you — I'll write in your notes that we've discussed the reasons, the risks and the alternatives, that a nurse was present, and that you agreed.'

(2) Passing: 'hold the penis upright at a right angle with a little stretch — straightens the water pipe; feed the tube in slowly. About two-thirds of the way there's a muscle ring guarding the bladder; when I reach it I lower the penis towards your toes with steady, gentle pressure until it slips past. Pressure, not pain. I never force it' ('if it doesn't go?' → 'I stop and ask urology — forcing is how the pipe gets damaged') · ★ 'I push the tube all the way in, right up to where it splits in two, even after urine starts coming — because the little balloon sits back from the tip, and if I blew it up too early it would be inside the water pipe. Once I can see urine draining, and only then, I fill the balloon with sterile water — the exact amount is printed on the tube, about two teaspoons. Then pull back gently until it sits snugly.' · (3) Finish: closed drainage bag below the bladder; ★ 'I make sure the foreskin is pulled back forward — if it's left back it can swell'; tape to the thigh with slack; clean up and cover; measure and chart the volume; daily review — out once walking and off the morphine, then a trial without it; safety-net: fever/shakes, back pain, no urine in the bag for four hours, heavy bleeding → nurses

From the pack: sterile drape as the working surface, gallipot for sterile sodium chloride, gauze swabs and plastic forceps for cleaning, the fenestrated drape. I add sterile gloves, apron and eye protection, a 2% lignocaine gel syringe, ★ a 10 mL syringe of sterile water — not saline, which crystallises in the inflation channel so the balloon may not deflate — a closed drainage bag and a securing device. I confirm the balloon volume printed on the catheter, and check the expiry date and integrity of every package before opening.' · 'why not bigger?' → 'size is chosen by what has to pass through the lumen, not the size of the patient' · close: 'I'll get the nurse and the trolley. Background if asked: up twice a night, slow stream for a year; never catheterised; no prostate surgery; no stricture; no trauma; no blood at the tip; legs normal ('why — should they not?'); no latex allergy; BP tablet only. Asks: 'will it hurt? be straight', 'will I be knocked out?', 'how long am I stuck with it?', 'how soon will I feel better?'

Findings given: bladder palpable, scan 780 mL; HR 96, BP 138/84, afebrile; pain 6/10. Trolley: two-way and three-way Foley catheters of various sizes, catheter pack, lignocaine gel, syringes, sterile water and saline ampoules, drainage bags, securing device, gloves

Numbers: 14 Fr default adult male (12–16); funnel colours 12 white, 14 green, 16 orange, 18 red, 20 yellow, 22 purple; Fr ÷ 3 = mm outer diameter; male catheter 40–45 cm; three-way 20–22 Fr for irrigation; balloon 10 mL sterile water (volume printed); lignocaine 2% gel 6–11 mL, dwell 3–5 min VERIFY; hand rub 20–30 s, soap and water 40–60 s; residual 780 mL — >1000 mL → hourly output, U&E; post-obstructive diuresis >200 mL/h × 2 h or >3 L/24 h VERIFY. CAUTI risk ~3–7%/catheter day; contraindications — suspected urethral injury (blood at the meatus, perineal haematoma, high-riding prostate), known stricture/false passage; relative — recent urethral/prostate surgery (contact the surgeon); alternatives — suprapubic catheter (urology), intermittent catheterisation; post-op retention risk — anaesthesia, opioids, anticholinergics, pelvic/anorectal surgery, BPH, IV fluids

Aftercare: closed system below bladder level, secure, daily necessity review, TWOC when mobile and off opioids (consider tamsulosin before TWOC if BPH VERIFY), measure residual, document; safety-net — fever/rigors, loin pain, no drainage 4 h, frank haematuria/clots, bypassing, pain · TIS 131 450 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 (rural)
fails: ★ Not offering a chaperone, or exposing without explicit permission; taking 'just do whatever you have to' as consent
★ Omitting the contraindication screen (urethral injury, stricture, latex, cauda equina); jargon to the patient (meatus, urethra, Foley, aseptic field)
★ 'Insert and inflate' in one breath — balloon before urine; ★ forgetting to replace the foreskin; skipping the gel or the wait
★ Consent never asked for, agreed to, or documented; 'it's very safe' to the brother's infection instead of validate–quantify–mitigate
Choosing a three-way for simple retention; filling the balloon with saline; letting consent eat Task 3; refusing the bounded retry without offering anything

setting: Telephone station — MO on duty, no patient, a desk and a phone; the ward nurse is calling. Four tasks, but resuscitation outranks the printed order: say 'I am treating this as sepsis' and give four instructions with a read-back before listing bloods. Cultures before antibiotics, antibiotics within the hour (don't let specimens delay past ~45 min); ask what the penicillin allergy actually was before naming a drug. Automatic fails: accepting oral trimethoprim; never treating as sepsis; antibiotics before cultures with no caveat; never saying 'catheter-associated'; naming a drug without asking about the allergy.
stem: Mr Trevor Nolan, 60, known BPH, attended ED two days ago in acute urinary retention; catheterised, catheter removed yesterday. Today he has re-presented exhausted and feverish. T 39.5 · BP 80/50 · tachycardic · saturations low. The ward nurse has telephoned to discuss him.
tasks: Explain your diagnosis to the nurse
Discuss the investigations you require
Discuss your immediate management
Discuss the long-term management (may be held back — offer it once the first three are complete)
time: 8 min. 'Dr —, MO on duty — am I speaking with the nurse looking after Mr Nolan? May I take your name?' · 'tell me in your own words what's happened, and his full observations — ★ respiratory rate, conscious state, urine output, allergies' (RR 26, sats 91%, HR 122, 'a bit vague', no urine since morning, penicillin allergy) · ★ dx in both halves, causally: 'a catheter-associated urinary tract infection — seeded when he was catheterised two days ago — that has progressed to sepsis; with 80/50 he may be in septic shock — I'll know once we see the response to fluid'; four reasons: instrumented 48 h ago, 39.5, hypotensive/tachycardic, hypoxic/drowsy · 'we've got oral trimethoprim' → ★ no — 'oral isn't enough, absorption unreliable in shock' · ★ sepsis door first: (1) oxygen to 92–96% (2) two large-bore cannulae (3) 500 mL crystalloid over 15 min then repeat BP and tell me the number (4) obs every 15 min + bladder scan (retention again?) → ★ 'can you read those four back to me?' · investigations in two buckets, before antibiotics: urine MCS — midstream or from the sampling port of a NEW catheter, never the bag; bloods — two sets of blood cultures separate sites, FBE, UEC, CRP, LFT, coags, ★ VBG with lactate, BSL, group and hold; bedside — ECG, CXR ('I won't assume the urine is the only source') · 'no urine since morning' → bladder scan first (620 mL) → recatheterise, specimen from the new catheter, relieves obstruction · ★ 'before I name a drug — what does the chart say about allergies, and what actually happened?' (rash as a teenager → cephalosporin reasonable: IV ceftriaxone; or gentamicin + amoxicillin if no allergy; immediate reaction → no beta-lactams, gentamicin + advice) · within the hour, narrow at 48 h · continuous monitoring, hourly obs, strict fluid balance, hourly urine · ★ 'I'm walking down now and I'll call the registrar myself' · ring me if BP doesn't come up, more confused, stops passing urine · long term: 7 days (10–14 if slow), IV→oral when afebrile, narrow; the prostate — alpha blocker, 5-ARI, urology (TURP) — fewer catheters prevent the next one; no prophylactic antibiotics at insertion/removal · summary, 'anything worrying you I haven't covered?'

back.dx: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (catheterised 48 h ago for retention, removed yesterday — within the 48-hour definition) that has progressed to sepsis, possibly septic shock (T 39.5, BP 80/50 → MAP 60, HR 122, RR 26, SpO2 91% RA, vague/drowsy, no urine since morning — bladder scan 620 mL = retention again). Sepsis bundle by phone: oxygen 92–96%, two large-bore IVs, 500 mL crystalloid bolus over 15 min (repeat towards 20 mL/kg with reassessment), obs q15 min, bladder scan → recatheterise (aseptically) and take the urine from the new catheter's port; cultures (urine MCS, two sets blood cultures), FBE/UEC/CRP/LFT/coags/VBG+lactate/BSL/G&H, ECG, CXR; IV antibiotics within 60 min — gentamicin (weight/renal-dosed loading) + amoxicillin, or ceftriaxone if delayed-rash penicillin allergy; avoid all beta-lactams and seek advice if immediate hypersensitivity; escalate — walk down, call the registrar, ICU if not fluid-responsive. Long term: 7 days (10–14 if delayed response), IV→oral when afebrile, narrow at 48 h; treat the BPH (tamsulosin ± finasteride, urology/TURP) — fewer catheters is the single best prevention; no antibiotic prophylaxis at insertion/removal.
plan: Pick up, sit, pen ready: 'Hello, Dr —, medical officer on duty. Am I speaking with the nurse looking after Mr Nolan? May I take your name?' → Jane · 'I've read his notes — could you tell me in your own words what's happened, and give me his full observations, ★ including respiratory rate, conscious state, urine output and allergies?' → 39.5, 80/50, HR 122, RR 26, sats 91% air, 'a bit vague', little urine, penicillin allergy → 'thank you — particularly the respiratory rate and that he's vague'

★ 'Here is what I think is going on. Mr Nolan has a catheter-associated urinary tract infection — an infection seeded when he was catheterised two days ago — and that infection has progressed to sepsis. With a blood pressure of 80 over 50 he may already be in septic shock; I'll know that once we see whether he responds to fluid. Four things: instrumented 48 hours ago; temperature 39.5; hypotensive and tachycardic; hypoxic and drowsy — a systemic picture, not a bladder one.' · 'we've got oral trimethoprim — shall I start it?' → ★ 'No — oral is not enough and absorption is unreliable when someone is shocked.'

★ Sepsis door: 'Before we talk about tests, I am treating this as sepsis and I want a few things started now. One — oxygen, titrate to saturations of 92 to 96. Two — two large-bore cannulae. Three — 500 mL of balanced crystalloid over 15 minutes, then repeat his blood pressure and tell me the number (saline is fine if that's what you have). Four — observations every 15 minutes, and a bladder scan — I need to know whether he's in retention again. ★ Can you read those four back to me?'

★ Investigations, two buckets, before antibiotics: 'urine — a sample for microscopy, culture and sensitivity; midstream if he can, and if we recatheterise him, from the sampling port of the new catheter, never from the bag. Bloods — two sets of blood cultures from separate sites, FBE, UEC, CRP, LFT, coagulation, ★ a venous gas with a lactate, a blood sugar, and a group and hold. Bedside — an ECG and a chest X-ray, because I don't want to assume the urine is the only source' (cannula site, chest, wounds asked) · 'he hasn't passed urine since this morning' → 'then bladder scan first (620 mL). If there's urine he can't pass — catheterise, take the specimen from the new catheter; that also relieves the obstruction. Don't let the urine hold the antibiotics past about 45 minutes.'

★ 'Before I name a drug — the chart says penicillin allergy. What actually happened?' → 'a rash as a teenager' → 'that's a delayed rash, not an immediate reaction — a cephalosporin is reasonable: please prepare IV ceftriaxone at therapeutic dose; I'll confirm the choice and dose against the guideline when I'm with you. I want it in within the hour, and we'll narrow it when the cultures come back at about 48 hours.' (no allergy → gentamicin loading dose by weight/renal function + IV amoxicillin; 'lips swelled, couldn't breathe' → avoid all beta-lactams, gentamicin + on-call physician/ID advice, flag the allergy) · 'what dose?' → 'IV, empirical, therapeutic dosing, checked against the guideline' (never invent a number) · 'continuous monitoring, hourly observations, strict fluid balance and hourly urine measurement. ★ I am walking down now, and I will call the registrar myself. Ring me immediately if his blood pressure doesn't come up after that fluid, if he becomes more confused, or if he stops passing urine.' ('ICU?' → if not fluid-responsive — vasopressors; discuss with the registrar/ICU)

Long term, offered: 'once he's stable — two threads. The infection: seven days of antibiotics if he responds promptly, 10–14 if delayed; IV to oral once afebrile and tolerating intake; narrow when sensitivities return. The prostate — the part that stops it happening again: review anything worsening his outflow, an alpha blocker such as tamsulosin 400 mcg daily, finasteride or a combination if the gland is large; urology for a TURP or a newer endoscopic procedure if medical treatment fails or he re-obstructs. If we treat his prostate properly he shouldn't need catheterising again — and fewer catheters is the single best way to prevent this infection.' (no prophylactic antibiotics at insertion/removal/change) · ★ 'Thanks Jane. To summarise: oxygen, fluids, cultures, antibiotics within the hour, obs every 15 minutes. I'm on my way down and the registrar is being called. Anything you're worried about that I haven't covered?'
ask: ★ 'Am I speaking with the nurse looking after Mr Nolan? May I take your name?' / ★ 'Could I have his full observation set — respiratory rate, conscious state, urine output, allergies?'

★ 'A catheter-associated urinary tract infection that has progressed to sepsis.' / ★ 'Before we talk about tests, I am treating this as sepsis.' / 'Oral is not enough and absorption is unreliable when someone is shocked.' / ★ 'Can you read those back to me?'

★ 'Cultures first — but do not let them delay the antibiotic past 45 minutes.' / 'Midstream if he can manage it; if we recatheterise him, take it from the sampling port of the new catheter, never from the bag.' / 'An ECG and a chest X-ray, because I do not want to assume the urine is the only source.'

★ 'Before I name a drug — what is his allergy, and what actually happened?' / ★ 'I am walking down now, and I will call the registrar myself.' / ★ 'Ring me immediately if the blood pressure does not come up, if he becomes more confused, or if he stops passing urine.'

Catheter still in situ, cloudy smelly urine → 'Then the catheter comes out. Antibiotics are only transiently effective around a colonised catheter, because the bacteria sit in a biofilm the drug cannot reach. Remove it; if he still needs drainage, insert a new one aseptically and take the specimen from the new catheter's port — not the old bag.' / immediate penicillin allergy → 'That is an immediate hypersensitivity, so I will avoid all beta-lactams — no penicillins and no cephalosporins. I will use gentamicin and take advice from the on-call physician or infectious diseases on the second agent before we give it. Please make sure the allergy is flagged properly in the chart.'
pefe: Role-player: Jane Coulthard, 34, RN, six years on a busy surgical ward, 7 pm, one nurse short; brisk, practical, respectful; gives full answers to open questions but volunteers nothing — withholds RR 26, sats 91%, 'vague and drowsy', no urine since morning, and the penicillin allergy unless asked. Pushes once early: offers oral trimethoprim (accepting it = fail, uncorrected). Pushes at the antibiotic: 'what dose?' — notes a confidently invented number. Anxious at 4 min if nothing started: 'is there anything you want me to start? he doesn't look well.' At 6 min if never asked: 'the notes say he's allergic to penicillin — does that matter?' 'A rash as a teenager' — or, if you've coped well, 'his lips swelled and he couldn't breathe'. Won't read back unless asked. Bladder scan if asked: 620 mL. IV access: one small hand cannula; saline and Hartmann's available; no cough, cannula site fine, sore over the bladder

Observations: T 39.5 · BP 80/50 (MAP 60; target ≥65) · HR 122 · RR 26 · SpO2 91% RA · vague · anuric since morning · bladder 620 mL. Catheter-associated = catheter in situ or removed within 48 h. Sepsis red flags: hypotension, RR ≥22, altered mentation (qSOFA ≥2), lactate >2, oliguria

Sepsis bundle (Sepsis Kills/SA Health VERIFY): oxygen to 92–96%, IV access, cultures (blood ×2 + urine + relevant sites) before antibiotics, lactate, IV antibiotics within 60 min, fluids 500 mL boluses to 20–30 mL/kg reassessing, hourly urine output, escalate (MET criteria); vasopressors (noradrenaline) if MAP <65 after fluid → ICU. Empirical urosepsis antibiotics VERIFY TG: gentamicin 4–7 mg/kg IV loading (renal/weight-adjusted, ideal body weight, single dose then review) + amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly; delayed non-severe penicillin rash → ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV daily acceptable; immediate hypersensitivity → no beta-lactams, gentamicin ± advice (e.g. ciprofloxacin); narrow at 48 h; duration 7 d (10–14 if slow/complicated); no post-treatment culture unless prostatitis; catheter removal if colonised; source control — relieve retention (recatheterise), exclude abscess/obstructing stone (USS/CT if not improving 48–72 h)

Long term BPH: tamsulosin 400 mcg daily; finasteride 5 mg daily (up to 6 months; halves PSA); combination; urology — TURP/laser/UroLift/Rezum; TWOC planning with alpha blocker; no antibiotic prophylaxis at catheter insertion/removal/change VERIFY. Telephone conduct: identify both ends, structured handover (ISBAR), closed-loop read-back, state you are attending and escalating, document · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 (rural)
fails: ★ Accepting oral trimethoprim, or never treating as sepsis; following the printed order — two minutes listing bloods while MAP is 60
★ Antibiotics before cultures without the 45-minute caveat; forgetting lactate or blood cultures; specimen from the bag; assuming the urine is the only source
★ Never saying 'catheter-associated' ('urosepsis' hides the catheter); asserting septic shock as certain before any fluid
★ Naming a drug without asking what the allergy was; inventing a dose; naming a penicillin in a documented allergy
No read-back; four instructions in a monologue; not coming down/escalating; starting with the prostate while he is hypotensive; no summary/check of the nurse's concerns

setting: General practice. Three numbers in the stem do the work: HbA1c 8% (uncontrolled diabetes), BP 150/90 (uncontrolled), atenolol (a recognised cause — but prescribed for his heart). 'Further interventions' means investigate, fix the chronic disease first, then treat the ED — and ask about nitrates BEFORE prescribing a PDE5 inhibitor. Clear fail: PDE5 without the nitrate question; stopping atenolol unilaterally; never defining the complaint; blaming; omitting the psychosocial assessment.
stem: James Corrigan, 60, presents with erectile dysfunction for a number of months. T2DM diagnosed 5 years ago; MI 4 years ago. Medications: metformin, atenolol. HbA1c 8%. BP today 150/90.
tasks: Take a history from the patient
Explain the possible causes to him
Discuss further interventions
time: 8 min. Intro, confidentiality → 'things aren't working downstairs' → ★ acknowledge + normalise + warning shot: 'not easy to bring up; common; a medical problem; in most men we find the reason. I need to ask some quite personal questions — about erections, intercourse and masturbation — I ask every man with this problem; tell me if anything's uncomfortable' · ★ define and grade: how long (6 mo), every time, worse · 'getting and keeping an erection, or finishing sooner than you'd like?' · 'able to start intercourse, or does it go before that?' (loses it part-way) · ★ 'still getting early-morning or spontaneous erections? change in sex drive? ★ same difficulty on your own?' (reduced; same libido; same alone → organic) · ★ impact on him and the relationship (wife thinks he's gone off her) · genital/prostatic: bend/curve/lump/pain, LUTS, surgery pelvis/prostate/back · ★ cardiovascular: 'chest pain or breathlessness on exertion?' (puffed on the hill — pursue), claudication; smoking (quit 5 y), alcohol (3–4 beers most nights), exercise, diet, weight, snoring · endocrine (cold, constipation, fatigue; breast enlargement/discharge; headache/vision) · ★ psychosocial: mood (flat), sleep, enjoyment, home (32 y, strained), work; ★ risk question when mood is low · neuro: back pain, ★ numbness (feet numb), weakness, bladder/bowel · meds incl chemist; changes · ★ four questions ×2: diabetes — when, what, ★ 'in an average week how many doses do you miss? most people miss some' (2–3/week — stomach), reviews (none >1 y), complications; MI — when, stent, chest pain since, rehab (2 sessions), cardiologist · causes: vascular explanation without blame — diabetes (8%, missed doses, small vessels then nerves — numb feet), atenolol, MI ('penile arteries are smaller — show trouble first'); hormones, thyroid, penis, prostate, nerves, mood · three boxes: investigate → ★ fix diabetes and BP (matters most; don't stop atenolol — write to the cardiologist; back to rehab) → PDE5 with ★ the nitrate question inside the sentence → GTN spray in the glovebox → rules + teach-back · counselling for both; safety-net (chest pain, priapism >4 h); review 2 wk.

back.dx: Organic (vasculogenic + neuropathic + drug-related) erectile dysfunction — six months, progressive, loses the erection part-way, reduced morning erections, preserved libido, same on his own; drivers: poorly controlled T2DM (HbA1c 8%, metformin missed 2–3×/week for GI upset, no review >1 year, numb feet = sensory neuropathy), atenolol (post-MI beta-blocker — do not stop unilaterally), ischaemic heart disease (MI/stent 4 y, rehab abandoned, new exertional breathlessness on the hill — needs cardiac reassessment before PDE5 use), hypertension 150/90, alcohol 3–4 beers nightly, overweight, snoring; mood flat (consequence and amplifier; no self-harm thoughts); relationship strained (wife thinks he's gone off her). Interventions: (1) investigate — morning testosterone ×2 + LH/FSH/prolactin, HbA1c, lipids, TSH, UEC, home/24-h BP; (2) optimise — fix metformin tolerability (XR/with food), add an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 with CV benefit VERIFY, add an ACE inhibitor once BP confirmed, write to cardiology re atenolol and the exertional symptoms, cardiac rehab, diabetes reviews, weight/exercise/alcohol; (3) ED — sildenafil on demand or tadalafil daily, only after the nitrate check (GTN spray in the glovebox → 24 h/48 h rules, cardiology first), needs stimulation, side effects; vacuum device/intracavernosal injections/urology if unsuitable; couple counselling; safety-net chest pain and priapism; review 2 weeks. Hidden: father died of an MI at 62 — 'does this mean my heart is getting worse?'
plan: 'I'm Dr —; am I speaking with James? May I call you James? Everything we discuss is completely confidential. What's brought you in?' → 'awkward… things aren't working downstairs' → ★ 'Thank you for telling me — I know that isn't easy to bring up. It's common, it's a medical problem, and in most men we can find the reason and do something about it. Before we go on: to sort this out properly I need to ask some quite personal questions — about erections, intercourse and masturbation. I ask these of every man with this problem. Tell me if anything's uncomfortable. Is that alright?'

★ Define/grade: 'how long? every time or comes and goes? getting worse?' (6 mo, almost every time, worse) · 'can you describe exactly what you mean — the difficulty getting and keeping an erection, or finishing sooner than you'd like?' (getting and keeping) · 'able to start intercourse at all, or does it go before that?' (starts, loses it part-way) · ★ 'still getting early-morning or spontaneous erections? any change in your sex drive? ★ same difficulty on your own?' (now and then, not like before; same drive; same alone) · ★ 'how is this affecting you, and your relationship?' (wife thinks he's gone off her — 32 years) → 'that sounds hard for you both — I'll come back to that'

Genital/prostatic: bend, curve, lump, pain on erection; LUTS — difficulty, nocturia, dribbling; surgery to prostate/genitals/pelvis/back → no · ★ cardiovascular: 'ever told high sugar, BP, cholesterol? ★ chest pain or breathlessness when you exert yourself? calf pain walking that eases with rest?' → 'puffed going up the hill — put it down to age' → 'that's important and I'll come back to it' · smoking (quit 5 y; pack/day before), alcohol (3–4 beers most nights), exercise (little), diet, weight (few kilos), snoring/unrefreshed (yes)

Endocrine: cold intolerance, constipation, fatigue; breast enlargement/discharge; headaches/vision → no · ★ psychosocial: 'how has your mood been? sleep? still enjoying things? who's at home, how are things between you? work — stress?' → flat; sleep ok; married 32 y, strained → ★ 'when you say flat — any thoughts of harming yourself?' (no — fed up) · neuro: back pain, ★ numbness/tingling in the legs or feet (feet numb for a while), weakness, bladder/bowel control → 'that's relevant' · ★ 'what medications, including anything from the chemist? anything changed?' (metformin, atenolol, a cholesterol tablet, aspirin)

★ Diabetes ×4: 'when diagnosed? what are you taking? ★ in an average week how many doses do you think you miss — most people miss some? regular reviews? complications — the numbness, foot ulcers, blurred vision, kidneys checked?' → 5 y; metformin bd; 'if I'm honest 2–3/week — upsets my stomach'; no review >1 y; numb feet → 'thank you for being straight with me' · ★ MI ×4: 'when? stent? chest pain since? cardiac rehab completed? seeing a cardiologist?' → 4 y, one stent, no pain except the hill, two rehab sessions then stopped

★ Causes, without blame: 'James, erections depend on healthy blood vessels — blood has to flow in quickly and be held there; anything that damages small vessels affects it. First and biggest, your diabetes: your recent test was 8% where we aim for around 7, and missing doses will be part of that. Over years, high sugar damages the small blood vessels and later the nerves — the numbness in your feet tells me that damage has already started elsewhere. Second, one of your tablets — atenolol is known to cause this in some men. Third, your heart attack: the arteries that supply an erection are much smaller than the ones in the heart, so they often show trouble first. I also thought about hormones — a low testosterone level, which I'll test; thyroid; the penis itself — a curvature — or the prostate; nerve or spinal causes; and stress and mood, which are both a cause and a consequence. This is a physical, treatable problem — not a failing on your part.' · 'so it's my fault for skipping the tablets' → ★ 'No — the metformin upset your stomach, and that's a real side effect, not a character flaw. There are ways around it, and that's a problem we can solve together.'

★ Three boxes: (1) 'tests — a morning testosterone with a couple of related hormones, repeat sugar test, cholesterol, thyroid and kidney tests, and your blood pressure properly — at home over a week or a monitor for a day' · (2) ★ 'and this is the part that matters most: getting the diabetes and blood pressure under control. Tell me what makes the metformin hard to take — there are ways around the stomach upset. Then a second diabetes tablet from a group that also protects the heart and kidneys. Once we confirm the blood pressure, a different type of tablet for that. ★ I'm not going to stop your atenolol on my own — it's protecting your heart — but I'll write to your cardiologist and we'll look together at whether there's a better option, and about that breathlessness on the hill. Back to cardiac rehab, back to regular diabetes reviews; weight, exercise, cutting the beers back helps the diabetes, the heart and the erections all at once' · (3) ★ 'treatment for the erections themselves: sildenafil, taken when you need it, or tadalafil as a small daily dose — sildenafil is off patent, so cheaper. Before I prescribe either: ★ do you ever use a spray, or a tablet you put under your tongue, for chest pain?' → 'a little spray in the glovebox — never used it' → ★ 'that's exactly why I asked. That spray is a nitrate, and taken close together with these tablets it can drop your blood pressure dangerously. It doesn't necessarily mean you can't have the tablet, but we need clear rules and I want to discuss it with your cardiologist first. The rule: if you take one of these tablets, no spray for about a day afterwards — longer with the daily one. Chest pain in that window — call an ambulance and tell them you've taken this tablet. Can you tell me that back?' · 'the tablet needs sexual stimulation to work; headache, flushing, indigestion' · alternatives: vacuum device, injections, urologist · ★ 'I'd like to offer you and your wife a session with a counsellor — not because I think it's in your head, but because it affects both of you' · father at 62 → honest: risk factors treatable, the breathlessness gets checked · review 2 weeks with readings/results · ★ safety-net: chest pain/breathlessness at rest or during sex → stop, ambulance; erection >4 hours → hospital

I ask these of every man with this problem.' / ★ 'Can you describe exactly what you mean — getting and keeping an erection, or finishing sooner than you'd like?' / ★ 'Are you able to start intercourse at all?'
