setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION + discharge conversation. Cardiology ward; you are the hospital MO. This is a HEART FAILURE examination — six places read for congestion; every negative is the evidence for task 2. Stop examining at 4:30 wherever you are and reserve 3½ minutes for a six-step conversation: bridge → state → ask → solve → risk → respect. Decide now that the answer is neither yes nor no. Automatic fails: telling a competent adult he is not allowed to leave; 'yes, you can go' with no examination-based reasoning; never bridging; letting him leave with no red flags/follow-up/medication plan.
stem: Ron Prescott, 70, admitted three days ago with decompensated heart failure. History: hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, coronary artery bypass graft. He is insisting on being discharged today.
tasks: Perform a relevant physical examination with running commentary to the examiner
Advise the patient whether he can be discharged
time: 'Are you the one who can let me out?' → ★ 'I am, and I'll give you a proper answer in a few minutes once I've had a look at you' → WIPE (hands, eyes, pulse, heart, lungs, tummy, ankles; chest uncovered; any pain?) · general appearance: ★ alert/orientated, not drowsy, ★ 'not breathless at rest or on speaking', no cachexia/jaundice/cyanosis, no O2/infusion · hands: xanthomas, splinters, clubbing, peripheral cyanosis, ★ warm and well perfused · pulse 78 regular; ★ BP — 'what limits how far we push his heart-failure medications' · face: xanthelasma, arcus; ★ 'Examiner, I would like to perform fundoscopy' (hypertension) → skip · mouth; ★ JVP at 45° (sternal angle, vertical height); carotid bruits · praecordium: ★ midline sternotomy scar named + drain scars, ★ no device box, apex (unable to comment on displacement), heave, thrills; ★ bell at the apex for a THIRD HEART SOUND — 'no gallop rhythm'; ★ 'no murmur, so I'm deliberately not doing the manoeuvres' · lung bases (→ skip → name it: three points each side, bases to the anterior axillary line, bibasal crepitations) · abdomen without flattening the bed: liver from the RIF; ★ abdominojugular reflux — warn, 'breathe normally through an open mouth', hold 10 s, 'no SUSTAINED rise' · legs: press and hold 15 s, ★ long saphenous harvest scars · ★ offer sacral oedema, daily weights, fluid balance chart, electrolytes/creatinine · 4:30 summarise ('clinically euvolaemic and compensated') · six steps.

back.dx: Compensated (euvolaemic) heart failure on day 3 of treatment for decompensation — alert, not breathless at rest or on speaking, warm, pulse 78 regular, JVP not raised, no displaced apex, no S3, no bibasal crepitations, no hepatomegaly, no sustained abdominojugular reflux, no peripheral oedema; sternotomy + saphenous harvest scars (ischaemic cardiomyopathy the likely aetiology), no device. Discharge: clinically possible, not advised today — the oral diuretic dose and renal function are unconfirmed and the precipitant is unresolved (readmission within a month likely); if he chooses to go he has capacity and it is his right → discharge safely: written medication list, bloods, GP review within 7 days, red flags (more breathless, can't lie flat, PND, ankle swelling, weight up >2 kg in 2 days, chest pain, blackout), daily weights, door stays open. Hidden reason: wife Marg in a motel at $160/night, three hours from home → PATS.
plan: 'Are you the one who can let me out of here?' → ★ 'I am, and I'll give you a proper answer in a few minutes — I just want to have a look at you first so I'm telling you something useful rather than guessing. Good morning Mr Prescott, I'm Dr —. I'll look at your hands and eyes, feel your pulse, listen to your heart and lungs and press gently on your tummy and your ankles. I'll need your chest uncovered — is that all right? Any pain anywhere?' (gloves, sanitiser, blot; bed at 45° — never repositioned)

'Examiner, on general appearance Mr Prescott is ★ alert and orientated, not drowsy, comfortable at rest and ★ not breathless at rest or on speaking. No cachexia, no jaundice, no central cyanosis. Not on oxygen, no infusion running.' · 'may I see your palms… turn them over — no tendon xanthomas, no splinter haemorrhages, no clubbing, no peripheral cyanosis, and ★ the hands are warm and well perfused' → 'skip the peripheral signs' → 'Thank you — moving to the pulse and blood pressure. Rate 78, rhythm regular. ★ I'd also like his blood pressure, since it's what limits how far we can push his heart failure medications.'

'On the face no xanthelasma, no arcus. ★ Examiner, I would like to perform fundoscopy — he has hypertension in his history and the retina is the one place I can see end-organ damage.' → 'skip that' → take it (you've scored for asking) · 'open your mouth and lift your tongue — no central cyanosis, membranes moist. Turn your head to your left. ★ Examiner, at 45 degrees the JVP is not raised, and with the bell either side of the trachea there are no carotid bruits.' ('how do you measure it?' → 'vertical height of the top of the venous pulsation above the sternal angle at 45° — ≤3 cm normal')

'On inspection of the chest there is a ★ midline sternotomy scar consistent with the bypass grafting in his history, with drain scars below it. ★ I cannot see a device box beneath the left clavicle. No visible apex beat, no chest wall deformity.' → 'what does the scar tell you?' → ★ 'That he has established coronary disease, which makes an ischaemic cardiomyopathy the most likely reason he has heart failure at all — as opposed to what tipped him into this admission, which is a separate question.' · 'I cannot feel the apex beat, so I am unable to locate it or comment on displacement. No parasternal heave. No thrills at the mitral, tricuspid, pulmonary or aortic areas.' · ★ 'I'm starting with the bell at the apex specifically to listen for a third heart sound… S1 and S2 normal, no murmurs, no added sounds at each area. There is no gallop rhythm. There is no murmur, so I'm deliberately not performing the dynamic manoeuvres.'

'Examiner, I'd like to auscultate the lung bases' → 'skip the respiratory examination' → 'Thank you — I would have listened at three points each side with the bases out to the anterior axillary line, for bibasal crepitations. Moving to the abdomen.' · 'Mr Prescott, I'm going to press on your tummy — tell me if it's sore. I'm leaving you sitting up.' → 'no hepatomegaly, no liver tenderness. Now the ★ abdominojugular reflux — I'll press here for about ten seconds; ★ breathe normally through an open mouth, don't hold your breath' → 'there is ★ no sustained rise in the JVP'

'I'll look at your legs and press on your shin for about fifteen seconds — it may feel firm. Examiner, no peripheral oedema, and there are ★ long saphenous vein harvest scars on the medial calf and thigh, consistent with the graft. ★ I would also like to check for sacral oedema, and to review his daily weights, fluid balance chart and most recent electrolytes and creatinine.' → 'skip those — please summarise' → ★ 'A 70-year-old man on day three of an admission for decompensated heart failure. Alert, comfortable, not breathless at rest or on speaking, warm peripherally, pulse 78 regular. No features of ongoing decompensation: JVP not raised, no visible or displaced apex, no third heart sound, no bibasal crepitations, no hepatomegaly, no sustained abdominojugular reflux, no peripheral oedema. Sternotomy and vein-harvest scars consistent with his bypass; no device. He appears clinically euvolaemic and compensated on current treatment, which I'd confirm against his weights and renal function.' STOP.

★ 1 BRIDGE: 'Mr Prescott — can I tell you what I found? The blood tube in your neck, which stands up when there's too much fluid on board, is flat. Your lungs are clear at the bases — that's where fluid collects. Your liver isn't enlarged and your ankles aren't swollen. None of the signs that your heart failure is still overloaded are there today.' · ★ 2 STATE: 'So the treatment has worked. I do want to be straight with you though — the fluid has gone, but the heart condition hasn't. We've got you back under control; we haven't cured anything.' · ★ 3 ASK, then stop talking: 'Before I answer about home — can I ask what's pulling you home today? Something specific, or just three days of this place?' → 'the wife's in a motel at $160 a night, three hours from home — and I feel fine'

★ 4 SOLVE: 'That's a real problem and I'm glad you told me — there's a scheme that covers exactly that: travel and accommodation for country patients and an escort. I can get the paperwork started this morning. I can also ask the team to see you first on the round tomorrow.' (cigarettes → patch within the hour; somewhere to be → leave from the ward) · ★ 5 RISK, specific: 'What I'd want you to know is what isn't finished. Your fluid tablet has only just gone back to tablet form and we haven't checked your kidneys on the new dose. We haven't worked out what tipped you over this time — and if we don't find that, there's a fair chance you're back in here within a month.' · 'so can I go or not?' → ★ 'Clinically you're in good enough shape that going home is possible — so I'm not going to tell you that you can't. What I'm telling you is that it isn't what I'd advise today, and why. If you still want to go after that, we'll do it properly rather than have you walk out with nothing.'

★ 6 RESPECT: 'Having said all that — this is your decision, and you're entitled to make it. If you decide to go I'm not going to stand in your way. What I'll do is write your tablets down, get a blood test organised, ring your GP so you're seen within the week, and give you a list of things that mean come straight back: getting more breathless, not being able to lie flat, waking at night short of breath, your ankles swelling, or your weight going up more than two kilos in two days. Weigh yourself every morning. And if you change your mind tonight, come back — nobody will be annoyed with you. Does that sound fair?' · examiner 'yes or no?' → 'Clinically he is compensated, so discharge is possible. It is not what I would advise today, because his oral diuretic dose and renal function are unconfirmed and the precipitant is unresolved. If he chooses to go, he has capacity and that is his right — I would discharge him safely, with a written medication list, bloods arranged, GP review within seven days and red flags.'

I'm not going to stand in your way.' / 'If you change your mind tonight, come back — nobody will be annoyed with you.'

Variants: already dressed, bag packed ('just sign something') → 'There's nothing you need me to sign — you're not a prisoner and you don't need my permission. What I'd ask for is four minutes: let me examine you so that what I tell you before you walk out is worth something, and then I'll help you go properly.' / angry ('three days and nobody has told me a thing') → 'That sounds genuinely frustrating, and I'm sorry it's been like that. Can I do that now? I'll examine you, then tell you exactly where things stand and what's left.' (apologise for the experience, never defend the system) / ★ Variant D — 'JVP raised at 6 cm, crepitations at both bases' → 'those are features of ongoing congestion, so he is not compensated and I would not be advising discharge today at all. Ron — what I found is different from what I hoped: there is still fluid on your lungs and the pressure in your neck is still up. The treatment isn't finished; going home today carries a real risk of getting worse quickly and I'd strongly advise against it. I still can't stop you — but I'd be failing you if I didn't say that plainly.' (steps unchanged; step 6 identical) / Variant E — 'my wife's got dementia and there's nobody with her tonight' → 'That changes what matters here. Social work this morning, an urgent aged-care assessment, respite if we can get it. If we can cover tonight, would you give us another day? If we can't, I'll help you go home safely rather than pretend that's not what's happening.'
pefe: Role-player: Ron Prescott, 70, retired grain farmer, Wallaroo, three hours from Adelaide; admitted 'full of fluid', much better since yesterday; hypertension, cholesterol, CABG eight years ago; not breathless, ankles fine, walking to the bathroom. Blunt, not hostile. Opens 'are you the one who can let me out of here?'; allows a few minutes if asked. Reason (ONLY if asked what's pulling him home): Marg in a motel at $160/night. 'So can I go or not?' at least once, presses if dodged. Told he can't leave or must sign something → irritated: 'you can't keep me here'. Examiner: skips at the peripheral signs (~1:20), fundoscopy, respiratory (~3:45), sacral oedema; asks 'what does that scar tell you?' (silence if you never mention it — marked), 'how do you measure the JVP?', 'please summarise' at 4:30, 'yes or no — can he be discharged?' at the end. Second run: Variant D findings

Heart-failure examination = six congestion sites: JVP · apex (displacement) · S3/gallop · lung bases · liver + abdominojugular reflux · peripheral/sacral oedema — plus 'not breathless on speaking' (most sensitive bedside marker), warm vs cool peripheries (perfusion), BP (limits therapy), daily weights and fluid balance, U&E/creatinine on the oral diuretic. Sternotomy + saphenous scars = CABG → ischaemic cardiomyopathy (aetiology) vs precipitant (ischaemia, arrhythmia/AF, infection, non-adherence, NSAIDs, salt/fluid, anaemia, thyroid, uncontrolled BP). Discharge readiness: euvolaemic, stable on oral diuretic ≥24–48 h, renal function checked on the oral dose, precipitant identified/addressed, GDMT titration plan, education (weights, 2 kg/2 days rule, fluid/salt), GP review within 7 days, HF nurse/telehealth. Capacity — Consent to Medical Treatment and Palliative Care Act 1995 (SA): a competent adult may refuse/leave; document the discussion; discharge against advice done safely

SA: PATS (Patient Assistance Transport Scheme — travel and accommodation + escort for country patients) · Country Health Connect · heart failure nurse · GP within 7 days · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450
fails: ★ Telling a competent adult he is not allowed to leave / must sign something; fear or coercion ('you'll die if you walk out')
★ 'Yes, you can go' with no examination-based reasoning and no unfinished business named; ★ 'you can't' — indefensible
★ Never bridging — examining thoroughly then discussing discharge without reporting a finding to the patient in lay words; never asking why he wants to go

Generic general-appearance list (missing conscious level and breathless-on-speaking); not asking for fundoscopy; walking past the sternotomy; 'added sounds' instead of S3; flattening the bed for the liver; pressing the abdomen/exposing without warning
Still auscultating at 6:00 and improvising a verdict; ★ Variant D — still advising discharge is reasonable; no red flags/2-kg rule/GP follow-up/medication list
numbers: Stop examining 4:30 · six-step talk 3½ min · JVP ≤3 cm above the sternal angle · AJR 10 s, 'sustained' · oedema press 15 s · weight rule >2 kg in 2 days · GP review ≤7 days
Six negatives: JVP · apex · S3 · bases · liver/AJR · oedema · the answer is 'clinical state → advice → autonomy', never yes or no · PATS · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION, two task versions. Version 1 (secondary causes excluded in the stem): CVS exam hunting complications → explain the implications and findings. Version 2 (no exclusion sentence): add the secondary-cause screen (Cushingoid features, radio-radial/radio-femoral delay, other arm, Mallampati, striae, kidneys, renal bruits, thyroid) → diagnosis and differentials. The station is won at the fundus — ask for fundoscopy at ~2:30 and describe the photograph; never asking is an automatic fail. Reserve the last two minutes (half the marks). Expect to be skipped at the hands and the respiratory exam.
stem: James Whitmore, 25, referred after a BP of 160/100 was recorded when he attended to donate blood. Otherwise well, no symptoms.
tasks: Perform a cardiovascular examination with running commentary to the examiner
V1: Explain the implications of the high blood pressure and your findings to the patient · V2: Explain the diagnosis and the differential diagnoses to the patient
time: Decide the version at the door; fix the eye block (arcus, xanthelasma, ★ fundoscopy) · WIPE: hands/eyes/pulse/BP/heart/lungs, chest uncovered, any pain? ★ 'I'll just sit the bed up to 45°' (in the opening line) · general appearance — ★ name absences, not searches (no central cyanosis, cachexia, jaundice; V2: no moon face, no supraclavicular fat pad, no plethora) · hands (xanthomas, nicotine, peripheral cyanosis, clubbing) → skip → pulse 84 regular (V2: ★ no radio-radial delay; ★ 'I need to feel the pulse in your groin, is that all right?' — no radio-femoral delay; other arm) · BP: cuff 1–2 cm above the fossa, marker anterior, one finger under → examiner '160/100' → ★ 'I'll take that as 160 over 100 — stage two hypertension in a 25-year-old' · face: no arcus/xanthelasma → ★ 'Examiner, I would like to perform fundoscopy' → photograph → AV nicking, silver wiring, disc margin sharp → 'sure no papilloedema?' → answer both ways · mouth (V2 Mallampati) · JVP at 45° (sternal angle, vertical) · praecordium: inspection, apex ('unable to comment on displacement'), heave, thrills, bell then diaphragm 2–3 s each, ★ 'no gallop rhythm', carotids; ★ decline the manoeuvres aloud · lung bases → skip → name it · abdomen: liver from the RIF, AJR ('breathe normally', 'sustained'; V2 striae, kidneys, ★ renal bruits) · legs: oedema, posterior tibial pulses · V2 last: 'I'd complete with a thyroid examination' · ★ stop at 6:05 · summary: six HF negatives + the one positive · task 2.

back.dx: Primary (essential) hypertension with end-organ damage in the eye — BP 160/100 (stage 2) in a well 25-year-old, no features of cardiac decompensation (JVP not raised, no displaced apex, no gallop, no bibasal crepitations, no hepatomegaly, negative abdominojugular reflux, no oedema), posterior tibial pulses present and equal; fundoscopy: arteriovenous nicking and silver wiring with a sharp disc margin = hypertensive retinopathy (a blurred/swollen disc = accelerated/malignant hypertension → same-day assessment). Task 2 (V1): never diagnosed on one reading → 24-h ambulatory monitor; end-organ damage in plain words (eyes, heart, kidneys, brain, leg vessels); heart normal, eye changes present and imply duration; kidneys can't be examined by hand → urine ACR + eGFR, ECG, lipids/glucose. V2: working diagnosis primary hypertension; secondary causes examined for — thyroid, renal artery stenosis (renal bruits), coarctation (radio-femoral delay), Cushing's/Conn's/phaeo (adrenal), renal disease, OSA — and white-coat hypertension named; bloods incl hormone levels, urine, ECG, 24-h monitor.
plan: 'Hello James, I'm Dr —. I've been asked to examine your heart and circulation — I'll look at your hands and eyes, feel your pulse, take your blood pressure, and listen to your heart and lungs. I'll need your chest uncovered — is that all right? Any pain anywhere? ★ I'll just sit the bed up to forty-five degrees.' (gloves, sanitiser, blot) · 'Examiner, on general appearance this is a well-looking young man, comfortable at rest. There is no central cyanosis, no cachexia and no jaundice.' (V2: 'no moon face, no fat pad at the base of the neck, no facial plethora')

'May I see your palms… turn them over… nails together — no tendon xanthomas, no nicotine staining, no peripheral cyanosis, no clubbing.' → 'skip the peripheral signs' (~1:15 — help, not judgement) → 'Thank you — I'll move to the pulse and blood pressure. Rate 84, rhythm regular.' (V2: 'feeling both radials together — no radio-radial delay. Now the right radial with the right femoral — ★ James, I need to feel the pulse in your groin, is that all right? — no radio-femoral delay, which argues against a coarctation. I would also record it in the other arm.') · 'I'm going to put a cuff on your arm — it will squeeze for a few seconds' (cuff 1–2 cm above the fossa, marker anterior, one finger underneath) → 'his blood pressure is 160 over 100' → ★ 'Thank you — I'll take that as 160 over 100, which is stage two hypertension in a twenty-five-year-old.'

'James, may I look at your eyes? Look straight ahead. Examiner, there is no arcus and no xanthelasma. ★ Examiner, I would like to perform fundoscopy.' → photograph, 'tell me what you see' → ★ 'This is a fundus photograph. There is arteriovenous nicking at several crossings, and the arterioles show silver wiring rather than the normal red. The optic disc margin is sharp. These are the changes of hypertensive retinopathy.' → 'are you sure there is no papilloedema?' → ★ 'I can draw a clean line around the whole disc margin and it doesn't appear to bulge forward, so I don't think so. If it were blurred I would be calling this accelerated hypertension and asking for same-day assessment.' (V2: 'while the mouth is open I'm noting the Mallampati score — class two') · 'open your mouth and lift your tongue — no central cyanosis. Turn your head to your left. Examiner, at 45 degrees the JVP is not raised.' → 'how do you measure it?' → 'the vertical height of the top of the venous pulsation above the sternal angle, at 45 degrees; three centimetres or less is normal'

'On inspection of the chest no visible apex beat, no scars, no chest wall deformity. On palpation I cannot feel the apex beat, so ★ I am unable to locate it or comment on displacement. No parasternal heave. No thrills at the mitral, tricuspid, pulmonary or aortic areas.' · 'I'm going to listen to your heart now' — bell at mitral, diaphragm mitral, tricuspid, pulmonary, aortic, 2–3 s each — 'S1 and S2 normal, no murmurs, no added sounds at each area, ★ there is no gallop rhythm, and at the carotids no bruits. ★ There is no murmur, so I am deliberately not performing the dynamic manoeuvres — I'd rather finish the complication screen.'

'Examiner, I'd like to auscultate the lung bases' → 'skip the respiratory examination' → 'Thank you — I would have listened at three points on each side and at the bases in the anterior axillary line for bibasal crepitations. Moving to the abdomen.' · 'James, I'm going to press on your tummy — tell me if it's sore.' → 'no hepatomegaly. Now the abdominojugular reflux — ★ breathe normally through an open mouth, don't hold your breath… there is ★ no sustained rise in the JVP.' (V2: 'no striae; I'd like to ballot the kidneys' → skip; 'auscultating two to three centimetres above and lateral to the umbilicus with the diaphragm — no renal bruits')

'I'll look at your legs and feel your ankles. Examiner, no peripheral oedema, and the posterior tibial pulses are present and equal.' (V2: 'Examiner, I'd like to complete with a thyroid examination' → skip) · ★ STOP at 6:05 · 'Examiner, in summary: a well twenty-five-year-old man with a blood pressure of 160 over 100 and a regular pulse of 84. No features of cardiac decompensation — no raised JVP, no visible or displaced apex beat, no gallop rhythm, no bibasal crepitations, no hepatomegaly, a negative abdominojugular reflux and no peripheral oedema. The one positive finding is on fundoscopy: hypertensive retinopathy with arteriovenous nicking and silver wiring. My diagnosis is primary hypertension with end-organ damage in the eye.'

★ V1: 'James, your blood pressure today is 160 over 100, so it's high again — the same as at the blood bank. The first thing I want to say is that we never make this diagnosis on one reading. Blood pressure goes up when people are nervous, and giving blood makes most people nervous. So I'd like you to wear a small monitor for twenty-four hours that checks it while you go about a normal day. The reason we take it seriously is what it does over the years: high pressure quietly damages the eyes, the heart, the kidneys, the brain and the blood vessels in the legs — and that's exactly what I was examining you for today. The good news is that your heart examination was completely normal, with no sign of strain or fluid, and the pulses in your legs are strong. But when I looked at the back layer of your eye, I could see some early changes from the pressure in those very small blood vessels. That matters, because it suggests this has been going on for a while rather than just this week. I can't check your kidneys with my hands, so I'll arrange a urine test and a blood test for those, along with a tracing of your heart and a cholesterol level. Is that all right?' · 'is it dangerous? I feel fine' → 'Not today — no immediate danger, and feeling fine is exactly why it goes unnoticed. It's a long-game problem: left alone for years it raises the risk of stroke, heart attack and kidney damage. Finding it at twenty-five is actually good luck. Shall I organise the monitor and those tests?' · 'tablets forever?' → 'not at tablets yet — confirm with the monitor first; at your age salt, alcohol, weight and exercise shift the numbers more than people expect' · 'can I still donate?' → 'I'd check the current Lifeblood criteria rather than guess — let's sort the numbers first' · 'dad had it and was fine' → 'family history makes yours more likely and is useful to know — it also means we look after yours properly'
V2

★ 'James, my working diagnosis is primary — or essential — high blood pressure: high pressure without one single cause behind it. I say working because a number of conditions can push it up, and today I examined you for the ones I can pick up with my hands: your thyroid gland; a narrowing of the artery to the kidney — that's why I listened over your tummy; a narrowing of the main vessel leaving the heart — that's why I compared the pulse at your wrist with the one in your groin; a hormone condition from the glands above the kidneys; kidney disease itself; and a sleep-breathing problem. stem: Jack, 5, brought to ED by his mother with tiredness, lethargy and worsening shortness of breath. Previously well; recent sore throat. Vital signs provided. A chest X-ray is available.
tasks: Explain the chest X-ray to the examiner
Perform an anterior chest and abdomen examination on the mannequin and explain your expected findings to the examiner
time: FILM (≤60 s): 'AP chest radiograph of a young child; trachea central, bones/soft tissues unremarkable, adequate inspiration. ★ The striking abnormality is the cardiac silhouette — CTR well over 0.5: cardiomegaly. Caveat: AP magnifies the heart and a young child tolerates a higher ratio (~0.55) — but at this degree I think it's genuine. ★ Second, the costophrenic angles are blunted with fluid at the bases — pleural effusions — and increased interstitial markings, pulmonary congestion. ★ Putting it together — previously well five-year-old, recent sore throat, breathless, big heart, effusions — my working diagnosis is acute rheumatic fever with carditis. A globular silhouette can also be a pericardial effusion; an urgent echo distinguishes them.' · consent from the mother + 'I'll talk out loud so the examiner can follow' · general appearance: level of consciousness (expect tired, lethargic, rousable), respiratory distress (tachypnoea, nasal flaring, tracheal tug, recession — ★ 'I would expect to find them'), central cyanosis; hydration offered → 'stick to your task' · praecordium: ★ expect a visible apex beat (film); JVP offered with the paediatric caveat — lean on the liver edge · palpation: apex — normal position named (5th ICS MCL) → ★ expect displaced laterally and inferiorly; heave expected; thrills possible · auscultation: bell at the apex — ★ expect a gallop rhythm, a murmur of valvulitis (apical pansystolic MR ± early diastolic AR), possibly a pericardial friction rub, listen for a Carey Coombs murmur; no manoeuvres on a mannequin · respiratory ALL FIVE steps anterior with expectations: reduced movement/expansion at the bases, trachea central, stony dullness at the bases, reduced breath sounds + ★ bibasal crepitations (two findings, two causes), reduced vocal resonance · abdomen: mild distension, hepatomegaly from congestion (1–2 cm normal at this age — degree and tenderness matter), hepatojugular reflux — ★ 'sustained' · lower limbs excluded — facial/periorbital puffiness in a child · 'to complete: the other Jones features — arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules' · diagnosis and plan.

back.dx: Acute rheumatic fever with carditis (pancarditis) in a previously well five-year-old three weeks after an untreated sore throat — cardiomegaly (CTR >0.5 on an AP film, conceded and committed), bilateral pleural effusions and pulmonary congestion; expected: respiratory distress, displaced apex, parasternal heave, gallop rhythm, apical pansystolic murmur of mitral regurgitation ± early diastolic AR ± Carey Coombs murmur ± pericardial rub, bibasal stony dullness with reduced breath sounds (effusions) plus crepitations (oedema), congestive hepatomegaly with a sustained hepatojugular reflux. Plan: urgent echocardiogram in any case (subclinical carditis is itself a major criterion; excludes pericardial effusion), streptococcal serology (ASOT/anti-DNase B) + throat swab, ESR/CRP, ECG (PR interval), urinalysis (post-streptococcal GN also follows a sore throat and overloads a child), admit, penicillin, heart-failure treatment, notification/registration with the RHD control program, secondary benzathine penicillin prophylaxis for at least ten years.
plan: 'Thank you. Examiner, this is an anteroposterior chest radiograph of a young child. Trachea central, bones and soft tissues unremarkable, adequate inspiration. ★ The striking abnormality is the cardiac silhouette — the cardiothoracic ratio is well over 0.5, so there is cardiomegaly. ★ Second, both costophrenic angles are blunted with fluid at the bases — pleural effusions — and the lung fields show increased interstitial markings in keeping with congestion.' → 'how do you know that is cardiomegaly and not just an AP film?' → ★ 'I don't, from the film alone — an AP projection magnifies the heart and a young child tolerates a higher ratio than an adult, up to about 0.55. But at this degree, and with a breathless child, I think it is genuine. I'd also note that a globular silhouette can be a pericardial effusion rather than a dilated heart, and an urgent echocardiogram would distinguish them.'

★ 'Putting it together — a previously well five-year-old, a recent sore throat, now breathless with a big heart and effusions — my working diagnosis is acute rheumatic fever with carditis. May I move to the examination?' · to the mother: 'Hello, I'm Dr —. I'm going to examine Jack's chest and tummy — looking at his breathing, feeling and tapping his chest, listening, and pressing gently on his tummy. Is that all right? ★ I'll talk out loud as I go so the examiner can follow me.'

'Examiner, on general appearance I'd assess his level of consciousness — I would expect a tired, lethargic but rousable child. I'd look for respiratory distress — tachypnoea, nasal flaring, tracheal tug, intercostal and subcostal recession — and with pulmonary congestion and effusions ★ I would expect to find them. I'd look for central cyanosis. I'd also assess hydration —' → 'stick to your task' → 'Of course. Moving to the praecordium. On inspection ★ I would expect a visible apex beat, because the film shows an enlarged heart. I'd also look at the neck — I would expect a raised JVP, ★ though it's unreliable at this age, so I'd rely more on the liver edge.'

[flat hand left lower chest] 'I'm palpating for the apex beat, ★ normally in the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line, and I would expect it displaced laterally and inferiorly towards the axilla, because of the cardiomegaly.' [heel at the left sternal edge] 'I would expect a parasternal heave with right ventricular loading.' [pads] 'Thrills at the mitral, tricuspid, pulmonary and aortic areas — possible if the valvulitis has produced a loud murmur.' · mother: 'is it his heart? he was fine a month ago' → 'It does look like his heart, yes — and the sore throat he had is probably part of it. I'll explain properly as soon as I've finished, and we'll get a scan of his heart today. Is it all right if I keep going?'

'On auscultation — bell at the apex first, then the diaphragm at the mitral, tricuspid, pulmonary and aortic areas. ★ I would expect three things: a gallop rhythm, meaning decompensation; a murmur of valvulitis, most likely an apical pansystolic murmur of mitral regurgitation and possibly an early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation; and a pericardial friction rub. I'd listen specifically for a Carey Coombs murmur — the short mid-diastolic murmur of acute mitral valvulitis. I'm not performing the dynamic manoeuvres on a mannequin.'

★ Respiratory, all five steps, anterior: 'Inspection — chest movement at the upper zones and bases; I'd expect reduced movement at both bases. Palpation — trachea central, which I'd expect with bilateral effusions; chest expansion, reduced at both bases. Percussion — apices, mid-zones, bases, comparing sides; ★ I'd expect stony dullness at both bases. Auscultation — I'd expect reduced or absent breath sounds at both bases from the effusions, and ★ bibasal crepitations from pulmonary oedema — two separate findings with two separate causes. Vocal resonance — I'd ask him to say ninety-nine, or count to three, and I'd expect it reduced over the effusions.'

'To the abdomen. On inspection I'd expect mild distension. Palpating for the liver from the right iliac fossa with the radial border of my hand up towards the costal margin — ★ I'd expect hepatomegaly with the edge well below the costal margin, from hepatic congestion; a centimetre or two is normal at this age, so it's the degree and any tenderness that matter. Then the hepatojugular reflux — pressing over the right upper quadrant for ten seconds while watching the neck — ★ I'd expect a sustained rise in the JVP that persists while I press and falls when I let go.' · 'I'm not examining the lower limbs since the task is chest and abdomen — though in a child I'd look for facial and periorbital puffiness rather than ankle oedema. To complete, I'd look for the other features of rheumatic fever: migratory arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules.'

'What is your diagnosis, and what would you do?' → ★ 'Acute rheumatic fever with carditis — pancarditis, given the recent sore throat in a previously well child. An urgent echocardiogram in any case, because subclinical carditis is itself a major criterion; streptococcal serology and a throat swab; ESR, CRP and an ECG for the PR interval; and a urinalysis, because post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis also follows a sore throat and also overloads a child. He needs admission, penicillin, treatment of his heart failure, notification and registration, and ★ secondary penicillin prophylaxis for at least the next ten years.' · mother 'will he be all right?' → 'He's quite unwell today and we'll be admitting him. This is treatable and most children come through the acute illness well. The longer view: this can leave scarring on the heart valves, and the thing that prevents that is a regular penicillin injection every few weeks, for years — it sounds like a lot, and it is, but it's the single most important thing we can do for him. Can I go through it properly once he's settled?'

Carditis = pancarditis: endocardium (MR — apical pansystolic; Carey Coombs; AR), myocardium (gallop, failure, cardiomegaly), pericardium (rub, effusion). Management: admit; benzathine benzylpenicillin IM (or 10 days oral phenoxymethylpenicillin) to eradicate GAS; heart failure — diuretics, ACEi, restrict fluids, rarely steroids for severe carditis VERIFY; aspirin/naproxen for arthritis once the diagnosis is secure (NSAIDs mask the arthritis criterion) VERIFY; bed rest; notify (ARF/RHD notifiable in SA VERIFY); register with the RHD control program; secondary prophylaxis benzathine benzylpenicillin every 21–28 days for a minimum of 10 years after the last episode or until age 21, whichever is longer (longer with RHD); dental care; echo follow-up

stem: A 40-year-old woman returned from New York two days ago. Shortness of breath and chest pain worse on deep inspiration. On the oral contraceptive pill. RR 20 · SpO2 95% · T, BP, pulse normal.
tasks: Perform a physical examination with your running commentary
Explain your diagnosis and differentials
time: WIPE 30 s: look/feel/tap/listen; ★ 'I'll need to expose your chest — I'll keep you covered in between, and I can offer you a chaperone'; ★ 'could you move up and sit on the far end of the bed?' (access from above and behind); wash · general appearance: ★ describe what's in front of you — tachypnoeic, respiratory distress, not cyanosed, alert/anxious, ★ 'not able to complete a full sentence in one breath' (don't argue with RR 20 in the stem) · hands — two justified signs: peripheral cyanosis/CRT; clubbing + small-muscle wasting 'because malignancy is a risk factor for venous thrombosis' (no tar staining today) · face: central cyanosis, Horner's · neck: tracheal tug, ★ trachea central — nothing else (JVP challenge → time decision; raised JVP + loud P2 = RV strain) · inspection: chest movement from above (clavicles) and behind · palpation: expansion front AND back, thumbs to the xiphisternum, lifted off · percussion apices → bases, same levels both sides, front and back · ★ auscultation: bell at the apices, diaphragm two further levels each side, ★ a full breath at each spot · ★ vocal resonance 'ninety-nine' · ★ 'That completes the five steps… given my working diagnosis is a PE, the most useful thing with my remaining time is the lower limbs for the source of the clot' — unilateral swelling, dilated veins, redness, warmth; ★ tape: tibial tuberosity → 10 cm below → circumference both sides; ★ 'deliberately not squeezing the calf or forcing dorsiflexion — Homans' sign is unreliable' · dx PE — 'a normal examination does not exclude it' — risk factors · long ordered differential, respiratory first · Wells, ECG, CXR, CTPA; anticoagulate while arranging transfer; stop the pill.

Ordered differential: respiratory — pneumothorax, pneumonia/pleurisy, asthma, interstitial lung disease, lung cancer (a red flag twice — malignancy causes clots); cardiac — ACS, arrhythmia, pericarditis, endocarditis; musculoskeletal chest pain (not settled on until the clot is excluded); anxiety/hyperventilation (diagnosis of exclusion); anaphylaxis only if onset over minutes; reflux far down. Plan: Wells score, ECG (sinus tachycardia commonest; S1Q3T3 uncommon), CXR (usually normal), CTPA (V/Q if contrast contraindicated or pregnant); high suspicion + imaging delay (no CT on site) → therapeutic anticoagulation while arranging transfer, MedSTAR; stop the combined pill and replace it before she leaves.

I will look at your chest, feel it, gently tap on it, and then listen with my stethoscope. ★ I will need to expose your chest — I will keep you covered in between and I can offer you a chaperone. Is that all right? ★ Could you move up and sit on the far end of the bed for me? That gives me room to look from above and to reach around behind you.' → wash hands

She is not able to complete a full sentence in one breath — speaking a few words at a time and pausing to breathe.' (describe what's in front of you; the RR 20 mismatch is built in)

'At the hands: nails for peripheral cyanosis and capillary refill. I will also look for ★ clubbing and wasting of the small muscles of the hand, because malignancy is a risk factor for venous thrombosis. I am not spending time on tar staining today. At the face: central cyanosis at the lips and tongue, and as part of a respiratory examination I would look for a Horner's syndrome.'

'Moving to the neck. On inspection there is no tracheal tug. Palpating the trachea — fingers into the suprasternal notch, pressing up and back until I find it — ★ the trachea is central.' → 'are you not going to assess her JVP?' → 'Not as part of this examination, because of time — but I would want it. A raised jugular venous pressure with a loud pulmonary second sound would suggest right ventricular strain and a large embolus; I would come back to it at the end if I had time.'

'The one thing I want from inspection is chest movement. For the upper lobes I look from above at the level of the clavicles — take a deep breath in and out — ' (shallow breath, winces) 'I'm sorry, I'll be as quick as I can — movements are symmetrical. For the lower lobes from behind — another breath — symmetrical and equal.' · 2:45 'Chest expansion, front and back: hands on the sides of the chest, ★ thumbs towards the xiphisternum and lifted off the skin. (if the whole anterior left chest is unusable — say so, do the left posteriorly if he can lean at all)

'Now I'll listen — just breathe normally, don't force a deep breath if it hurts.' [bell at the apices, diaphragm elsewhere, off the bruise] 'Air entry is present, equal and symmetrical, with no added sounds. Now say ninety-nine each time I move — vocal resonance is normal and equal.' ('that's enough, mate' → 'that's all I needed — thank you')

★ 'Examiner, I've already inspected the neck veins. I'll feel for the apex beat — no bruising there — it is not displaced. I'll auscultate the four valve areas, specifically listening for muffled heart sounds because tamponade is a consideration after chest trauma. First and second heart sounds are normal, no murmur, and the heart sounds are not muffled.' · ★ 'Finally the abdomen. James, I'm just going to look and press very gently at the top. Examiner, no Cullen's sign and no Grey Turner's sign.' [gentle palpation, both upper quadrants and epigastrium, patient left at 45°] 'The upper abdomen is soft and non-tender with no guarding. I'm examining for injury to the liver and the spleen, which sit beneath the lower ribs. I've kept him at 45° rather than repositioning him, so this is a limited abdominal examination.'

'Please request one further investigation' → ★ 'A CT chest with intravenous contrast — to assess for pulmonary contusion, occult pneumothorax or haemothorax, and mediastinal or great-vessel injury, which a plain film can miss in multiple rib fractures. I'd also make sure he has adequate multimodal analgesia and incentive spirometry, because the complication I am trying to prevent is atelectasis and pneumonia.' · Version A (investigations): 'At the bedside an eFAST — free intraperitoneal fluid, pericardial fluid, pneumothorax and haemothorax in about ninety seconds. Then CT chest, and abdomen if indicated, with IV contrast. An echocardiogram if concerned about tamponade. Bloods: FBE, group and hold with crossmatch, blood gas. An ECG, with troponin if I suspect blunt cardiac injury.' ('why not a FAST first?' → 'if he were unstable I would — eFAST is the bedside first line; he is stable and the question the X-ray leaves unanswered is the parenchyma and the mediastinum, so CT is the higher-yield next test')

pefe: Role-player: James, 40 (or Jenny, 52), fell ~3 m from a ladder two hours ago onto the left side; analgesia hasn't touched it; large makeup bruise over the left lower chest; deep breaths sharply painful, normal breathing bearable. No abnormal findings (never invents wheeze/crackles). THE RULE: percuss/press/spring on or beside the bruise, or squeeze the chest between two hands → 'AH! That really hurts!' and pulls away → automatic fail. No empathy → 'aren't you going to give me something for this pain?'. Asked to sit up → levers up slowly, wincing, a full minute unless stopped; stopped → 'thanks', cooperative. 'Take a deep breath' → 'Ah — I can't.' Lie flat → 'No — don't. I can't lie flat.' Ninety-nine ×4–5 → 'that's enough, mate'. Silent skip → marked; skip with a reason → ticked. Three archetypes: easy-going (tests completion incl. gentle rib check), in pain (default), grumpy (refuses to sit, cries out early; female version with the bruise under a sports bra)

Definitions: flail chest = ≥3 adjacent ribs each fractured in ≥2 places (paradoxical movement); Beck's triad = hypotension + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds; 'the box' = nipple to nipple, clavicles to costal margins → cardiac wound. Signature pairs: hyper-resonant + quiet = pneumothorax; stony dull + quiet = haemothorax; dull + bronchial + increased resonance = contusion/consolidation. Anatomy: left lower ribs → spleen; right lower ribs → liver; 1st rib/scapula → high-energy — think aorta. Investigations: eFAST (four abdominal windows + both pleural views; rules in, not out); CT with IV contrast definitive in the stable patient; ECG/troponin for blunt cardiac injury; ABG; G&H. Rib fracture care: multimodal analgesia (regular paracetamol, NSAID if no contraindication, opioid, consider regional — serratus anterior/erector spinae block VERIFY), incentive spirometry/deep breathing, early mobilisation, admit if ≥3 ribs, elderly, hypoxia, poor pain control; watch for delayed pneumothorax/haemothorax and pneumonia

fails: ★ Never acknowledging the pain / no promise to be gentle and stop; the patient cried out and you continued or didn't apologise

'Primary survey complete' deleting the respiratory rate and saturation; jumping from general appearance to the chest (losing the trachea and the neck veins); 'I can see a bruise' with no flail/emphysema

setting: PAEDIATRIC PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — ED, regional. Do I have that?' wash; keep covered · observations + 'move him to resus — a pneumothorax can tension' → 'stick to your task' · general appearance (distress, colour, sentences), hands (peripheral cyanosis, pulse volume — low volume = tension) → 'skip' → face (central cyanosis) · ★ NECK: no tracheal tug, ★ no engorged neck veins, ★ no swelling of subcutaneous emphysema (neck discomfort), palpate the supraclavicular fossae for crepitus, ★ trachea midline · inspection (surgical emphysema; movement — 'the mannequin doesn't move, but I would expect reduced on the left'), expansion (thumbs lifted, expect reduced left) · percussion (expect hyperresonant left) · auscultation bell apices + diaphragm two levels (expect absent/reduced air entry left, no wheeze/crackles) · ★ vocal resonance — 'a 5-year-old can say ninety-nine; expect reduced on the left' · to complete: apex, four valve areas · summary: secondary spontaneous pneumothorax complicating asthma; DDx exacerbation (signs unilateral), inhaled foreign body; O2, monitor, admit, MedSTAR to WCH; decompress if deviation/compromise.

back.dx: Left-sided simple (non-tension) secondary spontaneous pneumothorax complicating asthma in a 5-year-old — lucent left hemithorax with a visceral pleural line and collapsed lung, midline trachea, no mediastinal shift, sharp costophrenic angles, no consolidation, rib fracture or surgical emphysema; expected unilateral left signs — reduced movement and expansion, hyperresonance, reduced/absent air entry, reduced vocal resonance, midline trachea, no engorged neck veins. Differentials: asthma exacerbation (less likely — signs are unilateral; asthma is the risk factor, treat both), inhaled foreign body (no choking episode). Plan: oxygen, continuous monitoring, admission, retrieval to a paediatric centre (MedSTAR Kids → WCH); decompress immediately if tracheal deviation or haemodynamic compromise — tension is a clinical diagnosis. V-B: eleven features of infant respiratory distress named individually, plus conscious level, colour/mottling, observations, hydration/feeding, apnoea; examination adapted to an infant; ENT add-on — never the throat with stridor.
plan: 'Examiner, this is a chest X-ray of a 5-year-old boy. In practice I would confirm his name, the date and the side marker. AP or PA — for these findings it doesn't change my interpretation; adequately penetrated, reasonably rotated.' (one sentence) · 'Systematically: clavicles, ribs and spine, trachea, cardiac shadow, both hemidiaphragms and both lung fields.' · ★ 'On the left there is a lucent area with no lung markings, bounded by a fine visceral pleural line, with the lung collapsed towards the hilum. That appearance is a pneumothorax.'

'What is the single most important thing?' → ★ 'The position of the trachea. It is midline, and the mediastinum is not displaced, so radiologically this is a simple, non-tension pneumothorax. I would add that a tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis — if this child were shocked with a deviated trachea I would decompress him immediately and not wait for a film.' · 'To complete my search: the costophrenic angles are sharp, no consolidation, no rib fracture, and ★ no surgical emphysema in the soft tissues of the neck or chest wall — which I am looking for specifically, given his neck discomfort. In summary: a left-sided simple pneumothorax in a known asthmatic, with no radiological evidence of tension. May I move on to the examination?' → 'we do not need the full three minutes'

(to the child) 'Hello — I'm going to look at your chest, feel it, tap on it and listen with my stethoscope. I'll need your top off for a few minutes.' → (to the examiner) ★ 'Before I expose and examine a 5-year-old I would confirm consent from his parent, who is his legal decision-maker — his own agreement is not consent. Do I have that?' → 'mother has consented' → wash hands; 'I will keep him covered between steps' · 'Before I touch him I would like his observations — RR, saturation, HR, BP, temperature — and I would move him to the resuscitation cubicle, because a pneumothorax can tension.' → 'stick to your task'

'On general appearance I am looking for features of respiratory distress, his colour, and whether he can speak in full sentences. He is not cyanosed. At the hands, nails for peripheral cyanosis and the pulse volume — a low-volume pulse would concern me about tension.' → 'skip the peripheral signs' → stop mid-sentence: 'Thank you — moving to the face for central cyanosis at the lips and tongue, and then to the neck.'

★ NECK: 'On inspection: no tracheal tug, no engorged neck veins — which I would expect in a tension pneumothorax — and no swelling to suggest subcutaneous emphysema, which I am looking for specifically because of his neck discomfort. I would palpate the supraclavicular fossae for crepitus. Palpating the trachea now, two fingers either side of the suprasternal notch: the trachea is midline.' (examiner nods)

'Inspecting the chest, again for surgical emphysema. For chest movement I look from above at the level of the clavicles for the upper zones, and at the lower chest for the lower lobes, assessing symmetry. ★ The mannequin does not move, but in this child I would expect reduced movement on the left.' [hands on the lateral chest, thumbs to the xiphisternum, lifted off] 'Chest expansion — watching my thumbs move apart — I would expect reduced expansion on the left.'

[percuss apices → bases, comparing sides] 'I am listening for hyperresonance, and I would expect the left to be hyperresonant.' [bell at the apices, diaphragm at two further levels each side] 'I am assessing air entry — absent, reduced or normal — and listening for added sounds. I would expect absent or markedly reduced air entry on the left, with no wheeze and no crackles.' → 'anything further?' → ★ 'Yes — vocal resonance, the fifth step. A 5-year-old can say ninety-nine, so I would ask him to repeat it while I listen at the same points, and I would expect it reduced on the left.' · 'To complete, I would palpate for the apex beat and auscultate the mitral, tricuspid, pulmonary and aortic areas.' (the task is the anterior chest — do not turn him)

★ Summary: 'A 5-year-old boy with known asthma, acutely breathless with cough and neck discomfort. His film shows a left-sided pneumothorax with a midline trachea — simple, not tension. I would expect unilateral signs on the left: reduced movement and expansion, hyperresonance, reduced air entry and reduced vocal resonance, with a midline trachea and no surgical emphysema. My leading diagnosis is a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax complicating asthma; I considered an asthma exacerbation — less likely because the signs are unilateral — and an inhaled foreign body, possible but less likely without a choking episode. I would give oxygen, monitor him continuously, admit him and arrange retrieval to a paediatric centre — MedSTAR to the Women's and Children's Hospital. If he developed tracheal deviation or haemodynamic compromise I would decompress immediately without waiting for another film.'
V-B

VIDEO — head down, feature by feature: 'nasal flaring · tracheal tug and head bobbing (sternocleidomastoid pulling the head with each breath) · grunting · audible stridor or wheeze · accessory muscle use and recession — suprasternal, substernal, intercostal, subcostal · paradoxical see-saw abdominal breathing · tachypnoea · apnoea. In this video I can see intercostal and subcostal recession, tracheal tug, head bobbing and paradoxical abdominal movement; he is tachypnoeic. I cannot see nasal flaring, cannot hear grunting or stridor, and saw no apnoeic pause.' → ★ the half most leave out: 'behaviour and level of consciousness — alert, irritable or drowsy — colour including mottling, RR, saturation, HR, BP, temperature, and hydration, because a baby working this hard often stops feeding; I would specifically ask about apnoeic episodes.' · DOLL: general appearance (cyanosis, conscious level, no apnoea seen); hydration — CRT on the chest, turgor on the abdomen, mucous membranes, sunken eyes, sunken fontanelle; inspection for symmetry, deformity, Harrison's sulcus; expansion scaled down; gentle percussion over two or three levels (distinguishes pneumothorax from effusion); auscultation bell apices/diaphragm below — air entry, intensity, wheeze (continuous), crackles (interrupted), bronchial breathing; no ninety-nine — compare the transmitted cry · ★ ENT add-on: throat, ears, nose, cervical nodes — 'I would not examine the throat if there were stridor at rest — keep him with his parent, avoid distress, oxygen if tolerated, senior and anaesthetic help early'

Findings: film — left pneumothorax, visceral pleural line, collapsed lung, midline trachea, no mediastinal shift, sharp costophrenic angles, no consolidation/rib fracture/surgical emphysema. Obs RR 34, SpO2 93%, HR 128, BP 96/62 (tachypnoea/tachycardia for age; not shocked). Pneumothorax signs — unilateral: reduced expansion, hyperresonance, reduced/absent air entry, reduced vocal resonance; tension adds tracheal deviation away, distended neck veins, hypotension. Infant respiratory distress — eleven features: nasal flaring, tracheal tug, head bobbing, grunting, audible stridor/wheeze, accessory muscle use, suprasternal/substernal/intercostal/subcostal recession, paradoxical abdominal movement, tachypnoea, apnoea. Consent: parent, not child (Consent to Medical Treatment and Palliative Care Act 1995 SA; a mature-minor assessment does not apply at 5). Management: high-flow oxygen (reabsorption ×4), monitoring, IV access, analgesia, CXR-guided — small/asymptomatic → observe with repeat film; large/symptomatic → needle aspiration or intercostal catheter; secondary pneumothorax (asthma) → lower threshold for drain and admission VERIFY; treat the asthma (salbutamol, steroid) alongside; retrieval — MedSTAR Kids 1300 13 12 33 → WCH; decompression site: 4th–5th ICS anterior to mid-axillary line (adult); 2nd ICS MCL acceptable — confirm paediatric cannula size locally VERIFY

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — ED. The most failed physical examination station in the whole exam, and it is not failed on knowledge. Gloves are given and there is no hand sanitiser in the room. Everything turns on one discipline: she screams at the first light touch, and you must still test THREE quadrants before the word 'generalised' leaves your mouth, then narrate every omission with its reason. Automatic fails: announcing generalised peritonitis after the first scream; pressing again without apologising, explaining and asking permission; skipping deep palpation, rebound and percussion silently; deciding a 52-year-old does not need a pelvic examination.
stem: Emergency department. A 52-year-old woman with sudden onset abdominal pain, already given analgesia by the nurse; observations are in the notes. BP 104/62 — HR 112 — RR 22 — T 37.9. Gloves are provided and you will be told to put them on; there is no hand sanitiser in the room; the bed is in the centre of the station.
tasks: Perform a focused abdominal examination, with a running commentary to your examiner
State your most likely diagnosis, with your reasons
Give your differential diagnoses
time: DOOR: gloves on, 'may I have the vital signs · blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and temperature?' → name the abnormality out loud ('tachycardic at 112 with a soft blood pressure · I will keep that in mind') · never accept 'stable' silently · WIPE 30-45 s: name and date of birth, four steps (look, gently feel, gently tap, listen), expose whole tummy, wash hands, and offer analgesia; she says 'you do it' → 'is it all right if I lower your trousers a little so I can see the whole tummy?' · peripheries (do NOT skip · dehydration and blood loss are the point, and one recall scores hydration separately): general appearance, CRT, turgor, palmar creases, cold peripheries, pulse volume, sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, conjunctival pallor · inspection: Cullen and Grey Turner BY NAME in every case, scars, distension, masses, redness, then bend down and look across the abdomen · cough: 'could you cough and tell me if it hurts, and where?' → 'I can't' → don't push; 'she is unable to cough, which itself suggests significant peritonism' · superficial palpation starting away from the pain → she SCREAMS on the lightest touch → apologise, offer more analgesia, explain why you must press again, ask permission · switch maps out loud: 'given the severity I will assess by quadrant rather than nine regions' → quadrant 2 tender, quadrant 3 tender → 'I am not going to test the fourth. There is guarding; there is no rigidity.' · the skip, spoken in full: 'I am stopping superficial palpation here, skipping deep palpation and rebound and skipping percussion, because they would add nothing and cause unnecessary pain' · what still costs her nothing: auscultate, request groins, request DRE with consent and chaperone, and offer a PELVIC examination with consent and chaperone, naming all the bimanual items · diagnosis with reasons → causes as rupture / progressed obstruction / ischaemia / pancreatitis → plan.

back.dx: Generalised peritonitis — she was unable to cough and had severe tenderness with guarding in three separate quadrants on LIGHT palpation (guarding present, rigidity absent); on the verbal pelvic examination, cervical motion tenderness with bilateral adnexal tenderness. Causes, grouped: rupture — perforated peptic ulcer (she takes ibuprofen most days), perforated appendix or diverticulum, ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, and in a woman a ruptured ovarian cyst, tubo-ovarian abscess or, if younger, a ruptured ectopic pregnancy; obstruction that has progressed — tumour, strangulated hernia, faecal impaction; then mesenteric ischaemia and acute pancreatitis. Plan: nil by mouth, two large-bore cannulae, bloods with lactate and beta-hCG, fluid resuscitation, adequate analgesia, erect chest X-ray and CT abdomen and pelvis, surgical referral now; at a rural SA site start all of that and call MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 while the workup runs.
plan: Gloves on. 'Good morning, Examiner. Before I begin, may I have the vital signs, please — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and temperature?' → 'BP 104/62, pulse 112, RR 22, temperature 37.9' (or 'all observations are stable' / 'assume they are normal'). Say what you heard: 'Thank you — she is tachycardic at 112 with a soft blood pressure; I will keep that in mind as I examine her.' Move to the patient's right side.

WIPE: 'Hello, I'm Dr -, one of the doctors in the emergency department. Can I check your name and date of birth? Thank you, Jane. I've been asked to examine your tummy — I'll look at it, gently feel it, gently tap on it, and at the end listen with my stethoscope. I'll need to see the whole tummy, so could you pull your top up and lower your trousers a little? You can stay lying as you are. Let me wash my hands — and before I start, are you in pain now? Would you like something for it?' → 'the nurse gave me morphine twenty minutes ago, it hasn't touched it' → 'I'm sorry — I'll ask her to review that as soon as we finish.' → 'you do it' → ask, then act: 'Of course. Is it all right if I lower your trousers a little so I can see the whole tummy?'

Peripheral survey — do not skip it: 'Examiner, on general appearance she is alert but in obvious pain and distress, lying very still, guarding her abdomen. No pallor. Jane, may I see your hands? Capillary refill under two seconds, skin turgor normal, no pale palmar creases, no cold peripheries, radial pulse of good volume. Face — no sunken eyes, no dry mucous membranes. Look up for me — no conjunctival pallor.' ('skip the peripheries' → stop mid-sentence and move on.)

Inspection, exposing xiphisternum to below the umbilicus: 'No Cullen sign, no Grey Turner sign, no scars, no distension, no visible masses, no redness. Bending down to look across the abdomen — movement with respiration is shallow and symmetrical.' Then the cough: 'Jane, could you give me a cough, and tell me if it hurts and where?' → 'I can't. I really can't.' → 'That's absolutely fine, don't force it. Examiner — she is unable to cough, which in itself suggests significant peritonism. The stem does not localise the pain, so I will begin superficial palpation in one corner and work across.'

The scream and the recovery script. Lightest touch, left upper quadrant → 'AAH! Don't — please don't!' → 'Jane, I am so sorry. I did not realise you were in that much pain. Would you like some more pain relief before I go on? I do need to feel your tummy once or maybe twice more, so that I can understand what is happening inside. I know it hurts, and I will be as gentle as I can. Is that all right?' → '...Alright. Be quick.' (Ask 'shall I continue?' without explaining and she hands it back: 'It's your call, doctor.')

Switch maps OUT LOUD and test three quadrants: 'Examiner, given the severity I am going to assess by quadrant rather than by nine regions. Second quadrant -' (scream) '- tender. Third quadrant -' (scream) '- tender again. I am not going to test the fourth, because I am now confident this is generalised and I do not want to cause unnecessary pain. There is guarding; there is no rigidity.'

The skip, spoken in full: 'Examiner — on that basis I am stopping superficial palpation here. I am skipping deep palpation and rebound tenderness, and I am skipping percussion, because they would add nothing and would cause unnecessary pain. I will continue with the rest of the examination.'

What still costs her nothing: 'Jane, I'm just going to listen with my stethoscope — this won't hurt. Examiner, bowel sounds are present. I would like to inspect the inguinal regions for hernias' → 'normal'; 'a digital rectal examination, with consent and a chaperone' → 'normal'; 'and as this is a woman with lower abdominal pain, a pelvic examination, with consent and a chaperone: on inspection — bleeding, discharge, rash or swelling? On speculum — bleeding or discharge from the cervix, tissue at the os, is the vaginal wall normal? On bimanual — cervical motion tenderness, uterine size and tenderness, adnexal masses or tenderness? And a urine dipstick.' → CMT present, uterus normal size, bilateral adnexal tenderness, dipstick negative.

Diagnosis with reasons, then grouped causes, then plan (see dx). Examiner probes and the answers: 'why no pulsatile mass?' → 'the aorta lies deep and I cannot reach it without a deep palpation this patient cannot tolerate — I would exclude an aneurysm with a bedside ultrasound.' 'Why no shifting dullness if you think there is free blood?' → 'both shifting dullness and a fluid thrill require percussion, and percussion here would be uninterpretable as well as painful.' 'Would you do the appendicitis tests?' → 'no — once peritonism is generalised, localising it to the appendix does not change the management, which is theatre.' Her worry, if it surfaces: 'Am I going to need an operation? My husband's at home on his own.'

Variants: Version A (localised, mild-moderate) — everything unchanged; at the tender area press, hold, WARN, release in one movement, then percuss for tenderness, auscultate, groins, rectum, and finish with the special test matching the quadrant: 'tenderness in the right lower quadrant, rebound negative, tenderness on percussion — that is localised peritonitis.' / Version B (localised, screams on DEEP palpation) — correct to proceed to deep palpation, because that pain is necessary; still take rebound on that single press: 'severe tenderness with rebound in the right upper quadrant. I am going to skip percussion, because peritonism is already established and percussion would only add pain.' The Version-B error is asking her permission to move from superficial to deep — she will say 'it's your call' and you lose both the mark and the time.
pefe: Role-player: Jane Hollis, 52, retired teacher. Sudden severe pain across the WHOLE abdomen three hours ago while watching television, 10/10, unmoved since; no vomiting; bowels opened normally yesterday; ibuprofen most days for her knees and occasional indigestion (Gaviscon); periods stopped four years ago; no operations; rarely drinks, never smoked. Frightened and exhausted, not difficult — lies very still, knees slightly drawn up, breathing shallowly. Asked to cough: 'I can't' (pushed twice: 'I really can't, it's too sore'). Screams loudly and immediately at the FIRST touch anywhere; screams again on the second and third quadrant, tensing the abdominal muscles — that tensing is the guarding. Apologise + explain + ask → 'Alright. Be quick.' Ask without explaining → 'It's your call, doctor. I don't know.' Asked to expose → 'you do it' the first time. 'At my age? No' to pregnancy. If nobody asks her worry: 'Am I going to need an operation? My husband's at home on his own.'

Numbers and technique: capillary refill under 2 s — postural drop >=20 mmHg systolic or >=10 mmHg diastolic — normal liver span 8-12 cm (not tested here) — bowel sounds listened for 2-3 minutes before being called absent VERIFY — THREE quadrants before the word generalised — WIPE in 30-45 s — diagnosis spoken by 7:00. Rebound is press, hold, warn, release in one movement — never lift off and come back to test it separately, that is the same pain inflicted twice.

Four scored domains, only one of which is knowledge: (1) choice and technique of examination — below 4 here and the station fails whatever else you do; (2) accuracy — a press-and-yelp is not a Murphy sign and a shallow prod is not deep palpation; (3) approach to the patient — consent, warning, apology, offer of analgesia, stopping when you have what you need; (4) diagnosis and differentials — structured, by system, delivered before the bell.
fails: ★ Announcing generalised peritonitis after the FIRST scream — the commonest automatic fail in the station; you have not tested for what you are claiming
★ Pressing again without apologising, explaining why and asking permission; or asking 'shall I continue?' with no explanation and losing the mark to 'it's your call'
Skipping deep palpation, rebound and percussion SILENTLY — every omission is narrated with its reason

Skipping the peripheral survey as 'not relevant to the abdomen'; naming only general inspection findings and never Cullen and Grey Turner; insisting on the cough three times and treating the refusal as non-cooperation rather than a finding
Deciding she is 52 and therefore needs no pelvic examination; never offering groins or rectum; a flat list of diagnoses instead of grouped causes

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — ED. The fever at the door chooses the diagnosis, and the Murphy sign is the scored moment: out, press, IN — in that order, or the role-player is briefed to give you nothing. Look for jaundice TWICE (general appearance, then sclerae). Palpate for the liver EDGE but do not drift into the chronic liver disease station — no liver span here. Automatic fails: taking the temperature and not reacting to it; refusing to go on to deep palpation because superficial hurt; pressing first and then asking for a breath out; leaving out the ECG and the respiratory examination in upper abdominal pain.
stem: Emergency department. A 35-year-old man with pain in the right upper abdomen that began after dinner last night, constant and severe, radiating to the right shoulder blade. He has vomited once and feels feverish. BP 118/74 — HR 104 — RR 18 — T 38.4.
Common variant: a 45-year-old woman, same history, with mild scleral jaundice.
tasks: Perform an abdominal examination with a running commentary to your examiner
State your diagnosis and differential diagnoses
time: DOOR: vitals including TEMPERATURE → 'he is febrile at 38.4 and mildly tachycardic, which makes an inflammatory or infective cause more likely than simple biliary colic' · WIPE, expose whole tummy, wash, offer analgesia · jaundice twice: 'on general appearance he is not jaundiced' then 'look up for me · no conjunctival pallor and no scleral icterus' · inspection Cullen/Grey Turner, scars, distension, masses, bend down · cough → he points under the right ribs · superficial palpation starting away: mild RUQ tenderness with guarding, no rigidity → PROCEED to deep palpation (mild superficial tenderness is a reason to continue, not to stop) → he screams → keep the hand still, warn, release in ONE movement → 'severe tenderness with guarding and positive rebound in the RUQ; I am going to skip percussion, because localised peritonism is established and percussion would only add pain' · liver EDGE from the RIF upward on each expiration ('not palpable, no palpable gallbladder') · NO liver span · auscultate, groins, DRE with consent and chaperone · MURPHY: warn, 'breathe all the way out... and out... pressing in under your right ribs... now take a deep breath in' → arrested inspiration → 'Murphy sign is positive; repeating on the left produced no pain, so the sign is specific' · the two closing offers: ECG (inferior MI) and respiratory examination (right lower lobe pneumonia) · plain-language explanation, then diagnosis with system-grouped differentials.

back.dx: Acute cholecystitis — right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right scapula, fever 38.4 with tachycardia, RUQ guarding with positive rebound, a positive Murphy sign, and no jaundice. Differentials by system: biliary — biliary colic, ascending cholangitis; gastrointestinal — pancreatitis, peptic ulcer disease, perforation, hepatitis; cardiorespiratory — inferior myocardial infarction, right lower lobe pneumonia, pulmonary embolism; urinary — right pyelonephritis, renal colic. Investigations: ECG, bloods with LFTs and lipase, FBC/CRP, right upper quadrant ultrasound; expect raised WCC and CRP with normal or mildly deranged LFTs — a markedly raised bilirubin and ALP point to a stone in the common bile duct or cholangitis, a raised lipase to pancreatitis. Management: nil by mouth, IV fluids, analgesia, IV antibiotics and surgical referral for cholecystectomy VERIFY TG; rural SA — discuss transfer with the receiving unit and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if unwell.
plan: Gloves on. 'Examiner, may I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and temperature?' → '118/74, pulse 104, RR 18, temperature 38.4.' → 'Thank you — he is febrile at 38.4 and mildly tachycardic, which makes an inflammatory or infective cause more likely than simple biliary colic.' (Taking the numbers and moving on loses the mark: the fever is the fact that chooses the diagnosis.)

WIPE: name and date of birth, the four steps, 'I'll need to see the whole tummy — could you pull your top up and lower your trousers a little? Let me wash my hands. Are you in pain now — would you like something for it?' → 'It's bad. They gave me something twenty minutes ago.'

Jaundice twice, and the peripheries: 'Examiner — on general appearance he is alert, in obvious pain, lying still, NOT JAUNDICED and not pale. Jake, may I see your hands? Capillary refill under two seconds, turgor normal, no pale palmar creases, no cold peripheries, pulse of good volume. Could you look up for me? No conjunctival pallor, and NO SCLERAL ICTERUS.'

Inspection and cough: 'No Cullen sign, no Grey Turner sign, no scars, no distension, no masses, no redness. Bending down — the abdomen moves symmetrically with respiration. Jake, could you cough for me and tell me where it hurts?' → 'Ah! Up here, under my right ribs.'

Superficial then deep — do not stop: 'I'll feel your tummy very gently, starting on the far side. Tell me the moment it hurts.' → 'ooh, there. That's sore.' → 'Examiner — mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant on superficial palpation, with guarding and no rigidity. Jake, I need to press a bit deeper now to feel underneath. Tell me if it hurts.' → he SCREAMS → 'I'm so sorry. I'm keeping my hand exactly where it is for a second... now I'm taking it away. Tell me if you get a stab of pain.' → 'Ow! Yes, that was worse.' → 'Severe tenderness with guarding and positive rebound in the right upper quadrant. I'm going to skip percussion, as localised peritonism is established and percussion would only add pain.'

Liver edge — not a span: 'Starting in the right iliac fossa and moving up towards the costal margin on each expiration — the liver edge is not palpable and there is no palpable gallbladder.' Then 'auscultating below the umbilicus — bowel sounds are present. I'd like to inspect the inguinal regions for hernias' → 'normal' — 'and a digital rectal examination, with consent and a chaperone' → 'skip that.' (Percussing a liver span here costs you the minute you need for Murphy and the differentials.)

THE MURPHY SIGN, in three named steps: 'Jake, one more test. I'll ask you to breathe all the way out, then I'll press in under your right ribs, then I'll ask you to take a deep breath in. It may be uncomfortable — is that all right? ... Breathe all the way out for me... and out... good. Pressing in under the ribs now... and take a deep breath in.' → he starts to inhale, catches his breath and stops: 'Ah — ! No, I can't.' → 'Thank you, I'm sorry. Examiner — Murphy sign is positive: he arrested inspiration as the gallbladder descended on to my fingers. Repeating the manoeuvre on the left produces no pain, so the sign is specific.'

The two offers, then the explanation: 'Examiner, given the site of the pain I would also like an ECG, because an inferior myocardial infarction can present as upper abdominal pain, and I would like to examine the respiratory system for a right lower lobe pneumonia.' → 'Jake, I think your gallbladder is inflamed — that's a small bag under your liver that stores bile to help digest fat. If a small stone blocks its outlet the bag gets inflamed and infected. That fits everything: pain after a meal, the temperature, and catching your breath when I pressed. I'd like blood tests and an ultrasound. You'll need antibiotics through a drip and most likely an operation to take the gallbladder out.' → 'Do I have to have the operation?' → 'The surgical team will discuss it, but a gallbladder that has made one stone usually makes more, so removing it is the usual advice — you can live perfectly well without it.'
Present: most likely acute cholecystitis, with the system-grouped differential list and the investigations (see dx).

'I'm keeping my hand exactly where it is — now I'm taking it away.' / 'I am going to skip percussion, and this is why.' / 'Moving up from the right iliac fossa on each expiration — the liver edge is not palpable.'

Variants: jaundiced and rigoring → 'RUQ pain, fever with rigors and scleral icterus — that is Charcot triad, and my diagnosis is ascending cholangitis. He is also hypotensive and confused, which makes this Reynolds pentad. I would resuscitate, take blood cultures, start IV antibiotics and arrange urgent biliary drainage by ERCP — antibiotics alone will not treat an obstructed, infected biliary tree.' / settled and afebrile with a negative Murphy → 'more consistent with biliary colic: outpatient ultrasound, dietary advice about fatty food, and referral for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.' / 'how can the abdominal examination be normal in a myocardial infarction?' → 'because the pain is referred — visceral afferents from the inferior wall enter the cord at the same levels as upper abdominal structures, so the patient localises it to the epigastrium even though nothing in the abdomen is inflamed. That is why a soft, non-tender abdomen does not reassure me and why I want the ECG.' / 'what would you expect on the bloods?' → raised WCC and CRP with normal or mildly deranged LFTs; markedly raised bilirubin and ALP → CBD stone or cholangitis; raised lipase → pancreatitis.
pefe: Role-player: Jake Morrissey, 35, diesel mechanic. Fish and chips last night, severe pain under the right ribs an hour later, constant, 8/10, radiating to the right shoulder blade; vomited once; hot and shivery; two or three milder episodes this year after big meals, always settling in a couple of hours; four or five beers on a Friday, non-smoker, no medicines, allergies or operations. In real pain, slightly impatient, not hostile. Coughs, winces, points under the right ribs. Superficial RUQ: 'ooh, that's sore', nothing elsewhere. Deep RUQ: SCREAMS and says stop, tensing the muscles. On release: 'ow — that was worse.' THE MURPHY IS THE KEY MOMENT — he reacts ONLY if you ask him to breathe out first, then press, then ask him to breathe in; if you simply press and ask if it hurts he says 'yes' and nothing more. Repeat on the left → 'no, that's fine.' Worry near the end: 'Am I going to need an operation? I've got work on Monday.'

Numbers: gallbladder wall over 3 mm on ultrasound — common bile duct over 6 mm VERIFY — biliary colic settles in 1-6 hours; cholecystitis is constant beyond six hours with fever — Charcot triad is three (RUQ pain, fever/rigors, jaundice), Reynolds pentad is five (plus hypotension and confusion) — Murphy done by 6:30, diagnosis started by 7:00. Three biliary syndromes to keep separate: biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, ascending cholangitis.

Scored behaviours: asked for the temperature and commented on the fever — jaundice commented on TWICE — proceeded to deep palpation despite superficial tenderness — rebound taken in a single movement — percussion skipped OUT LOUD with a reason — liver edge palpated and no span measured — groins and rectum requested — Murphy in the correct order with the left-sided control — ECG and respiratory examination offered — plain-language explanation plus a system-grouped list.
fails: ★ Taking the vitals and not reacting to the fever — it is the fact that chooses the diagnosis
★ Reporting jaundice only once; the sclerae are a separate observation and yellowing appears there first
Stopping at superficial palpation because it hurt — mild superficial tenderness is a reason to continue to deep palpation, not to stop; or lifting off and coming back to test rebound separately
Murphy performed in the wrong order (press first, then ask for a breath out) — the gallbladder has to be out of reach before your hand goes in; and never testing the left side to show specificity
Drifting into a liver span and the chronic liver disease examination; leaving out the ECG and the respiratory examination in upper abdominal pain
