time: TWO-MINUTE PLAN: inspect all four limbs ONCE; upper limb seated tone → power → reflexes, C5 C6 C7 C8 T1; LIE DOWN; lower limb POWER → reflexes → tone, L2 L3 L4 L5 S1; OFFER sensation and coordination and take the skip; TIA = temporary blockage, fully resolved, warning sign; ladder brain → cord → nerve → NMJ → muscle · OPENING under 30 s and FLAG THE LIE-DOWN ('I will start with you sitting and ask you to lie down part-way through') · the stroke question arrives: 'that is exactly what I need to work out · let me examine you first and I promise I will not leave without answering that' · INSPECTION of all four limbs in ten seconds · UL TONE wrist/elbow/shoulder both sides · UL POWER: C5 push the ELBOWS not the shoulders, C6 'don't let me pull', C7 'push against my hands', C8 'don't let me pull my fingers out', T1 press GENTLY · UL REFLEXES biceps and triceps only, TWO TAPS per tendon, no brachioradialis (say why if challenged) · LIE DOWN → LL POWER first: L2 thighs, L3 shins, L4 calves, L5 dorsum, S1 soles, commentating each root as you finish it · LL REFLEXES knee L3/4 and ankle S1/2 supine · LL TONE ankle, knee, hip · OFFER sensation (C4-T1 and L1-S2) and coordination → take the skip · normal examination IS the finding → TIA, defined plainly, framed as a WARNING, plus differentials and 'do not drive'.

back.dx: An entirely normal neurological examination — inspection, tone, power C5-T1 and L2-S1 bilaterally, reflexes, and (by report) sensation and coordination all normal. With a RESOLVED unilateral motor deficit, a normal examination and a normal glucose, the diagnosis is a transient ischaemic attack. To the patient: 'a temporary interruption to the blood supply to part of your brain — the blockage cleared on its own.' Then the framing that scores: it resolved, which is good news, BUT a TIA is a warning sign, the risk of a full stroke is highest in the next few days, so this is not something he goes home with — urgent brain and carotid imaging, an ECG for the heart rhythm, bloods, treatment started today, and no driving until reviewed. Differentials by ladder: brain — stroke or small bleed, tumour, multiple sclerosis; cord and nerve roots in the neck; individual nerves of the arm and leg; neuromuscular junction; muscle. Mimics named in patient words: hypoglycaemia ('a low blood sugar can mimic this exactly — we checked yours and it was normal') and Todd paresis after a seizure. Same-side arm AND leg with a normal examination points firmly to the brain.
plan: ID and gloves. 'Hello Gary, I am Dr -. I have been asked to examine your arms and legs. I will look at them, check the strength of your movements, tap them with this hammer and check sensation with cotton wool. I WILL START WITH YOU SITTING AND ASK YOU TO LIE DOWN PART-WAY THROUGH. Is that alright?' → 'Doctor, is this a stroke? My father had one.' → 'That is exactly what I need to work out. Let me examine you properly first and then I will explain everything — I promise I will not leave without answering that.'

Inspection of ALL FOUR limbs at once, ten seconds: 'no wasting, no fasciculations, no tremor, no abnormal posture or scars.' Then upper limb tone: 'Gary, relax completely and let me move your joints' — wrist, elbow, shoulder, both sides — 'tone at the wrist, elbow and shoulder is normal, and the same on the left.'

Upper limb power, root by root, commentating each: 'Copy my movement, arms out to the side — don't let me push your ELBOWS down. C5 normal both sides. Bend your elbows, don't let me pull — C6 normal. Straighten, now bend and push against my hands — C7 normal. Squeeze my fingers, don't let me pull them out — C8 normal. Spread your fingers, don't let me close them — T1 normal.' (Pushing the shoulders at C5 or pressing hard at T1 both produce false weakness.)

Upper limb reflexes, two taps per tendon: 'biceps and triceps reflexes are present and normal, both sides.' → 'you did not check brachioradialis' → 'I omitted it deliberately — it shares roots with biceps and I prioritised completing both limbs within the time.' (Re-tapping an absent reflex is the single biggest clock-killer in this station.)

'Gary, could you lie down for me now?' (he takes 15-20 seconds — do not fill it with counselling). LOWER LIMB POWER FIRST: 'I will put my hands on your leg and ask you to press against them. Press up — L2 normal. Bend your knees, feet flat, press forward — L3 normal. Pull your heels back — L4 normal. Straighten your legs, press up — L5 normal. Now press down — S1 normal. All bilateral.' Target: both limbs' power done by 5:00.

Lower limb reflexes then tone: forearm under both thighs — 'knee reflex L3 and L4, present and normal both sides'; foot dorsiflexed — 'ankle reflex S1 and S2, present and normal both sides'; then 'tone in the lower limbs is normal bilaterally.' If the bell goes first: 'I would complete the examination with lower limb tone and with gait' — say it regardless.

OFFER sensation and coordination by name — 'I would test sensation with cotton wool in each dermatome, C4 to T1 in the upper limbs and L1 to S2 in the lower limbs, and then coordination with finger-nose and heel-shin testing' → 'both normal — skip.' Never assume the skip; offer, then accept.

Bell. Summary: 'tone, power, reflexes, sensation and coordination are normal throughout. This is an entirely normal neurological examination. With a resolved unilateral motor deficit, a normal examination and a normal glucose, my diagnosis is a transient ischaemic attack.' Then to Gary: the plain definition, the warning-sign framing, the plan, no driving, and the differentials in patient words (see dx). 'So it wasn't a stroke — that's a relief?' → hold the frame: 'it is good news that it resolved, but I want to be straight with you: a TIA is a warning sign.'

ask: 'I will start with you sitting and ask you to lie down part-way through.' / 'That is exactly what I need to work out — let me examine you first and I promise I will not leave without answering that.' / 'Examiner, power at C5 is normal, both sides.' / 'Biceps and triceps present and normal, both sides.' / 'Knee reflex L3 and L4 — present and normal.'

Resistance instructions: 'Don't let me push your elbows down' (C5) / 'Don't let me pull' (C6) / 'Push against my hands' (C7) / 'Don't let me pull my fingers out' (C8) / 'Don't let me close your fingers' (T1). When the bell beats you: 'I would complete the examination with lower limb tone and with gait.' / 'I omitted brachioradialis deliberately — it shares roots with biceps and I prioritised completing both limbs.'

Explaining: 'This is an entirely normal neurological examination.' / 'A temporary interruption to the blood supply to part of your brain.' / 'The blockage has cleared on its own — that is why the weakness has settled.' / 'It is good news that it resolved, but I want to be straight with you: this is a warning sign.' / 'The risk is highest in the next few days, which is why we act today.' / 'I need you not to drive until you have been reviewed.' / 'A low blood sugar can mimic this exactly — we checked yours and it was normal.' / 'A seizure can leave temporary weakness afterwards.'

Variants: the deficit has NOT resolved (right arm 4/5, upgoing plantar, brisk reflexes) → 'these are upper motor neurone signs and the deficit has not resolved — this is a STROKE, not a TIA. Time-critical: urgent CT brain and immediate stroke team referral to assess for reperfusion therapy' — escalate out loud rather than politely finishing. / irregular pulse noted incidentally while positioning → 'I incidentally noted an irregularly irregular pulse. That raises atrial fibrillation as a cardioembolic source, which would change treatment from antiplatelet to anticoagulation. I would request an ECG' — noting it is fine, hunting for it is not the task. / stem says 'RELEVANT examination' → carotids and pulse come back into scope: 'I would auscultate both carotids for a bruit, assess the pulse for irregularity, and auscultate the praecordium — looking for a carotid or cardioembolic source.' Read the task on the door; it decides this, not the recall. / recalled as UPPER LIMB ONLY → same sequence, same commentary, same diagnosis, and you now have time to do sensation and coordination properly rather than offering them. / the frightened patient ('my father died of a stroke — am I going to end up like him?') → 'I can hear how frightening this is, especially with what happened to your father. Here is what I can tell you honestly: this was a warning, and it is a warning we can act on. Most of the risk is in the next few days, and the treatments we start today reduce it substantially. You have come in at exactly the right time.' Do not promise he will be fine.
pefe: Role-player: Gary Feldman, 58, sitting on the edge of the bed; right arm and leg weak for about ten minutes forty minutes ago, now completely resolved and he feels fine; his father died of a stroke at 66. EVERY FINDING IS NORMAL — push back firmly and equally on every movement, limbs floppy for tone, normal reflexes. HIS JOB IS TO COST TIME: at thirty seconds he interrupts once with 'Doctor, is this a stroke? My father had one' — if the candidate stops to counsel now, let them, and note it. Asked to lie down, he takes a genuine 15-20 seconds. He gives the skip for sensation and coordination ONLY if they are offered by name. After the explanation: 'so it wasn't a stroke — that's a relief?' (testing whether the warning frame survives) and 'what else could it have been?' (testing differentials). A stopwatch runs and at exactly six minutes: 'Doctor, time' — stopping them dead, mid-movement.

Sequence and pacing: opening under 30 s with the lie-down flagged; inspection of all four limbs at 0:40; UL tone by 1:35; five roots by 2:50; biceps and triceps by 3:25; lie down; LL power L2-S1 done by 4:55; LL reflexes and tone; offer sensation and coordination; bell at 6:00. C5 push the elbows, not the shoulders; T1 press gently; two taps per tendon maximum; lower limb power BEFORE tone; knee and ankle reflexes supine — do not sit him up.

Pass guide 17 or more of 22 with all four starred items, and failing to complete both limbs before the bell is a fail on its own. Also scored: warns about the lie-down, inspects all four limbs together naming wasting and fasciculation, starts UL power at C5 not C4 and LL power at L2 not L1, volunteers sensation and coordination by name, does NOT auscultate carotids or hunt for AF, states that the normal examination IS the finding, names TIA and defines it in plain words, frames it as a warning rather than reassurance, gives differentials across brain, cord, nerve and at least one mimic, and mentions urgent investigation and not driving.
fails: ★ Being drawn into the stroke conversation at thirty seconds and never recovering the minute
★ Reaching the bell with the legs unexamined — the default failure of this station
Doing lower limb tone before power, or re-tapping an absent reflex instead of moving on
Pushing the shoulders instead of the elbows at C5, or pressing hard at T1 — both manufacture false weakness; starting UL power at C4 or LL power at L1

Assuming the skip for sensation and coordination instead of offering them by name; hunting for AF or auscultating carotids when the task did not ask; letting 'that's a relief' stand instead of holding the warning frame
numbers: 6-min bell, both limbs' power done by 5:00 · opening under 30 s · inspection of all 4 limbs in 10 s · 2 taps per tendon · C5-T1 and L2-S1 · knee L3/4, ankle S1/2 supine · BGL 6.1 mentioned

BP 158/92, HR 78 regular · normal examination IS the finding · TIA risk highest in the FIRST FEW DAYS · urgent brain and carotid imaging, ECG for AF, bloods, treatment today, NO DRIVING · mimics: hypoglycaemia, Todd paresis

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice, often a REAL patient face to face. The tremor is obvious from the door and the trap is starting the Parkinson's tests: the first block of marks is the upper limb neurological examination you were literally asked to do, and the PIVOT LINE tells the examiner which half of the marking sheet you are on. Free marks sit on inspection before you touch anything — hypomimia, reduced blink, stooped posture. Automatic fails: omitting the upper limb neurological examination and going straight to the Parkinsonism tests; mobilising the patient unsafely (no falls question, candidate seated or across the room, or a pull test with nothing behind him); talking through the father's death without acknowledging it; diagnosing confidently and never mentioning a differential.
stem: General practice. A 68-year-old man whose family have noticed his right hand shakes; he has become slower over six months and his handwriting has become small. Vital signs stable.

Findings: upper limb neurological examination normal apart from tone — right-sided 4-6 Hz pill-rolling REST tremor that damps on movement; COGWHEEL rigidity at the right wrist, enhanced on activation; finger tapping shows DECREMENT; hypomimia, reduced blink, soft monotonous speech; micrographia; gait stooped and short-stepped with reduced right arm swing and an EN-BLOC turn. No asterixis, no cerebellar signs, no postural drop.
tasks: Perform an upper limb neurological examination
Perform the relevant physical examination
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: DECLARE (10 s): 'I will complete a full upper limb neurological examination first, characterising the tremor as I go, and then perform the additional examination relevant to Parkinsonism' · WIPE 30 s + the GLOBAL LOOK that scores before you touch: reduced facial expression, reduced blink rate, stooped posture · ITPRSC at speed 140 s: inspection (tremor at rest named), tone with SUPINATION AND PRONATION and an ACTIVATION manoeuvre ('while I move this wrist, tap your other hand on your knee'), power 5/5 C5-T1, reflexes, sensation, coordination (finger-nose, rapid alternating · slow on the right) · THE PIVOT LINE: 'Examiner, that completes the upper limb neurological examination. I will now characterise the tremor' · TREMOR 60 s: REST with distraction ('rest your hands in your lap and count backwards from twenty'), POSTURAL (arms out, palms down, fingers spread, 15 s), ACTION (bring this cup up as if to drink), ASTERIXIS (wrists cocked back, 30 s) → '4 to 6 hertz pill-rolling tremor, present at rest, damping with voluntary movement, asymmetrical, more marked on the right; no asterixis' · BRADYKINESIA 45 s: finger tapping for AT LEAST TEN repetitions → decrement · FACE, SPEECH, WRITING, GLABELLAR 50 s ('British constitution'; write a sentence; tap from ABOVE AND BEHIND, not in front of the eyes) · GAIT 55 s: ask about falls first, walk beside him, and DEMAND THE TURN · then postural stability (pull test with a chair behind) and a lying and standing BP · then STOP after naming the diagnosis and let it land.

back.dx: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease: an asymmetrical 4-6 Hz pill-rolling REST tremor damping with movement, cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist enhanced on activation, bradykinesia with DECREMENT on finger tapping, hypomimia, micrographia, and a stooped short-stepped gait with reduced right arm swing and an en-bloc turn — with the relevant negatives of no intention tremor, no cerebellar signs and no asterixis. Differentials given to the patient in plain English: essential tremor (a shake that runs in families), medications that cause the same picture, thyrotoxicosis, and problems with the balance part of the brain. Plan: bloods, a full medication review, neurology referral to confirm and start treatment, physiotherapy; then the driving conversation — raised by you, framed as rules you have to follow rather than a licence taken away today, with the offer to have his daughter present. Safety-net: return sooner for a fall, a faint, or confusion. Explain dopamine in one sentence, and never promise a course — 'Parkinson's varies enormously between people, and treatment today is far better than it was in your father's time.'
plan: Declare the plan, then WIPE: 'Hello, I am Dr -, one of the doctors here. I have been asked to examine your arms and look into the shakiness your family have noticed. I will look at your hands, move your joints gently, test your strength and reflexes, and then ask you to do a few simple tasks including walking. Tell me if anything hurts. Is that all right? Could I please expose both arms to the shoulders?'

The global look, before touching: 'On inspection there is no wasting, no fasciculation and no abnormal posture, but there is a tremor of the right hand present at rest. I also note REDUCED FACIAL EXPRESSION and a REDUCED BLINK RATE, and a slightly stooped posture.'

ITPRSC at speed. Tone: 'Please let your arms go floppy' — flex, extend, SUPINATE and PRONATE both wrists and elbows — 'there is increased tone at the right wrist with a cogwheel quality. I will confirm with an activation manoeuvre — while I move this wrist, could you tap your other hand on your knee? Yes, the cogwheeling is enhanced.' Then power 5/5 C5-T1, biceps/supinator/triceps symmetrical, sensation intact C5-T1, coordination: 'no dysmetria and no intention tremor; rapid alternating movements are performed but are slow on the right.'

THE PIVOT LINE, then the tremor: 'Examiner, that completes the upper limb neurological examination. I will now characterise the tremor. Please rest your hands in your lap and COUNT BACKWARDS FROM TWENTY for me' (the rest tremor becomes coarser) '... now hold both arms straight out in front, palms down, fingers spread ... now bring this cup up as if to drink ... and finally, arms out with your wrists cocked back like you are stopping traffic, and hold.' → 'This is a four to six hertz pill-rolling tremor, present at rest, damping with voluntary movement, and asymmetrical — more marked on the right. There is no asterixis.'

Bradykinesia and the face: 'Please tap your index finger and thumb together, as big and as fast as you can, and keep going until I say stop' — watch TEN or more repetitions — 'over ten repetitions there is progressive reduction in amplitude and speed on the right — that is bradykinesia with decrement.' Then 'say British constitution for me... now would you write this sentence out... and I am just going to tap gently on your forehead FROM ABOVE — please try to keep your eyes open': soft monotonous speech, micrographia shrinking along the line, blinking that fails to habituate.

Gait and postural stability: 'Before we do this — have you had any falls? Good. If you feel safe, please walk to the wall, turn around, and walk back to me. I will walk beside you.' → 'the gait is stooped and short-stepped with reduced right arm swing and an EN-BLOC turn. I would complete the assessment with a pull test for postural stability with a chair behind the patient, and with a lying and standing blood pressure.' (Omit the turn and you lose the most sensitive sign in the station.)

Summary to the examiner with the relevant negatives, then TO THE PATIENT, ideas first: 'Mr Doyle, may I share what I have found? First — what did you and your daughter think might be going on?' → 'She thinks it's Parkinson's. Is it?' → 'I think she may be right, and I am sorry to be confirming something you were worried about.' Then STOP. Let it land. → 'That's what my father had. He ended up in a wheelchair.' → acknowledge it before saying anything else: 'That must be a very frightening thing to have in your mind. Can I say something about that?' Then dopamine in a sentence, the honest differentials, the plan, the driving conversation with the daughter present, and the safety-net (see dx).

ask: 'I will complete a full upper limb neurological examination first, then perform the examination relevant to Parkinsonism.' / 'Examiner, that completes the upper limb neurological examination.' / 'Please let your arms go completely floppy.' / 'While I move this wrist, could you tap your other hand on your knee?' / 'Please rest your hands in your lap and count backwards from twenty.'

'Hold both arms straight out in front, palms down, fingers spread.' / 'Wrists cocked back, as if you are stopping traffic — hold it there.' / 'Tap your index finger and thumb together, as big and as fast as you can.' / 'There is progressive reduction in amplitude and speed — bradykinesia with decrement.' / 'This is a four to six hertz pill-rolling tremor, present at rest and damping with movement.' / 'Please walk to the wall, turn around, and walk back to me.'

To the patient: 'Before I explain — what did you think might be going on?' / 'The brain slowly loses cells that make a chemical called dopamine, which helps control movement.' / 'I would rather you heard about the driving rules from me than from a letter.' / 'Come back sooner if you have a fall, if you faint, or if you become confused.' Avoid in front of him: bradykinesia, cogwheeling, extrapyramidal, hypomimia, micrographia, dysdiadochokinesia.

Variant A — ESSENTIAL TREMOR (62M): tremor ABSENT at rest, appears with the arms outstretched and worsens through movement, symmetrical, no rigidity, no decrement, normal gait with full arm swing → 'this is a symmetrical postural and action tremor, absent at rest, with no cogwheel rigidity, no decrement on finger tapping, normal arm swing and a normal gait. The negatives are as important as the positives here: this is NOT Parkinsonism.' To the patient: often familial, often settles briefly with alcohol, and propranolol if it interferes with life. Trap: saying 'BENIGN essential tremor' — drop 'benign' and still ask how much it affects his work, his writing and his confidence.

Variant C — DRUG-INDUCED PARKINSONISM (28M on risperidone): SYMMETRICAL findings, rigidity and bradykinesia dominating over tremor, onset over weeks, a young patient, possibly akathisia → 'there is symmetrical bradykinesia and rigidity in a 28-year-old developing over weeks since a dose increase of risperidone. This is drug-induced parkinsonism rather than idiopathic Parkinson's disease, which is asymmetrical, insidious and a disease of later life.' To the patient: usually reversible; 'I will not change anything today on my own — I will speak with your psychiatrist about lowering the dose or switching, because stopping it suddenly could make you unwell again.' Trap: ceasing the antipsychotic yourself, or missing neuroleptic malignant syndrome — febrile, rigid, confused and unstable means stop examining and escalate. Harder turns: 'am I going to end up like my father?' → 'I can't promise you a course, and I won't pretend to. What I can tell you is that it varies enormously and that treatment now is much better than it was.' / 'don't tell them about my licence' → acknowledge what it means in a country town, explain the duty is not discretionary in South Australia, and offer to work through transport options together. / 'what if he were 34?' → screen for Wilson's disease with caeruloplasmin, urinary copper and a slit-lamp examination.
pefe: Role-player: Frank Doyle, 68, retired shearer in a country town; his daughter made the appointment because his right hand shakes and he has 'gone slow' over six months. Embarrassed rather than frightened. His father had Parkinson's disease and died in a nursing home — mentioned ONLY once the diagnosis is named. No regular medications except a fluid tablet; two beers most nights; still drives to the shops and the footy. HOW HE PLAYS IT: speaks softly and flatly, keeps his face still and blinks less than feels natural, right hand rolling gently in his lap and stopping the moment he reaches for anything; finger tapping starts big then gets smaller and slower with a stall around tap eight; writing small and shrinking; rises slowly, short steps, right arm hanging still, four or five little steps to turn — and if asked to walk with NO turn, he walks in a straight line only and never volunteers it. If the candidate talks over 'that's what my father had', he goes flat, stops answering, and marks it down.

Numbers: 4-6 Hz Parkinsonian rest tremor; 6-12 Hz essential tremor. At least TEN repetitions before you may call decrement. Postural tremor held 15 s; asterixis held 30 s. Normal glabellar habituation is 3-4 taps. More than 2 steps of retropulsion is an abnormal pull test. C5-T1 upper limb myotomes and dermatomes. Under 40 — screen for Wilson's disease. Weeks to months for drug-induced parkinsonism to resolve after the drug is stopped.

Three moments that carry the station: the PIVOT LINE, which tells the examiner exactly which half of the marking sheet you are on; counting backwards from twenty, fifteen seconds that turn an equivocal tremor into a diagnostic one; and the PAUSE after 'that's what my father had' — candidates who talk through that line lose the communication domain no matter how good the examination was. Also scored: tone tested including supination/pronation with an activation manoeuvre, asterixis tested, speech and handwriting assessed, falls asked about before mobilising, the walk AND the turn requested, a structured summary with relevant negatives, ideas elicited before naming the diagnosis, and three or more differentials in plain English.
fails: ★ Going straight to the Parkinsonism tests because the tremor is obvious from the door — the first block of marks is the neurological examination you were asked for
★ Mobilising unsafely — no falls question, examining from a chair or across the room, or a pull test with nothing behind the patient
Talking through the father's death without acknowledging it; saying 'Parkinson's' and continuing straight into management without letting the word land

Three taps and a diagnosis — decrement cannot appear in three taps, and slowness alone is not bradykinesia; testing tone only in one plane; tapping the glabella from in front of the eyes so you elicit a visual blink reflex
Testing posture and action but never rest, or never distracting with counting — a subtle rest tremor only appears when the patient is counting; diagnosing confidently with no differentials
numbers: 4-6 Hz rest tremor (essential 6-12 Hz) · >=10 taps before calling decrement · postural hold 15 s · asterixis hold 30 s · glabellar habituates in 3-4 taps · >2 steps retropulsion = abnormal pull test

Pivot line after the neuro exam · count backwards from 20 to bring out the rest tremor · activation manoeuvre for subtle cogwheeling · the EN-BLOC TURN is the most sensitive gait sign · Wilson's if under 40 · drug-induced resolves over weeks to months

setting: VIDEO / TEACHING STATION — your general practice, 8 minutes. A monitor plays a short clip of the patient and a MEDICAL STUDENT is in the room; there is no live patient. You watch the clip ONCE without talking, then teach head to foot in plain English. The two things that fail it: never saying the word BRADYKINESIA, and claiming a finding the video cannot show — tone, cogwheeling, power, or special tests being performed. The correct construction is 'if he were in front of us, I would expect...' and examiners specifically listen for it.
stem: General practice. Mr Ray Dolan, a 68-year-old retired shearer, has come in complaining of shakiness of his hands. A monitor plays a short video clip; a medical student attached to your practice is in the room. No observations and no results are provided.
tasks: Watch the video of the patient
Describe and explain to the medical student the abnormalities you see
Tell the medical student what further examination you would perform
State your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses
time: 0:00-0:45 greet the student and SET THE STRUCTURE ('I'll watch the whole clip once without talking, because if I start commentating I'll miss things; then head to foot; then what I still don't know') and start the clip · 0:45-2:00 WATCH IN SILENCE, one viewing only · 2:00-3:45 four things before any special test: POSTURE stooped even seated; FACE mask-like with reduced blink and mouth slightly open; TREMOR right hand at rest, pill-rolling, settling on reach; SPEECH slow to start, low volume, monotonous · then the teaching point: ALL FOUR ARE BRADYKINESIA · 3:45-5:30 the four special tests seen on screen: finger tapping with DECREMENT (the cleanest bradykinesia there is), hand flipping SLOW but accurate (slow = bradykinesia; clumsy and irregular = dysdiadochokinesia and a cerebellar differential), finger-to-nose accurate with the tremor SETTLING on the reach, glabellar tap with failure to habituate = Myerson's sign · 5:30-6:30 the gait in SIX parts: hesitation starting, short steps, reduced foot clearance with no heel strike, festination, reduced arm swing, and the EN-BLOC turn · 6:30-7:00 what you would add at the bedside, six things, phrased as 'if he were in front of us I would expect' · 7:00-8:00 diagnosis and differentials in GROUPS, DRUGS FIRST.

back.dx: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease: bradykinesia with decrement, an asymmetrical rest tremor, a mask-like face, hypophonic speech, a stooped shuffling festinating gait with reduced arm swing and an en-bloc turn, and a positive glabellar tap. Differentials IN GROUPS, drugs first because that group is reversible: DRUGS — antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, valproate; OTHER DEGENERATIVE — progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy, dementia with Lewy bodies; STRUCTURAL AND VASCULAR — vascular parkinsonism, normal-pressure hydrocephalus; OTHER TREMORS — essential tremor, thyrotoxicosis, and Wilson's disease if he were under forty. There is NO test that confirms Parkinson's disease — it is a clinical diagnosis; investigations exclude the mimics (TSH, UEC, LFT, FBE, B12, calcium; MRI) and a good response to levodopa supports it afterwards. Assess driving against Austroads with the SA reporting duty under the Motor Vehicles Act 1959, and refer to neurology. To the student's last question: treatment helps a lot with slowness and stiffness and often the tremor, but never promise the tremor will disappear — and much of what helps is not a tablet: physiotherapy for walking, speech pathology for the voice, and making the house safe.
plan: Set the structure before the clip: 'Before we watch this, let me tell you how I'm going to do it. I'll watch the whole clip once WITHOUT talking, because if I start commentating I'll miss things. Then I'll go through the patient from head to foot — face, posture, tremor, speech, the special tests, and the gait — and I'll tell you what each one means. Then we'll talk about what I still don't know and how I'd find out.' Start the clip; do not wait for permission. ONE viewing — rewatching loses the commentary time.

The four things before any special test: 'His POSTURE. Even sitting still, his trunk and neck are bent forward — a stooped posture. His FACE. Watch it for ten seconds — it barely changes; he's blinking far less than you or I would and his mouth sits slightly open. That's a mask-like face; it doesn't mean he feels nothing, it means the muscles of facial expression have become slow. His HANDS. There's a tremor of the right hand while it rests in his lap, with a pill-rolling quality, and crucially it's there AT REST and settles when he reaches — the opposite of the tremor you see in cerebellar disease. His SPEECH. Slow to get started, low volume, flat and all on one note — hypophonic and monotonous. Now — all four of those are the same thing underneath. They are all BRADYKINESIA: slowness in starting and in carrying out voluntary movement.'

The four tests, each taught: FINGER TAPPING — 'he starts reasonably, then slows, hesitates, and the fingers come closer and closer together. That shrinking is DECREMENT, and it is the single clearest demonstration of bradykinesia there is — the same reason his handwriting shrinks as he writes, micrographia.' HAND FLIPPING — 'he can do it, it's just very slow. That's still bradykinesia. If the movement were CLUMSY and IRREGULAR rather than slow, I'd call it dysdiadochokinesia and I'd be thinking about the cerebellum, not Parkinson's.' FINGER TO NOSE — 'he gets there, no overshooting, no past-pointing, and the tremor settles as he reaches — that confirms a rest tremor rather than an intention tremor.' GLABELLAR TAP — 'if I did that to you, you'd blink two or three times and stop. He keeps blinking every single tap — that failure to habituate is Myerson's sign; a feature of Parkinson's disease, though on its own not specific.'

The gait, six parts: 'One, he HESITATES before he starts. Two, the steps are SHORT. Three, he barely lifts his feet — REDUCED FOOT CLEARANCE, no heel strike, which is why it looks like shuffling. Four, once he's going the steps get quicker and shorter, as though he's chasing himself — FESTINATION, and that is different from shuffling; he has both. Five, his ARMS BARELY SWING. Six, the TURN — instead of pivoting he turns slowly and stiffly in several small steps, EN BLOC, like a statue rotating.'

What the video cannot show — the sentence examiners listen for: 'Now, what I can't tell from a video. I haven't touched him, so I can't comment on tone, power or reflexes, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. If he were sitting in front of us, six things. One, tone at the wrist and elbow with slow passive movement — I would EXPECT increased tone, that's rigidity, and where the tremor is superimposed it feels like a ratchet, which is cogwheeling. Two, ask him to write his name and draw a spiral, looking for micrographia. Three, lying and standing blood pressure. Four, his eye movements, especially looking down. Five, a full medication list — particularly antipsychotics, metoclopramide and prochlorperazine, because those cause exactly this picture and it's reversible. Six, ask about falls, hallucinations, memory and acting out dreams.'

Diagnosis and the grouped differential, drugs first (see dx), and the closing honesty on treatment. Student probes to answer cleanly: 'what test confirms Parkinson's disease?' → 'none — it's a clinical diagnosis; investigations exclude mimics and a good levodopa response supports it afterwards.' 'Is it just his age?' → no; this is never normal ageing. 'Is that dysdiadochokinesia?' at the hand flip → no: slow but accurate is basal ganglia; irregular and uncoordinated is cerebellum, and it changes the whole differential.

back.dx: Alcohol-related cerebellar degeneration — ten positive cerebellar signs with no nystagmus: unsteady in sitting, broad-based gait, loss of balance on Romberg WITH THE EYES OPEN, dysdiadochokinesia bilaterally, intention tremor with past-pointing, upward drift, rebound, slurred staccato (scanning) speech, pendular knee jerk, abnormal heel-shin, and truncal ataxia — in a man with chronic heavy intake and gradual onset. Differentials IN SIX GROUPS: BRAIN — cerebellar stroke or TIA, posterior circulation ischaemia, tumour or metastasis, multiple sclerosis; NUTRITIONAL — Wernicke's encephalopathy, B12 deficiency; DRUGS — phenytoin, carbamazepine, lithium, sedatives; SENSORY — alcoholic or diabetic peripheral neuropathy causing sensory ataxia; VESTIBULAR — vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis, Meniere's; LOWER LIMB — arthritis of hip or knee, lumbar radiculopathy, cauda equina. Plan: PARENTERAL THIAMINE BEFORE ANY GLUCOSE (a glucose load in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate Wernicke's), bloods including LFTs, magnesium and B12, MRI brain, and referral for withdrawal management, falls prevention, physiotherapy and an OT home assessment. Raise driving. SA: DASSA ADIS 1300 13 1340, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, PATS, TIS National 131 450.
plan: 'Good morning Ben, I'm Dr -. I've been asked to examine you today. I'll look at your arms and legs, check your eyes, listen to your speech, and I'll ask you to stand and take a few steps. I'll be right beside you the whole time — if you feel like you're going, I've got you. Any pain anywhere? Happy for me to go ahead?' → 'Just don't let me go over.' Acknowledge the fear once, then move. 'No particular exposure or position is required for this examination.'

General appearance BEFORE the gait: 'Examiner, on general appearance my patient is alert and orientated. There is no obvious wasting or fasciculation. Notably, he is unable to maintain his balance even in a SITTING position — he is swaying from side to side as I speak to him.' (Do not call it truncal ataxia yet; that has a specific test at the end.)

GAIT, two or three steps only: 'Ben, I'd like you to stand up and take a few steps for me. I'm going to put my arms around you as you go — I won't hold you, but if you go I'll catch you. Ready?' (stand beside him, arms bracketing, walk backwards with him) 'That's plenty — let's sit you back down.' → 'On gait he places his feet wide apart from each other in order to maintain balance — a broad-based gait.'

ROMBERG, eyes OPEN: 'Now bring your feet together, side by side, and let your arms hang by your side. Stay just like that for me — I'm right here.' Count to five; he lurches at about two seconds — CATCH HIM. 'Got you. That's enough, sit yourself back down.' → 'On Romberg testing the patient lost his balance WITH THE EYES OPEN. I did not proceed to eye closure because he had already lost balance and I was concerned about a fall.'

THE COMMITMENT SENTENCE: 'Examiner, before I go on — a broad-based gait together with loss of balance on Romberg with the eyes open points to a CEREBELLAR cause rather than a proprioceptive one. I'm therefore going to focus the rest of my examination on a full cerebellar screen rather than a general neurological examination, and I'll call out each finding as I go. I'm also going to omit tandem gait, because he has already demonstrated loss of balance and I don't think it is safe.'

Hands and arms: 'Copy my movement — tap the palm of one hand with the palm and then the back of the other, as fast as you can. Now swap hands.' → 'dysdiadochokinesia, present on both sides.' 'Now touch your nose, then touch my finger, as quickly as you can' (finger at FULL arm's reach, two or three positions) → 'intention tremor that worsens as he approaches the target, and past-pointing — he does not reach my finger.' 'Stretch both arms out in front, palms facing up. Now close your eyes and hold them there.' → 'both arms show an UPWARD drift — the cerebellar pattern; a downward pronator drift would indicate an upper motor neurone lesion.' 'Arms out again. I'm going to press down and I want you to resist me' — press, then release suddenly → 'there is a rebound phenomenon — the arms overshoot well beyond their starting position.'

Face and lower limb: 'Keep your head still and follow my finger with your eyes only' (H-path, pausing at the extremes) → 'I can see no nystagmus on eye movements.' 'Can you repeat after me — West Register Street.' → broken syllable by syllable → 'his speech is slurred and staccato — scanning dysarthria.' Then SITTING with the legs hanging free, tap the patellar tendon → 'the knee jerk is PENDULAR — four or five swings before it settles, which reflects the hypotonia of cerebellar disease.' Lying: 'touch my finger with your big toe' → intention tremor and past-pointing; 'run your heel down your other shin in a straight line — now the other leg' → abnormal bilaterally; 'cross your arms and sit up without using your hands' → he cannot do it in one movement — TRUNCAL ATAXIA.

'Examiner, I have ten positive cerebellar signs and no nystagmus. Those localise to the cerebellum, and in a man with chronic heavy alcohol intake and a gradual onset my most likely diagnosis is alcohol-related cerebellar degeneration.' Then the six groups and the plan (see dx). 'Why thiamine before glucose?' → 'a glucose load in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy.'

pefe: Role-player: Ben Whyte, 55, former shearing-shed hand, lives alone in a unit in Kadina, divorced, two adult children in Adelaide he rarely sees, disability pension. A cask of wine and several beers most days for about twenty years, first drink around ten in the morning, never been to detox, eats one meal a day. Unsteadiness crept up over eighteen months, no sudden onset, no headache or vomiting; three falls in six months, no head injury; NO numbness or pins and needles in the feet (this keeps the case cerebellar rather than sensory); no spinning, no hearing loss or tinnitus; no medications. Flat, defensive about alcohol, embarrassed about falling. If the candidate is kind about the drinking he softens and asks 'will it come good if I stop?'; if judgemental he goes quiet and answers in single words.

How the signs are played: sways gently while seated the whole time; plants the feet very wide and lurches when walking; on Romberg starts to fall at about two seconds with the EYES STILL OPEN; hand tapping slow, irregular and messy on both sides; finger-nose steady at the nose then shaking more and more towards the target and missing it; arms drift UPWARD with eyes closed; arms fly up past the start on rebound; smooth eye movements with NO nystagmus; speech broken into syllables; knee jerk swinging four or five times; toe-to-finger shaking and missing; heel-shin wandering on both legs; cannot sit up with the arms crossed without two or three attempts. Three role-player mistakes that break the case: falling only once the eyes are closed (that is the sensory variant), making finger-nose merely slow rather than tremulous and missing (slow is Parkinson's), and volunteering the alcohol history before being asked.

Reference points: Romberg — falls with the eyes OPEN means cerebellar or vestibular; steady open then falling closed is a POSITIVE Romberg and means proprioceptive loss; count to five. Dysdiadochokinesia and heel-shin must be done on BOTH sides. Pendular reflex: knee jerk sitting with the legs hanging, 4-5 swings instead of 1-2. Drift: cerebellar is UPWARD with palms up; a downward pronator drift is UMN. DANISH — Dysdiadochokinesia, Ataxia, Nystagmus, Intention tremor, Scanning speech, Hypotonia. Wernicke's triad: confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia — thiamine before glucose, and correct magnesium.

plan: 'Good morning Nick, I'm Dr -. I understand you've had the result of the biopsy from your neck, and I'm sorry — that must have been a difficult thing to hear. What I'd like to do today is examine you to work out where it has come from, because that's what decides the treatment. I'll start with your arms — some movements, testing the feeling with cotton wool, and I may tap with a reflex hammer. Any pain? Happy for me to go ahead?' (washes hands) → 'They said it's cancer but nobody's told me where it started. And my right hand's been useless for a couple of months — is that part of it?' → 'That's exactly what I want to find out.' Do NOT deliver a warning shot or re-break the news.

INSPECTION, front and back — the finding most candidates walk past: 'On general appearance he is alert and comfortable at rest. On inspection of both arms and hands, front and back — there is WASTING OF THE SMALL MUSCLES OF THE RIGHT HAND with dorsal guttering between the metacarpals, and wasting of the thenar and hypothenar eminences. There are no fasciculations and no tremor. The left hand is normal.' Then tone, normal and symmetrical.

POWER and REFLEXES: 'Arms out to the side like a chicken, don't let me push down... bend your elbows, pull me towards you... now push me away' → C5, C6, C7 normal and symmetrical. 'Squeeze my fingers as hard as you can' (two fingers of each hand, compared directly) → the right is loose, 'that's all I've got, doc' → 'power of C8 is reduced on the right.' 'Spread your fingers apart and don't let me push them together' → right collapses → 'power of T1 is reduced on the right.' Biceps C5-C6, supinator C6, triceps C7 with a C8 contribution — present and symmetrical.

SENSATION, including the medial forearm: cotton wool demonstrated on the sternum, 'close your eyes and tell me if it feels the same on both sides' — C5 lateral shoulder, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 MEDIAL FOREARM, both sides at the same level → 'sensation is normal in C5, C6 and C7. There is sensory loss in C8 and T1 on the right.' Offer coordination and skip it with a reason: 'the findings already localise the lesion and I'd rather use the time on the relevant examination.'

THE LINKING SENTENCE: 'Examiner, to summarise task one: wasting of the small muscles of the right hand, with reduced power and sensory loss in C8 and T1 on the right, and normal C5 to C7. That is a LOWER BRACHIAL PLEXUS lesion, not a single peripheral nerve. A C8 and T1 lesion, in a smoker, with a metastatic squamous node in the neck, makes me think of a lesion at the LUNG APEX involving the lower trunk of the brachial plexus. For my further relevant examination I'd like to look for Horner's syndrome, examine the skin of the face, scalp and neck and the oral cavity for a primary, and then examine the respiratory system.'

The relevant examination: 'I'd like to look for Horner's syndrome — specifically ptosis and miosis' → photograph card → 'partial ptosis and miosis on the right. ANHIDROSIS CANNOT BE ASSESSED FROM A PHOTOGRAPH — I'd look for it clinically.' Then the skin survey said out loud ('suspicious moles, ulcers or non-healing lesions') over the face, behind the ears and the scalp; 'open your mouth and say ah' for masses or ulcers; then palpate the node groups and BOTH supraclavicular fossae → a hard, fixed, non-tender node in the left supraclavicular fossa.

Respiratory BY REQUEST, asked specifically and in order: 'Is chest expansion symmetrical?' → reduced right lower zone. 'Is the trachea central?' → central, so the effusion is not large enough to displace it. 'On percussion, both sides — any dullness?' → stony dullness at the right base. 'Is air entry equal? Diagnosis and the five concerns, each linked to what you did (see dx), then the management sequence and the plain-English explanation to Jimmy. If he asks 'am I going to lose it?' — answer honestly on what you found: the blood supply and nerves to the foot are working normally today.

Plan: TSH (the screening test) and a NECK ULTRASOUND (first-line imaging), with ultrasound-guided FNA if a suspicious nodule is seen, and review with the results. Safety-net: return sooner if the swelling grows quickly, the voice becomes hoarse, or there is trouble swallowing or breathing, or a hard lump appears. If the clock beats you, drop the differentials — never the plan. Regional SA: check what imaging is available locally first, and PATS helps with travel and accommodation if she has to go to Adelaide.

If she is wearing a scarf: 'Would you mind slipping that off for a couple of minutes so I can see the whole neck? I can pull the curtain across, and I'm happy to have a chaperone with us.' Examiner, on inspection from the front I can see no visible swelling and no visible mass, no engorged veins, and no scars to suggest previous thyroid surgery. Palpation from BEHIND, warned and consented: 'Jane, I'm going to come and stand behind you and feel your neck — is that all right? Please tell me if it's tender anywhere. Examiner, I'm displacing the trachea to the left and palpating the right lobe... displacing to the right and palpating the left lobe... and palpating the isthmus just below the cricoid. Examiner, THE KEY POINTS: the size is normal, I can feel the lower border, the consistency is normal, I cannot feel any nodules — Jane, is that painful at all? — no, so the gland is not tender.'

Thrills, second sip, nodes, trachea: 'I'm placing the pads of my fingers over each lobe — no palpable thrills. Jane, another sip, hold it... swallow now. Cervical nodes: submental... submandibular... pre-auricular... post-auricular... occipital... anterior cervical or jugular chain... posterior cervical... and SUPRACLAVICULAR. Then the patient explanation: the butterfly-shaped gland that sets the speed the body runs at, everything checkable at the bedside normal and reassuring, but an examination alone cannot tell everything and she has definitely noticed something — so a blood test and an ultrasound, FNA if the scan shows something to look at more closely, and review with both results, plus the red-flag safety-net.

The hidden agenda surfaces: 'Is it cancer?' → 'That's exactly the right question to ask, and I'd rather you asked it than worried on your own. What I can't do is promise you that from an examination alone, and I don't want to give you a reassurance I can't back up. That's exactly why we do the blood test and the ultrasound — so we're not guessing. Whatever the results show, I'll go through them with you and we'll decide what happens next together.' Also expect: 'my aunt had her thyroid out', 'will I need an operation?', 'do I have to go to Adelaide?' (PATS).

back.dx: Graves' disease — thyrotoxicosis with a DIFFUSE, smooth, symmetrical hypervascular goitre (palpable thrill, audible systolic bruit) plus ORBITOPATHY, which occurs in Graves' and not in the other causes: anxious and restless with facial sweating, fine tremor on paper, tachycardia ~105 regular with a wide pulse pressure, brisk biceps jerk, bilateral lid retraction, lid lag and mild proptosis with full movements. Negatives worth naming: no onycholysis or acropachy, no proximal myopathy, no ophthalmoplegia or diplopia, no lymphadenopathy, central trachea, resonant percussion, negative Pemberton's, no gynaecomastia, no pretibial myxoedema. Differentials: toxic multinodular goitre and toxic adenoma (both less likely with a diffuse rather than nodular gland), thyroiditis (less likely with a non-tender gland). Plan: ECG for AF, TSH-receptor antibodies, baseline FBC and LFTs; beta-blocker for symptom control now; carbimazole after baselines WITH the agranulocytosis rule and teach-back; endocrinology referral for definitive treatment (radioiodine or surgery); ask about smoking, the single biggest modifiable factor for eye disease, and offer cessation; review in four weeks with repeat thyroid function.
plan: WIPE and exposure: '...I'll look at your hands and your eyes, feel your pulse, test the strength in your shoulders, tap your arm with this little hammer to check your reflexes, examine the gland in your neck, and have a look at your shins. I'll need your ARMS, NECK AND SHINS uncovered, and I'd like you sitting on the edge of the bed.' Then, out loud: 'Examiner, given the blood results I'm going to perform an examination for THYROTOXICOSIS, working from the general appearance through the hands, eyes and neck.'

Appearance, hands, tremor, pulse: 'From the end of the bed the patient is alert and orientated but appears anxious and restless. There is VISIBLE SWEATING OF THE FACE. He appears thin for his frame... no onycholysis — separation of the nail from the nail bed — and no thyroid acropachy... no palmar erythema, and the palms are warm and sweaty [FEEL them]. Could you hold both arms straight out in front, palms down, fingers spread? No coarse tremor. I'll now test for a fine tremor [lays the PAPER across the dorsum] — the paper is oscillating: there is a fine tremor. [radial pulse] The pulse is approximately 105, regular, normal character and volume, with a wide pulse pressure of 148 over 62. No evidence of atrial fibrillation — I would confirm with an ECG.'

Proximal myopathy and the reflex, straight on: 'Could you hold your arms out to the sides like wings, and stop me pushing them down? Shoulder abduction is 5 out of 5 bilaterally — no proximal myopathy. I would also ask whether he has difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs.' Then PICK UP THE HAMMER: 'Let your arm go floppy for me. Examiner, the biceps jerk is BRISK — hyperreflexia, consistent with thyrotoxicosis.' ('I would also check the reflexes' earns nothing; all four limbs burns the clock.)

THE EYES, four manoeuvres: FRONT — 'look straight ahead at the wall behind me. There is bilateral LID RETRACTION — sclera visible above the iris on both sides — with mild proptosis, no chemosis or conjunctival injection and no periorbital swelling.' ABOVE — 'may I stand behind you and look down over your forehead? From above there is mild bilateral proptosis, the globes protruding slightly beyond the orbital rim.' MOVEMENT — 'keep your head still and follow my finger with your eyes only — tell me if you see double or if it hurts. [H-pattern] Full movements, no ophthalmoplegia, no diplopia.' LID LAG — 'I'm bringing my finger down slowly from above; keep watching it. [pen above eye level, midline, lowered slowly] There is LID LAG bilaterally — the upper lid falls more slowly than the globe and upper sclera is transiently exposed.'

The neck IN FULL despite the obvious diagnosis, then chest and shins: 'the key points: the gland is diffusely and symmetrically enlarged, roughly twice normal size; lower border palpable; smooth and firm without discrete nodules; not tender; moves with swallowing. There is a palpable THRILL over both lobes and on auscultation a systolic BRUIT — a hypervascular gland. No lymphadenopathy, trachea central, percussion resonant, Pemberton's negative.' Then 'no gynaecomastia; heart sounds dual with no systolic flow murmur. Could I look at your shins? No pretibial myxoedema and no peripheral oedema. To complete I'd take a full set of observations including blood pressure, record the weight, and perform a full cardiovascular examination.'

The 45-second summary, committing to Graves' with reasons, plus the plan (see dx). Examiner: 'why Graves' rather than a toxic multinodular goitre?' → THREE reasons: the gland is diffuse and symmetrical rather than nodular; it is hypervascular with a thrill and a bruit; and there is orbitopathy, which occurs in Graves' and not in a toxic MNG — confirmed with TSH-receptor antibodies.

Explain in plain English: the thyroid as the accelerator pedal stuck too far down; Graves' disease as an autoimmune antibody that switches the gland on and won't let it switch off — common, very treatable, nobody's fault, and the cause of the eye changes. Three parts to treatment: a beta-blocker now for the racing heart and shakes (better within days), a tablet to turn the gland down, and later a permanent fix — radioiodine or surgery — which he does not decide today. Bloods for blood count and liver before the second tablet.

THE SAFETY COUNSELLING, said out loud: 'The tablet for the gland is called carbimazole. It works well, but it has one rare and serious side effect: in about one person in three hundred it can drop the white cells that fight infection. So this is the rule, and it matters more than anything else I've said today — if you develop a SORE THROAT, MOUTH ULCERS, A FEVER, or you just feel unwell and fluey, STOP THE TABLETS AND GET A BLOOD TEST THE SAME DAY. Don't wait to see if it settles. Ring the practice, or go to the hospital after hours. Can you tell me back what you'd do if you woke up with a sore throat?' Then smoking cessation offered, and review in four weeks.

I want to be clear about something. THAT IS NOT LAZINESS AND IT IS NOT IN YOUR HEAD. There is a real, measurable, physical reason for how you've been feeling, and it's one of the most treatable conditions we see.' Then Hashimoto's — the same condition her mum has, nobody's fault — and levothyroxine: first thing in the morning on an empty stomach, FOUR HOURS apart from iron, calcium or indigestion tablets; repeat TSH at 6-8 weeks, not sooner; report chest pain or a racing heart; tell you early about pregnancy or planning one, because the dose needs to go up. On the weight: some is fluid and will settle, the rest gets easier as energy returns — do not promise it all comes off.

Variant 1 — THE HEADSCARF STATION ('I'd rather keep this on, if that's all right'): 'Of course — thank you for telling me, and I want to do this in a way you're comfortable with. Can I explain why I'm asking? The gland I need to examine sits at the front of the neck and I have to see it and feel it directly; through fabric I'd miss things that matter to your diagnosis. What would make this easier? I can close the door and pull the curtain so nobody can see in, I can ask a female colleague to do this part or to stay with us, and you can uncover just the neck yourself and cover up again straight after. It will take about two minutes.' If she still declines: 'That's your decision and I respect it. What I'd like to do then is arrange an ultrasound of the neck instead, and book you back with a female doctor so we can examine you properly. I don't want to leave that unchecked.' Working around the fabric, or silently abandoning the neck, both fail.

Variant 2 — POST-ABLATIVE, ON AMIODARONE: 'on inspection of the neck there is a faint transverse scar just above the sternal notch, consistent with a previous thyroidectomy... the gland is impalpable... the pulse is 48 and regular. This is post-ablative hypothyroidism — the scar makes the diagnosis. He is also on amiodarone, which independently causes hypothyroidism, so both may contribute; I would not stop it without cardiology input. Given his age and the bradycardia I'd start levothyroxine LOW and increase slowly, check for angina first, and recheck TSH at six to eight weeks' VERIFY. The scar is only found if you INSPECT before you touch. / Variant 3 — MYXOEDEMA COMA: hypothermic at 34.8, bradycardic at 42, hypoventilating, drowsy and difficult to rouse with marked non-pitting oedema → 'this is myxoedema coma and it is a medical emergency: A to E, airway support and oxygen, cardiac monitoring, IV access, bloods including TSH, fT4, CORTISOL, sodium, glucose and cultures, passive rewarming. INTRAVENOUS HYDROCORTISONE BEFORE THYROID HORMONE — coexisting adrenal insufficiency is common and thyroxine alone can precipitate an adrenal crisis — then IV thyroid hormone after specialist discussion. Look for a precipitant: infection, cold, sedatives, a missed dose. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval to a tertiary ICU.'
pefe: Role-player: Helen Marchetti, 40, council administrator in Wallaroo, husband and two primary-school children; non-smoker, occasional wine, no medications or allergies, no previous surgery; her MOTHER has Hashimoto's (only if asked). Four months of exhaustion sleep doesn't fix, cold all the time in February, bowels every third day, 6 kg on without changing anything, rings don't fit, skin so dry she's been through three tubs of moisturiser, husband says she sounds different on the phone, rereads the same email four times, eyebrows gone sparse which she put down to age, periods heavier. She speaks at a noticeably reduced rate with a deeper croaky voice and pauses before answering — flat, a little defeated, telling herself she is lazy and useless and half-expecting to be told nothing is wrong. Wears layers and keeps them on until asked; RESISTS ONCE ('do I have to? I'm freezing') then agrees if given a reason, privacy or a chaperone; if no reason is given she keeps them on and makes them ask again; if they examine through the fabric she lets them and marks them down; if they reach for her clothing she pulls back. After the tendon strike she lets the arm come back down slowly — count one-and-two before it settles. If the diagnosis is delivered coldly she pushes once: 'so there really is something wrong with me? Everyone's been telling me I'm just busy.'

Numbers: FOUR signs you must not miss — the clothing, the eyebrows, the bradycardia, the delayed relaxation. TWO named signs — Hertoghe (eyebrows) and Woltman (delayed relaxation). ONE reflex, the biceps jerk, watched for a full second. Repeat TSH at 6-8 weeks VERIFY. FOUR hours between levothyroxine and iron, calcium or a PPI VERIFY. Start low and go slow in the elderly and in ischaemic heart disease. Hydrocortisone before thyroxine if adrenal insufficiency is possible. TSH tells you which way, free T4 tells you how far. Clock: exposure in the WIPE, reflex 2:30, neck 3:15, stop 4:50, reporting done 5:40.

Scored domains, with exposure and consent the highest-weighted: commented on the clothing as a clinical sign, asked the PATIENT not the examiner, gave a reason, offered privacy and a chaperone, let her uncover herself, asked inside the WIPE rather than at minute four, did not examine through fabric, did not silently abandon the neck. Then technique (felt the palms, pulse rate and rhythm, proximal myopathy against resistance, reflex elicited AND the relaxation watched, face examined close up with the eyebrows named, neck inspected for a scar before palpation, complete thyroid examination including percussion, auscultation and Pemberton's, heart and lung bases, ankles pressed to show non-pitting oedema); language (no insulting descriptor in her hearing, reflex described as delayed relaxation rather than 'normal', correct direction); diagnosis (committed, TSH and fT4 interpreted, differentials including drugs, post-ablative and central causes, TPO antibodies, FBC, lipids, sodium, ECG); and communication (levothyroxine explained plainly, the self-blame addressed directly, realistic about the weight, pregnancy raised, chest pain and palpitations safety-netted, follow-up arranged).
fails: ★ Examining through the scarf, asking the examiner for exposure instead of the patient, reaching for her clothing, or leaving the request until minute four when there is no time left
★ Striking the tendon and not watching the relaxation — the jerk looks normal in size, so 'reflexes normal' is reported and the best sign in the station is lost
Describing her as 'mentally sluggish', 'slow', 'dull' or 'obese' in her hearing — a role-player took audible offence and marked it down
Inspecting the face from a metre away and missing the eyebrows; looking at the palms instead of feeling them; palpating the neck before inspecting it and missing a thyroidectomy scar

Premature closure — shortening the neck examination (usually dropping auscultation) because you already know the answer; a technically perfect plan that never addresses the self-blame; promising the weight will all come off
